My highly beloved patron, Blessed Henry Suso, you who are flooded with heavenly delights in Heaven, yet—even in the perfect state you now occupy—burn with a much stronger and greater love for God and your neighbor. For this reason, you have willed that these your posthumous writings—among so many most precious writings which you, out of great humility on earth, did not wish to come to light but rather to remain hidden—these alone should come forth and now come to light in the German language. To this end, you have deigned to make use of my lowliness <note>literally "my nothingness," a common humble rhetorical device of the period</note>, which I then heartily and gladly, through the help of Divine Grace, have put into effect as much as was possible for me. I have done so as gladly as I have long and fervently desired to make my beloved brothers and sisters of the German fatherland partakers of this noble treasure, and to serve those inexperienced in the Latin language. 

Your love—as one who well knows how much the honor of God (who is honored through the honor of his saints) will be increased through this work, and the salvation of the neighbor promoted—has obtained this from the Divine Majesty for our latter times. These are times in which love will grow cold and decrease in many hearts, because living faith and the hope springing from it have already noticeably decreased, so that the majority of people look only to human means. Through this mistrust, the wells of the rivers of Divine Grace are blocked; and where they could have daily seen and experienced the wonders of God, just like the former holy friends and children of God, they make themselves unworthy of these wonders...

## Preface to the Following Dialogue.

<image-desc>A decorative row of repeating floral ornaments (fleurons) spans the top width of the text area.</image-desc>

Everyone knows that from the beginning, man was created by God primarily for this reason: so that he might enjoy Him as the true, highest, and eternal Good. Therefore, not only do humans desire this by their nature, but all creatures seek the highest Good, because nothing can be found among all created things that does not partake of this same Good to some extent. For from Him, as the foremost and inexhaustible fountain, a portion of this goodness is directed toward all things; and as the Psalmist <note>Reference to Psalm 145:16: "You open your hand and satisfy the desires of every living thing."</note> speaks: **When He opens His hand, all things are filled with goodness.** No one can truly be called or be "blessed" except according to how much they cling to or are united with the highest and true Good, in which alone the soul—adorned with the **image of God**—enjoys perfect peace and rest. The further the soul deviates from this Good, the more wretched and miserable it becomes. Therefore, by the impulse of nature, we all wish to be well-off, and all our labors, toil, and diligence aim toward one thing: namely, that we may be blessed <term>glückselig<gloss>A term denoting both earthly happiness and the state of eternal divine beatitude.</gloss></term>. Thus, some strive to accumulate possessions, others to achieve honor, and others to enjoy pleasures, for no other reason than that they might be blessed through the acquisition of these things.

But so that you may understand how God-loving souls can be fulfilled by nothing other than the highest Good, observe that wretched people, devoted to the aforementioned vanities, are not only failed by these things in finding happiness or satisfaction, but the more they have, the more they are tormented by an unceasing thirst and desire. They wander miserably, seeking more and more, envying others when they see them possessing an abundance, and spending their whole lives burdened with vain worries and anxieties. In this very fact they provide enough testimony that true blessedness does not consist in these things; and yet, when they chase these things, their only intention is to enjoy blessedness. This error has taken hold of almost all people, causing them to neglect the fountain of true blessedness and—as the Prophet Jeremiah <note>Reference to Jeremiah 2:13: "They have forsaken me, the spring of living water, and have dug their own cisterns, broken cisterns that cannot hold water."</note> says—to dig for themselves **cisterns** that are broken and hold no water, seeking blessedness in places where it cannot be found. Oh, the blindness of the human mi— <note>The text breaks off mid-word (likely "Gemüt" or "Geist," meaning mind or spirit) at the bottom of the page.</note>

<summary>This preface introduces the theological foundation of the book, arguing that all human desire is ultimately a search for God, the "highest Good," though most people mistakenly seek it in worldly vanities.</summary>
<keywords>highest Good, blessedness, image of God, vanity, Psalm 145, Jeremiah, spiritual fulfillment, human nature</keywords>

### Preface.

...plainly; they are rightly to be mourned! O most wretched condition of Man, which has deviated so far from its original dignity! It was not for this reason that we were so excellently created by God, that we should cling to these dreams and worthless things, these amusements of the world, and (as the Prophet speaks in Psalm 39 <note>Reference to Psalm 39:6: "Surely every man walks like a shadow... he heaps up riches, and does not know who will gather them."</note>) to false vanities, as if they were our ultimate goal and end. Not for this cause did the Son of God suffer so many torments <term>tormenten<gloss>Derived from the Latin "tormenta," referring to the physical and spiritual agonies of the Passion.</gloss></term>, so much misery, and a shameful death, that we should desire to live in wretchedness forever: your Lord and God has prepared other treasures for you, O man, from eternity. What business have you with these visible things? All things of this world God has cast under your feet, so that you might learn to despise them and not to desire them. God promises you the dwellings of Heaven, and why do you love the earth more? He calls you to the freedom of His children, and why would you rather be a slave to the Devil and to your own flesh?

Thus (God have mercy) the greatest part of mankind is blinded by evil spirits, turned away from the Creator, and wallowing in the filth of worldly lusts, as they never lift their eyes to behold the heavenly things for which they were ordained. Who would not weep for this folly of man even with bloody tears? Meanwhile, countless wretches hasten to Hell, and instead of the very brief pleasures of the flesh, they suffer eternal punishment. The infinite benefits of the most generous Redeemer <note>A reference to Jesus Christ.</note>, especially those He showed us in His assumed nature <term>angenommenen natur<gloss>A theological term for the Incarnation, when God took on human form.</gloss></term>, have fallen into forgetfulness for almost everyone, and no one strives to bring them back into fresh memory—even though our Lord Jesus left us the Sacrament of His Body and Blood so that they might constantly remain incorporated into our hearts.

The **four last things** <term>vier lezte ding<gloss>In traditional Christian teaching: Death, Judgment, Heaven, and Hell.</gloss></term>, which the Wise Man <note>A common historical reference to the author of the biblical Book of Sirach.</note> exhorts us to remember, are either considered by no one at all, or only superficially. Finally, what is conducive to salvation <term>Seligkeit<gloss>A word encompassing both "blessedness" and "eternal salvation."</gloss></term> is rejected, while that which is harmful is desired. And yet, unless we set our minds upon that which serves our salvation, and unless we gladly hear or read from others what leads us to eternal joy, we cannot attain salvation—just as a sick person cannot recover unless they take the means and medicine that are beneficial to their health. Certainly, we do not lack countless books from whose reading we might achieve health of the soul, learn to hate vice, and love God. And passing over others, there is presented here before our eyes the **Dialogue** of the blessed man **Henry Suso** <note>Original Latin: "Henrici Susonis." Suso was a famous 14th-century German mystic.</note>, which is indeed brief in

### Preface.

...words, yet very significant in spiritual maxims, which clearly explain in brief terms what can be beneficial for a blessed life. For herein are contained the foremost incentives to salvation <term>salvation<gloss>Seligkeit—often translated as blessedness or salvation; the state of eternal happiness with God.</gloss></term>, so that this little book—should other things be lacking—if it is read through, can lead even an ignorant and unwise person, even a lazy and stubborn one, yes, even an ungrateful one who has turned away from God, back to God as the fountain of life and the author of salvation. It is unnecessary to praise this book with many words, for it will make itself known to the reader. May Jesus Christ grant that we finally take care for our salvation; many, God have mercy, have spent their time poorly learning vain things, from which they have become neither better, nor more blissful, nor more understanding. From this little book, everyone who wishes can draw the greatest wisdom and attain the knowledge of God as well as of himself; which, when he has attained it, he will become understanding. But if he does not know this, however much else he knows and is capable of, he will be all the more unlearned and inexperienced. Many know much, yet do not know themselves, and as the Poet says:

### The First Chapter.

> Her I have loved, and from my youth on I have diligently sought after her, and I have intended to marry her as a bride. <note>original: "Sap. 8" refers to the Book of Wisdom (Sapientia) 8:2, a Deuterocanonical book often cited in mystical literature.</note>

<image-desc>Ornamental initial 'D' containing a miniature illustration of a landscape with a figure, possibly a saint or the author in prayer.</image-desc>

These words are written in the Book of Wisdom and belong to the most graceful and lovely Eternal Wisdom. There was a youth in the bloom of his age who had moved to a foreign <note>German: "vngleiches Land" (unequal/different land), implying a place far from home or spiritually alien.</note> land and had separated himself far from his parents; to him, Eternal Wisdom appeared in a spiritual, ineffable form, and drew him through sweet and sour <note>An idiomatic expression meaning through both joys and hardships.</note> until she brought him onto the path of Divine truth. As he considered within himself the lovely and glorious approach of God, he spoke to the Lord: "From the very beginning of my life, O sweetest God, my soul has chased after one thing with burning thirst and desire; but what

<column-break/>

it may be is unknown even to me. For many years I have pursued it completely, but have never been able to attain it according to my wish; for what it truly is remains somewhat unknown to me at this time. Yet there is something that pulls my heart and soul toward it and draws me in, so that I cannot be entirely at rest. Indeed, in my youth, like others, I endeavored to seek this in creatures <term>creatures<gloss>Creaturen—in this theological context, refers to any created thing (nature, people, worldly goods) as opposed to the Creator.</gloss></term>, but the closer I approached them, the further I strayed from this [goal], and the more I searched in them, the less I found. For all types of visible things, before I had fully searched through them or felt any rest in them, spoke to me internally thus: 'We are not that which you seek...'"

**Eternal Wisdom.** Do you not recognize that which embraces you so sweetly, and which has so often blocked your wrong paths until it united you with itself?

The great power of my love appears from the unutterable bitterness of my suffering, no differently than the sun from its radiance, a blooming rose from its scent, or a kindled fire from its heat. Therefore, notice with all diligence and fervor of spirit how lovingly, and also how painfully, I have suffered for your sake.

# What our Lord suffered before the Crucifixion.

## Chapter 2.

After holding the last supper with my disciples, when I presented myself on the Mount <note>Refers to the Mount of Olives and the Garden of Gethsemane.</note> and was determined to suffer death—as I also felt how it would soon attack me—I sweat blood from the anguish of my tender heart and the torments of my whole body; afterward I was cruelly captured, bound hard, and led away in a pitiful manner. In that same night, I was mockingly treated with blows, spitting, and the veiling of the eyes; I was unjustly accused before Caiaphas and condemned to death. Great was my sorrow to see my most pure Mother surrounded with unutterable pain of heart, from that time when she saw me struggling in such anguish until I was fastened to the Cross. With great shame they led me to Pilate, and falsely accused me as one who deserved death. They stood before me with a terrifying gaze, no differently than monstrous giants; but I was among them like a gentle little sheep. Before Herod I was—even though I am Eternal Wisdom itself—mockingly scorned in a white garment <note>The "white garment" was traditionally placed on Christ by Herod as a sign of mockery, marking him as a "fool" or a mock-king.</note>; my most graceful body was most cruelly torn by scourging; they pierced my most holy head with thorns; and my most beautiful face was filled with spit and blood; because I was then condemned to death,

But now I desire with all my heart to obtain that thing—and although I have often experienced what it is *not*—it is still unknown to me what it *is*. **Eternal Wisdom.** Do you not recognize that which so sweetly embraces you, and has so often blocked your wandering path until it united you with itself?

**Servant.** I have never been able to see nor hear it; therefore, I do not know what it is.

**Wisdom.** It is right that this has happened to you, for the company of creatures and the negligence of the soul <note>German: "saumseligkeit." This implies a spiritual sluggishness or a lack of focus on divine matters.</note> have caused this. But now look with internal eyes, and see who I am. For I am **Eternal Wisdom**, who have bound myself to you from eternity through providence. I have so often fenced your path with thorns—as often as you had separated yourself from me—no differently than if I had abandoned you. Thus in all things you have experienced something adverse which opposed you; this is the surest sign of my chosen ones, that I wish them to be entrusted to me.

**Servant.** Are you then the loveliest Wisdom, whom I have sought so long, and for whom my soul has always carried a longing? And why have you made such a long delay in explaining yourself to me until now? Oh me, how many difficult paths have I wandered?

**Wisdom.** If I had made myself known to you then, you would not understand and recognize my goodness so much

<column-break/>

as you understand and recognize it now.

**Servant.** O infinite goodness, how sweetly, how pleasantly you have shown yourself to me. When I was not, you created me; when I left you, you did not depart from me; when I wanted to depart far from you, you caught me lovely. If, therefore, my heart were divided into a thousand pieces and could embrace you as its joy—if I could spend every day of my life in constant love and full praise with you—this would be my greatest wish. For truly **blessed** is the one whom you meet so generously, that you allow him to enjoy no true rest until he wishes to rest in you. Because you then, **O Eternal Wisdom**, are that very one whom I love, I pray you: do not despise me, your unworthy creature. Look how my heart is quite heated against all things of this world—both the joyful and the adverse—do you then want it to be always silent before you? O sweetest God, allow my poor soul to speak a single word with you, for my overflowing heart can no longer contain itself, because in this whole world it has no one in whom it can delight but only in you, O sweetest Heart, most beloved Brother. You alone, my Heart, know and recognize the affection of a loving heart, and it is not unknown to you that it can love nothing unless it recognizes it. Because you then alone desire to be loved, give me full knowledge of yourself, so that I may embrace you with full love.

Therefore, take note with all diligence and fervor of spirit, how lovely and also how painfully I have suffered for your sake.

# What our Lord suffered before the Crucifixion.
## Chapter 2.

After holding the Last Supper with my disciples, when I presented myself on the Mount <note>The Mount of Olives, specifically the Garden of Gethsemane.</note> and was determined to suffer death, as I also felt how it would soon fall upon me, I sweated blood from the anguish of my tender heart and the torments of my whole body. Afterward, I was cruelly captured, bound tightly, and led away in a miserable manner: in that same night treated mockingly with blows, spit, and the veiling of my eyes, unjustly accused before Caiaphas <note>Original: "Caipha." The Jewish High Priest who presided over the initial trial of Jesus.</note>, and condemned to death. Great was my sorrow to see my most pure Mother surrounded with unspeakable pain of heart from the time

<column-break/>

she saw me struggling in such anxieties until I was fastened to the Cross. With great mockery they led me to Pilate <note>Original: "Pilato." Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea.</note> and falsely accused me as one who had deserved death. They stood before me with a terrifying appearance, no differently than monstrous giants, but I was among them like a gentle little lamb. Before Herod <note>Original: "Herode." Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee, who mockingly dressed Jesus in royal white.</note>, I myself—though I am Eternal Wisdom—was mockingly scorned in a white garment; my most graceful body was most cruelly torn by lashes of the whip; they pierced my most holy head with thorns, and the most beautiful face was filled with spit and blood, because I was then condemned to death,

# The Dialogue of the Blessed Henry Suso
<note>Original title: "Deß Seeligen Henrici Susonis gespräch." Henry Suso (c. 1295–1366) was a German Dominican friar and a central figure in medieval mysticism.</note>

...true, they led me out with the cross in a shameful and pitiable manner to endure the sentence of blood and death; terrifying were their voices and cries, so that it was heard from afar: Crucify, crucify the wicked man.

**Servant.** Oh my heart! If the beginning of your suffering is so bitter, how then will be the end? In truth, if I were to see an unreasoning beast treated in this way, I could hardly endure it; with how great a pain then must my heart and soul not be flooded by your suffering? Yet I find here something wonderful; for I, O sweetest God, desire only to know your Divinity, and you speak to me of your Humanity; I wish and seek to taste your sweetness, and you place your bitterness before me; I was pleased only to hang at the breasts <note>A common medieval metaphor for the soul receiving easy spiritual comfort or "milk" from God before transitioning to the "solid food" of suffering.</note>, and you instruct me for battle. What does this mean, my heart and God?

**Wisdom.** No one can reach the height of my Divinity, nor the extraordinary sweetness, unless he be led through the bitterness of my Humanity; for the higher one strives to ascend without this, the deeper he will fall. My Humanity is the way upon which one must wander; my suffering is the door through which everyone must enter who seeks what you seek. So cast off the faint-heartedness of your heart and betake yourself here into the brave circle of war. For it is impermissible that the servant wallows in pleasures while he sees his Lord fighting courageously in the war. I will put my armor on you, for it is necessary that you taste all my suffering according to all your

<column-break/>

powers. Take courage then, with the assurance that you must endure frequent death of the heart before you bring nature under the yoke; also from the anguish of the bloody sweat, which the manifold bitter torments—through which I will make you suitable for me—will press out of you. For I will strew your spice garden <note>In mystical literature, the "spice garden" represents the soul's interior life where virtues grow.</note> with red flowers; against your custom and deep-rooted habits, you will be entangled and bound with bonds: by my adversaries you will be persecuted with secret slanders and publicly shamed. Many insolent judgments will be passed against you. My suffering you will carry about in your heart with maternal loyalty and inward love. Many judges and slanders you will always have, even because of your spiritual life; thus it will happen that even your holy intentions will often be laughed at by others as if foolish, because they are contrary to their habit of living. Your unpracticed body will be scourged and chastised by the rough and hard manner of living, and through the belittling of your holy life you will be crowned <note>Likening the soul's social humiliation to Christ's Crown of Thorns.</note>, through which it will be pushed to the ground; from there you will be led out with me to walk the sorrowful path under the cross, if you will renounce your own will, deny yourself, and make yourself so free, empty, and loose from all creatures in those things that might put any hindrance in the way of your eternal <term>Bliss (Seeligkeit): The ultimate state of spiritual union with God.</term>, just like one who now wishes to bid the world farewell and have no fellowship with this life in the future.

**Servant.** Hard and very difficult are the things, O Heart, of which you now make mention,

# How our Lord <note>original: "Herz", likely a variation of "Herr" (Lord) or referring to Christ as the "Heart" of the world</note> on the Cross was constituted according to the outer man.
## The 3rd Chapter.

**Wisdom.** When I was hung upon the high wood of the Cross (which I did out of great love for you and all people), my entire beauty and physical form were changed in a pitiable way; my bright-shining eyes lost their light, the divine ears were filled with mockery and blasphemy, the excellent sense of smell was filled with foul stench, thirst tormented the sweetest mouth, and the most tender sense of touch was struck with hard blows. Not a single rest or relief could the whole world provide me. For my most holy head bowed with pain and discomfort, the well-formed neck was crushed by blows, the most radiant face was defiled by stinking spit, and the most delicate color was changed into a pale one. Ultimately, all the beauty of my body departed from me so completely that no difference could be found between me and a leper; indeed, I seemed almost to be nothing, though I was the Wisdom who is much more beautiful than the sun.

**Servant.** O bright-shining Mirror of all graces, into which the angels carry a longing to gaze, in which they delight their countenances: would to God that I might have your lovely face, surrounded by this form of death, before me for so long until I might abundantly

<column-break/>

-fore <note>Continuing "Derhal-" from the previous column: "Derhalben"</note> I pray you, that you would set before me the treasure of your suffering entirely, and treat of it more extensively.

moisten <note>Continuing "be-" from the previous column: "befeuchtigen"</note> it with the tears of my heart, and might well behold the shining cheeks, the tender mouth—now entirely pale and deceased—and thereby satisfy my soul with my lamentation and song of mourning. O Heart, one finds some who are so vehemently moved by your passion that they observe it with great lamentation and the shedding of many heart-felt tears. Oh, if only I could offer today all the mournful cries of the pious alone; could I shed the tears of all other people; if it stood in my power to speak with the mournful voices of all tongues, I would certainly declare in deed how your bitter passion torments me.

**Wisdom.** No one gives a truer testimony of his heart regarding the pain for my suffering than he who performs the same together with me in deed. Much more pleasing to me is a heart which is freed from all transitory love and strives with steady diligence toward the highest perfection according to the prescribed image of my life, than one who constantly weeps for me and sheds as many tears for my suffering as there are raindrops that have ever fallen from the air. For through the bitter death on the Cross, I sought and desired only this: that humanity should follow me, although godly tears are also very dear and pleasing to me.

# How faithful Christ's suffering was.
## The 4th Chapter.

---

**Servant.** Although I have to some extent, O Heart <note>original: "Herz"; the Servant continues to address the personified Wisdom/Christ as "Heart," emphasizing the emotional and mystical union between them</note>, forgotten your excellence, your gifts, and the benefit that has grown for us from your suffering, as well as all other benefits, yet there is something that moves me deeply as I thoroughly and diligently consider not only the way of our restored salvation, but also the immeasurable faithfulness that is united with that way. Many people grant such favors to others so that their love and faithfulness might be revealed through the manner of doing good rather than through the gifts themselves; and certainly, even a small gift is often much more acceptable when it comes from great faithfulness than a large benefit shared in another way. But your benefit, O Lord, is not only excellent, but the way and manner of it is joined with an infinite faithfulness. For not only have you suffered death for my sake, but you have also sought out the furthest reaches of love—that which is most hidden and inward—that

<column-break/>

-one is willing and able to suffer. For you have acted just as if you were saying: Consider, all you people, whether ever a heart was filled with such love; and even if all my limbs had been that most noble limb, namely the Heart, I would have had them all pierced, murdered, cut, and divided piece by piece, so that nothing would remain in me which I did not share with you, so that you might thus fully recognize my love. I ask you, my Heart, how did you feel, or what came into your mind, that you suffered such heavy pain? You could indeed have redeemed us with less effort.

here and there some old pieces of high buildings stand / in them is a great number of people / among whom many—indeed the greatest part—though in human form, are in no way different from wild animals. By this city I see the wretched pilgrim <note>In the context of this allegory, the pilgrim represents Christ or Divine Wisdom seeking a home in the human soul.</note> walking up and down / waiting to see if anyone will offer him a helping hand / but I notice that he is turned away by many with great anger / and because of the business with which they are entangled / they hardly deem him worthy of a look / nevertheless a few stretch out their hands toward him / but on the contrary the wild people see this with displeasure and seek to prevent it / at this the wretched pilgrim sighs before them / and speaks thus: "Ah, let heaven and earth be moved / have compassion for me / since I have endured such hard labor for the sake of this city / yet I am received here so poorly / while on the contrary / those who never moved a foot for its sake / are treated so friendly and well." Lord / this vision has just been presented to me / but what does it mean / is it something true / or is it a deception?

**Wisdom.** In this vision there is no deception / hear, my son, a lamentable thing / and let your heart have mercy regarding this. I, I am the rejected and cast-out stranger / whom you have seen / in former times I was held in great honor by the inhabitants of this city / but now I am banished into misery / and pitifully driven away.

**Servant.** Lord / what kind of city is this / and who are its inhabitants?

**Wisdom.** This decaying and almost desolate city signifies the brave and earnest spiritual or monastic life <term>Monastic life: a way of life dedicated to religious vows, typically involving poverty, chastity, and obedience.</term> / in which I was indeed formerly served with great

<column-break/>

reverence and propriety / and where the holiest and most secure life was led / but that same life is now for the most part falling away / its ditches are collapsing / the walls are tearing apart / that is to say, devout obedience / voluntary poverty / and noble purity and chastity wedded to holy simplicity / are beginning to perish / only some peaks of high buildings are still seen under the appearance of external statutes / customs / or habits. The people who indeed appear in human form / but yet are not different from wild animals / signify those people who, under the spiritual religious habit <term>Habit: the distinctive clothing worn by members of a religious order.</term>, carry a heart which is devoted to the world / and who turn me away from their minds and souls because of external worldly affairs. But that you saw some stretching out their hands toward me / but being pulled away by others / signifies / that the good will and spiritual beginning of some is destroyed and perverted through the talk and godless examples of others. The staff upon which I leaned / as I stood before them / is the Cross of my bitter suffering / because I do not cease to admonish them / that they should be mindful of me / and direct the love of their hearts to me alone. Finally, the cry and pitiful sighing / that you heard / is nothing else / than that my death is now beginning to call out / and that it will always call out against those / in whom neither infinite love / nor my most painful death can bring it about / that they never reject / and turn me away.

**Wisdom.** Hear a strange and pitiful thing. **Servant.** From whence comes such folly to them / or what does this mean / O most holy God?

**Wisdom.** They think indeed / and strive to avoid the cross and the burden of my service / and they fall into the midst of others [burdens]; because they will not carry me / I who am the infinite good / and my sweet yoke / they will / by the decree of my strict justice /

be loaded with many and heavy burdens / and while they fear the frost / they fall into the snow <note>An old German proverb meaning "to fall from the frying pan into the fire"—by trying to avoid a small difficulty, they fall into a much greater disaster.</note>.

**Wisdom.** At all times I am willing and ready to help / if only they were ready; I do not withdraw myself from them / but that they withdraw themselves from me is manifest.

**Servant.** Heart, it pains greatly / when a beloved is separated from his beloved.

**Wisdom.** It is indeed true / if I did not wish to most faithfully and abundantly repay / and not exceed / the love of all lovers with a loving heart.

**Servant.** But it is difficult to leave the old habit.

**Wisdom.** But it will be much more difficult to endure the future pains.

**Servant.** Perhaps they are so constituted within themselves / that this does them no harm.

**Wisdom.** I was better constituted than all others / and yet no one was less devoted to vain love / and how can that which by its nature disturbs the heart / unsettles the mind / withdraws the heart from devotion / and from the practice of the inner life <term>inner life: "innerliches leben" — the mystical practice of focusing on the soul's relationship with God rather than external rituals</term> / and takes away peace / be rightly ordered and well-constituted?

## Interpretation of three difficulties that can be particularly distressing and hindering to one who loves God; the first is, in what way and how it can happen that God, who is so lovely, shows Himself so terrifyingly.

### The 8th Chapter.

---

**Servant.** Most kind Lord, I marvel greatly at three things. The first is that, although you are entirely lovely in yourself, you are nonetheless such a strict judge toward sinners. Truly, when I properly consider your strict justice within myself, I cry out with a mournful voice of the heart: woe, woe to all those who have ever consented to sin. For if the sharp justice were known to them, which you silently exercise without contradiction against every sin—even against those who are dear to you—they would much rather strike out their own teeth or tear out their hair than anger you in any way. Oh, your angry face is very terrifying; your turning away, moved to vengeance, pains unbearably; the reproachful words you speak penetrate and cut through like a fire, heart and soul. <column-break/>

harbor the slightest suspicion that you have turned your face from me because of my sin, it is so unbearable to me that nothing similar in the whole world seems as grievous to me; in what way then, O most faithful Father, should I endure your angry face? Truly, as often as I diligently consider your angry face within myself, my soul becomes so disturbed and all my powers are shattered with such terror that I can explain it no better with any other comparison than if the sky were covered with black clouds, the fire raged in the clouds, the earth moved, and the lightning breaking out from the clouds were shot straight at the person. Most kind God, no one can trust in your long-suffering, <note>Long-suffering refers to God's patience and delay in punishment.</note> since it will one day break out into a terrifying thunderclap. ## The second difficulty: why God often withdraws his sweetness from his friends, and how one can perceive his true presence.

In this context, "Englisch" refers to angels (Engel), not the English nationality.</note> spoke to me, nonetheless, this unquenchable love would aim only for the one thing it longs for, and strive only to attain that. Certainly, the soul ignited with your love would choose you even in place of Heaven; by your leave:

**Servant.** Lord, it would befit you to give a somewhat greater trust to those who labor out of love for you, who tire and exhaust themselves out of desire for you, who so often sigh so inwardly toward you, their most beloved, and cry out to you in a piteous manner, saying from the bottom of their heart: "Turn back, turn back" <note>original: "Cant. 6." This refers to Chapter 6 of the Song of Songs (Cantica Canticorum), a book of the Bible central to medieval mystical thought.</note>. Those who ultimately seek so anxiously and speak: "Have you perhaps offended him? Could he have truly forsaken you? Will he grace you again with his honey-sweet presence, so that you might lovely embrace him with the arms of your heart and press him to your breast, so that all your pain and hardship might vanish?" You hear this, and you indeed know it, O Lord <note>original: "Herz", literally "Heart." As noted previously, this is the Servant's intimate address to Wisdom.</note>, and yet you remain silent.

**Wisdom.** Yes, I know it, and I look upon it with no small delight of heart. But give me an answer to my question, since such a great, though hidden, wonder has taken hold of you: what is it that is most acceptable and best-pleasing among all things to the highest created spirit?

**Servant.** Ah Lord, this question exceeds my understanding; I pray you, explain it to me.

**Wisdom.** Look, I will satisfy your request. To the highest angelic spirit <note>original: "Englischen Geist." In this context, "Englisch" is an archaic form meaning "angelic," not the English language.</note>, nothing is dearer nor more pleasant than to fulfill my will in all things—so much so that, if he knew it would serve my praise to root out nettles and other weeds, he would perform this with the highest desire.

**Servant.** Truly, Lord, your answer gladdens me greatly, for I sense that you desire this from me: that as far as love is concerned,

<column-break/>

I should be of a free and surrendered spirit, and seek your praise alone, as much in dryness and barrenness as in sweetness.

**Wisdom.** There is no more perfect and excellent surrender than to be resigned and surrendered in one's abandonment.

**Servant.** But Lord, that is very painful.

<margin>2</margin>
**Wisdom.** Where is virtue tested, if not in adversity? Know this for certain: that I often come and desire that the entrance to my house stand open to me, and yet I am turned away. Very often I am treated as a pilgrim <note>original: "Pilgram." Here meaning a traveling stranger who relies on the hospitality of others.</note>, poorly received, and soon shown the door. But to a soul that loves me, I do not only come, but I remain and dwell with her lovely. This happens, however, in such silence that it is unknown to all people, except for those who live withdrawn and separated from men, observe my ways, and constantly apply diligence to this, so that they might obey my grace and satisfy its demands. For according to my Godhead, I am the purest spirit, and in pure spirits, I am received and taken in a spiritual manner.

**Servant.** Lord, from what I sense, you are a secret and hidden lover; therefore I pray you, give me some signs by which I may recognize your true presence.

**Wisdom.** You can recognize my certain presence by nothing better than when I hide myself and withdraw what belongs to me from the soul. Then you recognize well enough what I am and what you are. Without doubt, I am the eternal Good, without which no one has anything good.

# The Dialogue of Blessed Henry Suso

"Because I, then, who am the infinite Good—which I am myself—kindly share and pour myself out, all things to which I impart myself take on some goodness, from which one can undoubtedly conclude my presence, just as the sun is recognized by its rays, which otherwise cannot be seen in its spherical shape. When you notice me, go into yourself; learn to distinguish the roses from the thorns and to gather the flowers from the grass."

**Servant.** Yes, Lord <note>original: "Herz", literally "Heart." Suso frequently addresses Divine Wisdom as "Heart" to signify an intimate, mystical bond.</note>, I feel a great difference within myself. When I am forsaken, my soul behaves like a sick person whose sense of taste is corrupted, to whom nothing is pleasant, but everything is tasteless. The body is overtaken by laziness, the spirit weighed down; inwardly I feel dryness, outwardly sadness. What comes before the eyes or ears is unpleasant, even if it is good. I am inclined toward vices, weak in resisting enemies, cold and lukewarm toward all good things. Whoever approaches me finds an empty house, for the Master of the House <note>original: "Haußvatter." A metaphor for God's presence dwelling within the soul.</note> is not at home—he who can order everything well and encourage the whole household. But as soon as the **Morning Star** <note>A traditional reference to Christ or divine illumination dawning in the soul.</note> rises in the middle of the heart, all pain vanishes at once, the darkness is driven away, and a bright, shining radiance arises. The heart laughs, the spirit is lifted, the soul rejoices; everything within me is happy and joyful; whatever is in and around me is all used for your praise. What previously seemed hard, heavy, tedious, and impossible becomes light and sweet in an instant. The suffering of fasting, vigils, and prayer—the enduring and avoiding—finally, all the roughness of life seems to have no burden,

<column-break/>

if only you are present. I take on a great confidence and magnanimity, which I nonetheless do not follow nor experience when I am forsaken. The soul is showered with clarity, truth, and sweetness, so that it forgets all labor. The heart is delighted and has an abundance of sweet contemplations; the tongue knows how to speak of high things; the body is ready and prepared to suffer all kinds of hardships; and whoever comes to me for advice obtains very wholesome counsel according to their wish. Finally, it seems to me that I am no different than one who has retreated from all place and time and stands in the forecourt of eternal bliss. But O Lord, who will grant that I remain so for long? God have mercy, in a swift moment everything is withdrawn from me, and I am left so bare and naked, as if I had never received such a thing, until it is given back to me after long and many sighs of the heart. Lord, are you then that thing, or am I? Or what else is it?

**Eternal Wisdom.** Certainly, you have nothing of yourself but sin and defects; so it is I, and this is the **game of love.**

**Servant.** What is the **game of love**?

**Eternal Wisdom.** As long as the one who is so loved is with the lover, the lover does not know how pleasant the beloved is to him; but when the beloved is separated from the lover, then the lover understands for the first time how delightful the presence of the beloved had been.

**Servant.** This is a vexing game. But I pray you, O Lord, are any to be found in this life with whom this alternation of your presence has ceased?

# Of Eternal Wisdom and Her Servant.

**Wisdom.** Very few of these are to be found, for to never be deprived of my presence is not granted to this temporal life, but rather to the eternal one.

**Servant.** But who are they, and what is the nature of those who enjoy your presence at all times?

**Wisdom.** The purest ones, and those most similar to eternity.

**Servant.** But who are they?

**Wisdom.** Those who have cast off and freed themselves—as much as was possible for them—from every mediator <note>original: "mittel." In Suso's mysticism, "means" or "mediators" refer to any created thing or worldly attachment that stands between the soul and the immediate presence of God.</note> and vice.

**Servant.** Kindest Lord, I pray you, teach me how I should conduct myself in this matter according to my imperfection.

**Wisdom.** When things go well for you, remember that they can go poorly again; and when they go poorly, remember they can go well again (Ecclesiastes 11). Thus it will happen that you neither fall into pride from my presence, nor fall into heavy sorrow of heart from abandonment and despair. If, however, out of your imperfection, you cannot yet fully renounce the delight you receive from me, then at least await me with patience and search for me lovingly.

**Servant.** Hope that is deferred, kindest Lord, torments the soul (Proverbs 13).

**Wisdom.** By necessity, he who wishes to devote himself to my love in this life must taste now the bitter, now the sweet. Do not think it enough if you give me

<column-break/>

a certain little hour of the day, but rather he must constantly dwell within himself, whoever wishes to sense and feel God inwardly, and whoever desires to understand His secret inspiration and inner, mystery-rich speech. But why do you wander about so thoughtlessly with your eyes and your mind, when the eternal and most beautiful Wisdom is always present to you and stands by you, never turning its gaze away from you for a single moment? Why do you let your hearing be drawn to strange and outward things, when so many loving words are placed before you inwardly through my inspiration? Why do you so miserably and harmfully forget yourself, when you are surrounded by the presence of the highest and eternal Good? Finally, why is your soul entangled and occupied with any external thing, when it carries the Kingdom of God so secretly within itself?

**Servant.** Lord, what kind of Kingdom of Heaven is this, which you say the soul carries within itself?

**Wisdom.** It is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.

**Servant.** Lord, from your words I perceive that you have many hidden paths in the soul which are unknown to it, and that you stand within the secret passages of the mind, and also lead and entice it sweetly and kindly to love your high Divinity <note>original: "Gottheit." This refers to the abstract, infinite nature of God beyond physical form.</note>, which previously was only attentive to your most pleasant Humanity <note>original: "Menschheit." Suso describes a spiritual progression from meditating on the human life of Christ to contemplating the divine nature of the Trinity.</note>.

# The third grievance: why God allows his friends to experience so much adversity in this world.

## Chapter 10.

**Servant.** O most kind God, there is still something lying in my heart; ah, if only I could report it to you. Ah, if only I could dispute and hold a conversation with you, as we read of the Holy Jeremiah <note>A reference to Jeremiah 12:1, where the prophet questions God's justice regarding the prosperity of the wicked and the trials of the righteous.</note>. Ah, most kind God, hear me without being burdened, according to your goodness. Some believe that although your love is **flowing with honey** and your friendship is very intimate, nonetheless, through your providence, they obtain these things with much labor and pain because of the diverse and very heavy tribulations and crosses that you allow to come upon them. Such as: that they are held in contempt by the whole world, and many adverse events—both internal and external—befall them. For as soon as someone enters into your friendship, they must immediately prepare themselves to endure all adversity with a strong, unbroken spirit. Lord, I ask you through your goodness, what sweetness can they experience in this? Or in what way can you tolerate this happening to your friends? Or is it of no concern to you to know this?

<margin>John 15</margin>
**Wisdom.** Just as my Father has loved me, so I love my friends. I deal no differently now with my friends than I have dealt from the beginning of the world until this very day.

**Servant.** Lord, this is exactly what some interpret poorly, and therefore, they say, you have few friends because you treat them so roughly and harshly in this world. From this, it also happens that many, after

<column-break/>

they have been accepted and received into your friendship—and they should now be proven and strengthened through tribulations—fall away from you. This I cannot say without great heartache and the shedding of hot tears; they return to those things to which they had given a *letter of separation* <note>original: "schedbrieff." Historically a legal document for divorce or formal separation; here it refers to a total renunciation of worldly pleasures.</note> and said goodnight for your sake. Lord, what is your answer to this?

**Wisdom.** This is the complaint of those who are of little faith and meager works, who also have a lukewarm life and an untrained spirit. But you, my beloved, step steadily out of the deep and miry pool of bodily pleasures, and with opened inner senses and spiritual eyes, look diligently at who you are, where you dwell, and where you are going. From this, you will recognize to some extent that I am very useful and favorable to my friends. For according to your natural being, you are a **mirror of the Divinity**, an **image of the Holy Trinity**, and a **pattern of eternity**. And just as I, according to my Divinity, am the infinite good, so you have an unfathomable desire. Therefore, just as a single drop of water does nothing to increase the incomprehensible, wide, and great sea, so nothing that the whole world can perform or give can fulfill your desire. Meanwhile, you hover in this **valley of tears** <note>original: "jammerthal." A traditional Christian metaphor for earthly life, full of sorrow and trial, as opposed to the joy of heaven.</note> where joy is mixed with adversity,

# Concerning the Lamentable, Everlasting Pains of Hell.

## Chapter 11.

<margin>2.</margin> **Wisdom.** Look now, my beloved, and observe with an attentive mind that unspeakable misery; behold where those are now who previously, with joy and pleasure in this momentary life, gave themselves over to the lusts of the body and delights. What does the manifold temporal joy benefit them now, which has vanished as quickly as the fleeting time, as if it had never been? How short is this happiness; what a pain follows it which will have no end? O foolish men, where is it now, what you said exultantly: "Come, you great-spirited sons, be away with all sorrows, let us give ourselves to the best of joys." <note>This echoes the speech of the ungodly in Wisdom of Solomon 2, who advocate for a life of pure hedonism before death.</note> What benefit do you draw from all the received pleasures? With injustice you may weep with a lamentable voice and say: "Woe, woe, woe, that we were ever brought into this world! Oh, how the short time has so miserably deceived us; oh, how craftily has the unavoidable necessity of Death tripped us up. <note>original: "hindersichlichen" — literally to pull someone backward or ambush them from behind.</note> Oh, is there anyone still left in the world who is as deceived as we are deceived? Or is there one who, from the harm of others,

<column-break/>

becomes wise and cautious?" Truly, if a man had to endure the crosses of all others alone for a thousand years, such a thing, compared to our account, would be considered as nothing. O truly blessed and very happy is he who has accepted no joy or pleasure against God's will, and who for His sake has not had a single happy day during the entire time of his life. We fools <note>The speaker here adopts the perspective of the damned looking back at the righteous.</note> thought such men were forgotten and abandoned by God; but see, how sweetly has He embraced them in eternity? How greatly has He honored them and exalted them before the entire Heavenly Host? What harm have they now from all the tribulation and contempt of themselves, which is now changed for them into such great happiness and into such great joy? But how is everything that we loved turned into nothing? O pain and unending tribulation! Oh, what is the pain that knows no end? What is eternal misery? Think on this: it will have no end. O death, bitterer than all death—constantly dying and never being able to die. I say to you the eternal farewell; <note>original: "Valet" — a formal Latin leave-taking.</note> I take my departure from you, my father, mother, and all friends, whose friendship I can henceforth never again enjoy...

See, this most delightful city shines with pure Gold, set with precious Pearls; the foundations of the walls are adorned with pure gemstones; its streets are pure Gold, transparent like glass; from red roses, white lilies, and all kinds of green flowers, this Fatherland shines. Now look more closely at the heavenly, pleasant fields. Here is the lovely summer; here are the blooming meadows of spring; here is the fruitful valley of true joys; here is the most pleasant...

<column-break/>

...sight of true friends upon friends; here the harps and lutes sound; there one sings and leaps, shouts for joy and dances incessantly; there one devotes oneself to all joys; there one has everything according to their wish; there all joy is without sorrow, with constant security. Look at the innumerable multitude, how they drink from the life-giving, incessantly gushing fountain according to their heart's desire; see how they cast their eyes upon the purest and most excellent **Mirror of the present Godhead** <note>This refers to the "Beatific Vision," the direct perception of God which was believed to be the ultimate source of knowledge and happiness in heaven.</note>, in which everything appears bright and clear to them. Go even further inside and see how the honey-flowing Queen of the Heavenly Fatherland <note>A reference to the Virgin Mary.</note>, whom you love so fervently, far surpasses all inhabitants of heaven in happiness, joy, and dignity; she has an abundance of joy, and out of tenderness she leans upon her beloved, **Cant. 8** <note>original: "Cant. 8"; a reference to the Song of Solomon (Canticle of Canticles) 8:5: "Who is this coming up from the wilderness, leaning on her beloved?"</note>, surrounded with roses and May-flowers. See how her most excellent beauty fills all heavenly citizens with the highest joy and exultation; and so that you yourself may rejoice, lift up your spirit: see how the most kind Mother of Mercy turns her most kind eyes so sweetly upon you and upon all sinners who call upon her, with what great power and authority she protects them and reconciles them with her Son. Look with the eyes of your understanding how the high **Seraphic Spirits** and the souls of that same order are endowed with the hottest love and are ignited without ceasing with the fervent heat of love toward me; how the bright-shining **Cherubim** and the souls beneath them enjoy the shining influence of my constant, inconceivable light and share it with others; how the high **Thrones** <note>Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones are the three highest ranks of the nine choirs of angels in traditional Christian theology.</note> and the souls joined to them...

Literally a "morning-gift" given by a groom to a bride the day after the wedding; here used for the soul's reward in heaven.</note>. Technical theological terms for the glorified body: 'subtle' meaning it can pass through matter, and 'impassible' meaning it can no longer feel pain or suffer.</note>.

<column-break/>

Besides this, I set upon her head a decorative Golden Crown, and alongside it, I give her yet another **accidental crown** <note>original: "zufällige kron." In scholastic theology, the 'essential' reward is the vision of God, while 'accidental' rewards are extra honors for specific deeds.</note>.
**Servant.** Lord, I pray you, what is this good thing, or wedding-gift? What is this golden crown, and what is this accidental crown, or little wreath of honor?
**Wisdom.** The wedding-gift, which is otherwise called a gift on account of the marriage, is a clear and manifest **contemplation** <note>original: "beschawligkeit." Refers to the 'Beatific Vision' or seeing God face-to-face.</note> of those things that we here only believe, and a present grasping of that which you here only think upon, and also a lovely and friendly enjoyment of that which you here love. The golden crown signifies the **essential reward**, but the little wreath of honor signifies the **accidental reward**.
**Servant.** I would like to have this explained to me even more clearly.
**Wisdom.** The accidental reward is a special joy which the soul has from its heartfelt works through which it was victorious here; this is enjoyed by the excellent teachers, the invincible martyrs, and the undefiled virgins. The essential reward consists in the contemplative union of the soul with the **pure Godhead** <note>original: "blossen Gottheit." Literally 'naked Godhead,' referring to God's essence stripped of all images and forms.</note>. For the soul can never enjoy full peace until it is raised above all its powers into the natural **essence** <note>original: "essenz." The inner nature of God.</note> of the Divine Persons, and is led into the simple purity of the essence, where it then receives in this **object** the true delight and eternal **Blessedness**. Now, the more detached and swift this departure is, the freer is the ascent; and the freer the ascent, the nearer and deeper it goes...

# On the infinite worth and utility of temporal tribulations.

## The 13th Chapter.

**Servant.** Lord, I pray you, explain to me clearly what you mean by the Cross and trials <note>The original German "anfechtung" refers to spiritual trials, temptations, or assaults on the soul.</note>, which you say are so excellent and profitable; for I inwardly desire to receive a precise account of this, so that, if perhaps through your providence something adverse should happen to me, I might receive and accept it with joy and gladness as coming from your Fatherly hands.

**Wisdom.** I mean this to be said of every Cross and trial, whether it is accepted voluntarily or comes from elsewhere against one’s will—where necessity is commonly transformed into a virtue—provided that the person does not seek to be exempt from such a Cross against my will, and bears it for my praise with humble and loving patience. The more such a Cross is united with greater love and a more inclined will, the more noble and acceptable it is to me. Hear me speak further of these trials, and what I say, write it in the innermost part of your heart, and let it be placed before your soul’s eyes as a spiritual sign. Hold this for certain: that I dwell in a soul as in a paradise of delights; therefore, I cannot endure that it should cling with love and pleasure to any other thing, for it is by nature inclined to harmful lusts; therefore, I—

<column-break/>

—fence its way with thorns, and all its paths (whether it brings them joy or sorrow) I block with adversity, so that the soul might not escape from my hands. All its ways I strew with trials, so that it might set its heart's delight on no other thing than on the height of my Divinity. Believe me, if all hearts were melted into one, they could not in this life endure even the smallest reward that I will give in the other, eternal life, for the slightest Cross that someone has carried for my sake; for thus it has been ordained and decided by me from eternity, and it may not be changed: that all excellent things, and those united with virtue, are at once difficult and laborious. Whoever does not wish to be diligent in this, but wishes to turn away from me, may indeed turn away. For many are called, but few are chosen. <note>Matthew 20:16.</note>

**Servant.** Perhaps, Lord, it cannot be denied that trials are very useful, provided they are not so very great, so cruel, and so unusual. You, my Lord and God, who alone know all hidden things, who have created everything in number, weight, and measure <note>A reference to Wisdom of Solomon 11:20: "But thou hast arranged all things by measure and number and weight."</note>, it is known to you that my Cross is heavy beyond measure and exceeds my strength; I truly do not know if anyone in the whole world is more and more harshly tor—

...be united. And how can I endure it? If you, O Lord, visited me with common burdens, I would bear them; but how I can endure such strange, unusual tribulations, which penetrate my soul and mind in such a secret way and are known to you alone, I do not see.

**Wisdom.** Every sick and ill-conditioned person believes his sickness to be the heaviest of all, and a thirsty person considers no one more wretched than himself; so too, if I had tormented you in another manner, you would feel exactly the same as you feel now; therefore, surrender yourself in all adversity to my will with a courageous heart, and do this without reservation or exception of this or that burden. Do you also know that I alone desire much more earnestly than you yourself what is useful and advantageous for you? It is also unknown to you that I am the eternal Wisdom, who knows best of all what is most beneficial for you. Now I believe that you have also experienced how the Cross laid upon you by me—if one only knows how to use it—touches more closely, penetrates more inwardly, and leads more quickly to God than any other voluntarily chosen Cross <note>Suso emphasizes that trials sent by God are more spiritually refining than penances one chooses for oneself, as they require deeper surrender.</note>. Why do you still complain: why do you not rather say, "Most Kind Father, deal with me according to your pleasure."

**Servant.** Lord, this is indeed easy to say, but the present tribulation, because of its excessive pain, is hard to bear.

**Wisdom.** If the Cross did not cause pain—

<column-break/>

—then it could not defend its name. Nothing is more honorable, nothing more lovely and desirable, than bearing the Cross. Cross and tribulation have indeed a short pain, but long joy; to him who is against it, the Cross is burdensome, but to him who bears it with love, it is not vexatious. In truth, if you always had such an overflow of spiritual joy, divine comfort, and nourishment that you were constantly melting from the heavenly dew <note>A common mystical metaphor for the grace or presence of God felt in the soul.</note>, the consideration of all this would not increase your merit so much, nor would I give you so much thanks for it, nor would I be bound and obligated to you in a similar way as for a single Cross borne with love, or a state of abandonment of yourself in the soul’s poverty, in which you serve me with love. And ten of those in great pleasure and lovely sweetness of heart could more quickly turn away and depart from me than just a single one who is visited with constant tribulation and adversity. If you had the knowledge of all the star-gazers <note>original: "Sternseher"; referring to astronomers or astrologers.</note> and could speak as gracefully of God as the tongues of all angels and men; if you were finally endowed with such learning alone as all the wise teachers of this world, all this would not be as advantageous for your fear of God and holiness as if you could surrender yourself entirely to God in all your tribulations. For those things are common to both the good and the evil, but this belongs only to the chosen. Oh, if one could weigh time and eternity with a righteous judgment, he would much rather lie enclosed in a fiery oven for a hundred years than be robbed of the reward of a single small tribulation which he will therefore receive in heaven; for the former has an end, but the latter knows no ceasing.

**Servant.** Most kind Jesus, that which you say is to an afflicted person just like a sweet-sounding lute. My heart, if you would present such lovely melody to me while I lie under the Cross <note>original: "Creutz"; Suso uses the "Cross" as a central metaphor for all forms of suffering, trials, and spiritual burdens.</note>, I would rather bear the Cross than be without it.

**Wisdom.** Well then, listen diligently to the sweet melody and the pleasant sound of the taut strings of a person living in adversity; notice how beautifully they ring out. Tribulations are indeed contemptible to the world, but in my eyes, they are held in great honor. Adversity destroys my anger, brings my grace and friendship, and makes a person pleasing to me and conformed to my likeness. Tribulations are a hidden good that no one can ever fully repay; so much so that if someone were to beg me for a Cross on bended knees for a hundred years, he still could not worthily deserve it. The Cross turns an earthly person into a heavenly one. The Cross alienates a person from the world and leads him into my eternal fellowship; it may decrease one’s friends, but it increases grace. He who wishes to enjoy my loveliest friendship must be separated and forsaken by the whole world. The Cross is the surest and shortest path. Believe me, if one truly recognized the utility of the Cross, he would receive it as nothing other than an excellent gift from the hand of God. Oh, how many were very near to eternal destruction and lay in a dangerous sleep, whom tribulation has stirred and awakened to a better life. How many people are kept by a constant Cross just as untamed wild animals and birds are kept in a cage, where

<column-break/>

they—if the opportunity of time and place were given to them—would immediately fall into eternal harm for their salvation. The Cross preserves one from a heavy fall, gives a person knowledge of himself, and keeps him in check so that he may lead himself and keep faith with his neighbor. It maintains the soul in humility, teaches wisdom, protects chastity, and brings the crown of eternal salvation. There is hardly anyone for whom tribulation is not useful, whether he is still entangled in sins, or has begun to improve his life, or is among those who are increasing in virtue, or is one of the perfect. For fire cleanses iron, purifies gold, and adorns precious gemstones. Temptation <note>original: "anfechtung"; in this context, it refers to spiritual trials or assaults on the soul rather than simple enticement to sin.</note> soon takes away the burden of sin, lessens the punishment of Purgatory <note>original: "Fegfewr"; the state of purification after death in Catholic theology.</note>, drives away temptation, uproots vice, renews the spirit, and brings a true confidence, a pure conscience, and a steadfast and noble mind. Temptation is a healing medicine and a health-giving herb above all other herbs of Paradise. It chastises the body, which will soon rot, and feeds the soul, which is far nobler and will live eternally. Just as the lovely-smelling roses are moistened by the dew of greening May, so does temptation make the soul fruitful. It endows the mind with wisdom and makes a person experienced. What does he know who has experienced no temptation or trial? Temptation is a rod full of love and a fatherly chastisement of my chosen ones. Temptation draws and forces a person to God, according to Ecclesiasticus 34 <note>The text refers to the Wisdom of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus), which discusses how an untried man knows little.</note>, whether he wills it or not. To him who shows himself joyful in adversity, sorrow and joy, friend and foe, are useful and serving. How often have your struggling

# Of Eternal Wisdom and her Servant.

—enemies overcome / when you praised me with a joyful heart / and kindly suffered adversity? I would rather create trials <note>original: "anfechtungen"; refers to spiritual tests, temptations, or attacks that challenge a believer's faith.</note> out of nothing / than let my friends be without a Cross. For in suffering all virtues are strengthened / the person is adorned / the neighbor is encouraged to a better life / and God is praised. Patience in adversity is a living Host <note>original: "Hoſtien"; the sacrificial bread of the Eucharist, symbolizing a holy offering to God.</note> / and a sweet balsamic scent in the presence of my Divine Majesty / at which the whole heavenly host wonders. For never has a brave fencer / or knight engaged in such a public combat / and thus drawn the tongues and hearts of men to himself / as the whole heavenly host looks upon a person bearing tribulation with gentleness. All the saints have already tasted the drink of the afflicted / because they have experienced trials enough and in abundance / and they unanimously testify / that in affliction there is no poison / but rather a healing medicine. To maintain patience in affliction is better / than giving life back to the dead / or performing other miracles. Affliction is the narrow way / which leads us to the gates of heaven / it raises a person to the company of the Martyrs / it carries the praise and the victory over all enemies / it clothes the soul with a purple-colored garment / it makes wreaths and crowns of roses / and scepters of green palm branches / it is hung as an excellent gemstone upon the breast of virgins / it sings a new song in eternal life with a sweet voice and a free heart / which even all the angelic spirits cannot sing after them / because they never endured a Cross—

<column-break/>

—endured, and to say it in few words / the world calls the afflicted people miserable / but I call them blessed / because I have chosen them for myself.

**Servant.** It appears very beautifully from this / that you are Eternal Wisdom / because you can bring the truth so clearly to light / so that nothing therein is to be doubted. Now it is no longer a wonder / that the king endures affliction / when you praise it so. In truth, O Lord, you have through your honey-sweet words brought this about in me / that in the future every Cross / and burden will be more bearable / and more lovely to me. **Wisdom.** But what do you think of this matter now?

### The Dialogue of the Blessed Henry Suso

**Servant.** Most gracious Jesus, what you say is to a sorrowful person like a well-tuned lute. My heart, when you present such lovely melody to me / even while I lie beneath the Cross <note>The "Cross" here is a metaphor for personal suffering, trials, or burdens borne for the sake of faith.</note> / I would rather bear the Cross / than be without it.

**Wisdom.** Well then, listen diligently to the sweet melody / and the pleasing sound of the taut strings of a person living in adversity; mark how lovely they ring out. Troubles are indeed contemptible to the world / but held in great honor by me. Adversity wipes away my anger / brings my grace and friendship / makes a person pleasing to me / and conformed to my image. Troubles are a hidden good / which no one can repay / so that / even if one begged for a Cross from me for a hundred years on bended knees / he could not worthily earn it. The Cross makes a heavenly person out of an earthly one. The Cross alienates a person from the world and leads him to my eternal fellowship / it diminishes friends, but increases grace. He must be summoned away from the whole world / and be forsaken / who wishes to enjoy my most lovely friendship. The Cross is the safest and shortest way. Believe me / if one correctly recognized the benefit of the Cross / he would take it as nothing other than an excellent gift from the hand of God. Oh, how many were very near to eternal destruction / and lay in a dangerous sleep / whom trouble has cheered / and awakened to a better life. How many people are held back by a constant Cross like untamed wild beasts and birds in a cage / where 

<column-break/>

they yet / if the opportunity of time and place were given to them / would immediately fall into eternal harm in their wantonness <note>original: "geiligkeit"; implies worldly lust or unrestrained, wild behavior.</note>. The Cross preserves from a heavy fall / gives a person knowledge of himself / keeps him in check / so that he might rule himself / and keep faith with his neighbor. It keeps the soul in humility / teaches wisdom / protects chastity / and brings the crown of eternal bliss. There is hardly anyone for whom trouble is not useful / whether he is still entangled in sins / or has begun to better his life / or is among the number of the progressing <note>original: "zunemmenden"; a technical term for those who have moved past the "beginner" stage of spiritual life but are not yet "perfect."</note> / or is one of the perfect. Trial <note>original: "anfechtung"; refers to spiritual testing, temptation, or hardship that challenges one's faith.</note> soon takes away the burden of sin / lessens the punishment of Purgatory / drives away temptation / roots out vices / renews the spirit / brings true trust / a pure conscience / and a steadfast and high mind. Trial is a healing medicine / and a health-giving herb above all other herbs of Paradise. It chastises the body / which will soon rot / and feeds the soul which is much nobler / and will live eternally. Just as the lovely smelling roses are moistened by the dew of greening May / so trial makes the soul fruitful. It endows the mind with wisdom / and makes a person experienced. What does he know / who has experienced no trial or temptation? Trial is a rod full of love / and a fatherly chastisement of my chosen. # Of the unspeakable benefit and fruit / which springs from the contemplation of the Passion of Christ.

## The 14th Chapter.

**Servant.** How much benefit and fruit can be drawn from your Passion <note>original: "leydens", referring to the suffering and death of Jesus Christ.</note>, O Lord / if one would apply place, time, and leisure to it / I believe no one is sufficiently aware. Oh, what a certain way is the way of your suffering / which leads the person through the way of Truth to the highest summit of all perfection. Well have you, Saint Paul, you great and excellent Light among all the stars of heaven / held this view / when you were so highly exalted / and thus led into the secret chamber of the Divinity / so that you heard hidden words / which no person is permitted to speak. 2 Cor. 12. <note>original: "2. ...melted away in tears and sweetness; for in such a way, you perform a work of virtue out of love, not seeking yourself. Now, if there is a great sinner, who perhaps has defiled himself more than a thousand times with heavy mortal sins, for whom—according to the requirements of spiritual laws <note>This refers to Canon Law and the "penitential canons" of the Middle Ages, which prescribed specific lengths of penance for specific sins.</note>—a seven-year penance would be required for every single sin; but if he is overtaken by death and departs from this world without having made satisfaction <note>original: "gnugthuung"; the theological concept that a sinner must make amends for the harm caused by their sin, even after being forgiven.</note>, he would have to pay the unpaid punishment most precisely in the burning furnace of the sharp Purgatory. Who does not see how long she will have to remain in that punishment? But behold: everything she has to suffer can be paid in a short time through my innocent suffering. And surely, she can make the treasure of my suffering her own in such a way that, even if she were meant to be tormented in Purgatory for thousands upon thousands of years, she would—in a short time—dissolve and pay both the guilt and the punishment at once, and go straight to heaven without Purgatory.

**Servant.** Lord, teach me how such a thing can happen, for I wish to make myself a partaker in the treasure of your suffering.

<column-break/>

**Wisdom.** With a contrite heart, one must often consider the number and magnitude of his heavy sins, with which he has so unsuitably offended the eyes of his heavenly Father. He must hold the works of his own satisfaction in low esteem, as they, when compared with his sins, are no more than a single drop against the whole sea. But the infinity of my satisfaction he must exalt, praise, and honor; for a single little drop of the precious Blood, which flows so richly from my whole body, would have been more than sufficient to wipe out the sins of a thousand worlds. Nevertheless, each person receives and appropriates for himself from my satisfaction only as much as he makes himself conformable to me in compassion <note>original: "mitleydon," meaning "suffering-with." This is a key theme for Suso: the believer must not just observe Christ's pain but spiritually share in it.</note>, and as much as he—with all humility—sinks the insignificance of his own satisfaction into the infinity of my payment, and lifts it up there. And to say it in a single word: know that neither the masters of arithmetic <note>original: "Rechenmeister"</note>, nor the surveyors, nor the paymasters together can calculate all the infinite goods that lie hidden in the constant meditation on my suffering.

**Servant.** Lord, since this is so, I beg you: let all things go through which I have strayed, and lead me into the inner, hidden treasures of your lovely suffering.

# What Christ suffered on the Cross, concerning the compassion of His Mother, and how we should make ourselves conformable to the Crucified.

### The 15th Chapter.

**Servant.** Lord, you have explained to me above in some measure the anxieties with which your outer man <note>In medieval theology, the "outer man" refers to the physical body and the sensory nature, as opposed to the "inner man" or the spirit.</note> was surrounded when you hung on the high Cross; how he was entirely laden with wounds and entangled and surrounded by the bonds of wretched death. Now I would like to know what happened beneath the Cross, whether anyone was present to whose heart your lamentable death went painfully, and how you behaved then toward your sorrowful Mother.

**Wisdom.** Listen to a lamentable matter and have compassion with me; when I hung on the Cross before my enemies in a wretched manner, surrounded by manifold anxieties (as you have heard) and pains, they stood against me, tormented and crucified me with mockery and blasphemy, laughed at me, and shook their heads at me, and esteemed me so little in their hearts as if I had been the most contemptible little worm. In all this I stood unmoving and prayed fervently to my Father for them. <note>original: Marc. 15; see the Gospel of Mark, chapter 15.</note> And though I was the most innocent little Lamb, I was numbered among the godless, <note>original: Luc. 23; see the Gospel of Luke, chapter 23.</note> one of whom mocked me, but the other called upon my faith and help, whom I graciously received without delay, forgave him his sin, and opened the heavenly Paradise to him. Hear what is to be wept over: as I turned my eyes here and there, I

<column-break/>

found myself robbed of all human help; but my friends and acquaintances who followed me stood from afar, and my dearest disciples had departed from me. I hung naked, robbed of all clothes; I was without strength and brought under the power of my enemies; they held me cruelly without mercy. Meanwhile, however, just like a silent little sheep, I was completely gentle. Wherever I turned, I was filled with bitter heart-sorrow and anxieties. Beside the Cross stood my most sorrowful Mother, <note>original: Johan. 19; see the Gospel of John, chapter 19.</note> and suffered in her motherly heart what I suffered in my body, which cut most severely through my heart, for I alone recognized the cruel pains of her heart. When I saw her mournful gestures and heard the lamentable words, I comforted her as best I could, although I must now be separated from her through death, and I commended her to my dearest disciple John, so that he might show her the loyalty due to a mother; likewise, I commended the disciple to her motherly loyalty and care.

**Servant.** Lord, who can refrain from deep sighs and bitter tears here? Oh most beautiful Wisdom, oh most gentle and kind little Lamb, how could the fierce lions and ravening wolves treat you so cruelly against your dignity? Ah, that to me, your wretched and unworthy

**Wisdom.** When you take care to always do, according to your ability, what seems best to you—even though others laugh at you for it and behave disgracefully toward you, and also despise you in their hearts as someone who can neither protect nor defend himself—and yet you, meanwhile, are not only not moved to anger,

When you also renounce all human fellowship, profit, and comfort—except for what strict necessity requires—then your abandonment and desolation take the place of all those who abandoned me on the Cross. But when, out of love for me, you withdraw from all friends as if they did not concern you (specifically in those things that might cause some hindrance between you and me): in this fortune you show yourself as my most beloved disciple and brother, who stands under the Cross and bears compassion with me. By maintaining the heart's freedom, stripped of all things, you thereby cover and adorn my nakedness.
