**Servant.** Lord, I pray you that, according to the desire of my soul, you fulfill the likeness of your pitiable death in my body and soul—whether I will it or not—to your highest praise and according to your most pleasing will. I also desire from my heart that you would explain the infinite sorrows of your most sorrowful Mother somewhat more extensively, and tell how she conducted herself under the Cross while you suffered for us.

**Wisdom.** It is permitted for you to seek this out from her.

# Of the unspeakable pain and compassion <note>Original: "mitleyden." In this context, it refers to "suffering-with" or "co-passion," the theological idea that Mary shared in Christ's physical and spiritual suffering.</note> of the Mother of God.

## The 17th Chapter.

Who will give to my eyes as many drops of tears as there are letters I intend to write, so that I might write and recount with tear-water the pitiable weeping which flowed from the infinite heart-pain of the Most Holy Virgin? I pray you, immaculate Lady, most excellent Queen of Heaven and Earth, touch my stony heart with a single little drop of your hot tears, which you shed so abundantly under the Cross because of the unspeakable agonies of your only-begotten Son, so that it might become soft and feel your pain to some extent. For the nature of a very sharp pain is manifest to no one except the one who has experienced it. Therefore, O most kind Lady, touch my heart with your sorrowful words, and for the sake of remembrance, explain to your servant what your heart endured, and how you conducted yourself under the Cross, when you saw your most beloved Son—eternal and most excellent Wisdom—die such a wretched death.

**Mary answers.** You will not hear this without sadness and heart-pain; for although I am now free of all misery and

<column-break/>

pain, I was then of a different state. Indeed, before I stood under the Cross, I had already taken in very great and unspeakable heart-agonies, especially from the place where I first saw my Son being struck down, beaten, plucked <note>Original: "gerupfft." A reference to the "Plucking of the Beard," a common motif in medieval meditations on the Passion based on Isaiah 50:6: "I gave... my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair."</note>, and evilly tormented. When I saw this, I was robbed of all my strength until I followed him to the Cross. What I suffered there, what my condition was, and how I behaved, you shall hear in part, as much as can be grasped by you; for never has a person been born into the world who can fully fathom it. For just as a single little drop of water is to be considered as nothing compared to the entire sea, so all the pains of a person cannot be compared with the immeasurable agonies and tribulations with which my maternal heart was then tormented. This you can note from this: that the more someone is dear, lovely, and pleasant to another, the more intolerable and bitter is their death or loss. But who on earth was born more lovely, who was more pleasant than my only-begotten Son, the beloved of my heart, in whom I alone had everything that to me the entire [world]...

Because I then saw such a friend—my only-begotten Son—hanging before me on the Cross as he wrestled with death, what anguish and pain do you think this sight brought me? # How our Lord’s inner being was disposed at that time.

## Chapter 18.

**Servant.** Lord Jesus, the more one strives to fathom your suffering, the more unfathomable it seems. You truly endured great anxiety before the crucifixion, but the pain of the Cross caused you even greater agony according to your senses and outward powers, which then tasted the present bitterness of death. But, my heart, what did your inner being—namely, your most noble soul—feel at that time? Was it showered with any comfort or sweetness, as we read of certain martyrs whose pains you softened and made bearable? Or when did your pain reach its end?

**Wisdom.** <note>In Suso’s work, "Wisdom" is the personification of Jesus Christ as the Eternal Wisdom of God.</note> Although you have heard many sad tidings from time to time, yet nothing sadder will have come to your ears than what I am about to tell you. According to its higher powers, my soul then recognized the Divine Essence no less than it does now; however, the lower powers of both the inner and outer man were so forsaken and devoid of comfort in all bitterness that there has never been such distress. And as I hung there on the Cross, robbed of all help and abandoned, with dripping wounds, weeping eyes, outstretched arms, and the veins of all my limbs opened, surrounded by the agonies of death, I cried out to the Father with a plaintive and piteous voice: *My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?* <note>original: "Matth. 27." Reference to Matthew 27:46.</note> Nevertheless, meanwhile, my will was united with the eternal

<column-break/>

decree and the good pleasure of His will. When all my blood had been shed and my strengths were weakened, a very great thirst overcame me from the agony of death; yet I thirsted even more for the salvation of all people. While I suffered this unbearable thirst, they gave me gall and vinegar. When all was accomplished that was necessary for the restoration of human blessedness, I cried out: *It is finished.* <note>original: "Jo-an. 19." Reference to John 19:30.</note> Thus I rendered full obedience to my Father even unto death. And after the words: *Father, into your hands I commend my spirit* <note>original: "Luc. 23." Reference to Luke 23:46.</note>, my excellent soul departed from the Divine Body, yet in such a way that the Divinity did not depart from it. After this, they pierced my right side with a lance, from which immediately flowed a small stream of precious blood and a fountain of living water. See, my child, with such labor and pain I have purchased you and all the elect, and with the life-giving sacrifice of my innocent blood, I have redeemed you from eternal death.

**Servant.** Lord Jesus, my purest lover, you have purchased me very dearly; how you have loved me and graciously set me in freedom! How shall I be grateful to you, O sweetest Wisdom, for such great love and for such bitter suffering? # On the taking down of Jesus from the Cross.

## The 19th Chapter.

**Servant.** Most kind Mother, venerable Lady, likewise explain to your servant how the great pain you endured from the suffering of your Son finally reached its end.

**Mary answers.** I will fulfill your desire, but you must listen to my words only with sighing and compassion. After my only, most beloved Son gave up His spirit, hung dead before me, and all the strength of my heart and senses left me—because I could do nothing else—I frequently cast my eyes upon Him in a pitiful manner. But when I perceived those who came to take Him down from the Cross, I felt as if I were raised from the dead again. With what maternal affection I received His lifeless arms, and with what faithfulness I pressed them to my bloody cheeks; with what love and longing I laid Him in my maternal lap, embraced Him with my arms, and pressed Him to my breast! How I kissed the fresh, still bloody wounds of His pale face! Into what ugliness was that previously unspeakable beauty changed—the beauty which all the angels longed to see with the highest joy.

# Of Eternal Wisdom and Her Servant

**Servant.** Lord Jesus, what do you wish to teach me?

**Wisdom.** How to live and how to die, and how you should likewise receive me in the most holy Sacrament with love and devotion, and praise me worthily. For such things are properly your concern.

**Servant.** Most kind Jesus, if I had the choice to select anything, I would wish for nothing better than to know how to die to myself and all things, and to live for you alone; to love you with my whole heart, to receive you out of love in the most holy Sacrament, and to praise you worthily. Blessed and thrice-blessed is he who knows this and spends his life in this pursuit. However, it is somewhat unclear to me whether you wish this to be understood as <term>spiritual death</term> <note>This refers to 'mortification,' the mystical practice of 'dying' to worldly desires and the ego to be united with God.</note>, which your bitter and pitiable death has so inwardly and lovely commanded and explained to me—or if you mean bodily death.

**Wisdom.** It is to be understood as both.

**Servant.** Lord, what use is it to be instructed about bodily death, since when it arrives, it will teach enough of itself?

**Wisdom.** Whoever wishes to learn the art of dying only when he must depart from life will find himself deceived.

**Servant.** Lord, I confess that even now the memory of death and the talk of it is quite annoying and unacceptable to me.

**Wisdom.** Consider, however, how unavoidable and unforeseen death creeps around both in monasteries and cities, and how many are taken away; indeed, death had entangled you yourself in its snares in a secret and cunning way, and it lacked little that it would have snatched you away like countless others. From among their number, I will set one before your eyes. Now, open your inner eyes and ears; behold the example of a terrifying death in your neighbor, and listen diligently to his lamenting voice and sighs.

<column-break/>

**Servant.** Meanwhile, I heard with the ears of the soul the wretched cry and piteous words of a person perishing through unforeseen death, in this manner:

> Oh my heart and God, why was I ever born into this world? The beginning of my birth started with weeping, and the last day ends with sad and hot tears. The sighs of death have surrounded me, and the pains of Hell have encompassed me.

Now the terrifying words of death resound in my ears: neither friend, nor riches, nor knowledge, nor any effort and labor will be able to rescue you from my hands; you must necessarily surrender to me. ### The Dialogue of the Blessed Henry Suso

...that I was ever born! O Death, O terrifying Death, what will you do with me?

**Servant.** For what reason do you find yourself in such a state? This is a common law for both the rich and the poor, for the young as well as the old; and far more have died by an unforeseen death than a prepared one. Do you expect to be the only one exempted from death? This is surely a great folly.

**The man dying unexpectedly answers.** This comfort is very distressing. I have not been robbed of my reason; certainly, those who have not lived in such a way that they are ready to die, and yet do not fear death at their end, are blind and foolish. They die like cattle, ignorant of the danger in which they hover. I do not weep because I am dying, but because I die unprepared. I must necessarily die, yet my affairs are in such a state that dying is not profitable to me. Not only do I mourn the loss of my life, but also the good days that I used poorly and allowed to slip away without fruit for my soul. I now see no difference between myself and a blossom falling from a tree in springtime; my days have passed more quickly than an arrow through the air. I am forgotten as one who never was, like the path of a bird flying through the sky, which can no longer be recognized as soon as it has passed. Therefore, my speech is in bitterness, and my words are full of pain. <margin>Job 23</margin> Who will grant me, miserable as I am, to set that precious past time before my eyes, and to know now what I know far too late? Woe is me, who held the present time granted to me in low regard, and let it slip away in vain and foolishly.

<column-break/>

Now it has flowed away; I can never recall it nor reach it again. Not a single hour, however short, has passed that I should not have valued more highly and received with greater gratitude than if a whole kingdom were given to a poor beggar. Now my eyes shed tears because I cannot recover those vanished hours. Oh, my Lord and God, why have I let so many days pass so fruitlessly, from which I now have no benefit? Why did I not learn to die well throughout all that time? Oh, you blooming roses, you young people whose age has not yet withered, but who still live in the bloom of youth: look at me and learn to become wise from my danger while there is still time. Turn yourselves immediately to God; spend your years with Him alone, so that such misery does not one day seize you. Oh, how poorly I invested my young years! My Lord and God, have mercy on me. Wretched as I was, I would then believe no one, even if he admonished me rightly; I would give ear to no one. Now I have fallen into the snare of Death. Time has vanished, youth has flown; it would have been much better for me if my mother's womb had become my grave, so that I had not employed that most noble time so poorly.

**Servant.** My brother, turn yourself to God and feel sorrow for your sins. If the end is good, then all will be good.

**Dying Man.** You speak of vain things. This should move the old as well as the young; and while there is still time, gather merits in this life, so that you do not want to beg at the final end and yet can obtain nothing.

*Servant.* My brother, your anxieties crucify my soul. I adjure you by the living God that you instruct me on what is to be done so that I do not one day fall into this same danger.

...day, or would die within that very week. Imagine that your soul should be detained in Purgatory <note>original: "Fegfewr"; in Catholic theology, a place of temporary suffering where souls are purified before entering Heaven</note> for whole years for its sins, and were actually being held there now, but that you were granted only one year of life to come to its aid whenever you wished. In the meantime, look upon it often and hear its pitiful voice as it calls to you: "My dearest and most trusted friend, reach out your hand to me in my misery; have mercy on me, help me, so that I may be drawn out of this pain and these cruel flames in time. For I am entirely inconsolable and poor, and no one offers themselves as a faithful helper to me except you alone; the whole world has forgotten me, for everyone seeks only their own interests." <note>This is a reference to the Bible, Philippians 2:21.</note>

**Servant.** There is no doubt that this teaching of yours is most excellent, provided that one could experience in deed what you are feeling in the present. But even though your words are powerful and piercing like a sword, they are nonetheless little regarded by men; they have ears and hear not, eyes and see not. Almost no one wants to die until the soul departs from the body.

**Dying Man.** When they are then caught with death’s hook, they will indeed sigh, but they will rightly not be heard. Believe me, it has come to this: just as among those in religious orders <note>monks, nuns, and friars</note>—to say nothing of others—barely the hundredth person is moved to improvement and conversion by my words; so among a hundred, you will barely find one who dies well-prepared. Therefore, almost all, just like me, fall suddenly into death's snare. This even happens sometimes to those who do not die entirely without repentance and without

<column-break/>

reason. For vain honor, the profit and pleasure of the body, the love of worldly things, and the anxious toil to maintain the body blind many people. But if you, along with the few, wish to escape the agonies of an unforeseen death, then give ear to my words: the constant meditation on death, and the faithful help—which you must remember—that your poor soul (subjected as it were to the pains of Purgatory) pitifully demands of you, will quickly lead you to the point that you not only do not fear death, but await it with heartfelt longing. Contemplate this not just superficially, but often and with diligence, and write my words upon the innermost part of your heart. ## What Diligence Should Be Applied to the Inner Life.

### Chapter 22.

**Servant.** LORD, there are various exercises and many ways to live; some follow these, others follow those. Holy Scripture is also unfathomable <note>original: "vnerforschlich"</note>, and the instructions and commandments are innumerable. So I ask you then, O Eternal Wisdom, teach me briefly what I should do on the journey of true life, and whom I should follow.

**Wisdom.** The truest, most useful, and shortest thing that you can gather from all writings, and make useful for yourself for the perfection of life, is this instruction: Live withdrawn and separated from all people; keep yourself free and pure from all internal imaginings <note>original: "einbildungen"; refers to mental images or distractions that pull the mind away from God.</note>; free yourself from everything to which your mind might cling and which can bring you any care or anxiety. Lift your mind incessantly to earnest, hidden, and Divine contemplation <term>contemplation: "beschawlichkeit," a state of deep, prayerful focus on the presence of God.</term>, in which you always set me before your eyes as a goal, from which you do not turn your eyes for a single moment. As for other lesser exercises—such as poverty, fasting, vigils, and other bodily mortifications <term>mortifications: "kasteyungen," physical disciplines like fasting or lack of sleep intended to subdue the body's desires.</term>—direct them all toward this goal, and take on as much of them as is necessary and beneficial to you for this purpose. In this way, you will ascend to the highest perfection, which hardly one in a thousand otherwise reaches, because they set their goal on other outward exercises and are therefore led around for many years, yet remain far removed from perfection

perfection.

**Servant.** Lord, who can look upon your Divinity with steady eyes at all times and remain in this unchanging contemplation of the mind?

But where you perceive yourself led away from this goal, consider that you are deprived of eternal bliss; therefore, return there at once so that you may reach again what was lost and take care over yourself. For as often as you deviate from this, it is no different for you than for a sailor who has lost his oars and rudder during a storm and does not know where he should go. If you cannot do this at all times, then apply yourself so that the often-repeated conversion to the inner life—by which you gather yourself again as often as you have failed—may finally make you steadfast, as much as can happen in this life. # The Conversation of the Blessed Henry Suso

...how rich you are in your gifts? My God, look upon the desire of my heart. No king or emperor was ever received with such honor, no foreign guest was ever so welcome, no bride has been led home with such preparation and adornment, nor held more dearly or heartily, than my soul desires to receive you—the most invincible Sovereign, the most friendly Guest, and the most beloved Bridegroom of my soul. **Servant.** Lord, all these things work heartfelt works and bring great benefits.

**Wisdom.** These things seem great and hearty to you because you can see them with your eyes; but the very smallest gift proceeding from the most holy Sacrament <term>Sacrament|The Eucharist or Holy Communion, central to medieval Christian life</term> shines and glows in all eternity much more clearly than the radiance of the sun. It is much brighter than the rising morning star and adorns you with eternal beauty much better than the earthly spring has ever adorned the earth. Do you perhaps doubt that my most radiant Divinity, which is more glowing than the sun; that my most beautiful Soul, which is more shining than all the stars; and that my glorious Body, which is more delightful than all the loveliness of summer, are truly shared with you in the most holy Sacrament?

**Servant.** Lord, since this is so, why does one not feel it? For I often approach so dry, cold, and stubborn <note>The author refers here to "spiritual dryness," a common state in mystical theology where a believer feels no emotional or sensory connection to God despite their devotion.</note> that it seems to me I receive no more light, grace, and sweetness than one born blind who has never looked upon the light of the sun. **Wisdom.** The less one asks for testimonies and proofs, the purer the faith and the greater the reward. You see that God, as the author of Nature, gives to countless trees the most beautiful and wonderful growth and increase—and does so in such a hidden way that it can be grasped neither with the eyes nor any outward sense,

<column-break/>

until they are perfect. In the Holy Sacrament, I am not a light that breaks out [visibly], nor such a good that works externally; but the more spiritual such a thing is, the more excellent it is.

**Servant.** Oh my God, how few there are who rightly weigh what they receive in the Holy Sacrament! They approach in a common, unthinking manner; therefore it happens that just as they approach, so they also depart—namely, without grace and devotion—for they do not think upon the Food and do not contemplate what they are to receive.

**Wisdom.** To the well-prepared, I am the Bread of Life <note>original: "Brodt deß Lebens"; a reference to John 6:35</note>; to the poorly prepared, a dry bread; to the unworthy and unprepared, a temporal punishment, a deadly fall, and an eternal curse.

**Servant.** LORD, what you say is terrifying; but whom do you call the well, the poorly, and the unworthy or badly prepared?

**Wisdom.** I call "well-prepared" those who are purified from sins; "poorly prepared" those who still have some obstacle; but "unprepared" those who, either by will or deed, voluntarily persist in mortal sins.

**Servant.** If someone in that same hour has hearty remorse for his sins and exerts himself according to his ability so that he may be pronounced free of his sins according to the church order <note>Referring to the rite of Confession and Absolution</note>, is that then enough?

**Wisdom.** Then he is no longer burdened with any sins.

**Servant.** Lord, as much as it seems to me, it is to be reckoned among all the difficult things of this world that one prepares himself worthily for you; for who can do such a thing?

I 3

...if someone were already endowed, renowned, and adorned with all the natural purity of angels, with all the perfection of the saints, and with all the good works of all mankind, he would still not be worthy enough to receive me in the **Holy Sacrament**.

**Servant.** Since this is so, O most kind **Jesus**, with how great a fear must we then approach—we who are deprived of all devotion and grace?

**Wisdom.** When a person does what is within their power, nothing more is required of them, because God makes up for the rest. A sick person must cast aside all fear and submit to the advice of an experienced physician until they regain their health.

**Servant.** But what is most advisable: to receive you often or rarely in the **Holy Sacrament**?

**Wisdom.** Whoever feels that grace and devotion grow within them from the <term>reception|original: 'geniessung', referring to the act of consuming the Eucharist</term> of the Sacrament, it is advisable for them to approach often.

**Servant.** But what if someone notices neither an increase nor a decrease—indeed, often feels entirely dry and barren in their spirit?

**Wisdom.** As long as they do what they can, they must not be too disturbed by this dryness or hardness. For the salvation of the soul—which by God's providence is burdened with a state of dryness or hardness <note>In mystical theology, "dryness" (Ariditas) refers to a period where a believer feels no emotional or spiritual "sweetness" during prayer or rituals, testing their faith.</note>—is made perfect in the light of pure faith no less than in great sweetness. I am a treasure of such a kind that is increased through frequent reception and diminished by sparing use. Thus...

<column-break/>

...it is then more useful to go to the most holy **Sacrament** out of love than to abstain out of fear. It is much better to receive it once every week with true and deep humility of heart than only once a year with presumption of one's own righteousness or with pride of spirit.

**Servant.** At what time does the grace of the **Holy Sacrament** work within a person?

**Wisdom.** In the very moment when they receive it.

**Servant.** But what if someone had a great desire to receive you present in the most holy **Sacrament**, but it could not happen?

**Wisdom.** Many of them, even if they do not receive me physically, are nevertheless abundantly satisfied by me; whereas many others who receive me at the Altar go away hungry. The latter receive me <term>sacramentally|The physical act of eating the consecrated host</term>, but the former receive me in a <term>spiritual manner|Also known as 'Spiritual Communion,' where the believer receives the benefits of the Sacrament through desire and faith when the physical rite is impossible</term>.

**Servant.** Do they then benefit more who receive you both sacramentally and spiritually than those who receive you only spiritually?

**Wisdom.** Tell me, whom do you judge more blessed: he who enjoys both me and my grace, or he who partakes of my grace alone?

**Servant.** This is an easy question. But my Lord, tell me briefly: how long do you remain with your bodily presence in the one who has received you?

**Wisdom.** So long as the <term>forms|original: 'gestalten', referring to the 'accidents' or physical appearance of bread and wine</term> of the **Sacrament** remain.

<summary>In this dialogue, Eternal Wisdom explains that the Eucharist should be received frequently out of love rather than fear, even during times of spiritual dryness. **Wisdom.** Whoever thinks they can praise me worthily labors in vain; nevertheless, it is permitted to you, as to all other creatures, to praise and glorify me with all your strength. For there has never been a creature, great or small, good or evil, that does not praise me and deem me worthy of praise; and the more closely a creature is united to me, the more praiseworthy I am to it. For the more similar and closer your praise is to the praise of the Heavenly Fatherland <note>original: "Himlischen Vatterlands", a common mystical term for Heaven</note>, the more it honors me. Yet, it is closer to that heavenly praise the more it is detached from the imaginings of all created things, and the more united it is with me through true devotion. For without doubt, the devout meditation of the heart sounds much better in my ears than the praise spoken with mere lips without the heart's devotion and attentiveness. And the inner sighing of the heart is more pleasing to me than the loud shouting of the mouth. Finally, humble lowliness <note>original: "niederträchtigkeit"; in Suso's time, this meant "lowliness" or "humility" rather than the modern German sense of "meanness" or "malice"</note>—where one submits themselves not only to God the Lord but also to all people, so that they wish to be nothing and held in no esteem—surpasses all melodious songs in my eyes. When I lived on Earth, I praised God the Father most when I hung on the Cross, completely disfigured and dying at every moment. Some praise me with the beautiful words of their lips, but their heart is far from me; I hold their praise in low regard. Others praise me diligently when everything goes according to their wish; but when misfortune blows upon them and they are buffeted by the contrary wind, their praise also diminishes, which must necessarily displease me. This, then, is the worthy and

<column-break/>

acceptable praise in my eyes: that you praise me with heart, word, and deed no less devoutly and diligently in adversity as in prosperity—in sorrowful and unpleasant things just as much as in joyful and desired things. For thus you will truly declare that you look more upon me than upon yourself.

**Servant.** Lord, I dare not ask for any cross or trial from you, and I will strive not to deserve to be tested; nevertheless, I surrender myself entirely to your eternal praise. # Of Eternal Wisdom and Her Servant

In [those] years, every week; and of those many weeks, every day; and of those days, every hour; and of those hours, every moment—that I might praise you in my name with such a pleasing and perfect praise as any saint in the true radiance of the saints has ever praised you. And [to do] this so many countless times, as many as the dust motes <note>original: "gestüb", referring to the fine particles of dust visible in a beam of light</note> that fly in the sunbeams, so that they might fulfill my good desire, just as if I had completed it myself in this temporal life. Lord, it is not I, but you; you, I say, are the one yourself upon whom I look, whom I will, whom I love, and whom I seek. All is known to you; you know the hearts of all men; you know me to be of such a mind that even if I were aware that I should be eternally tormented in Hell <note>original: "Höllen"</note>, and even if the deprivation of your most delightful face should torment me most vehemently, I would still wish to withhold nothing from your praise. Indeed, if I could, I would gladly recall the past times of all people, chastise <note>original: "Casteyen", referring to the practice of spiritual discipline or mortification of the flesh</note> sin through penance, and make satisfaction for them, and repay and atone for all the wrongs shown to you with your praise. <column-break/>

abyss of Hell would penetrate Hell, the Earth, the Air, and all the Heavens, until it reached you. But because no one in Hell thanks or praises you, I will in the meantime praise you all the more fervently and insistently on Earth. Deal with me, who am your lowliest creature, according to your greatest praise; for however and whatever happens to me, I will praise you, my Lord, in my life as long as breath is in me. And when my tongue and voice shall fail, I wish that the movement or stretching out of a finger might be a confirmation and conclusion of your praise, which I have ever offered to you. And when my flesh has rotted away, I wish that from every little speck of dust <note>original: "stäublein"</note> your most fervent praise might break forth, passing through stone, through rock, and through all the heavens until it stands before your face, until the Judgment Day <note>original: "jüngsten tag"</note>, when body and soul, reunited, shall praise you in eternity.

*Wisdom.* Persevere steadfastly in this desire and holy purpose <note>original: "vornemmen"</note> until the end, and do not doubt that such praise is very pleasing to me.

*Servant.* Lord, since you desire to be praised by me, a wretched man, I pray you tell me whether the praise which happens with words or song is of any use.

*Wisdom.* It is of no small benefit, primarily because it rouses the inner person <note>original: "innerlichen Menschen", a mystical term for the soul or the spiritual self</note>, who is often spurred on by this, especially in those who are beginning a good life.

*Servant.* Yes, Lord, I am constantly called inwardly, because I have a joy in beginning in this life what one will do for all time in eternity—that I may strive unceasingly to praise you, and not cease from your praise for a single moment. In this desire

# The Conversation of the Blessed Henry Suso

I remember having often said: "O Heaven, why do you hurry so much? Why is your course so fast? Stand still a little while until I shall praise my most beloved Heart according to my heart's desire." and when it happens, O most kind Jesus, that I turn away from your praise for a short time and do not attend to you, when I come back to myself, I speak thus: "O, a thousand years have passed in which I have not once been mindful of my beloved Lord!" Because my body and soul are still united <note>The Servant refers to being alive on earth, where the physical body often distracts the soul from spiritual focus.</note>, teach me, Lord, in what way I should honor you with an unceasing praise.

**Wisdom.** Whoever aims at me in all things, abstains from sins, and is devoted to virtues, never stops praising me. But because you wish to know the highest way to praise me, I will explain it most perfectly: It can be said of the soul that it is like a light feather; when nothing clings to it, it is raised high into the air because of its natural mobility; but if something heavy <note>In this metaphor, "something heavy" refers to the weight of sin or worldly attachment.</note> clings to it, it is thrown down to the earth. Even so, a soul freed from sins and driven by the wind of spiritual contemplations is raised on high; when the soul is then freed from the desire for visible things and set at rest, so that its whole intention and mind is inseparably attached to the unchanging Good, such a person praises and prizes me at all times. For in such purity—more than can be expressed in words—human reason is so swallowed up and transformed from the earthly into a spiritual and angelic likeness, that whatever the soul receives outwardly or inwardly, whatever it does or works, whether it eats, drinks, sleeps,

<column-break/>

or wakes, all of this is nothing other than the praise of God.

**Servant.** Lord, your teaching is entirely pleasant, yet I would still like to be instructed in four points; the first is: from where should the material and opportunity to praise you be taken?

**Wisdom.** You will find the primary cause to praise me in the Wellspring and origin of all good, and thereafter in the little streams flowing from it.

**Servant.** Lord, I confess the origin surpasses my understanding; let the high cedars of Lebanon <note>A biblical reference to the tallest, most majestic trees, here representing the highest angels and saints.</note>—namely the heavenly and angelic spirits—praise you from that source. Yet, I will present myself before them for your praise as a rough and stinging thistle bush, so that they, moved by the stimulation of my desire (which I cannot fulfill on such a high level), may be reminded of their own high dignity. Thus, in their bright-shining clarity, they may be all the more encouraged to spread your praise with all attentiveness—just as the cuckoo encourages the nightingale <note>The cuckoo was often seen as a lowly bird whose simple call prompted the more talented nightingale to begin its beautiful song.</note> and gives her cause to sing sweetly. The little streams and the outflow of your goodness shall be praised by me to the highest; for when I consider who I have been, from what evils you have so often preserved me, and from what snares of fear, bonds, and plots you have freed me, it is a wonder that my mind does not entirely melt away in your praise. O my God, how long have you waited for me? How graciously have you received me when I turned to you? How sweetly you have very often, though secretly, come to me and inwardly exhorted me? And even though I have shown myself very ungrateful in everything, you have yet not ceased until you led me back to yourself. Should I then not rightly praise you for all of this?

<summary>In this passage, Eternal Wisdom explains that a soul purified from sin praises God through every action, even mundane ones like sleeping or eating. The Servant responds by marveling at God's mercy and personal providence, comparing his humble prayers to a thistle among cedars or a cuckoo prompting a nightingale.</summary>

Yes, I desire to praise you, just as all the angelic spirits <note>original: "Englische Geister." In this context, it refers to angels (from the German 'Engel'), not the English people.</note> praised you when they were strengthened in grace while seeing others cast out; or like the souls released from Purgatory and admitted before your Countenance; or like those on the streets of the Heavenly Jerusalem <note>A common medieval image of the afterlife where the saved dwell in a perfect, golden city.</note> after receiving the sentence of the Last Judgment, when the elect shall be separated from the damned with an eternal security. The second thing I desire to know is how I should direct all the good inclinations of nature toward your eternal praise.

**Wisdom.** Because in this temporal life no one can actually distinguish nature from grace by human art or science, if you therefore encounter something lovely—whether from nature or from grace, in the body or the soul—turn yourself immediately to the interior; attribute it to God and pray to Him that it be applied to His praise. For He is the Lord of nature and of grace; in this way, nature is raised above nature and shall be transformed into grace.

**Servant.** The third thing I desire to know is how I can draw and transform the evil suggestions of the wicked spirits to your eternal praise?

**Wisdom.** Whenever they whisper something evil or blasphemous to you, speak thus: "My Heart, as often as the evil spirit—or anyone else from his number—whispers evil and godless thoughts to me against my will, so often may the most pleasant praise be given to you by me in their stead from my free will for all eternity; the same praise with which the evil spirits would have praised you without ceasing had they remained in grace. Thus, through me, that which the fallen

evil spirits withdrew from your praise shall be restored."

**Servant.** Heart of Jesus, I see truly that for those who love you, all things work together for good <note>A reference to Romans 8:28.</note>, because in this way even the most harmful temptations of the Devil serve their benefit. Now tell me briefly the fourth: how can I direct everything I see and hear to your praise?

**Wisdom.** Whenever you see a great multitude of people and many well-formed men, speak from the heart: "My Heart, as often and as elegantly as this, shall a thousand times a thousand of your heavenly servants, and as often as ten times a hundred thousand times a thousand of your angels, praise and laud you today in my name. The wishes and desires of all the saints shall sigh through me to you, and their wondrously beautiful adornment shall honor you in my stead just as often."

**Servant.** Ah, my Heart, how much you have gladdened my spirit through your praise! The temporal praise has encouraged and exhorted my heart and soul toward your eternal, unceasing praise. But when, O most kind Jesus, will the bright day and the longed-for hour appear, when I may wander quite ready out of this misery to you, my most delightful Lord, to enjoy your loveliest vision eternally and praise you without ceasing? Truly, I wait for this with hearty longing. Ah, when will I come to you? O long while! How much the time is delayed in which I shall behold the joy of my heart face to face and enjoy it according to my heart’s desire. O misery, how burdensome you are to those who conduct themselves as exiles <note>The "exiles" or "outcasts" are those who recognize that their true home is in heaven, making earthly life feel like a period of banishment.</note>. <column-break/>

unceasingly, and with the infinite love with which the Heavenly Father embraces his only, most beloved Son, and with the most pleasant love of the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son. I desire likewise that this should ring out with precious-sounding melody, as lovelily as the harmony of all musical instruments has ever sounded in the heart of a living and well-disposed person.

I also desire that with this flame of love, a scent of your praise so pleasant should rise up, as fragrant as if all spices and choice herbs and all the most excellent and choice virtues were crushed into powder and made into incense <note>original: "rauchwerck."</note>. Finally, I wish that the sight of this praise through grace might be so lovely that no beauty of the green and blooming May <note>In medieval literature, the month of May was the ultimate symbol of natural beauty and renewal.</note> might be compared to it, so that God as well as the entire Heavenly Host may receive a special delight from it. I wish that the flame of love would always break forth with great force and rise up in every prayer which I perform with my mouth, with song, with contemplation, word, and work; so that it drives all my enemies to flight, erases and destroys all my failings and sins, obtains grace and forgiveness, and maintains for me a holy and blessed end of life—which may be the conclusion of my temporal praise and the beginning of eternally lasting praise. Amen.

# Description of a Vision or Revelation that Occurred to the Servant.
## The 26th Chapter.

When all this was completed and written down on paper, a small part was still missing at the end of a chapter about the Mother of God, where the Servant of Wisdom had left some space until it should be given to him by God; for grace had been withdrawn from him for several months, so that he could not complete the rest. Therefore, he turned to the Mother of God and desired that she complete the work. On the night of St. Dominic <note>St. Dominic (c. 1170–1221) was the founder of the Dominican Order, to which the author, Henry Suso, belonged.</note> after Matins <note>The midnight or early morning prayer service.</note> was finished, it seemed to him that he was in a chamber; as he sat there, he saw a beautiful youth with an elegant lute, and four others with trumpets <note>original: "Posaunen." While this word now means trombones, in a medieval/renaissance context it refers to heraldic or divine trumpets.</note> approaching him. The first stepped forward and began to play sweetly upon the lute. This pleased him well, and he said to the young lute-player: "When will you come to my dwelling, so that you might occasionally delight my soul with this music?" At this, the youth asked the brother whether he still maintained his usual exercise <note>Referring to Suso's rigorous spiritual disciplines or ascetic practices.</note>; when he answered yes, the youth said that such was a tedious game; he then immediately turned to the four youths and commanded them to blow upon the trumpets. At this, one replied that two of them would be enough; but he <note>The first youth with the lute.</note> further desired that they all blow at once, and he told them a certain melody, well known to him but unknown to the brother. Then they all blew; however, because of the wondrous speed, the brother heard no

<column-break/>

sound of music, but rather saw the youths holding in their hands an exceedingly beautiful image of the Mother of God, embroidered upon a cloth. The mantle of the image was entirely red inside, and purple-colored, interwoven with various strange craftsmanship, as tapestry-weavers <note>original: "Bildweber."</note> make it, very lovely to behold; but the space left blank by the brother was white as snow. At this, the brother marveled and rejoiced, and he paid close attention to see if they would complete it; then they began to fill the space, saying to the brother, "See, it is already increasing," and soon the image was entirely finished. One took a needle with thread and made two artistic curved lines across <note>original: "oberstwerch," meaning crosswise or transversely.</note> the tip of the mantle, which decorated the image of the Mother of God wonderfully. When he meanwhile came to himself, he realized without any doubt that it had been granted to him to complete the spiritual image <note>The "spiritual image" refers to the unfinished text of his book.</note> which had been denied to him for so long. For he was accustomed to having almost all things revealed to him by God; thus, on the following day, he finally completed the work he had begun.

# An Account of the Matters Dealt With in This Dialogue.

## The 27th Chapter.

A clergyman of the Order of Saint Dominic <note>The Dominican Order, to which Henry Suso belonged, known for its focus on preaching and scholarship.</note> once lamented before the image of the Crucifix after Matins <note>The night or early morning prayer service.</note> that he could not contemplate the Lord's suffering without great bitterness and vexation. Amidst this godly lamentation, he was, contrary to his habit, enraptured beyond himself, and a light like a flash of lightning illuminated and instructed him with these words: "You shall kiss the earth one hundred times daily, and at each kiss, use a special meditation on my suffering, and for each meditation, offer up specific prayers or sighs, and also write all my suffering spiritually into your heart; be prepared to endure such things for my sake and to follow me therein according to your ability." When he, illuminated by this light, wished to count the aforementioned meditations, he found no more than ninety. Therefore, he prayed thus to the Lord: "O most kind God, I know that You mentioned one hundred meditations, and I find only ninety." Thereupon the other ten were explained to him, which he had previously completed in the chapter house <note>The room where the monastic community met for business and disciplinary matters.</note> before he had, according to his custom, held the pitiful procession <note>original: "außgang." Referring to the Way of the Cross.</note> of the Lord Jesus to Mount Calvary <note>original: "Berg Calvariæ"</note> in an image, and had come to the representation of the Crucified. There he saw clearly that the hundred meditations very aptly encompassed the bitter suffering and death of Christ from beginning to end. After he now encouraged himself in this, as he had been instructed, his previous hardness was changed into the loveliest sweetness. He

<column-break/>

wished also that if perhaps another person, in the contemplation of Christ's suffering—wherein the entire salvation of man consists—should experience the same bitterness, he too might receive a remedy and medicine if he practiced the aforementioned meditations and did not cease until he attained the same grace. Therefore, he has allowed these meditations to be published in the common German language <note>original: "Teutscher Sprach." A significant choice, as most theological works of the time were in Latin; Suso wrote in the vernacular to reach a wider audience.</note> in which they were revealed to him. Thereafter, manifold and heartfelt inspirations of Divine Truth were given to him, in which he began to speak lovably and friendly with Eternal Wisdom; however, this did not occur through a physical conversation or through an imaginary answer, but through contemplation in the light of Holy Scripture, whose words cannot deceive. Thus, this answer is drawn either from the mouth of Eternal Wisdom speaking in the Gospel <note>original: "Evangelio"</note>, or from the most prominent Doctors of the Church <note>Highly influential theologians and saints recognized for their teaching.</note>, where they spoke either with the very same words, or in the same sense, or uttered a saying agreeing with the truth, which is not distinguished from the understanding of Holy Scripture or the opinion of the Teachers through whose mouths Eternal Wisdom has spoken. The visions touched upon above did not happen in a physical manner, but only through their likeness. What he reported regarding the painful compassion of the most blessed Virgin, he borrowed in part from the words of Saint Bernard <note>original: "Bernardi." Referring to St. Bernard of Clairvaux, a 12th-century mystic known for his devotion to the Virgin Mary.</note>, which he

# An Account of the Matters Dealt With in This Dialogue.

...therefore enclosed in a dialogue, so that the reading might be more pleasant; not as if he were its primary author, or had produced it of himself, but so that he might give a common teaching to all, from which he, as well as all others, might draw what is useful and pleasing to each. He conducts himself as befits one who wishes to instruct others. He takes upon himself the persona of all men—at one moment that of a sinner, soon he uses the words of a perfect and righteous man; now he takes the form of a God-loving soul, as the subject matter requires; but he always uses the name of a "Servant" speaking with Eternal Wisdom. The greater part aims at the virtues; in many passages, the diligent reader is also instructed how to pray rightly and well. The understanding of this book is indeed simple, and the words even simpler, as they proceed from a simple soul and are presented for the good of the ignorant and simple who have not yet entirely died to their vices <note>In mystical tradition, "dying to vices" refers to the process of purgation, where an individual detaches from worldly desires to focus on God.</note>.

It happened afterwards, however, when the Brother had begun to write the threefold subject matter—namely, the Passion of Christ and all the rest—and had now come to the place where mention is made of the heart's contrition in this manner: *Well then, my soul,* etc., that he became somewhat stuck and was delayed. One midday he fell asleep in his chair and clearly saw two monks sitting before him who deserved punishment, whom he rebuked with harsh words because they sat there idle without spiritual practice. It was shown to him, however, how he drew a thread through a needle given into his hands;

<column-break/>

the thread was threefold; two were somewhat subtle and thin, but the third was somewhat thicker; and when he tried to pull all three through at once, it did not succeed well. He then saw at his right hand the Lord Jesus, standing as if released from the pillar <note>Referring to the pillar where Christ was bound and scourged during his Passion.</note>, with such a kind and Fatherly gaze that he believed it was his Father; he noticed, however, that His body had a very beautiful natural color—not entirely white, but a mixture of white and red, which is the best natural color—and that His body was torn with fresh, bleeding wounds, some of which were round, some transverse, others elongated. In this manner, while the Lord stood before him in bodily form and looked at him kindly, He raised His hands up and down and exhorted him to [contemplate] the bloody wounds. In great haste, he joined the aforementioned threads together, by which it was given to him to understand that he could and should complete the work he had begun. He understood that God, with the purple-colored garment most ornamentally fashioned from His wounds, would wish to surround with eternal adornment those who spend their time in the contemplation thereof.

Here the reader is reminded to consider that just as there is a great difference between one hearing lovely music with his ears and, on the other hand, merely hearing others tell of it, so also the words received in Grace—flowing from a living heart and spoken with a living voice—are far different from those words written on paper, especially in the German language <note>original: "Teutscher sprach." Suso is reflecting on the difficulty of translating profound, "living" spiritual experiences into the vernacular German of the 14th century, fearing the written word loses the emotional heat of the original vision.</note>; for herein they wither and fade like no other...

# Several Sermons of D. HENRY SUSO, which briefly summarize what is useful for living well and blessedly. <note>Henry Suso (c. 1295–1366) was a German Dominican friar and a central figure in the "Rhineland Mystics" school.</note>

## On Overcoming Certain Very Burdensome Internal Temptations.

### The First Very Useful Sermon.

->Our little bed is flowery. <note>original: "Unser Bethlein ist geblümet." A reference to Song of Songs 1:16, a key text for medieval bridal mysticism.</note> Cant. 1.<-

There are some who are attacked and tormented with great anxieties of conscience / they accept no remedy / and follow no counsel / and thus they do not let the Lord Jesus make a dwelling place in their hearts / because of their unrest / which they ought to lay aside. ...blooming. <note>original: "grünend." This completes the thought from the previous page's citation of the Song of Songs 1:16, where the "flowery bed" represents a soul in a state of grace.</note> Come then, my most beloved friend / for nothing remains / but that you let me sleep sweetly in the arms of your infinite love. However, the consciences of many people are not adorned with flowers / but rather their hearts are defiled with dung and filth. These are the ones whose vices are openly revealed / who give themselves over to chasing the vain and fleeting pleasures and honors of the world / of whom we will speak no further now. There are others / whose temptations lie hidden within / and although there are very many of these / nevertheless three of them are found to be so heavy / and vexing / that they can hardly be compared with others. The first / is disordered sadness. The second / a disordered anxiety / or oppression of the soul. The third / a violent mistrust. As far as the first temptation is concerned / it is to be known / that sometimes a person is oppressed with such great sorrow of the soul / that he has no desire to do anything good / nor is he able to do so / although in the meantime he is unaware of what he lacks / even to the point / that / though he wishes to discover the cause of this pain within himself / he can nonetheless neither find nor grasp it. The pious King David seems to have felt this sadness when he says in Psalm 41 <note>In modern Bibles, this refers to Psalm 42:5: "Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you disquieted within me?"</note>: *Why are you cast down, my soul / and why are you so sad within me?* As if he wanted to say / surely you lack something / even if you yourself are not aware of what it is. *Hope in God / and you will find yourself better / for I will yet thank Him with joy.* This sadness generally takes its origin from natural temperament <note>original: "natürlichen gewonheit," referring here to a melancholic or depressive disposition.</note> / and it makes not a few people abandon that which they had well begun / as if it were something to be lamented. # Sermons of the Blessed Henry Suso

...weakness, do not neglect yourself / but pray to the Lord / and he will heal you. It would be quite foolish for one / who / when he is deprived of one eye / would wish to strike out the other as well. In these fearful people, six points are to be considered.

**The first** / that they often deviate from the truth / and in this do not easily grant belief to others / even those they should rightly believe / especially those / from whom they could otherwise receive help and comfort / whom they usually trust less / than those / who breathe burdensome and contrary things into them / and such happens to them out of inner heartache / which they bear almost constantly / also complaining to obtain counsel and help / and laying out their burdens to others / which is nonetheless not advisable to do without distinction / because they hardly obtain any means or help from it / indeed, the more means they seek for this evil / the greater their **anfechtung** <note>term: anfechtung — a German spiritual term referring to a trial, temptation, or a crisis of faith that feels like an attack on the soul.</note> becomes. It would be advisable for them, however, to seek a God-fearing and, in **Holy Scripture** <term>Holy Scripture: The Bible, considered the ultimate authority in theological matters.</term>, well-experienced man / whose counsel they should put into practice without any doubt / because on the Last Day God will demand an account not from them / but from this spiritual and learned man / provided they only do / what is within their power.

**The second** is / that they are troubled with manifold and vain fear / whereby it happens / that they imagine never to have confessed rightly / even though the **confessor** <note>confessor: a priest who hears confessions and gives spiritual guidance.</note> is learned. For even if they apply all possible diligence / they still never obtain true rest and peace of conscience / and the foremost cause is / because they do not know how to distinguish / which sins

<column-break/>

one must confess explicitly / and with distinction. For only **mortal sins** <note>mortal sins: grave offenses that break one's relationship with God. In Suso's time, these required specific confession.</note> must we / as much as is possible for us / confess explicitly / and with their certain circumstances / but for the lesser daily sins it is enough to accuse oneself in general. But because they are guilty of no mortal sin in the aforementioned temptations / it is not necessary—indeed, such people must not explicitly and with certain distinction confess the thoughts occurring to them / but it is enough / that according to the counsel of their sensible confessor they only reveal such things in general / for the hellish spirit intends to disturb the heart's rest / and peace through anxiety in confession / therefore one must resist him / for the more one obeys him / the more the conscience becomes entangled.

**The third** is / that they want to have certain information about those things / of which there is no sure knowledge / nor can there be / for some want to know and be assured / that they are burdened with no mortal sin. But when one believes **Holy Scripture** / no one in this life is found so blessed / pious / and learned / who can be assured / that he lives in the grace of God / unless it is revealed to him by God / in this case it is enough / if one finds no certain mortal sin after diligently searching the conscience; but wanting to know certainly in this matter / stems from ignorance / just as if a child wanted to know / what the **Emperor** <note>original: "Keyser" — likely referring to the Holy Roman Emperor, used here as an analogy for an unknowable, high authority.</note> had in his heart / and thoughts. Just as then a sick person must believe the doctor / as one to whom the illness is much better known than to the sick person himself / so must such people obey their sensible confessor / and follow his counsel.

->To live usefully and blessedly.<-
L 3
<meta>catchword: the</meta>

**The fourth** is that they show some impatience toward God, which takes its origin from the heavy **anfechtung** <note>term: anfechtung — a German spiritual term for a trial or crisis of faith that feels like an assault on the soul.</note> with which they are assailed. Because they are not practiced in other adversities, it happens to them just like an untamed horse harnessed to a wagon: when it is exhausted and worn out after long resistance and cannot pull away, it begins to behave well and submissively. So also, as long as these people resist their trials and have not entirely surrendered themselves to the Divine will to patiently bear every **cross** <note>In this context, "bearing the cross" refers to enduring personal suffering or spiritual burdens in imitation of Christ.</note>, they will be grievously tormented. And yet, they must endure such things until the Merciful God looks upon their labor and patience; He knows best when it is useful for them to be released from this burden. Thus, nothing is so necessary as to surrender oneself to bearing the cross as long as it shall please the Lord, and to call upon His help patiently through the prayers of pious people.

**The fifth** is that they err in no matter so much as when they hold conversation with the evil thoughts suggested to them, believe them, seek to oppose them with reason, and wish to fight with them. This is most to be avoided, for when they desire to fight with such thoughts, they become so entangled that they can hardly find a way out. It is enough, then, to turn away from them without strife or resistance and turn to whatever first comes before the eyes or the ears, as if to say: "Keep your suggestions; I have nothing to do with them; you are far too godless for me to deign to answer you." For the less attention one pays to them, the more quickly

<column-break/>

they are dismissed. This must be done as often as necessary until it has been turned into a habit; however, only those who have experienced this within themselves truly understand it.

**The sixth** is that the holier the time and the more fervently they desire to cling to God, the greater is their trial. It may reach a point where they cannot say even a single **Our Father** <note>original: "Vatter vnser"</note> or **Angelic Salutation** <note>original: "Englischen gruß" — the "Hail Mary" prayer, based on the Archangel Gabriel’s greeting to the Virgin Mary.</note> without such devilish suggestions. Because of this, they become almost despairing, abandon prayer, and speak thus to themselves: "What use could prayer be that is defiled with such sins?" But in this they fail greatly and obey their enemy, whose chief diligence is to hinder them in spiritual exercises. For they do not know in truth that their prayer—along with all the thoughts occurring to them, over which they do not rejoice but are instead saddened—is very pleasing to Almighty God. For (as **St. Gregory** <note>likely St. Gregory the Great, a 6th-century Pope and influential writer on the spiritual life.</note> says) a person's reason is often so confused that it cannot tear itself away; but because they are gripped by present pain, the adversity itself acts as their mediator and advocate before the eyes of God. The bitterness of suffering moves Him more than other exercises to come to the aid of such a person. Therefore, one must not neglect any good work, nor prayer, nor the visiting of churches—which is entirely contrary to the Devil—for what such a person lacks in the purity of prayer is added to them from the weight of the trial. This prayer is very pleasing to the **Creator** <note>original: "Erschöpffer"</note>; for it often happens that we are much more inclined to hear those who can barely speak than those who are healthy.

# Sermons of the Blessed Henry Suso

...of the voice and body. The more we desist from prayer, however, the more we obey our enemy. Since it has been abundantly shown that in such cases there is no sin, this question may be raised here: why does the Merciful God visit such people with such heavy **trials** <note>original: "anfechtungen" — a term for spiritual crises where one feels attacked by doubt, despair, or intrusive thoughts.</note>, when there is hardly any bodily pain that could be imagined which they would not rather endure than this trial concerning despair? Indeed, they—and some simple people who have neither knowledge nor experience—imagine it happens because of their own guilt. But that this is not so is clear because many holy people are also searched by similar temptations, as daily experience and **Holy Scripture** <note>original: "H. Schrifft"</note> testify. Conversely, even the most godless people feel and suffer nothing of the sort; indeed, these trials happen to some in their childhood when they have not yet committed any great sin. But if someone in a spiritual state, or after recognizing the truth, suffers them because of his sin, he must therefore give thanks richly to God the Lord. For as Holy Scripture says, it is a great sign of Divine love when He does not let sinners have their way, but punishes them quickly. But why the wisest God humbles people with the trial of despair, and tames them more strongly than with other trials, is counted among the secrets of His Majesty; for because He knows the hearts, minds, and customs of all men, He acts as an experienced physician toward each, using the most useful medicine. If anyone asks what benefit this trial has, I give him the answer that great and uncommon benefits can arise from it.

<column-break/>

For first, people who are proud by nature can be brought in no way better and more hiddenly to **humility** <note>original: "demuht"</note>, the mother of all virtue. For those who are visited with this temptation measure the greatness and holiness of sins by the abominableness of the thoughts occurring to them. But that this is not the case has been proven before; indeed, having even once taken a vain pleasure in oneself could make a person far more abominable before God than a thousand such cruel thoughts. This appears in **Lucifer**, who, feeling no such trial, nevertheless fell through ugly pride. But God allows a person to be assailed with this burden so that he, who previously would not know himself out of pride, may at least be brought to the knowledge of himself through this trial. Therefore, it happens that he who previously despised others now rightly appears contemptible to himself before all. What can be more useful to him and lead him more to God? For it is impossible that God would let a truly humble person be lost. Therefore, according to the teaching of Holy Scripture and the truth itself, those who carry such a **cross** should throw themselves at the feet of Almighty God and, as it were, "gild over" this temptation—through which they attain the grace of such an excellent virtue—with full thanksgiving toward God. For the trial draws the person out of the jaws of Hell, carries them into Heaven, and frees them from innumerable sins, in that it gives him so much to deal with that, meanwhile, he puts all vanities into forgetfulness. This is very useful and is thus a great advancement toward attaining the virtues; for they become thus...

For this trial <note>original: "anfechtung"</note> takes away a large part of Purgatory <note>original: "Fegfewrs"</note>, is very profitable for them, and increases their reward in an infinite way. For although they believe themselves guilty of many sins, they are nonetheless counted by God among the most eminent martyrs, because there is no doubt that such a constant trial is much more difficult than a stroke of the executioner when he

<column-break/>

strikes off the head. Finally, that this trial is an indication of God's great love is proven from Holy Scripture and from the truth itself, because namely an abundant grace and the revelation of many secrets will follow upon it. Thus, the aforementioned people must not only suffer patiently, but also gladly, with the assurance that the tribulation, which is temporal and light, works in them an eternal glory that is weighty beyond all measure. (2 Cor. 4). Of this we add a short example. A virgin devoted to God was attacked with one of the above-mentioned temptations; she appeared after her death and indicated that she had endured such things instead of Purgatory, and finally had been taken up by Almighty God into the heavenly Kingdom without any other means. May Jesus Christ, the blessed for eternity, also grant us this. Amen.

# Sermons of the Blessed **Henry Suso** <note>original: "Henrici Susonis"</note>
<meta>Catchword: appear</meta>

Members of religious orders lead such a life that they should be ashamed to recount such useless worldly news <note>original: "zeitungen" — in this era, it meant general reports or news, not necessarily a printed newspaper</note>. For what do they care for worldly matters? Others ask out of sheer curiosity; they want to know much and grasp things with their intellect, solely so that they may also know how to speak of lofty things; these people never grow, nor is there any hope of their progress as long as they remain so. Others ask questions in order to probe another's spirit <note>original: "gemüht"</note> and recognize it fully. These go just like the **Pharisees** in **Matthew 22** with flattering, cajoling words to someone and say, "Master, we know that you are truthful." And when they sense their own habits in him, everything is right; if not, his whole conduct is worth nothing. Therefore, they turn to others, ask them too, and there is no end to the questioning, so that they may hang a cloak over their godlessness, and from this they will not be turned away, no matter how one deals with them. The questions of others are praiseworthy, who from inward, heartfelt devotion most zealously seek the will of God; whether they eat, drink, sleep, write, or read, walk or stand, they always have this desire: in what way shall I recognize the most pleasing will of the most beloved God? Others ask nothing at all, and such have reached the highest peak of perfection. But where do we find such people? For these wonder at nothing; according to the testimony of **Augustine** and **Aristotle**, questioning arises from wonder, but these, as said, wonder at nothing; rather, because they are enlightened by Truth itself, they transcend all wonder. But so that we may return again to the **Gospel**, just as you heard before, the

<column-break/>

**Pharisees** with the Herodians asked **John** who he was. But what did the Heavenly Prince—yes, the Morning Star and the Archangel—give as an answer? He says, **"I am not he."** <note>original: "ich bins nit" — referring to John 1:21 where John the Baptist denies being the Christ or Elijah. Suso uses this to teach that we should not desire to be "something" in the eyes of the world</note> He confessed, says the Evangelist in **John 1**, and did not deny: **"I am not he."** These words—**"I am not he"**—no one wants to speak, and all human diligence is inclined toward avoiding and fleeing them. For who is there who does not desire to be something and to be held in honor, whether in spirit or in nature? But if someone could reach the point where they speak this word from the heart with **St. John**, they would certainly have found the best and shortest way in this life; for no one is excused from this, regardless of their age, how weak, how poor, or how rich they may be. But who can express what an inestimable essence is hidden in this word, **"I am not he"**? But no one wants to set out on this journey; indeed, we all are, we want to be, and have always wanted to be something. Almost everyone is so entangled in this snare that no one wants to abandon or deny themselves. Therefore, we perform ten outward works with less effort than we abandon ourselves just once completely. This is the goal of all struggle <term>original: "Kriegs" — literally "war," but here refers to the spiritual battle or "warfare" of the soul against the ego</term> and our labor. For this reason, worldly people amass many riches, make friends and relatives, and put their body and soul in a thousand dangers, namely so that they may be something—yes, so that they may be great and respectable in riches, honor, and power. What the members of religious orders and clergy also do, omit, and suffer in this regard, everyone can examine for themselves. Alas, all monasteries and cloisters are full of this harmful evil, so that everyone [desires] to be something and to
appear <note>The catchword "erschet" at the bottom of the page is a fragment of "erscheinen," meaning to appear or seem.</note>

### to live usefully and blessedly.

...desires to appear. Lucifer in heaven himself wanted to be something out of pride <note>original: "hoffarth"</note>, and in that same moment he was plunged into the deep abyss of nothingness, indeed into something even less than nothing. This cast our first parents, Adam and Eve, out of the most beautiful Garden of Paradise and has led all of us, who are born of them, into manifold misery, labor, and sweat. This is the cause of all our misery and lamentation; thence it comes that we—without God, without grace, without love, robbed and stripped of all virtues—enjoy neither outward nor inward peace. And it is why in many things we carry a displeasure toward ourselves, toward God, and toward men. All these evils arise from a single root: because we all seek to be something.

On the contrary, however, the desire to be nothing brings and maintains true, complete, and steadfast peace in all stations of life, in all places, and with all people. Nothing more fortunate, safer, or more excellent can happen to a person in this life than this. But how very much, alas, is this contrary to all of us—rich and poor, young men and maidens, the old along with the young! We read in the Gospel of Luke, chapter 7, that a Pharisee invited Christ the Lord to his table. Without doubt this work was good, to feed Christ and His disciples alongside other guests; the Pharisee did not lack good intentions either. What then? The most excellent phrase, "I am not," <note>German: "ich bins nit"</note> was lacking in him. How do we know this? Pay attention. During the meal there came a woman, a sinner, who threw herself at the feet of her Savior and confessed from the bottom of her heart, "I am not." Therefore, she was raised up—in my opinion—not only above all the heavens but also above many choirs of angels,

<column-break/>

for lying at the feet of Jesus, as was said, she confessed from the bottom of her heart: *Non sum* <note>Latin: "I am not"</note>, "I am nothing." But from that foundation there arose a constant, unceasing *Ego sum* <note>Latin: "I am"</note>, "I am something" <note>This refers to the mystical idea that by emptying the self of "being," one allows God's "being" to enter</note>; thus the most kind Jesus granted her what she desired. 

There sat the hospitable Pharisee, who, performing the great work, provided all the food and drink. He could not endure such a thing in his heart and said to himself: "Why does the Lord show such friendliness toward this open sinner?" But alas, the cursed phrase "I am" <note>German: "ich bins"</note> ruled within him, and not "I am not." Therefore he considered himself worthy of the Lord turning to him, listening to his speech, and speaking with him—but not with the sinful woman. 

What do you think, beloved? Are not similar Pharisees found even today among both the clergy <term>original: "Geistlichen" — those in religious orders or the priesthood</term> and the laity <term>original: "Weltlichen" — secular or worldly people</term>? The whole world is filled and overwhelmed with such people. Under black, white, red, ash-colored, and sky-blue clothing <note>These colors refer to the various habits of different religious orders, such as the Benedictines, Dominicans, or Franciscans</note> one finds many who—on account of their wealth, or power, or wisdom and learning, or their heartfelt understanding, or their almsgiving, or because of their habit <term>the distinctive dress of a religious order</term> (for which reason they prefer themselves in holiness over others), or the like—suppose it to be only right that all people should turn to them, speak with them, listen to their words, and do everything according to their pleasure. They therefore speak within themselves thus: "Should this happen to me from those for whom I have performed this or that, I who am so-and-so?" And certainly they would find themselves highly offended if they were not esteemed more highly by everyone than those in whom the aforementioned things are not perceived, of whom they say within themselves: "Who...

# How to Live Usefully and Blessedly

There are also many found in the spiritual estate <note>The "spiritual estate" refers to the clergy or those living in monastic orders.</note> who have spent almost their entire lives in this pursuit, who display a great and singular holiness, and tilt their heads toward their shoulders <note>A gesture of performative or outward piety, suggesting they are trying to look like saints.</note>; yet they will depart from this world in such a way that true **Resignation** <term>Resignation: From the German "Gelassenheit," meaning the complete letting go of one's own will and ego to be empty for God.</term> will not have happened to them for even a single moment.

A wise person may feel sorrow, and also laugh out of wonder at this, because these miserable people so deceive themselves. This is to be held as certain: that no one should flatter themselves regarding this surrender, or persuade themselves that they have truly given over, as long as a single drop of blood remains in their flesh, or the smallest bit of marrow is in their bones, which has not been "boiled out" and applied toward true surrender.

As long, however, as one has not attained the furthest point of true surrender, so long will they be held back from the **contemplation of God**, and they can taste true bliss neither in temporal nor eternal life. For it is necessary, if the grain of wheat is to bring forth fruit, that it first die; and once it has died, it will bring forth much fruit <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 12:24.</note>. It is necessary that we die and become nothing, and say from the heart: *Non sum* <note>original: "Non sum," Latin for "I am not."</note>, I am nothing. Not by desire, wishing, and praying alone does one reach this, but rather through works and the deed itself; for that which is worth nothing can have no value. If one could obtain surrender through desire and wishing alone, without cost, labor, and pain, it would be of no value. But such a thing cannot happen; for "He who created you without you," says **Augustine**, "will not justify you without you" <note>original: "der dich ohne dich erschaffen / spricht Augustinus / wird dich ohne dich nit rechtfertigen." This refers to a famous quote by St. Augustine (Sermon 169) meaning that while God created humanity without our help, He requires our cooperation and will to save us.</note>. Thus, no one should presume that God will lead us by a miracle

<column-break/>

to high mysteries. For even though He could bring forth the most beautiful roses from the earth in the cold winter time, He nevertheless does not do so; for He wills that they break forth and grow at the proper time (namely, in the Spring) through the frost and dew and other conditions of the weather.

It is to be lamented that many spiritual persons live thirty, forty, or more years in constant lukewarmness and everlasting complaining, and after so many passing years, they have not the slightest knowledge of themselves. How much better would it be to spend a single year dying to oneself and tearing the ropes with which they are entangled? Oh, when death comes and they see how poorly they have used their lives, what an irreparable loss they will feel, because in the future they must be deprived of everything they could have gained! This is unspeakable in words.

Rightly, every spiritual person should strive with great diligence and unceasing effort to reach **perfection**, and live with the desire to do more and more good, so that no day passes on which he does not see himself having made such great progress that he can hardly see the day that came before. It is pitiful that the lovers of the world take greater care to acquire temporal and perishable goods than the elect of God take to reach the Highest Good, which is God Himself. A spiritual monastic person should be so separated from their own will that nothing might be found in them but *Non sum*, I am not. One sees many inconsistent people who imagine different ways of living for themselves—who one moment live on water and bread,
