...soon wanting to go another way / and now undertaking this / then that. But I will show you the shortest and best way. Let each person withdraw into the **ground of their soul** <term>Ground of the soul (Seelengrund): A central concept in German mysticism referring to the deepest, innermost part of a person where they can meet God directly, beyond the senses and the ego.</term> / and diligently investigate there / what hinders them / and then cast this tether like a stone into the depths of the Rhine; otherwise, they may go wherever they wish / through all the lands of the world / but beyond this, they will carry away little or no profit from it. Just go into yourselves / and consider / how unequal you still are to the most perfect **Image of Jesus Christ** / whose **Resignation** <term>Resignation: The complete letting go of one's own will to be empty for God's will.</term> was so deep / that if the surrender of all people / who have been / who are / and who shall be / were melted together /

<column-break/>

it still could not be compared in the slightest degree. What was mentioned above / that sinners surrender themselves in Christ alone / must be understood in such a way that / when we abandon ourselves for God's sake / we also surrender everything to Him at the same time. But many indeed surrender themselves to God / and yet do not want to deliver themselves over to men / being satisfied to be tried and humbled by God / but not by men / but one must present oneself to God as it is pleasing to Him. If someone now guides us toward the contemplation of our own nothingness / we must receive this from them kindly and with a thankful spirit / so that we may be called in deed what we also are / <note>original: "Non sum," Latin for "I am not."</note> **I am nothing.** May Almighty God grant us / that we may thus arrive at the knowledge of our nothingness / so that we may be sunk / and swallowed up into the **Divine Essence**.
Amen..

### -> To live usefully and blessedly. <- ###

Thus, in the aforementioned first words of the Lord, the most sincere and truthful instruction is given, and the right, shortest, surest, and simplest path is shown. No matter where we turn, or what "sails of excuse" we spread, we must walk this path which the Lord himself walked if we wish to be with him, come to him, and be fully united with him. For as we have heard, he went forth from the Father, from the Fatherly Bosom and Heart, and came into the world, where for the entire time of his life he was tested beyond measure, burdened with constant misery, and attacked, so that he never allowed himself any worldly pleasure. Indeed, at the last, he was captured, bound, killed, and buried. Afterward, he rose again **impassible** <note>original: "vnleydlich" – in a theological sense, this means a body that is no longer subject to pain, suffering, or decay.</note>, radiant, and immortal; he returned to the Fatherly heart and enjoys for eternity a glory and blessedness equal to His. Now, whoever wishes to enter upon this journey, and wants to be "dead to themselves" and buried with Christ, will of necessity also rise with him. For "if we are buried with him, so shall we also rise with him," says the Apostle in **Colossians 3**, "for you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God." Of one who is so disposed, I can say that they, in some measure, rise up into heaven—indeed, into the very Fatherly Heart—**impassible**, indestructible, and immortal, fully united with the Son. They attain a blessedness equal to the Son and possess that very same inheritance; for what the Son has by **nature**, this person has through **grace** <term>Nature vs. Grace: A fundamental theological distinction where "nature" refers to what Christ is by right as God, and "grace" refers to what humans receive as a gift through spiritual union.</term>. Yet, one must constantly practice this. Such a person is as far preferred above other common men

<column-break/>

as a human being is preferred over an irrational animal. But those who do not wish to die with Christ, in what way shall they rise with him to the true life? Therefore, the Apostle exhorts us that if we have risen with Christ, we should strive for what is above and not what is on earth. There are many who, when they hear something good, desire to be pious and begin to live for God and the Spirit; but when everything does not go according to their wish, they fall away from their purpose and sink back into their former natural weakness. These can be compared to **students** who strive for the doctorate and other high dignities, even though they have hardly laid the first foundations and cannot yet speak Latin. Others, if they persevere in their studies, eventually attain the doctorate. Likewise, one finds some pious people who not only begin well but also move forward, increasing in virtues and persevering with the same diligence until the end. Others, however, make no progress in virtue; and because virtue sits upon a high seat, he who strives for great perfection must undertake great and weighty things. Specifically, there are **nine points**, of which we will show the four smallest and lowest. First, he must surpass all **sensuality** <note>In this context, "sensuality" refers to being governed by the physical senses and worldly comforts.</note> and bring all visible things under his feet. Second, all bodily and spiritual powers. Third, all desires that are united with **self-attachment** <term>Self-attachment (eygenthümb-ligkeit): The tendency to claim things, experiences, or even spiritual gifts as one's own "property" rather than seeing them as belonging to God.</term>. Fourth, all **imaginations**; but what I call "imaginations," I will explain hereafter.

Thus, one must first surpass all senses; but I am not speaking of those who, following their sensual pleasures, knowingly and—

Many undertake great things with their understanding and labor with their reason to grasp such strange and lofty things that they seem as if they wish to enter the innermost chambers of heaven; yet they rely and lean solely and alone upon their natural powers. Such men of understanding were **Plato** and **Aristotle**; though they were honorable in their character, it was a mere work of nature. It is necessary for such people to subdue their nature with great diligence and to guard against themselves. Conversely, there are others who are simple by nature, who from

their own simplicity turn away, surrender themselves, and gladly take up and accept everything. These make great progress in a short time; everything succeeds well for them internally, and they are capable of receiving Divine grace just as soft wax takes on every seal and image. However, just as wax is easily pressed back together and loses the imprinted image, so too do these simple people easily turn back from their purpose. On the contrary, just as an image is not carved into a rock without great effort, yet remains for many years and is not easily erased, so it is with the aforementioned people endowed with **acute understanding**. <note>original: "spizfündigem verstand," referring to a sharp, subtle, or sophisticated intellect.</note> Though they do not overcome themselves without great effort and diligence, if they persevere with a strong spirit, they occasionally obtain great grace and do not lose it easily.

Others have frequent visions and revelations; and even if these should be true for ten whole years, the evil spirit could finally mingle among them, transforming himself into an angel of light to deceive the unwary. Thus, they must take care to diligently weigh such appearances and revelations against the **Holy Scripture** and the **teachings of the Holy Fathers**, noting whether they agree with them. If they are found to be so, they may allow them; otherwise, they must reject them with all diligence and give them no belief, provided they do not wish to offend the grace of God and lose the salvation of their souls. They must therefore rise above such things so that they do not lean too heavily on any appearance or revelation of God or His saints, nor set their minds upon them with delight. Rather, they should surrender themselves entirely to the **Divine will**, clinging to Him in all things: in wealth and poverty, in comfort and distress, in good fortune and misfortune, following the example of our **Savior**. They should have Him present in their hearts at all times, constantly gazing upon how perfect His life, conduct, and behavior were—how <term>resigned<gloss>The original German 'resignirt' implies 'Gelassenheit,' a state of letting go of self-will.</term>, simple, withdrawn, humble, patient, and filled with all virtues He was. When they go to sleep, they should lay themselves down with Jesus—indeed, in all places and at all times. Among all people, they should consider Him present and take Him as a companion. I know of one person who, in order to make himself a partaker in the journeys of Jesus, went from one corner to another in a certain place, just as if he wanted to earn an <term>indulgence<gloss>A grant by the Church that was believed to reduce the temporal punishment for sins; here, the individual mimics a pilgrimage to gain spiritual merit.</gloss></term>, and meanwhile contemplated the life and suffering of our Redeemer. **St. Bernard** says that those beginning the spiritual life should place an honorable, distinguished man before their eyes, as if they were doing everything in his presence; and when they wish to do or omit something, they should first think whether they could do, omit, or say this in the presence of that distinguished man. Much more and much better can one present and imprint upon the mind the most lovely image of **Christ Jesus**, because He is closer and more inward to us than we are to ourselves; for in Him consists the best comfort, all good, and all joy; He is called "full of grace and truth." However, the **Image of Christ** can be understood both in an imaginary way <note>The German "einbildungs-weiß" refers to mental visualization or conceptual meditation.</note> and in a living way. When it is taken in an imaginary way, this must happen in an excellent, rational, and divine manner, and not in a sensory way, as if He were a pure creature <term>creature<gloss>In this mystical context, 'creature' (Creatur) refers to any created thing, including the human nature of Christ when viewed apart from His divinity.</term>. Many do this: when they wish to contemplate something regarding God, they represent Him in their thoughts as a creature, or just like a dear human being from whom they have received much kindness and who suffered great pain for their sake. From these thoughts, they draw a natural compassion toward Him. But one must behave far differently; namely, they must inwardly accept a divine and supernatural image—not the image of a creature—of the most amiable man Christ Jesus, as the Son of God, as God and Man, and as Man and God. Thus, they will never think of Christ except as He is simultaneously God and Man. When they understand Christ in this way and think of Him, they will never be without God; for where anything of God is, there God is entirely. In this way, they will never neglect what is best.

The **Image of Christ** is also understood in a living way, which occurs when a person finds no rest until, according to the full capacity of his powers,

> Love your enemies, and do good to those who hate you, etc. <note>original: "Liebet ewere Feind / vnd thut guts denen / die euch hassen / etc."</note>
is so pleasant to Love <note>Referring to the personified spirit of Charity or the state of being in Love with God.</note> that she is not satisfied merely to speak kindly to her enemies, but she loves them from the whole heart, wishes and desires for them from the bottom of the heart all honor and good, and excuses all their defects and faults to the best of her ability. Yet it must not be understood as if one should be so dull that he does not notice the manifest hatred or love of other people toward him; rather, according to the **Image of Christ**, so that he may follow Him in some measure, he must hold all such things in low esteem and, as it were, "not want to know" them.

It was said above that one must surpass all images <note>A core tenet of Suso's mysticism: moving beyond mental pictures to the formless reality of God.</note>; now one might doubt whether one should also set aside all images of Christ. > It is for your good that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Comforter will not come to you. <note>original: "Es ist euch nutz / daß ich hingehe / dann wann ich nicht hin gehe / so kombt der Tröster nicht zu euch."</note>

...depart; for as He departed from them in a physical manner and ascended into the Heavens, He led away with Him their whole mind, all senses, and all their love. Now that He has ascended into the Heavens and returned to His Father’s bosom, let us ascend up with Him—where He has gone before—with all our senses and with all love, to the Heart of the Almighty Father. There He remains, one life and one essence with Him: the radiance of glory, the form of His essence, the brightly shining **Mirror of His clarity**, and the **Image of the Fatherly Face**. This is not only in the form of an image, but also essentially in the complete likeness of the Person of God the Father, in the divine outflowing of <term>eternal birth<gloss>A mystical concept referring to the perpetual generation of the Son by the Father within the Trinity.</gloss></term>, being of one essence with Him. If he still does not attain it then, and departs from here burdened with certain debts <note>Refers to venial sins or temporal punishments not yet satisfied.</note>, he will indeed be sent to **Purgatory** so that he may be purified there. Nevertheless, he will enjoy it eternally in the Heavenly Palace, more or less according to how much or how little he strove for it during his life. Therefore, every person should rightly string the **bow of his desire** to the very best of his ability, so that no time, however small, might slip away in which he is not more fully united with God. For God will reward true desires, even though one does not attain his longing in this world; and He will judge every negligent and lukewarm conversation <note>Referencing "conversation" as one's general conduct and spiritual state.</note> most strictly. Now, even if someone finds that he has not reached the high level of Perfection, he should not despair because of it, but rather strive after it according to his ability. If he does not yet reach the desired Perfection, let him nonetheless love it with his whole heart and strive for it with all his desires. May Almighty God grant us that we may happily reach that Perfection of which we have spoken until now.

# On the threefold lack of surrender, and how we should altogether 
## leave ourselves and always renew the resolution to deny ourselves until we are fully transformed into Christ; and on the true poverty of spirit.

# The Fourth Sermon.

## Again I leave the world, and go to the Father. John 16. <note>original: "Joan. 16." This refers to Jesus’s words in the Gospel of John, signaling His departure from physical presence to spiritual union with the Father.</note>

Beloved, all the trouble, work, diligence, teaching, and examples of our Redeemer aimed only at leading His dear friends and disciples to the <term>inner ground of the soul<gloss>In German mystical tradition (Seelengrund), this refers to the deepest part of the human spirit where God dwells and where the soul is most like its Creator.</gloss></term> and to the light of Truth. However, when He saw how they were devoted only to the external man, and that they could not reach the true Good, He was forced to withdraw His physical presence from them. What does this mean? At this point, all interpretations and excuses must fall away: if <term>Eternal Wisdom<gloss>Suso’s preferred name for Christ, personifying the divine wisdom described in the Old Testament as the agent of creation and redemption.</gloss></term>, the only-begotten Son of the eternal Father, was a hindrance to His disciples <note>Suso suggests that even the physical presence of Jesus was a "creaturely" attachment that the disciples had to let go of to find Him spiritually.</note>, then without doubt there is no creature on Earth—whoever they may be, however named, or however clothed—who is not a hindrance to a person. Thus, we must leave all inconstant and mortal creatures if we wish to receive the most excellent Good, which is God Himself. 

One finds, however, three kinds of people: some turn away, others go forward, and the last go within. The first are the beginners, the second the progressing, and the third the perfect. Now, if someone intends to live rightly and to serve God, he must search every corner of his soul to see if he finds anything he has possessed with 

<column-break/>

disordered pleasure, or still possesses, or whether any mortal creature has any dwelling place within him. Whatever he encounters of this kind, he must drive out immediately. This is just as necessary for him as the first foundations of the A, B, C's are to a schoolboy. Even if everything does not go according to his wishes in the beginning, he should not be disturbed by this, but rather persist courageously; for even in schools, a lesson is repeated to the boys over and over until they fully grasp it. In the same way, such a person must deny himself over and over and say:

<margin>John 16</margin> **"Again I leave the world"**; that is, all transitory things. After he wakes in the morning, he should lift his eyes to God and address Him thus: "My most beloved and highest Good, God my LORD, again for Your sake I will begin to leave myself and everything." And he must do this a thousand times, and as often as he finds it advisable, and always resolve to go out from himself and to deny himself. In this self-denial consists the content of all perfection, without which no one—no matter where he turns—will be able to grow. Therefore it happens that many, after they have served God for fully forty years and [done] many... <note>The page ends mid-sentence with the catchword "viel" (many).</note>

<summary>In this sermon, Suso explains that spiritual perfection requires total self-denial and the removal of all creaturely attachments, categorized into three stages of spiritual growth. He emphasizes that just as Christ left the world to return to the Father, the soul must daily resolve to "leave the world" and its own ego to find God.</summary>

### Sermons of the Blessed Henry Suso ###

Others seek themselves again in a beastly manner. <note>German: "Viehischer weiß." Suso is not necessarily accusing the reader of gross sin, but of acting according to animal instinct rather than spiritual purpose.</note> No one should think that I speak here of those who, like cattle, wallow in the filth of their vices; rather, I speak of those who seek the highest and most excellent good—which is God himself—in a merely natural way. It is unseemly for a rational person to perform his works without reason, out of natural inclination, following nature just as cattle do; rather, he should act out of the will and with reason for the praise and love of God. In eating, drinking, sleeping, speaking, remaining silent, and in all his deeds, he should set aside the urges and inclinations of nature, as it were, and thus pray or think: "O my God, my lover, I eat for you, not for me; I sleep for you, not for me; I live and suffer for you; for your sake, not mine, I leave everything behind."

As a spiritual person <note>Likely referring to a member of a religious order, such as a monk or nun.</note> once carried a great desire for the perfect life, she was led in a vision to a school where many disciples were diligently occupied with study. The spiritual person addressed them and said, "Beloved, this is a heart-warming school of which I have heard much; but tell me, what science do you master here?" One among them gave as an answer: "Here we learn nothing else but to deny ourselves in all things." The spiritual person said: "Then I wish to remain here, prepare a chamber for myself, and dwell there, even if I should have to die a thousand times." The other spoke: "Do not do so, but go from here in peace, with the assurance that the less you *do* <note>Referring to outward "works" or busy-ness.</note> and the more you deny and leave yourself, the more you will always attain; people today are unfortunately quite blind; they want to

<column-break/>

do much and undertake many things, just as if they wanted to feed the Lord God himself, and this only out of themselves, from their own will, with their own pleasure, from their own judgment, and their own nature. For we do not reach perfection through the mere will, but through actual resignation <term>Resignation<gloss>Original: "Resignation." In this mystical context, it refers to "Gelassenheit," or the state of letting go of one's own will to be filled by God's will.</gloss></term>, mortification, and self-denial; for as long as there is still a single drop of blood in a person that is not rightly mortified, he still lacks true perfection. The third behave in a devilish manner after the fashion of Lucifer: God had created Lucifer and endowed him with the most excellent gifts and the most magnificent nature; but when that ungrateful, proud spirit took a vain pleasure in himself, he wanted to "be" something, and in that same moment he was cast out from heaven like lightning and became nothing. -> **on how to die usefully and blessedly.** <-

[in his] life, he was greatly honored not only by all other men but also by the Pope himself; yet he valued this no more than the filth of the earth. St. Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (c. 1225–1274), the influential Dominican philosopher and theologian.</note> has a memorable saying which I will mention in a few words: "If you wish to know," he says, "whether someone lives a perfect life, notice first whether he uses unseemly, childish words; secondly, whether he seeks honor, whether he flees from the disparagement of his person and does not endure such things with patience. If he is so inclined, whatever else he may do, do not consider him perfect, because he lacks the foundation of true virtue; for he who is unwilling to suffer is not far from a fall." This **poverty of spirit**, just like all other virtues, the most blessed Virgin possessed in the highest degree, and whoever wishes to follow her in this must diligently observe the four following points: First, that he should despise all earthly things; second, that he should not let himself be moved by prosperity

<column-break/>

and good fortune, for in this consists every hindrance to spiritual progress. Third, that he should despise all things, whether good or bad fortune, and with a thankful heart accept everything from the kind hand of the Lord—but not so much from men, who are only an instrument of God through which He works. Fourth, that he should always carry God in his heart and mind, observe His most lovely presence, and follow the blessed Mother of God in these things. This is the most useful service and obedience, and the one most pleasing to her, that can be shown to the most blessed Virgin, though there are many other services acceptable to her and wholesome for mankind. May Almighty God grant us that, following the example of the most blessed Mother of God, we may strive with unceasing diligence to deny, **mortify** <term>Mortification: The spiritual practice of "dying" to one's own ego, passions, and self-will to be more united with God.</term>, abandon, and shun ourselves. Amen.

## To the Reader.

We have placed these few sermons here—even though they are few—so that the pious reader may conclude from them how much it is to be lamented that the rest have perished through human negligence; for it is certain that Suso <note>Henry Suso (c. 1295–1366), the author and a famous German mystic.</note> was a famous preacher and presented the Word of God to the people with the highest praise and benefit; however, the reader may encounter his sermons, letters, and other writings here and there in the books of Tauler <note>Johannes Tauler (c. 1300–1361), a contemporary of Suso whose mystical writings were often collected together with his.</note>.

# Master Henry Suso’s Godly Epistles, Filled with Learning.
<note>The 'D.' in the original title likely stands for 'Dominus' or 'Doctor,' titles of respect for a learned master of theology.</note>

## Preface to the Reader.

There is no doubt that our Suso wrote many epistles; however, I have found only a few which we faithfully share with the favorable reader. Since they are filled with piety and learning, they cannot be read without great benefit.

---

## Concerning the true, righteous conversion of oneself to God, joined with a contempt for the whole world.

### The First Epistle.

->The kingdom of the world and all its finery have I despised for the love of my Lord Jesus Christ.<-
<note>original: "Regnum mundi..." This is a translation of a traditional Latin liturgical response used during the consecration of a nun, or "bride of Christ."</note>

When I heard you singing this most lovely melody and the virginal profession of the chosen bride of Christ, I thought thus to myself: it is only right that he can give good counsel to a dear friend who has obtained an even dearer friend—which truly happened to you today. Therefore, you must renounce the deceptive world with joy. See how the world deceives its friends and lovers; I had embraced a shadow, married myself to a dream, and seized upon a delusion. Where now is the form of the shadow? Where are the promises of the dream? Where is the persuasion of the false opinion? ...worthless thing / to serve God is to them instead of a dungeon / monastic discipline is to them a prison / and because they cannot reach the apple / they grasp at the scent / instead of rose-crowns <note>Likely referring to spiritual crowns or perhaps rosaries, contrasted here with earthly delights.</note> they put on painted violets / instead of purple-colored garments they strut about in a hair-cloth sack / and instead of the holy marriage they have made with God / they surrender themselves to vain worldly love / and friendship / from which they gain nothing else / than loss of time / disturbance of the heart / and the total destruction of the entire spiritual life. What happened to that monk also happens to them / upon whose mat / which he had put on instead of a cloak / the devil sat / and spoke to him with mocking words: "You miserable man / if you could do more / you would do more." <note>This anecdote warns that superficial asceticism—wearing a rough mat but lacking inner devotion—invites the devil's mockery.</note> Certainly it is a pitiable life / and like a forecourt of hell / to be unable to enjoy the world according to one's wish / and nonetheless be deprived of God / at once stripped of both worldly and divine comfort, and suffering loss on both sides. With what great shame and misfortune will they appear before enemies and friends on the Last Day. To diligently obey God the Almighty / and to serve Him cheerfully is a lovely / secure / and sweet life, both in this / and in the future world / such people live indeed according to the body in the world / but their <term>way of life</term> <note>original: "Conversation." From the Latin *conversatio*, meaning one's conduct, citizenship, or habitual social interaction; here it refers to the soul's true home being in heaven.</note> is constantly in Heaven / this yoke is in truth sweet / and the burden

<column-break/>

light / and even if they are occasionally tempted / it is still of little account / for who in the entire world is without a cross? <note>In this context, the "cross" refers to the inevitable suffering and trials of human life.</note> Truly no one. Neither those who dwell in castles nor in cities can flee the cross / no purple / nor any garment made of the finest cloth is able to drive the cross away from man / for commonly that which is entirely torn apart within appears whole on the outside. Now, if one must suffer something for the love of God, he should hold it in low esteem. Initially, the <term>mortification</term> <note>original: "abtödtung." A spiritual practice of "killing off" or subduing the desires of the flesh and the ego to make room for God.</note> and contempt of all things truly causes one great sorrow / but gradually it becomes pleasant / and then the previous burden falls away. Remember your former life / think of the days gone by / and the time of your earlier years / see how very long you have slept / consider whether it has not all been like a dream / through which you were amused. Wake up now / for it is time. The Lord has been turned away by you so often / yet He still does not depart / but it is impolite to turn away a good friend for so long / so let your heart stand open to Him / let your zealous lover enter into the dwelling of your heart / delight yourself with Him / and make up for the neglect of time past. He who opens slowly to his knocking friend / must hurry all the faster afterward. It is not with you as it is with other lazy / and negligent people / who love neither God the Lord / nor the world very much. God the Almighty desires / that you now offer Him your heart spiritually in every way / just as it was worldly before / whatever effort and diligence you previously spent on temporal things / now apply that same diligence to that which is steadfast / strong / and eternal.

# On the Humble Self-Denial of a God-
-> Loving Person. <-

## The Second Epistle.

### The wolf shall dwell with the lamb. Isaiah 11.

When God, the author and originator of Nature, came into the world in assumed human form, he wished to perform new miracles; thus he tamed the wild beasts and made the cruel animals gentle, as the prophet Isaiah says in chapters 11 and 65.

My beloved daughter in Christ, I remember having read in times past—which I only now truly understand—that love makes unequal things equal; for this reason, the image of the goddess Venus <note>original: "Göttin Veneris." In medieval spiritual writing, the "blindness" of the pagan goddess of love was often used as a metaphor for how divine love makes a person "blind" to their own worldly importance or social standing.</note> used to be painted blind and without eyes, because he who is seized by blind love loses his proper judgment. This is certainly true of worldly love; nonetheless, it also applies to spiritual love, because it has stripped and bared many people who were magnificently adorned with honors and dignities, so that many kings and princes left their kingdoms and domains and made themselves servants to poor beggars, so that they might make themselves like the tenderest Child, his heavenly Friend. Well then, my daughter, cast away your secret pride of heart, which springs from the nobility of your lineage, and all the meager comfort of your friends and relatives, which you have hitherto used harmfully and deceitfully under a spiritual appearance, and [have made a] mockery of yourself—

<column-break/>

—and let yourself down today to the sweetest little Child, the Lord Jesus, into the manger of humility, so that he may raise you to the throne of his glory and infinite dignity. He who sows sparingly shall also reap sparingly; and he who sows in blessings <note>original: "benedeyungen," following the Latin Vulgate "in benedictionibus."</note> shall reap in blessings. 2 Corinthians 9.

My daughter, do this courageously; lay yourself under the feet of men, no differently than if you were their footstool. You know that the cloth upon the feet is not burdensome, however one deals with it, because it is appointed for the feet. True humility, the suppression and denial of oneself, is the root of all virtue, of all health, and of salvation; from there springs a silent rest and a restful silence, united with true surrender of oneself, both toward the lowest and toward the highest. It certainly hurts to be wise and well-spoken and yet have to remain in silence, to hear words of insult and slander and not defend or avenge oneself; it hurts that a wise and honorable man should yield to a depraved and worthless person and say nothing in opposition. But in this, one truly becomes conformed to Christ. What, however, can be more useful to man and more praiseworthy to God? To this end, it is beneficial—

# How we should voluntarily surrender ourselves according to the example of Jesus Christ to bear every cross and temptation.

## The Third Epistle.

### I am black, but beautiful, you daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents.
-><note>original: "Cantic. I." — Song of Solomon 1:5</note><-

These are the words of a God-loving soul. Regarding the literal sense, they seem to be spoken by the most beloved spouse of King Solomon; because she was black like a Moorish woman, and nonetheless more pleasing to him than such a great number of wives and concubines, she brought amazement to the daughters of Jerusalem. Through this, the Holy Spirit indicated that a person who bears the **cross** <note>The "cross" here refers to personal suffering and hardships endured for the sake of faith.</note> patiently, and whom God visits with constant adversity and **temptation** <term>temptation: from the German "Anfechtung," referring to a state of spiritual trial, doubt, or inner conflict</term>, and who nonetheless surrenders themselves to God with patience, is more beloved to God than all others—even if the cross and suffering seem to make them entirely black like a Moor, in the eyes of men. Take heed, my daughter: it is easy to speak of and to hear about the cross, but its actual presence is painful. Tempted people sometimes fall into such anxiety that they believe God has forgotten them, and they may almost say to him: "Ah, gracious God, do you even know that we live? What do you think of us? Why is your hand so heavy and so hard against us, when your heart is yet so kind and compassionate?" To this friendly complaint, God gives an answer in this way: Look upon the many and innumerable saints; lift up your eyes

<column-break/>

to the living, most elegant, heavenly city of Jerusalem; see how its most radiant living stones <note>A reference to 1 Peter 2:5, where believers are described as "living stones" built into a spiritual house.</note> were previously cut, polished, and prepared through many kinds of trial, and with what wonderful brilliance they now shine and glow. Consider what the blessed widow **Elizabeth** <note>Likely St. Elizabeth of Hungary (1207–1231), who lived a life of extreme asceticism and service despite her noble birth.</note> suffered; **Paul** and other **Apostles** were the *offscouring of the world* <note>original: "kehrsal der welt" — based on 1 Corinthians 4:13</note>; **Job** and **Tobit** walked the same path. The holy **Athanasius**, Bishop of Alexandria, was attacked by such storms of persecution as if the whole world had conspired for his death. Note with diligence how all the saints shed either the blood of the heart alone, or the blood of the heart and the body together; all those who are troubled should rightly contemplate this, and in that contemplation they should rejoice and be glad, because through trial God wishes to make them conform to his most beloved friends. Let death then come, let all misery, cross, pain, and anxiety fall upon us, because so much benefit springs for us out of suffering; and even if we are not always resigned while bearing the cross, yet all hope of salvation is not taken from us, nor is Divine grace lost; *the evening and the morning make a whole.* <note>A reference to the creation narrative in Genesis, suggesting that both dark and light times are necessary to complete the spiritual "day."</note>

...stripped of the devotion of a loving heart, he was accustomed to withdraw deeply into himself and say: "My heart and God, what has happened to me? Oh, how unwisely and unknowingly I have fallen. Let us, O my soul, strive with all diligence to gather new merits, for the old ones have vanished." So he began to practice self-denial, to discipline the body, to avoid human company, to show a spiritual modesty, to guard himself, to fashion new prayers, to take up new exercises, and to renew every path upon which he thought he had fallen, practicing in this way day and night until he was again ignited with new Divine heat; and commonly, these later exercises suited him much better and brought him more abundant grace than all the previous ones. Meanwhile, with heartfelt contemplation, he buried the **old man** <note>The "old man" is a Pauline concept (Ephesians 4:22) referring to the sinful, unregenerate nature that a believer must "put off."</note>, as if he had never been, and thus found many ways to guard himself that he had never considered before. He thus became more cautious, and as often as he fell, he always began anew; and this perhaps happened to him an infinite number of times. Thus Eternal Wisdom teaches through his instrument, the Holy Father **Bernard** <note>original: "H. Vatter Bernardum" — St. Bernard of Clairvaux, a 12th-century mystic and doctor of the Church.</note>, who says: In this matter, the **elect** <term>elect: those chosen by God for salvation</term> are distinguished from the **godless**, because the godless, when they have fallen, do not strive to rise again, but the pious and the elect labor to rise and to move forward, for no one in this world can always stand upon one step <note>A reference to the "ladder" of spiritual perfection; one is either climbing or sliding.</note>. He who is just beginning

<column-break/>

to serve God can easily be led into error; but so that he may remain firm and steadfast with God, nothing is more useful to him than to avoid all outward affairs as much as he can, to pave the way to the **inner man**, and to remain within himself; for he who is very devoted to outward things without great necessity puts his inner heart-peace at risk. **Albertus Magnus** <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and teacher of Thomas Aquinas, known for his vast knowledge.</note> said that he never went among men without returning home a "lesser man" <note>This famous quote suggests that social interaction often leads to spiritual distraction and a loss of inner focus.</note>. Therefore, everyone must always and everywhere join themselves heartily with God; but so that he may do this better, he must apply himself to silence, devote himself to Divine contemplations, use fewer words, perform great and important works, accept with joy whatever God sends him to suffer, patiently bear the faults of all people, avoid the godless, not be too familiar with anyone, observe his senses, use time and words well, diligently watch over himself, submit to God and all men, speak honorably and well of all people, but hold himself in low esteem and accuse himself, serve God with joy, give a good example to his neighbor, avoid the smallest sins just like the great ones, mark and look upon God in all things, and thus spend all his time with God the Almighty; for in this way one can be united with God, lost time can be recovered, and new treasures of Divine grace and merits can be acquired. **Farewell.**

So then, everyone must at all times and everywhere be heartily united with God; but so that he may better be able to do this, he must apply himself to silence, be devoted to Divine contemplations, use few words, perform great and important works, accept with joy whatever God sends him to suffer, patiently bear the faults of all men, avoid the ungodly, be too familiar with no one, observe his senses, use time and words well, take diligent care of himself, subject himself to God and all men, speak honorably and well of all people, but hold himself in low esteem and accuse himself, serve God with joy, give a good example to his neighbor, avoid the smallest sins just like the great ones, notice and look upon God in all things, and thus at all times abide <note>original: "verzehren" — while literally meaning "to consume," in this context it refers to "spending" one's time or "communing" with the Almighty.</note> with God the Almighty; for in this way one can be united with God, bring back lost time, and acquire new treasures of Divine grace and merits. Farewell.

# How we should voluntarily surrender ourselves, following the example of Jesus Christ, to endure all crosses and trials.

## The third Epistle.

> I am black, but very beautiful, O daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents <note>original: "wie die hütten" — referring to the dark tents of Kedar mentioned in the biblical verse.</note>.
> ->Song of Solomon 1<- <note>original: "Cantic. 1." — shorthand for Cantica Canticorum, the Song of Solomon.</note>

These are the words of a God-loving soul. As far as the literal sense is concerned, they seem to be spoken by the most beloved spouse of King Solomon; because she was black like a Moorish woman <note>original: "Mohrin" — a historical term for a dark-skinned woman, used here to allegorize the soul darkened by the "sun" of suffering and tribulation.</note>, and was nonetheless more pleasing to him than the great number of other wives and concubines, she caused amazement among the daughters of Jerusalem. Through this, the Holy Spirit indicated that a person who bears the cross patiently, and whom God visits with constant adversity and trials <term>trials: the original "anfechtung" refers to spiritual assaults, temptations, or tribulations that test a believer's faith</term>, and who nonetheless surrenders himself to God with patience, is dear to God above all others—even if the cross and suffering seem to make him appear as entirely black as a Moor in the eyes of men.

Pay attention, my daughter: it is easy to talk and hear about the cross, but its actual presence hurts. People under trial sometimes fall into such anxiety that they believe God has forgotten them, and they may even say to Him: "Oh kind God, do you even know that we are alive? What do you think of us? Why is your hand so heavy and so hard against us, when your heart is so kind and compassionate?" To this friendly complaint, God gives an answer in this manner: Look upon the many and innumerable saints; lift up your eyes

<column-break/>

to the lively, most elegant, heavenly city of Jerusalem. See how its most radiant living stones were previously cut, polished, and finished through many kinds of trials, and with what wonderful brilliance they now shine and glow. Consider what the blessed widow Elizabeth <note>Likely St. Elizabeth of Hungary (1207–1231), who lived in forced poverty and service after her husband's death.</note> suffered; Paul and the other Apostles were the refuse <note>original: "kehrsal" — literally "sweepings" or "scum," referencing 1 Corinthians 4:13, describing the low status of the Apostles in the eyes of the world.</note> of the world; Job and Tobias walked the same path. The holy Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria, was attacked by such storms of persecution that it was as if the whole world had conspired for his death.

Note with diligence how all the saints shed either the blood of the heart alone, or the blood of both the heart and the body together. All who are distressed should rightly contemplate this, and in that contemplation, they should rejoice and exult, because God wants to make them conformable to His dearest friends through trial. Let death then come; let all misery, cross, pain, and anxiety fall upon us, because so much benefit arises for us out of suffering. And even if we are not always perfectly resigned <term>resigned: from "resignirt," meaning the total surrender of one's will to God's will</term> while bearing the cross, yet not all hope of salvation is taken from us, nor is Divine grace lost; the evening and the morning make a whole <note>A reference to Genesis 1: "And the evening and the morning were the first day." The author suggests that both the "darkness" of suffering and the "light" of grace are necessary parts of the spiritual life.</note>

There once came into the acquaintance of the **Servant of Wisdom** <note>Henry Suso's customary way of referring to himself in his writings.</note> a well-formed woman, so pleasing to the eyes of all people that many were wounded in their souls because she drew the hearts of all who looked upon her to herself. This pained the Servant of Wisdom, and he greatly desired to prevent the offense of so many souls and to draw them toward God, so that God might be praised thereby, the angels and all **angelic spirits** <note>original: "Englische Geister." In this context, "Englisch" is the archaic German form for "angelic" (Engel), not the nationality.</note> gladdened, and humanity edified. Therefore, he devoted himself entirely to praying to God the Almighty for her **conversion**; in particular, he turned to the most holy Mother of God and Virgin Mary, the bright-shining **Star of the Sea** <note>original: "Meerstern," translating the Latin title "Stella Maris."</note>, and sought her with all diligence, that she might enlighten the worldly heart of this woman—which was surrounded by the darkness of many vices—and turn her away from sin and lead her to God. She heard the petitioner and granted the worldly heart the grace that she converted to God in all haste; this brought such a great joy of heart to the servant that he was, as it were, poured over with heavenly joy, and wrote a letter to the aforementioned person. When, after some time, he made this small excerpt from all his letters and omitted everything else for the sake of brevity, he thought when he came to this letter that, because it contained nothing else but a heavenly rejoicing, it would be unpalatable and unacceptable to barren and stubborn people when they read it; for that reason, he discarded this letter. # Of the Blessed Henry Suso

Hear now, my beloved daughter in Christ / how you / and I / and those like us must behave toward almighty God. We should so arrange our lives in the future / that no one can take God the Lord from us / we should behave like a **kitchen maid** / whom a mighty and powerful King has preferred over his Queen; doubtless such a woman would show the King all gratitude / love him faithfully / praise him from the heart / and the more unworthy she recognized herself to be / the more fervently she would love him. So also should we strive to surpass those people who are innocent / and freed from sin / and when these have honored their Lord with one service / we should do so twofold; if they have loved him simply / we should love him a thousand times more / and just as we previously / when we were **blind in our souls** / applied all diligence so that we might be loved by all people / so should we in the future encourage all people toward improvement / and strive greatly to please God. Remember / my daughter / how pleasant it was for us / when we strove to please the world / when someone praised / extolled / and loved us above others / according to our opinion; how well will it go for us then / when God the Almighty / the **Supreme Good**, embraces us with even a small amount of love and regard. Think what great effort it cost / that we could enjoy a worldly friend / from whom one nevertheless received little and often no joy or pleasure; how much more proper is it then to endure some labor for God's sake? I believe /
> O **Eternal Wisdom** <note>In Suso's writings, "Eternal Wisdom" is a personification of the Divine, often identified with Christ, whom Suso serves as a "Servant."</note> / if the inner eyes of all men gazed upon You / as I do / then all transitory love would immediately be 

<column-break/>

> extinguished within them. Lord, I cannot wonder enough / (although I was previously of a much different mind) that a human heart can rest in anything other / than in You, the **unsearchable abyss**. And why do You not reveal Yourself / O most kind God / to the wretched? The deceitful lovers of the world / hide immediately whatever is unpleasant / ugly / and most vicious in them / but if they have any fictitious or false beauty / they put that on display / and it would grieve them if anything should remain hidden from their beloved / and yet if they weighed everything correctly / they would find themselves to be nothing other than a **bag of filth** <note>original: "drecksack." A common, if jarring, medieval ascetic term used to remind the reader of the physical body's mortality and corruption compared to the soul.</note> / of whom one can rightly think: if someone only peeled off your outermost skin / how quickly the truth would appear / and what a terrifying monster one would see. But You, O most heartfelt Wisdom, hide meanwhile in Yourself what is lovely / and show what is vexing. You put forth the bitter / and keep the sweet. Why do You do this, O most kind Jesus? Allow me to speak but one word / for I cannot restrain myself. Oh, that You loved me, O most kind Jesus / oh, that I might be Your friend. Is there anyone on earth who thinks as I do, that I am loved by my Lord Jesus? My soul longs for that / my heart leaps for joy merely thinking that You love me. When this comes to my mind, I become so joyful that it can be felt tangibly in me / whatever is in me / melts for pure joy. If I were allowed to wish for something / I would desire nothing higher / lovelier / or more wished-for / than that You embrace me with a special love / and look upon me with a special kindness. Who could doubt that this should be called the **Kingdom of Heaven**?

# How we should accept and receive Death with an undaunted mind.

## The 6th Epistle.

->Absalom, my son, who will grant it to me that I might die in your place? 2 Samuel 18.<- <note>original: "2. Reg. 18." In Suso’s time, following the Latin Vulgate, the books of Samuel were often titled 1 and 2 Kings.</note>

My most beloved son, who will grant to me—your dearest Father in Christ—that I might die in your place, my son, in whom I have placed all my hope? Truly, my child, although I am not permitted to die in the body, I will nevertheless die with you in my heart. In the body I am indeed far from you, but my heart stands beside you as you are dying, with bitter tears and with good and affectionate lamentations; I pray you, reach me your sick hands. If it pleases God that you should die, then hold fast to the Catholic <note>Universal</note> faith and die with joy; rejoice that your most beautiful soul (which is a pure, rational spirit made in the likeness of God) shall be released from the narrow, miserable, and heavy prison <note>The body, often described in medieval mysticism as a "dungeon" for the soul.</note> and shall hereafter be made a partaker—

<column-break/>

<margin>2</margin>
—of anything more praiseworthy can be found in any human being that is not found infinitely more abundantly and excellently in you. Thus, let all people see and behold: *Such is my beloved; he is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem.* Song of Solomon 5. <note>original: "Cant. 5." referring to the Canticle of Canticles.</note> O Almighty God, how blessed is the one whose friend you are, and who is eternally strengthened in this friendship of yours. Farewell, my daughter.

—of eternal salvation without hindrance. For the Lord himself says in Exodus: <note>original: "Exod. 23." but the verse cited is actually Exodus 33:20.</note> *No man can live who sees me.* One thing terrifies those who are inexperienced in death and makes death harsh and bitter for them: that as they place before their own eyes their past years, their poorly spent time, and their godless lives, they recognize themselves to be bound to God the Lord with great debt. In that hour, they do not see what they ought to do; in this case, however, I will give you good counsel, drawn both from Holy Scripture and from Truth itself, so that you may depart from here with certainty. Even if you know that you have lived poorly—as few men are without sin—you must not be too terrified in the final hour, provided that you have been provided with the customary Holy Sacraments of the Church.

...be provided; when it can be done fittingly, place the image of the Crucifix before your eyes, look upon it, and press it to your chest; lay yourself in the bloody Wounds of his infinite Mercy, and pray to him that he, through his Divine power in his bloody Wounds, may wash away all your sins to his Praise and according to your need. Hereafter, be certain upon my word, according to the faith of the *Catholic Church*, which can in no way deceive, that when you do this with a strong mind, you may enter Death with joy, freed from all hindrances. There is yet another thing for you to consider in your final hour, so that you may despise Death all the more.

There is in a certain land (as they say) a custom that when someone is born, all the relatives gather, sighing, howling, and weeping; but when someone dies, they laugh and engage in all sorts of pastimes. By this they signify that no one knows what misery and wretchedness a person must endure <note>A common medieval trope, likely derived from descriptions of the Thracians, used to emphasize that life is a "vale of tears."</note>, therefore they weep at the birth of a human being; and because such misery ends in Death, they rejoice over the dying. If one considers it truly, then a person's birth—when they enter this miserable world—may rightly be called Death, because of the misery, grief, and labor that await them. Conversely, the Death of the body may rightly be called a new Birth, because of the casting off of the heavy and troublesome body, and because of the free access and entry into eternal Life. He who has opened his eyes to recognize this well dies more easily; but he who cannot see this dies with great lamentation, fear, and the bitterness of an uncertain Death. Look—

<column-break/>

—everywhere at the world’s misery, cross, temptation, anxiety, and need; and if there were nothing else but the fear that drives us to sustain Body and Soul, and the changeable instability of the world, we should rightly desire to depart from here. If one encounter with prosperity occurs, ten misfortunes and adversities occur on the other hand. If many were asked, they would answer that in their whole lives they never had a single joyful day. The world is full of snares, deceit, and unfaithfulness, and no one may trust another, for everyone seeks their own interest.

Although the hour of Death is bitter, it must nonetheless be endured once. No one is exempt from the law of Death; he who is not ready today will perhaps be less ready tomorrow. Commonly, too, sins are increased with age, and many more people become worse rather than better. If the present Death is bitter, it brings an end to all bitterness. Now then, my son, lift up your heart, hands, and eyes to the Heavenly Fatherland, and greet it with your whole heart. # How one should conduct oneself in outward offices.

## The 7th Epistle.

->Christ became obedient for us even unto death. Philippians 2.<- <note>original: "Ad Phil. 2."</note>

Whoever refuses that which he is obliged to do out of obedience makes life vexing for himself. For when you do something small with reluctance, it is much heavier than when you perform many great things with a willing spirit. Since, then, the office <term>ambt: a position of responsibility or leadership, often within a monastery</term> commanded of you was laid upon your shoulders without your own effort or desire, by the ordinance of God—for there is no power except from God, as the Apostle says <note>referring to Romans 13:1</note>—carry it out in such a way that you do no injustice to God and inflict no notable distress upon yourself. It is indeed useful and necessary that you manage this office reluctantly; in this, I suspect you will find that where you hope for help and counsel, you obtain nothing but sorrow, harm, and bad advice; and where you expect to have good subordinates, you then find them to be stubborn and rebellious. Therefore it happens that in these times, to be in an office and position of dignity, and to fulfill it completely, is not an idle life, but a laborious and miserable

<column-break/>

<margin>2.</margin>
life. Take up this Cross then upon your shoulders for the sake of Him who in times past took the heavy wood of the Cross upon himself for your sake; and submit yourself voluntarily, because the will of those whom one must necessarily obey requires it; and never plead your weakness or ignorance as an excuse. For if you do what seems best to you, you will manage your office well; in all things, look more to God than to your own profit; and if you can, never permit any of the little sheep <note>Referring to the members of the religious community under the leader's care</note> entrusted to you to suffer any harm to their souls or any offense. Be consistent in the maintenance of monastic life, namely so that friends and enemies alike bear the yoke of Religion; for this brings peace. Keep the younger ones in good discipline, because poorly raised youth is the downfall of the Order. Be brave and earnest, yet sweet and friendly; seek more to be loved than to be feared, so that your commands are carried out more out of love than out of fear. Signify to the superior...

...what is beyond your strength; where one may not bite, at least bark. If you cannot make **monastic discipline** perfectly whole, then be careful that it does not diminish, nor suffer any harm under your rule; if you will not mend an old, torn garment, it will soon go completely to ruin. Where spiritual matters are neglected, temporal things will soon perish. He who neglects the small and trivial things gradually falls into greatness <note>meaning a great fall or great error</note>. <margin>Ecclesiasticus 19</margin> <note>original: "Eccl. 19." This refers to the Book of Sirach: "He who despises small things will fail little by little."</note> Always give your subordinates a good example, and teach them more through deeds than with words. One thing you must of necessity endure: that when you have applied all diligence to a matter, others will interpret it in the worst way; and those whom you have most endeavored to please and serve will be the most ungrateful and malicious toward you. No one can please everyone at once; if you strive to please all, you must necessarily offend God and the truth. The evil speech of the godless is the praise of the pious. Strive with all your might to break up bad company within the monastery and harmful friendships outside of it. Do what you can, and you will be safe. But woe to the monastery where these two pieces of advice are cast to the wind; for such a place first loses its peace, and secondly acquires an evil reputation. But if you say, "if I do this, destruction will immediately follow," I say: blessed is the destruction that brings eternal peace. Woe to those who look through their fingers <note>an idiom meaning "to turn a blind eye" or overlook faults</note> in this case, so that they may enjoy a peace of which Jeremiah says: <margin>Jeremiah 6</margin> *They have comforted the hurt of the daughter of my people with shameful lies, saying, "peace, peace," and yet there was no*

<column-break/>

*peace.* They chase after their own profit because they are delighted by temporal honor, and they buy such things at the expense of the entire monastery. But woe to them, for they have received their reward. But you, my son, do not follow their example; seek rather the honor, praise, and glory of God, just as the Lord Jesus sought His Father’s honor so greatly that He allowed Himself to be nailed to the Cross for it. You complain loudly, yet the blood does not yet run over your face, as happened in former times to the holy **martyrs**. In the old days, only the best and most stouthearted men were chosen for such <term>offices: "ämbtern," referring to positions of leadership or administration</term>, not those who sought their own gain. You would indeed prefer to enjoy rest in meditation and <term>contemplation: "beschawlichkeit," the practice of quiet, prayerful observation of God</term>; but the opinion of Saint Gregory <note>Gregory the Great, who wrote extensively on the "Pastoral Rule"</note> is that a superior must be able to satisfy both the **active life** and the **contemplative life**, as the situation requires. But because you, alas, have not yet reached this perfection, keep your own insignificance before your eyes and avoid pride. Remember who you are, and how soon you will be changed into dust. If you now wish to punish someone, first take yourself to task. Diligently strive to overcome evil with good; one devil does not drive out another. Speak mild and hard words from a gentle heart, as the matter requires. Above all things, promote **Divine service**; do not forget yourself, but enter into yourself often throughout the day, especially twice: namely, in the morning and the evening. Meanwhile, forget all outward business, lift your spirit to God, accept all pain and temptation from Him, and endure them for His sake.

# How one should conduct oneself in the abundance of Divine Sweetness.

## The 8th Epistle.

### Tell my beloved that I am sick with love. <note>original: "Cant. 5"; referring to the Song of Solomon 5:8</note>

If one person sat in a wine cellar and had drunk his fill according to his pleasure, while another lay in the open field by a rough juniper bush, plucking its berries so that he might slightly moisten his dry mouth; and if the one satisfied with wine should mock the other with the dry lips, saying that he should listen to the lovely sound of the lute in the tavern—then the latter would say with an angry spirit: "It is right that people take you for a drunkard, since you imagine everyone else is of the same mind as you. For I am of a very different condition, not being watered with the same juice as you." A full stomach easily lifts the head and makes it cheerful. My most beloved daughter,

<column-break/>

in this way it seems to me that I can address you, since you have sent me the most delightful letter, describing how the torch of most fervent love against <term>Eternal Wisdom</term> <note>Suso's frequent name for Christ</note> is kindled in your heart. You describe how it works strange and unusual things in you, wherein your heart has received a lovely wound, a delightful pain, and a loving melting away, and ultimately an ecstasy of the soul, of which you cannot express anything in words. You desire to be instructed by me on how you should behave most friendlily toward God and toward these strange things. Believe me, my daughter, I am unspeakably rejoiced because God shows Himself so loving and friendly—

This was a new, unheard-of, lovely song, such that he almost entirely melted away from inner heart-felt joy. 

In particular, they sang the ***Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus*** <note>Latin for "Holy, Holy, Holy," a central hymn of the Mass</note> with such melody and glory that he sang along with them. Afterward, he stepped to the altar where the **Body of the LORD** <note>The consecrated Host kept in the tabernacle</note> was reserved; and silently within himself, he sang this melody: *Blessed is he who comes* <note>original: "Gebenedeyt sey der da kombt"; the 'Benedictus' from the Mass</note>, etc., because the angelic voices still echoed in his soul. Farewell.

### The Ninth Epistle.

->In all things I have sought rest. Ecclesiasticus 24.<- <note>In this biblical passage, Divine Wisdom describes her search for a dwelling place among humanity.</note>

With these words, the Wise Man <note>Referring to the author of the Book of Sirach/Ecclesiasticus</note> teaches the erring how they should, as much as possible, attain peace during the ignorant course of this transitory life. Truth itself is indeed simple and bare, but we are by nature so constituted that we can only grasp it through certain parables <note>or "likenesses"</note> until we lay down this mortal body and the pure eye of Reason unwaveringly beholds the bright-shining, eternal Sun. # Of the purification, illumination, and perfection of Mankind.

## The Tenth Epistle.

-> Be perfect, even as your Heavenly Father is perfect. Matthew 5. <-

These words were spoken by the Eternal Wisdom, our Lord Jesus Christ, to his dear disciples who were striving after the perfect life. <term>St. Dionysius</term> <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian whose writings on "The Celestial Hierarchy" formed the basis for medieval Christian mysticism.</note> says in his book on the celestial hierarchy that the lesser angels are purified, illuminated, and made perfect by the greater ones, and that this happens through the radiance of the bright-shining, eternal, and <term>supersubstantial</term> <note>original: "vberwesentlichen," a term used to describe God's being as existing beyond all physical or created essence</note> Sun, and through the communication of the Divine outflowing with the overshadowing of new truth. We have a likeness of this among men in this temporal life.

<term>Purification</term> <note>original: "reinigung," the first stage of the mystical path (*via purgativa*), involving the cleansing of the soul from worldly attachments.</note> consists in this: that one excludes all created things from the heart, so that even the highest Seraphic spirit, or <term>St. John the Baptist</term>, or whatever else is created, is not allowed inward entry so far as their image is concerned, but rather that the person dies to them. Here, however, simple and faithful people could err, even if they did such things with good intentions; for a good intention is not always enough. In ancient times, the Lord commanded through Mo-

<column-break/>

-ses in Deuteronomy 16: "That which is right, you shall follow with righteousness," for otherwise what is right becomes evil and wrong. After purification follows <term>illumination</term> <note>original: "erleuchtung," the second stage (*via illuminativa*), where the mind is enlightened by divine truth.</note> and the clarity of light; for truth is the light that drives away the darkness of ignorance. This light is sometimes received through a medium <note>such as through scripture, nature, or other people</note> and sometimes without a medium <note>direct revelation to the soul</note>, and it renews the joy of the soul. It also fills the soul with Divine imaginings. The more fully this is accomplished in a person in this world, the more abundantly everything that is vain, earthly, and transitory dies within them, and the more the unfading crown of the future life and the eternal light is granted to them. This continues until they find a weariness and aversion toward all earthly things. From this, there immediately springs true <term>Perfection</term> <note>original: "Vollkommenheit," the final stage (*via unitiva*), where the soul achieves union with God.</note>, which consists in the highest union of one's powers with God, who is the beginning and origin of all things. This is achieved through high contemplation, fervent love, and the sweetest enjoyment of the Highest Good.

### His name was called Jesus. Luke 2.

<margin>p. ll</margin>
The Servant of Wisdom <note>A common self-designation for Henry Suso himself</note> had the most holy name of Jesus very gracefully painted in his chapel, and had beautiful sayings placed there. He did this so that he might stir the hearts of all people toward the love of God, and so that those being tempted might bear their cross more patiently. ### On the difference between temporal and Divine Love.

### The Body speaks.

Much is told to us of love, but I have resolved to love the body; for what can be more pleasant to the senses than strong wine and good morsels?

### Eternal Wisdom answers.

O lazy and stinking body, your reward is evil and rotten. Only the foolish and unwise desire to experience your pleasures, but not the wise, for they hate you.

### The Love of Honor and Riches speaks.

A sweet and lovely song of the world

<column-break/>

it is, to have an abundance of friends, honors, and goods; whoever has attained such things is held in great esteem, therefore I desire it too.

### Eternal Wisdom answers.

The world's wisdom, riches, and honor deceive many people in a terrifying way, and transitory goods have destroyed countless souls; therefore one must shun them and flee to God.

### Carnal Love speaks.

Nothing delights the heart more than the beautiful form of women, and to shun them is quite vexing and bitterer than death.

### Eternal Wisdom answers.

It is unspeakable how many people perish through the beautiful physical form of women; against this, neither wisdom nor physical strength prevails. The only remedy is flight <note>Suso follows the traditional monastic advice that carnal temptation cannot be fought head-on, but only escaped by "flight" (avoidance).</note>. But whoever wishes to please and obey women must endure much displeasure; if he does not do so, he loses their favor and bestows his love in vain. The wretched notice and avoid this, and thus learn to become wise.

> Is the garment of vain love.

### On the distinction between temporal and Divine love.

#### The Body speaks.

Much is said to us of love; but I have resolved to love the body, for what can be more delightful to the senses than strong wine and good morsels?

### Eternal Wisdom answers.

O lazy and stinking body, your reward is evil and rotten. Only the foolish and unwise desire to experience your pleasure, but not the wise, for they hate you.

#### The love of Honor and Riches speaks.

It is a sweet and lovely song of the world

<column-break/>

to have an abundance of friends, honors, and goods; whoever has attained such things is held in great esteem, therefore I also desire them.

### Eternal Wisdom answers.

The world's wisdom, wealth, and honor deceive many people in a terrible way, and these transitory goods have corrupted countless souls; therefore one must avoid them and flee to God.

#### Carnal Love speaks.

Nothing delights the heart more than the beautiful form of women; and to avoid them is quite vexing, and more bitter than death.

### Eternal Wisdom answers.

It is unspeakable how many people perish through the beautiful physical form of women; against this, neither wisdom nor physical strength prevails. The only remedy is flight. But he who wishes to please and obey women must endure much displeasure; if he does not have such things, he loses their favor and bestows his love in vain. The wretched ones notice and avoid this, and thus learn to become wise. <note>original: "witzig"; here meaning clever or sensible through experience.</note>

> In short: joy and long-lasting woe
> Is the garment that vain love will show.

Wisdom, born of GOD the Father, is the eternal Word in the Godhead, whose nature and essence is simple and incomprehensible to our understanding; all hearts long for Him, and yet no one is able to speak of it. ## **wherein Truth and the Disciple confer with one another.**

### **The First Chapter.**

> Behold, you have loved the truth; you have made known to me the uncertain things and the secrets of your wisdom. <note>original: "Sihe du hast geliebt die Warheit / du hast mir kund gethan das vnsicher / vnd die geheimnuß deiner Weißheit. # How a person surrendered to God <note>original: "Resignirter Mensch." In the tradition of German mysticism, this refers to "Gelassenheit"—a state of holy detachment and total surrender to the Divine will.</note> should begin in the truth / and end in it / and how the Divine Being is nameless and incomprehensible.
### Chapter 2.

Those who wish to be led back to their origin must first know their own beginning and the beginning of all other things / because in that same beginning is also the final end. Thus, it must be known / that everyone / who has ever spoken of the truth / agrees on this point: that there is something / which is the beginning / simple / and more eternal than all other things. When the <term>Holy Dionysius the Areopagite</term> <note>A 5th-century Christian philosopher whose "Mystical Theology" deeply influenced medieval thought by emphasizing that God is known through unknowing.</note> contemplated this unfathomable being / he said along with other teachers / that it is without a name / for because / as the worldly philosophers say / the name of a named thing must indicate its nature and properties / but since the nature of the aforementioned essence is infinite / and cannot be understood by any creature / it is certain among all scholars / that the incomprehensible essence is also without a name. Therefore, Dionysius says in <note>original: "Myst. Theol. c. 5"</note> *Mystical Theology*, Chapter 5: that God is nothing of those things which

<column-break/>

we attribute to Him according to our created understanding / for what we attribute to Him in this regard is false / and is only a pure denial of Him / so that He could therefore be called the **Eternal Nothingness** <note>In mystical writing, God is called "Nothing" not because He does not exist, but because He is "no-thing"—He does not exist in the way physical or conceptual objects do.</note>. However, if one is to speak of any matter / even though it surpasses all reason / one must nonetheless give it a name. This essence of quiet simplicity is His life / and His life is His essence / it is a living, essential mind / that understands itself / it is and lives in itself / and is its own life / I cannot express it more clearly with words. This I call the eternal and uncreated truth which is God Himself / because in this all things exist as in their origin and eternal fountain / where a surrendered person begins and leaves off / and orderly commits himself to the internal life / as will be explained hereafter.

->of Truth / and her Disciple:<-

[When we] read of the **Holy Trinity**, why do we not leave Him in His **simplicity** <note>In mystical theology, "simplicity" (einfältigkeit) refers to the state of being non-composite—the idea that God's nature is a single, unified essence without separate parts.</note> in which He exists? It seems to me that to this single, simple One, more than too many activities and distinctions are attributed; for how can the simple One be one, in whom there is such a great multiplicity?

   **Truth** answers: All this multiplicity is, at its core, nothing other than a simple unity.

   **Disciple**: What do you call the ground, or the origin?

   **Truth**: I call this the ground, or origin, from which the outpourings flow.

   **Disciple**: Lord, what is that?

   **Truth**: It is the nature and being of the **Godhead** <term>Godhead</term> <note>original: "Gottheit." Mystics often distinguished the 'Godhead' (the inactive, hidden essence) from 'God' (the active Persons of the Trinity).</note>; and in this inexhaustible abyss of the Persons, the Trinity is brought into a unity, and there all multiplicity falls away, as it were; where in this manner there is no external activity, but rather a peaceful, inner darkness.

   **Disciple**: My Lord, tell me: what is the first origin of the Divine outflow, and especially of His own activity, which is to share Himself?

   **Truth**: Such is His power and almighty strength.

   **Disciple**: What is His strength?

   **Truth**: The Divine nature, in which the Father is the beginning of the being; there-

<column-break/>

-fore He is called fruitful in birth and activity; for to speak in our way, and as much as our understanding can grasp, here the **Godhead** flows into **God**.

   **Disciple**: Is it then not one: the Godhead and God?

   **Truth**: Certainly they are one; yet the Godhead does not beget or act; rather, **GOD** begets and acts, which occurs through the distinction of the Persons, which the understanding distinguishes to a reasonable extent. In their ground, however, they are one; for in the Divine nature there is nothing but the essence, and the distinction of the Persons adds nothing to this essence, but they are one essence, even though one Person is distinguished from another. For when the Divine nature is taken according to that same ground, it is in itself no simpler than the Father or any other Person in the same nature; only your imagination troubles you, because you look upon them as you do upon created things.

   **Disciple**: I sense that I have fallen into the deep abyss of the highest simplicity, beyond which no one can go further unless they wish to stray from the truth.
