# How Man and All Creatures Existed in God from Eternity according to their Prototype; How They Flowed Out from God through Creation, and Will Return to Him Again.

## Chapter 4.

**Disciple.** Lord, I would dearly like to know how creatures existed in God from eternity?

**Truth.** They existed in Him as in their prototype <note>original: "vorbild." In mystical theology, this refers to the "divine ideas" or the perfect patterns of all things existing eternally in the mind of God before they were physically created.</note> or exemplar.

**Disciple.** What is a prototype?

**Truth.** The eternal essence of God, insofar as He allows Himself to be grasped and recognized by creatures through His self-communication; however, all creatures, according to their prototype, are God in God, and would not be essentially distinguished there. Rather, as has been said, as they are in God, they are one thing with Him—namely one life, one power, and one being—and no less than He. But in the manner that they have gone out from God through creation, each has received its own being with its own form <term>form</term> <note>In the Aristotelian sense used by Suso, "form" (gestalt) is what makes a thing what it is, giving it its specific identity.</note>, which then gives it its natural essence. For form creates a distinction between the Divine and other beings—as, for example, natural form gives the stone its nature. For its specific being is not the being of God; a stone is not God, and God is not a stone. Yet it is certain that the stone, like all created things, comes from God. And in this outflowing, all creatures have received the Almighty and eternal God; for where the crea-

<column-break/>

-ture recognizes itself as a creature, there it acknowledges God and its Creator.

**Disciple.** Lord, is the being of a creature more noble when it is in God than when it is in itself?

**Truth.** The being of the creature as it is in God is not a "creature" <note>This means that in God’s mind, the "idea" of a person is part of God's own infinite nature, rather than a limited, created thing.</note>; rather, the created being of each creature is more useful to it than the being it has in God. For this reason, a stone, a human, or another creature has nothing more in its created being than that it was one thing with God in God from eternity; for God has ordered all things most beautifully, so that they all may see their first origin.

**Disciple.** My Lord, from where did sin, malice, Hell, Purgatory, the devils, and such things arise?

**Truth.** When the rational creature should have turned toward its origin—which is God, singular and simple in nature—it instead withdrew with disorderly pleasure and self-will <term>self-will</term> <note>original: "eygenthumb." This refers to the soul claiming "ownership" of itself and its desires rather than surrendering to God's will; it is seen as the root of all sin.</note> and turned away from God. From this, the devils, Hell, and all malice took their beginning.

# On true inward turning of oneself, which should be done by a person who has surrendered themselves to Christ, the true God and man; and how we should deliver ourselves to him, unite with him, and withdraw into God.

## Chapter 5.

**Disciple.** I have heard enough concerning how the creatures proceeded out from God; now I would like to know how one might penetrate through all things, return to God through Christ, and attain blessedness.

**Truth.** It should be known that Christ, the Son of the eternal Father, has something in common with other men and something distinct from them. That which is common is human nature, because he is a true man. However, he assumed human nature, but not a human *person* <note>In medieval theology, this distinguishes between the "nature" (humanity) and the "person" (the Divine Word). Christ is one person with two natures.</note>; this is to be understood as his assuming human nature in "indivisible matter," as St. Damascenus <note>original: "H. Damascenus." Referring to St. John of Damascus, an influential 7th-century theologian whose writings on the Incarnation were foundational for medieval thinkers.</note> calls it. To this common, assumed human nature, the purest blood of the blessed Virgin Mary served, from whom he took that nature upon himself. Therefore, human nature considered in itself—not because it was assumed, but because the *person* of Christ was not a human person—has this right: that every man could, in the same way, be both God and man. However, only the Lord Jesus alone attained this incomprehensible dignity, for although he took human nature upon himself, he did so with such purity that neither original sin nor any other sin clung to him; therefore, he alone could redeem the human race which had been condemned to eternal damnation. Secondly, Christ has

<column-break/>

that which is distinct: namely, that the meritorious works of other people—which they perform with a true surrender <term>surrender</term> <note>original: "vbergab." This refers to *Gelassenheit*, a central concept in German mysticism meaning the letting go of self-will to become receptive to God.</note> of themselves—are made fit through the merit of Christ to receive eternal blessedness, which is the reward of the virtues. This blessedness consists in the full enjoyment of the Godhead, with the removal of all hindrances. But the unity of communication in Christ, because it exists in a Personal being, surpasses the union of blessed spirits with God. For from the first moment of his conception in the Virgin's womb, he was true God, so that the assumed man was the Word and the true Son of God. Other men have their essence <note>original: "essens." Referring to their fundamental being or *Wesen*.</note> in their natural being; and even when they withdraw from themselves and abandon themselves, they still do not enter into the Divine Person by losing their own essence. The third special privilege is that he is the Head of the Church, just as in the human body the head stands above the other members. Therefore it is written in Romans 8: "For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers." Whoever now desires to return to God and to become a son of the Father in Christ, let him turn away from himself and toward God; thus he will arrive where he was created to be, and where he ought to arrive.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the Disciple and Truth, moving from the theoretical nature of Christ's incarnation to the practical application of "resignation" or self-surrender. It provides a philosophical breakdown of the human "self" and the steps required to achieve mystical union with God.</meta>

->The Dialogue of the Blessed Henry Suso<-

**Disciple.** Master <note>The OCR reads "Herz" (Heart), but in the context of this dialogue, it is likely a transcription of "Herr" (Lord/Master), the standard address for a spiritual teacher.</note>: what is true resignation? <note>original: "resignation." In the German mystical tradition, this refers to *Gelassenheit*—the state of letting go of one's own will and ego to be receptive to God.</note>

**Truth.** Pay attention with great modesty to these two words: *to deliver oneself*. If you can weigh them rightly, recognize them well, and consider them with modesty, you will easily grasp the Truth. Come then, let us first take up the first word (read: "the self"). For every human being has a five-fold "self." The first is common to him and the stones, and is called *being* <note>original: "esse seyn." The most basic level of existence shared by all matter.</note>. The second he has in common with the plants, and it is called growth, or life. The third, he shares with the irrational animals, and is called sensation. The fourth, he shares with other humans; it is the rational human nature in which all men are equal. The fifth belongs to him specifically: his own person, according to its essence and its accidental traits. What then hinders man from eternal bliss? It is the last "self" (read: "the self"), where man turns away from God and toward himself. Where he should have committed himself to the internal life, he instead makes for himself a private "self"—that is, out of the blindness of his soul, he uses for his own purposes what belongs to God, wickedly pours himself out over created things, and devotes himself to the temporal. But if he wished to leave that "self" in an orderly way, he would have to make use of this three-fold internal contemplation. First, he should look internally and very deeply at the nothingness of his own essence, noting that his own being, as well as the being of all other things, is nothing when it is excluded from that Being <note>original: "wesen."</note> which is the sole power and ability of God. Second, he shall see that in this separation from God, man possesses his own essence only as he exists outside of God,

<column-break/>

therefore he must strive to kill his vice-laden nature, to deny it, and to lead it back to God, its origin. The third contemplation shall happen with a denial, a falling away, and a surrender of himself in all things where he looked upon himself as a creature—amidst the restless and unbearable multiplicity, against the Divine truth, in good fortune and misfortune, in doing and in leaving—so that with great strength he retreats from himself, never seeking himself again, and through eternity becomes one with Christ. Thus, through this unity, God may always work in him, he may accept God, and look upon all things in this simplicity. This surrendered "self" (read: "the self") becomes an "I" <note>original: "Ego ich."</note> conformed to Christ, as the Apostle says of himself in Galatians 2: *I live, yet now not I, but Christ lives in me.* <note>original: "Ich leb / aber nit jetzt ich / sondern es lebt Christus in mir." A central verse for Christian mystics describing the replacement of the human ego with the divine presence.</note> This word ("I"), when one weighs it well, creates a "self." The other word, namely, *to surrender* <note>original: "Resignare sich oberlieffern."</note>, desires that we should give ourselves over to God, abandon ourselves and despise ourselves—not indeed as if we could leave the only thing that we are, or turn into nothing, but that we despise ourselves out of true love for God with the deepest humility; in this case, all is well with us.

**Disciple.** Praise be to the Truth. Tell me, Master, whether anything remains even for the holy, surrendered person.

**Truth.** Without doubt it happens, when the pious and faithful servant is led into the joy of his Lord, that he is made drunk by the infinite abundance of the house of God. Then it happens to him in an inexpressible way, like a drunken man, that he forgets himself and is no longer master of his reason...

<meta>catchword: th (likely beginning the word 'that' or 'the' in the next page's sentence regarding the loss of self-awareness in God).</meta>

### Of Truth and her Disciple ###

seems to have departed from itself, goes into God, and becomes one spirit with Him—just as a single, small drop of water mixed with much wine departs from itself, as it takes on the taste and color of the wine. <note>This is a famous metaphor for mystical union, famously used by St. Bernard of Clairvaux. It illustrates how the soul is transformed by God without losing its underlying essence.</note> So too are the saints, in an inexpressible way, deprived of all human desire; they depart from themselves and sink entirely into the will of God. Otherwise, the saying of Holy Scripture in 1 Corinthians 15 would not be true: *that God shall be all in all*, if anything of the human remained in man of which he was not entirely divested. <note>original: "1. Cor. 15. ... das Gott alles in allem seyn werde." Reference to 1 Corinthians 15:28, a central text for describing the final state of creation.</note> His essence indeed remains with him, but it is clothed in another form, dressed in another Glory, and endowed with another power—and this occurs through the deepest surrender of oneself. 

But whether anyone in this life has so forsaken themselves that they have reached this perfection—never to look at themselves in either good fortune or misfortune, but to love themselves only for God's sake—I do not know. Whoever has attained such a thing in this life, let him step forward; in my opinion, it seems impossible. From this, you can answer your own question; for the true resignation <note>original: "Resignation." This refers to *Gelassenheit*, a key concept in German mysticism meaning a state of detachment and letting go.</note> of such an excellent person in this life follows after holy self-denial and resignation, of which it is said they have become more or less united or "one." 

But note especially, as was said, that such a person departs from himself and is moved into another Glory and power. What is this "other form" but the Divine nature and essence, into which nature humans are, as it were, melted and poured, so that they might be one thing with it through grace, not through nature? <note>This distinction is crucial to Suso: the soul becomes "one with God" through God's gift (grace), not because the soul is biologically or inherently the same as God's substance.</note> What is the other Glory, but to be

<column-break/>

illuminated with the essential light <note>original: "wesentlichen liecht." This refers to the "uncreated light" or the very essence of God's presence.</note> which never diminishes? What is the other power, but that from this same unity, a Divine power and strength is granted to the person to do and to avoid everything that belongs to his salvation? And in this way, as was said, the person departs from himself.

**Disciple.** Master, can this happen in this world?

**Truth.** The aforementioned blessedness <note>original: "seligkeit." Can mean both earthly happiness and eternal salvation.</note> can be grasped in two ways.

The first is according to the highest degree or step, which exceeds all human ability and cannot be attained in this life; for the body is joined to the human, and its manifold needs do not allow a person to reach that state.

The second occurs through a communication; and this, although it seems impossible to many, is nevertheless possible. This is truly right, because it cannot be grasped with the senses or reason. Regarding this, some write that chosen and practiced people are found who possess such a pure mind, conformed to God, that the virtues remain steadfast in them according to a certain likeness to God. This is because they have been changed into the unity of the first Image <note>The "first Image" is Christ, the archetype of humanity.</note>, as if having entirely forgotten temporal life, and being raised into the Divine Likeness, they have become one thing with it. But this can only be said of those who have attained this blessedness in the highest degree, or of a very few others, most perfect, who are still contained in this present life.

# Concerning several high and useful questions, which are demonstrated to the Disciple by Truth through the parable of a resigned person. <note>The word "resigned" (German: *resignirten*) here refers to the concept of *Gelassenheit*, a central theme in German mysticism meaning total detachment from one's own will and surrender to God.</note>

## The 6th Chapter.

Afterward, a desire came upon the Disciple to know whether a person on Earth could be so heartily resigned, thereby drawing Christ so into his inner self, that Christ would make himself known to him in a divine manner and make him a partaker of his secret conversation. While he was occupied with this earnest request, he was led into himself, rapt outside of himself, and it seemed to him that he was led into a familiar landscape, where he saw the figure of a man between Heaven and Earth beside the Cross with a friendly countenance. The figure's head stretched above the Cross and shone brightly. He also saw two kinds of people walking around the Cross, yet they did not approach it; some looked upon this figure inwardly, but not outwardly; others looked upon it outwardly and not inwardly. But both groups turned with a roughness and hardness toward the likeness or figure. Thereupon, the figure descended like a true human being, sat down beside him, and told him to ask anything according to his pleasure, because he would receive an answer to everything. At this he sighed heartily and began to speak thus: "O Eternal Wisdom, <note>Suso frequently addresses Christ as "Eternal Wisdom" (*Ewige Weißheit*), a personification drawn from the Book of Proverbs.</note> what does this vision signify?"

**Truth.** The figure that you saw signifies the only-begotten Son of God, as far as his human nature is concerned. But that you saw no more than one image, and yet one so very manifold and distinct,

<column-break/>

signifies the people who are his members, who through him and in him have become children of God, just as there are many members in one body. But that you saw the head shining signifies that he is the first- and only-begotten Son, according to the most excellent union with which, in him, the human nature is united with the Divine Person; the others, however, signify all pious Christians, who are transformed into that same image and are united with him. The Cross signifies that a truly resigned person, according to both the inner and outer man, should always willingly give themselves up to everything that God desires of them to do and to suffer, so that on every occasion they may receive and bear everything from the hand of God, to the praise of God the Almighty Father. Such people are inwardly and outwardly right, hearty, secure, and well-disposed. But that the figure beside the Cross showed a great friendliness signifies that, although these people suffer much, they yet think little of everything because of their surrender. Wherever the head turns, the body follows; this indicates that the faithful followers of a pure life and of his good instructions, to which they earnestly direct themselves, are endowed with wonderful simplicity. Those, however, who looked at him inwardly and not outwardly, represent to us

# How Blessedness is obtained through the imitation of Christ.

### The 7th Chapter.

**Disciple.** What is the name of the means by which one attains <term>Blessedness</term> <note>German: *Seligkeit*. This refers to the state of eternal happiness and salvation in God's presence.</note>?

**Truth.** One can call it the means of birth, as is written by St. John in the 1st chapter: *He gave them power to be called children of God, who are born in no other way than from God* <note>original: "Er hat ihnen gewalt geben Kinder Gottes genent zu werden / die nicht anderſter als auß Gott gebohren ſeyn", referencing John 1:12-13.</note>; which occurs in the usual manner of birth. For when in this way one thing aims at or gives birth to another, it becomes like it, both in essence and in effect; because then, in a <term>resigned person</term> <note>German: *reſignirten Menſchen*. Referencing the concept of *Gelassenheit*, or total detachment from the self.</note>, God alone is the Father, in whom nothing temporal is born according to its worldly property, his inner eyes are opened to understand himself, and there he receives a blessed life and essence, and is one thing

<column-break/>

with God, because there, in the one God, everything is one thing.

**Disciple.** I see mountain and valley, water, air, and various creatures; how then do you say that everything is one thing?

**Truth.** I will say even more: unless someone grasps and understands two contrary things simultaneously in one, it is truly neither safe nor easy to speak with him of this; for as soon as he understands this, he begins to walk on the path of this life of which I speak.

**Disciple.** What are the two contrary things or opposites?

**Truth.** The eternal Nothing, and the temporal being of oneself.

**Disciple.** All the academic schools deny that two contradictory parts can be said of the same thing at once.

**Truth.** I see that we do not meet one another on the same path; you wander on one, and I on another. Your question arises from human reason, but I speak from a meaning that surpasses all human understanding and reason. You must transcend all senses if you wish to arrive here, for Truth is better perceived in "unknowing" <note>This refers to *Apophatic theology*, or the "Cloud of Unknowing," where God is understood by setting aside all specific concepts or images.</note>. At that very time, the Disciple was wonderfully transformed; for occasionally, and indeed quite often, he was deprived of the use of his external senses for ten or twelve weeks, more or less. He did not know whether he was among or away from other people, and the function of his physical senses was so withdrawn from him that through everything and in all things, he perceived nothing but the simple, unique Being which is God. In that "One," he understood all things without the multiplicity of "this" or "that." There, **Truth** spoke to him inwardly in this way: "Well then, what has happened to you? Have I spoken the truth?"

<column-break/>

**The Disciple answers.** Yes; what I could not believe before, I now know for certain. But I wonder why this state does not remain forever.

**Truth.** Perhaps it has not yet become a habit.

**Disciple.** Where does the intellect of a <term>surrendered person</term> <note>original: *resignirten Menschens*. In mystical tradition, this describes someone who has achieved *Gelassenheit*—a state of letting go of the self and the ego to be filled by God.</note> end, or what is its goal?

**Truth.** A person can reach a point in this life where they understand themselves to be united with that which is "Nothing" of all those things that can be understood or expressed with words. This "Nothing" is commonly called "God," yet in Himself (if I may speak so) He is the most <term>super-essential</term> <note>original: *vberwesentlichste*. A term from Dionysian theology meaning a reality that exists beyond the category of "being" as humans understand it.</note> thing. Here, such a person recognizes themselves as united with the "Nothing," and without the effort of the intellect, they recognize the "Nothing" itself. But something lies hidden here, which admonishes us to go even deeper.

## How we should lose ourselves in the Nothingness which is God, so that God may become everything in all to us.

### Chapter 8.

**Disciple.** Do the Holy Scriptures or the Holy Fathers also speak of this "Nothing," which is not called so because it is truly nothing, but because of its inconceivable dignity?

**Truth.** Saint Dionysius <note>Referencing Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a foundational mystic who taught that God is "nothing" because He is above everything.</note> speaks of a "nameless thing" which can be called this "Nothing"; for when someone calls such a thing "God," or "Being," or by

<column-break/>

another name, these names do not actually reach Him in the way they are understood when applied to created beings.

**Disciple.** But what is the "hidden thing" into which one must go further, which you attributed to this "Nothing," and from whence (in your opinion) all things have flowed? Since it is a pure and transparent simplicity, how can there be a greater "entrance" or "exit"?

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Truth and the Disciple regarding the mystical state of "Nothingness." The previous page established that the Disciple had experienced a state of "unknowing" where he perceived only the simple Being of God. Here, Truth explains that true union transcends all language and sensory images, moving into a theological concept of the "Divine Nothing."</meta>

->of Truth / and her Disciple.<-

**Truth.** As long as a person understands the union, or anything similar that can be expressed with words, or feels it, he must go yet deeper. That **Nothingness** cannot go further into itself; but where we understand it beyond our intellect—that is, without possible mental images, which no intellect can reach through shapes and forms—there we can express nothing with words. For when we speak of such a matter that can be proven with reason, even if we say much about it, still it cannot be explained what that **Nothingness** is, even if a double portion of Teachers and Books were at hand. That this **Nothingness** is the intellect itself, the essence, or the enjoyment, is true in the way it can be told to us; but in truth, it is infinitely further away than the Heaven is separated from the Earth.

**Disciple.** What does it mean when it is said that the **Nothingness**, which is called God and can bring forth <note>original: *gebähren*. In Rhineland mysticism, this refers to the "birth of the Word" in the soul.</note>, when it turns into itself, a person cannot distinguish himself before it?

**Truth.** Then the **Nothingness** is indeed nothing in itself as far as we are concerned, in the way it works within us; but when it turns into itself, as far as we are involved, we do not know it, however much we are dependent upon it.

<column-break/>

**Disciple.** I would like to be better instructed in this.

**Truth.** Do you not grasp that the most powerful inner attention, which recedes from itself toward the **Nothingness**, loses all distinction in the deep abyss—not indeed regarding the essence, but regarding our intellect?

**Disciple.** I still remember the word where you said that a person can reach the point in this life where he finds himself united with the "One"; but how can this happen?

**Truth.** A Teacher <note>Likely referring to Boethius or Meister Eckhart, who defined eternity as the "simultaneous and perfect possession of boundless life."</note> says that <term>Eternity</term> is a life above all time, and encompasses all time within itself without a past or a future, or a "before" or "after." And when someone is inwardly drawn to the eternal **Nothingness**, he possesses all in all, and there is no "before" or "after" there. Indeed, if someone were raised up inwardly today, he would have been there no shorter a time—when looking at Eternity—than one who arrived there a thousand years ago.

**Disciple.** This inner admission, as the Scripture testifies, is what people expect after their death.

**Truth.** It is true, if you are speaking of the full possession, but not regarding the greater or lesser foretaste.

From this, one should and can understand how such a person looks upon all created things and all pleasures, and understands them in unity; yes, even the pleasure that is received from physical exercises without spiritual effect. But note here a distinction: the ancient philosophers <note>The "old world-wise" refers to Greek and Roman philosophers who relied on natural reason alone.</note> explored natural things only in the way they had a natural origin, cause, and beginning, and in this manner they spoke of them. **Disciple.** Is there then a difference here?

**Truth.** Yes. Whoever is rightly disposed knows and recognizes himself as a **creature** <note>In this context, a "creature" means any created being (human, animal, angel) as distinct from the Creator.</note>, not according to his vices, but according to the union of himself with God. To this end serves what we read in <term>Saint John</term> <note>original: *H. Joan.* (Heiligen Joannes)</note>, chapter 1: "What was made, that was the life in Him."

**Disciple.** How can this be according to the truth, since it seems that the soul is a twofold thing—namely, a created thing and an uncreated thing? How can the soul be a creature and at the same time not a creature?

<column-break/>

**Truth.** A human cannot be both a creature and God, according to our way of speaking; rather, God is Threefold and One. Likewise, a person can, in a certain way where he loses himself in God, be one thing with Him, and yet in an outward way or manner, he can observe, act, and be devoted to such things. Of this I give a likeness: when the eye looks at something, it forgets itself, for in the looking it is united with its object; and yet it remains in itself what it is.

**Disciple.** Whoever has ever read in the Scriptures knows well enough that the soul must either be transformed into the **Nothingness** <note>In German mysticism, "the Nothingness" (*das Nichts*) is a name for God's overwhelming presence, which is "nothing" because it cannot be defined as any specific "thing."</note> which is God, or must completely perish in its essence—which, however, does not happen here.

**Truth.** The soul always remains a creature. But in the fact that it has lost itself in this **Nothingness**, it does not think in the slightest whether it is a creature or this **Nothingness**—that is, whether it be a creature or not—just as it also does not think whether it is united with God or not. However, where reason can still perform its office, one perceives it well, and thus this remains entirely with the person.

**Disciple.** Is it then well with such a person?

**Truth.** Very well, because what he has is not taken from him, and besides that, something more excellent is granted to him, so that he understands it more clearly. **Disciple.** This union of the soul—does it happen through the essence of the soul itself, or through its powers?

**Truth.** The essence of the soul is united with the essence of the **Nothing**, and the powers of the soul <note>The "powers" of the soul traditionally refer to the intellect and the will.</note> are united with the workings of the **Nothing**, which are the workings the **Nothing** has within itself.

For those who are in this right state, they perform only one work, because there is only one birth and one foundation—namely, through the union <note>The mystical union where the human soul and the Divine become one in purpose and action.</note>.

**Disciple.** I do not see how it is possible for a person to perform only one work, since in Christ there was a twofold operation <note>A reference to the theological doctrine that Christ had both a divine and a human will and way of acting.</note>.

use to us, because it is only attributed to nature, which acts without grace and earns nothing; but the spiritual rebirth, after the full resurrection of man through grace in God, has as little to do with the body and with those things which nature alone works in man, as the actions of a human being are distinguished from the behavior of wild animals. And there remains almost nothing more for man to do than before his resurrection, except that he performs his works out of a virtuous habit—not by the guidance of nature, but of grace. In this way, a burnt, distilled, and prepared wine <note>likely referring to brandy or "aqua vitae"; the author uses the refining process of distillation as a metaphor for the soul's purification</note> has no less strength than a natural, unaltered one.

**Disciple.** Provide a distinction between the Eternal Birth and this Rebirth, which happens naturally in man.

**Truth.** This I call the Eternal Birth: because all created things have their origin, beginning, and cause in the single Almighty power, which is God. But Rebirth, which belongs to man alone, I call the leading back of every accidental or encountered thing to God, their origin, and this without any backward glance or view toward oneself.

**Disciple.** Since in this way the soul is deprived of knowledge, does the use of all natural things also cease within it?

**Truth.** All the powers of the soul are too weak to arrive at this **Nothing** in the manner previously described; but when the soul [lost itself] in this **Nothing**...

**Disciple.** Is the will also weakened in this Nothing?

**Truth.** It is indeed weakened according to its own self-willing; for although the will is entirely free, it then nonetheless attains true freedom <term>freedom</term> <note>The idea here is that true freedom is not the ability to do anything one wants, but the ability to perfectly align with the Divine Good without internal conflict.</note>, because nothing remains for it to will [for itself].

**Disciple.** How can a person's will be taken away from them, when Christ nonetheless retained His will?

**Truth.** Man loses his will because out of self-interest <note>original: "eygenthumb"; this implies a sense of "possessive selfhood" or acting out of ego rather than grace.</note> he wants to do now this, now that; here, however, his will is not united with any vice, as said before, but his will is endowed with freedom, so that he performs only one work, which he himself is according to the union; and he works this in time. And if one wishes to speak in the common manner, he wills no evil, but only to do good; but to speak precisely, his entire life is a pure freedom in God, which is undoubtedly his dwelling place, which he endures <note>original: "erduldet"; suggests a passive receiving or suffering of the Divine presence.</note>.

**Disciple.** The dissolution of the will is not of that nature.

**Truth.** This will is united with the Divine Will and wills nothing other than what it is itself, insofar as its willing is in God. But what has been said must

<column-break/>

not be understood as if man were entirely changed into God <note>A clarification to avoid the charge of Pantheism, which was a dangerous accusation for medieval mystics.</note>, but according to a certain translation and complete denial of himself, because such a man becomes so united with God that God Himself is his foundation.

**Disciple.** Does there then remain for man a distinct essence of his person in the ground of this Nothing?

**Truth.** All this must be understood according to man's turning toward the interior—that is, according to the vision that looks inward, in the manner of departing from oneself and considering neither this nor that. In this state, although God and man are internally united, each nonetheless remains what he is, as Saint Augustine says: 
> Take this good and take that good away, and behold the good in itself if you can, and that is the highest good toward which we strive. <note>original: "Nimb dieses / vnnd nimb jenes gut hinweg..."; quoting Augustine's *De Trinitate*, Book VIII, Chapter 3.</note>

# In what points those fail who follow false freedom, and of true modesty and right order.

## The 12th Chapter.

On a Sunday, in the clear light of day, the Disciple sat in his inner contemplation. As he enjoyed this inner peace and silence, there encountered him the rational form of a man who was subtle and sharp-witted in words, but in deeds and in life was little practiced. This form of a man we shall call a wild, unformed man—

<column-break/>

or rather, an Un-man <term>Un-man</term> <note>original: "Vnmensch"; Suso uses this to describe a person who has lost their proper human and spiritual orientation, often representing the "Brethren of the Free Spirit" who practiced a distorted form of mysticism.</note>. To this Un-man, the Disciple spoke: "Where do you come from?"

The **Un-man** answered: "From whence I never departed."

**Disciple.** "What are you?"

**Un-man.** "I am nothing."

**Disciple.** "What do you want?"

**Un-man.** "I want nothing."

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the soul's "Nothingness." Having heard Truth's explanation of the "inner ground," the Disciple now encounters a new character—the "Unman"—who represents the "False Free Spirits" that Henry Suso and other 14th-century mystics frequently criticized for misinterpreting spiritual freedom as a license to ignore moral laws.</meta>

->**Of the Truth and her Disciple.**<-

**Disciple.** You speak strange things; tell me, what is your name?

**Unman.** I am called an Unman <note>original: "Vnmensch"; literally "non-human" or "inhuman." In this context, it refers to a person who has lost their human identity in a negative, lawless way, often associated with the heretical "Brethren of the Free Spirit."</note> without a name.

**Disciple.** It is fitting that you are called an Unman, for you use such alien and strange speech; tell me, what is the aim of your reason?

**Unman.** Idle freedom <term>Idle freedom</term> <note>original: "müssige freyheit"; a term used to describe a state of spiritual apathy or antinomianism where a person believes they are above the law and moral requirements.</note>.

**Disciple.** What do you call "idle freedom"?

**Unman.** When one lives according to the pleasure of their own will without contradiction, without consideration or care for the past or the future.

**Disciple.** You miss the truth by a wide margin, for such freedom leads a person away from salvation <note>original: "Seligkeit"; refers to blessedness or eternal happiness in God.</note> and robs them of true freedom. You do not yet know how to distinguish true freedom from false; I speak of true freedom, but you, on the contrary, speak of the false and therefore fail. For whoever lacks discernment <note>original: "bescheidenheit"; in this period, it meant the ability to judge or discern correctly between right and wrong.</note> maintains no order; but whatever has no right order is sinful, as Christ himself says: **John 8.** *Whoever commits sin is a servant of sin.* But whoever enters into Christ with a pure conscience and a prudent way of life, surrendering themselves from the heart, attains true freedom, as our Lord testifies: **John 8.** *If the Son makes you free, you shall be truly free.*

**Unman.** What do you call "well-ordered" or "ill-ordered"?

**Disciple.** When nothing—neither external nor internal—of the aforementioned virtues belonging to the matter is neglected, I call it well-ordered; on the contrary, I call it ill-ordered when something of that kind is neglected.

<column-break/>

**Unman.** Idle freedom must renounce all these things and cast them to the wind.

**Disciple.** This outrage is entirely contrary to the truth and is identical to false freedom, because it neglects the order which the Eternal Nothing <term>Eternal Nothing</term> <note>original: "ewige Nichts"; a mystical term for God, describing His nature as being beyond all human categories and "things."</note> (which is God) has assigned to all things by way of birth or communication.

**Unman.** He who has become nothing in his Eternal Nothing knows of no distinction.

**Disciple.** The Eternal Nothing—which is sufficiently known to all well-ordered minds or to any right reason—is not called "Nothing" as if it were absolutely nothing at all, but rather because of its excellent and transcendent being. For this Nothing, according to its essence, knows no distinction within itself; yet, according to its fruitfulness, the orderly distinction of all things springs forth from it. And in this Nothing, a human is never so "annihilated" <note>original: "vernichtigt"; the process of the soul losing its self-will to be filled with God.</note> that the senses do not retain the distinction of their origin, and reason its power of choice—even if these things are not noticed or regarded in their first Ground <note>The "Ground" (grund) is the deepest point of contact between the soul and God.</note>.

**Unman.** But what if all these things are understood and taken as being only in and out of that same Ground?

**Disciple.** That cannot rightly happen; for they are not only in the same Ground, but the whole human is in himself a created being and remains what he is, and must also be understood as such. If he were to be robbed of all distinction according to his essence, as it is said, it would be intolerable; but such a thing does not happen, as was said above, which we must always understand with good distinction.

# The Dialogue of Blessed Henry Suso

**Unman.** I have learned from others that an excellent teacher <note>Refers to Meister Eckhart (c. 1260–1328), Suso's mentor. Suso wrote this text partly to defend Eckhart's complex teachings from being misinterpreted by radical groups.</note> rejects all distinction.

**Disciple.** That he "knows of no distinction" could be understood to mean that he speaks of the distinction of the Persons within the Unity, where the Persons are not divided, yet not in such a way as to ignore how the Persons are regarded in relation to one another, where they are certainly distinct. However, if you understand this as the inner departure <note>original: "abweichung"; here meaning the soul's turning away from its own self to sink into God.</note> of a person led toward God, it has been mentioned above that such a thing is to be understood not according to the essence, but according to our manner of speaking. Note also at the same time that separation is distinct from distinction; for a living body is not separated from the soul, yet the soul is distinct from the body—for the body is not the soul, nor is the soul the body, even though the soul is enclosed within the body and the body cannot live without the soul. Likewise, I believe that no thing can be separated from that simple essence <term>simple essence</term> <note>original: "einfältigen wesen"; refers to the pure, undivided nature of God.</note>, because it communicates being to all things; nevertheless, they are distinct from God because the Divine essence is not the same thing as the essence of a stone, nor vice versa, nor is the essence of one creature the essence of another.

**Unman.** The same teacher says in one place: Christ our Lord is an only-begotten Son and is not reborn.

**Disciple.** He is the Father’s natural and co-essential Son, as one who is born out of the Father’s substance and essence; but we humans are not natural children of God, thus our birth is rather called a "rebirth," because it is in some measure according to the image

<column-break/>

and conformity of His nature. He is the image of the eternal Father; we are *made* according to the image of God <note>A classic distinction: Christ is the "Image" (Identity), while humans are "made to the image" (Participation).</note>; and no one, whoever he may be, can say he is equal to the Son in this regard.

**Unman.** I have heard the mentioned teacher say further that such a man <note>A person who has achieved mystical union with God.</note> performs the very same work that Christ performs.

**Disciple.** But he says elsewhere: A righteous man does what Righteousness itself does; and this is true when a righteous person is a true, only-begotten son of Righteousness, as it is written in **John 3.** <note>original: "Joan. 3."</note> *That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.* And this, he says, is true in Christ alone and in no other human being, for He has no other essence than the Father’s essence, and the Father creates nothing without the Son; thus the Son does everything the Father does. This, however, is false in all other men. From this, you now have the truth of the mentioned words.

**Unman.** His words imply that whatever is granted to Christ is also granted to us.

**Disciple.** Understand this as the full enjoyment of essential bliss <note>original: "wesentlicher seligkeit"; the ultimate happiness of seeing God's essence in heaven.</note>, as Christ Himself says in **Matthew 11.** <note>original: "Matth. 11."</note> *The Father has given me all things,* and all this He has also given to us, but in a different manner. And he says this in many places: that Christ has all things by virtue of the Incarnation, but we have them through the God-conformable union <term>God-conformable union</term> <note>original: "Gottgleichförmige vereinigung"; a state where the human will is perfectly aligned with God's will through grace, not by nature.</note>. Thus Christ has all things more excellently, according to the magnificence with which He was able to receive them.

**Unman.** You will find how this teacher...

...anguish of conscience, and on the other hand, the disorderly and overly lax conscience of others?

**Truth.** Both still look upon themselves, but in different ways: the one in a spiritual manner, the other in a more fleshly way.

**Disciple.** Is such a **Resigned** <term>Resigned</term> <note>original: "Resignirter"; in the tradition of Rhineland Mysticism, this refers to a person who has achieved "Gelassenheit"—a state of total surrender where their own will is dissolved into God's will.</note> person always idle, or what is his activity?

**Disciple.** How does he conduct himself toward his fellow man?

**Truth.** He lives kindly with people without being swayed by imaginary impressions; he loves them without the attachment of the mind, and has compassion for them without anxious worry, dwelling in true freedom.

**Disciple.** Is he also required to go to confession?

**Truth.** Confession that arises from love is better than that which arises from sin.

**Disciple.** How does he pray, or does he perform any specific prayers?

**Truth.** His prayer is the most useful, for he penetrates the senses (because God is a spirit) and diligently searches whether any hindering obstacle has been placed between God and himself, or whether he is looking at himself according to the external objects of the sensory part. A light shines in his higher faculties which assures him that God is his essence and life, and works within him, while he is merely a bare tool, God's worshiper and co-worker.

**Disciple.** In what manner does such a person eat, drink, and sleep?

**Truth.** According to the external sensory part, the outward man eats; but if

<column-break/>

we wish to speak according to the inward way of life, he does not "eat" in the usual sense, otherwise he would merely be consuming food and resting according to the animal part. The same is to be held regarding all external things necessary to man.

**Disciple.** What is his outward **Conversation** <note>original: "Conversation"; here meaning social conduct and general manner of living among others.</note> like?

**Truth.** He does not have many rules or many words, and those he has are simple. His conduct is adorned with good manners; in his senses, he is still and quiet.

**Disciple.** Are all such people fashioned in the same way?

**Truth.** No; rather, according to opportunity, one has more and another less, but the primary goal in them is one and the same.

**Disciple.** Do such people have a full knowledge of the Truth, or are they still led by opinions or conjectures?

**Truth.** When they remain within themselves, they also conjecture; but when they depart from themselves into that which is the full knowledge of all truth—that is, into God—then there is no delusion, opinion, or conjecture in them. For they are united with Him, yet they take none of the credit for themselves. Let this be enough for you to have said until now; for it is not through asking, but through the total surrender of oneself that one reaches this hidden truth.

# Appendix or addition of several profound questions by the man renowned for the holiness of his life, Dr. Henry Suso.

---

## Concerning two kinds of people who project an appearance of some piety.

### The 13th Chapter.

->As an eagle stirs up its young to fly. Deuteronomy 32.<-

After the Servant’s spiritual daughter—of whom much is frequently mentioned in the Servant’s biography—had become like soft wax melted by the fire through his spiritual instructions regarding the holiness of the active life, allowing every seal to be pressed upon the outer man; and after she had been led in an orderly way for a long enough time through the model of the life of Christ (which is the surest path), the Servant wrote to her in this manner: My daughter, it is now time for you to venture further and to leave the nest of comforting preoccupations with the forms and images that are granted to those beginning their spiritual journey. Behave like a young eagle now fit for flight; that is, raise and soar with strong and now fully grown wings—namely, the higher powers of the soul—toward the height of Divine contemplation, just as perfected people are accustomed to do. You know what Christ said to his disciples when they were too deeply in love with his physical presence: *It is to your advantage,* he says, *that I go away, for otherwise the Comforter will not come to you.* <note>John 16:7</note> Furthermore, there is no doubt that your

<column-break/>

exercises will have been a support and a useful preparation for you to travel further through the wilderness of the animalistic and sensory life <note>Suso refers here to the "animal" or "sensual" state where a person is still ruled by physical desires and instincts rather than spiritual reason.</note> into the Promised Land of a pure and quiet heart, which is the beginning of the blessed life here and remains so for all time in the future. However, so that this high and rational path may become better known to you, I will light your way with the light of clear discernment <term>discernment</term> <note>original: "bescheidenheit"; in this mystical context, it refers to the spiritual gift of discretion—the ability to distinguish between true divine inspiration and mere human emotion.</note>, so that you do not fall into any error, even if you soar high with your senses. Now, take note: two-fold is the nature of those who project an appearance of piety; some follow the rational way, others the irrational way. The first group direct their reason and understanding so that everything they understand, do, or refrain from doing, is performed with true discernment, and according to the mind of the holy Catholic Church for the praise of God and the peaceful rest of all people. They also pay attention to their words and conduct so that, as far as it depends on them, no one is offended by them, unless someone should do so out of the malice of their own heart.

# Supplement of Several High Questions

...interpret it in the worst way; such an honest, well-guarded, and spiritual way of life is called good by nature and reason. Indeed, it is conformed to GOD and worthy of praise, because it shines within itself with steadfast truth, just as the heaven shines with the stars. Others, who wish to appear pious and yet lead an irrational way of life, are those who, looking only at themselves with an untamed and unmortified nature, merely use their reason to scrutinize things through contemplation. They know how to speak of these matters in a haughty manner to the unlearned, doing so in order to despise others—even if others show displeasure toward them in words and deeds. Their rational light shows itself externally but not internally; and just as **rotten wood** seems to glow at night, though it has no real light within it, so too is the internal light and external conversation <note>Here, "conversation" refers to one's conduct or way of living among others.</note> of such people completely unlike Christ, whom they ought to resemble. Generally, they are recognized by their untamed and bold words, of which we will cite only one as proof, from which the others may be recognized. One of them says in one place: *A righteous man has no means or hindrance to avoid.* This and similar sayings seem to have some weight to the ignorant and those who see little, but they are rejected by the wise because they rightly understand their intent and meaning. The cited saying, however, explains enough: namely, that the righteous man has no hindrance to avoid. Who then is righteous, and what is the hindrance? A righteous man, in the ordinary

<column-break/>

way of speaking, is understood as he was created, but not according to the Image <note>original: "Ebenbild." In Suso’s theology, the soul has an "uncreated image" or archetype eternally present in God's mind.</note> which he has in God; for a righteous man does not exist for himself, but requires a Person in whom he is called righteous. But what is the hindrance? Sin, which separates man from God. Should a righteous man then not avoid sin? Who does not see that this deviates from truth and right reason? It is indeed true that a righteous man has no "means" <note>In this context, "means" (mittel) refers to an intermediary or anything standing between the soul and God.</note> insofar as he—just like all other created things—is united with God in the **super-essential** <term>super-essential: (oberwesenlich) A mystical term describing God’s existence as being beyond or above the categories of created being or essence.</term> understanding of God. But in the simple and super-essential ground of the Godhead, a bodily man is not a "righteous man," for in God there is nothing bodily, just as there is no intermediary. But outside of this "ground," every man understands that he is this or that particular man; for here he is mortal, but there <note>i.e., in his eternal archetype in God.</note> he is not. Insofar as he is mortal, it is certain that he is covered with a corrupt nature, and it is necessary for him to avoid all harmful hindrances. If I were to imagine that I were not endowed with any created reason, and behave as if I did not exist, and wanted to perform all bodily works without any distinction between GOD and myself—as if the uncreated Image in God were performing them—this would be very wicked. Therefore, it is to be concluded that such sayings are contrary to reason. Yet this is not said as if we wished to reject rational instructions and those cautiously spoken sayings which lead man away from the **beastly manner** <note>original: "Viehischen manier," referring to living by animal instincts rather than spiritual reason.</note> and...

# On the difference between Orderly and Presumptuous reason.

### The 14th Chapter.

After the first battles, which are undertaken to mortify the flesh and blood, one arrives at a high path, from which many are plunged into the depths; and such is called **presumptuous reason** <note>Original: *vorwißige vernunfft*. This refers to an over-eager, intellectual curiosity that seeks to understand God through logic alone rather than humble experience.</note>. For after a person is freed from vices and the forms clinging to him, and rises with joy above time and place—where he was previously hindered from enjoying his natural dignity—the eye of reason opens. The person then receives a special delight, which is drawn from the knowledge of truth, the enjoyment of Divine bliss, the contemplation of eternity, and the like. The created understanding then perceives the eternal and inexpressible understanding partly within itself, and the person is seized with wonder in all other things as he considers himself—who he once was and what he is now. He finds that he was previously nothing but miserable, unworthy, deprived of God, blind, and far removed from God; but now he seems filled with God, nothing without God, but rather united with God in everything. In this way, he attacks all tasks with vehemence,
<column-break/>
fiercely and fervently, and his reason breaks forth like **new, fermenting wine** <note>Original: *sprungende Most*. Literally "springing must" or young wine that is still bubbling and volatile during fermentation.</note>. Therefore, he pours himself out upon that which he has grasped with his understanding—or which has been shown to him without discretion under an image of Him who is the only one he should cling to—and he wants to interpret and understand everything according to his own mind. 

From this, it happens that he denies all creatures—namely, Heaven, Hell, Angels, and the Devil—in their distinct natures, because he thinks he has grasped God within them. Yet he does not yet know these things insofar as they are distinct, insofar as they remain, and insofar as they deviate. Therefore, it happens to such people just as it does to **bees**: when they initially fly out of their hives, they wander to and fro, not knowing where they are flying; indeed, some are completely lost, while others come back to their dwelling properly and in good order. So too are these people: in wanting to behold God with **disordered reason** <note>Reason that is not guided by the proper "order" of the Church or humility.</note> as much as their natural understanding allows, they wish to renounce this and that, and yet do not know how such a thing is to be done. # How true Resignation may be distinguished from the False.

## The 15th Chapter.

At this point it is to be known that the essence <note>Original: *essenz*. In Suso’s mystical vocabulary, this refers to the core being or "is-ness" of a person or God.</note> has a threefold departure <note>Original: *außweichen*. This term describes an "ebbing out" or an ecstatic movement where the soul moves beyond its natural boundaries.</note>, or ecstasy. 

The first: when something loses its being entirely, so that nothing remains of it, just as a shadow becomes nothing. In this way, the spirit (that is, the rational soul) is not annihilated in its departure and denial; for the soul remains eternal because of its rational dignity and its God-like powers. Because God is a super-essential mind in whose image the soul was created, it cannot be destroyed or made into nothing, as the body is when it turns to dust and ashes.

The second is a partial departure, which requires its own place and time, as happens to those who are drawn into the essence of God Himself through contemplation <note>Original: *beschauhlichkeit*. This refers to a deep, meditative state of "beholding" the Divine.</note>, 

<column-break/>

as did St. Paul <note>The author refers here to the Apostle Paul’s account of being "caught up to the third heaven."</note> in 2 Corinthians 12; or externally, when one transcends all forms and images and exceeds oneself; which, however, is not long-lasting. When Paul came back to himself, he found the former man again, as far as the essence and being are concerned. 

The third departure is called an infinite resignation <note>Original: *Resignation*. In this German mystical context, it is synonymous with *Gelassenheit*, or the "letting-be" and total surrender of self-will.</note> of oneself, where one delivers oneself to God through the surrender of one's own will, wherever he finds himself, as if he knew nothing of himself, but God alone rightfully rules everywhere. This resignation cannot easily remain whole and uninjured as long as body and soul are together; for even if someone has abandoned themselves now and intends—as far as the emotional or sensory part is concerned—to have departed into God...

...so that in the future he will not resist himself and wish to make use of himself; in a single moment he turns, and his wicked nature turns back upon itself and is just as it was before—he must therefore, in this case, deny and surrender himself a second, third, and many more times. If someone, out of this frail resignation <note>The term "resignation" here is used as a synonym for the mystical concept of *Gelassenheit*, or "releasement," where one lets go of self-will.</note>, wanted to do as they pleased, they would fail in this; although it is true that, insofar as he departs from himself and is drawn into God through that departure, he stands in the truth in this regard. Furthermore, it is to be known that resignation is of two kinds: one is called **preceding**, the other **subsequent**, and this analogy serves the purpose: Thieves are incited by their corrupt nature to steal, but reason advises against doing it because it is wicked. If, in this case, the thieves denied themselves and followed reason, this resignation would be called a **preceding** one, and more excellent, for they would retain their innocence. If, however, they do not abandon themselves but choose to follow their evil lusts, and are afterwards captured and sentenced to death, resigning themselves willingly to death because necessity requires it, it is called a **subsequent** resignation. This is indeed good and imparts eternal salvation to them, but the first would have been infinitely and incomparably better. Thus, one must not boldly resign oneself to all vices, as some foolish people say—that one must pass through all vices and sins if one wishes to attain full resignation—because this is entirely contrary to the truth. No one would doubt that he who voluntarily throws himself into the mud so that he may afterwards be washed cleaner is to be considered insane.

<column-break/>

The foremost friends of God are so constituted that they wish to leave themselves entirely and, without repeating the use of themselves—as far as human weakness allows—to remain steadfast in the **preceding** resignation. When they do not sufficiently achieve this, they sigh and weep, although they have the advantage over others in that they can more briskly free themselves from all hindrances. While they are thus sighing, **subsequent** resignation arises within them, through which they are immediately restored to their former state; for they recognize themselves to be human, and yet they direct it to the praise of God. This subsequent resignation sometimes has its use from the knowledge of oneself, where the sighing ceases and they are suddenly born again to their former state. If, then, a perfect man were to obey in a deceptive and godless manner and follow his evil desires, and also think—should he happen to reclaim himself, make use of himself, and commit something viceful according to the external man—that such a thing is not harmful, as long as he remains of the same mind according to habit and according to his essence <note>Original: *essens*. This likely refers to the "essential" or inner being of the person as opposed to their outward actions.</note> without repeated use of himself: to such a person I say that he does not understand himself and does not know what he says. All learned men know this well, provided they recognize what an "accidental" thing is. We call this an accident or an occurrence, which can be in its substance or not be, without the destruction of the thing—such as the color in a board or a tablet. But here it is different, for the body and the soul, which they out of ignorance call attached or accidental things, are two...

Do you ask what should be the object of a resigned man in all things? It is this: to fall away from himself, or to surrender himself in all things; then all things depart together with him. Thoughts are the smallest medium between God and the soul, but the greatest medium is clinging to one's own will. A resigned person should let no hour pass in which he does not pay attention to God and to himself; he should look not only at what he needs, but also at what he can lack and do without. When such a resigned person strives to go to the internal and to cling to the truth, he should first endeavor to go within and to transcend the senses, for God is a Spirit. <note>original: *Ioan. 4*; refers to the Bible verse John 4:24.</note> Second, he should consider whether he has placed a medium or hindrance in the way. Third, he should investigate whether he seeks himself in any matter. Fourth, he should, in that same light, pay attention to the presence of the whole Divine Essence and hold that he belongs to it alone. The more one turns away from himself and all transitory creatures, the more he is united with God and made blessed. ### Addition of Several High Questions

...abandon what belongs to you. Close your senses to all present **imaginations** <note>original: *einbildungen*; these are mental images or sensory distractions that pull the mind away from spiritual focus</note>; be always freed from all things which reason, looking at the external, chooses—those which cling to the will and provide an agreeable pleasure—and rest in nothing outside of God. If something evil is committed in your presence, do not involve yourself in it, and do not participate. He who remains constantly within himself attains great powers. The bodily delight of a **resigned** <term>resignation: in this context, the word refers to "Gelassenheit" or the total surrender of one's own will to God's will</term> person is the narrow and necessary change, or the renewal of such works, from which he can turn away with a quick spirit. According to how much or how little a person is resigned, so he also directs his love and affection more or less toward temporal things.

When a half-resigned person felt heavy pains, he heard these words internally: "You should take such great care for my sake and so despise yourself—only so that it may go well with me—that you count it as nothing, however it may be with you." When a resigned person keeps still with their inner senses, the less help they find internally, the more they are crucified; however, the faster they die <note>meaning the "death of the self" or ego</note>, the more quickly they overcome and escape. The pouring out of the senses onto external things destroys the inner life and the soul’s devotion. See to it that you do not chase after business that draws you toward the external; but if such business seeks you, let yourself, as much as possible, not be found.

<column-break/>

Give yourself always cheerfully to the inner life. Natural life makes itself known in movements, in effects, and in the senses; but whoever leaves himself in these and deviates from his own self begins a supernatural life. Some rise up without hindrance but do not remain steadfast; therefore, embrace and follow pure resignation, for disordered desires can create a secret hindrance. A resigned person should so tame the powers of his soul that, when he looks inward at himself, he may see this. A resigned person remains so free from himself as if he knew nothing of himself, because in the "Only One," which is God, all things are well-ordered within him.

Strive so that the outer man may be united with the inner man, with the *crushing* <note>original: *zerknirschung*; a strong term for contrition or the grinding down of worldly desires</note> of all animal and sensual lusts. A resigned conversion, or return to God, is sometimes more pleasing to God than a self-pleasing perseverance. Withdraw your soul from external senses, through which it is scattered into the **multiplicity** <note>The state of being distracted by many worldly things rather than focused on the "oneness" of God</note> of external things. Return to the inner life, and return often to unity; enjoy God, remain steadfast, and never be satisfied until you attain in this temporal life—as much as is possible for human weakness—that which is always present in eternal life.

# What God Is.

## Chapter 17.

After this rational introduction of the outward man to the inward man, high insights arose in the Servant's spiritual daughter, about which she asked the Servant whether she was permitted to investigate further; he answered: "Indeed, because you have walked properly through the appropriate and convenient means and exercises, it is permissible for your spiritual reason to inquire about high matters. So, ask now according to your desire." She spoke: "My Father, tell me what God is, or how He is; that is, how He is one, and yet threefold." The Servant answered: "These are very high questions. As far as the first question is concerned—what God is—it must be known that all teachers who have ever lived cannot truly know it, because it surpasses all sense and reason. However, he who searches diligently and without ceasing will indeed obtain some knowledge of God, though it remains obscure; yet in the knowledge of God consists eternal life and man’s highest **bliss** <note>original: *Seligkeit*; refers to the state of perfect happiness or beatitude in the presence of God</note>. In this way, the excellent world-sages of old sought God, especially the subtle Aristotle, who investigated the beginner and author of Nature through Nature itself and its order. He searched diligently, and through the course and order of Nature, he found that there was a beginner and Lord of Nature, whom we call God. From this our God and Lord, we have this knowledge: that He is an un-

<column-break/>

mortal—that is, an eternal **Substance** <term>Substance: in a philosophical sense, this refers to that which exists in itself and does not change, the underlying reality of a thing</term> and Being before and after; yes, a **simple** <note>original: *einfältiges*; in medieval theology, "simple" means "not made of parts"—God is one unified whole</note>, pure, unchangeable Being, clothed in no body, but rather a Spirit. His most vivid intellect knows everything in Himself and through Himself; His Being in Himself is a deep abyss of all joys and delights; and lastly, He is the supernatural, inexpressible, and most lovely bliss of Himself and of all those who shall enjoy Him in the future life."

The Servant of Wisdom was once walking in the chapel, and his heart was filled with Divine Jubilee <note>original: "Jubel"; a technical term for a wordless, overflowing joy of the soul</note>; but the porter called him to a woman who wished to confess. When he would not come out, the woman began to weep with a troubled heart, went into a corner, and wept for a long time. Meanwhile, God quickly withdrew the delightful grace from the Servant, and his heart became as hard as a flint-stone. When he desired to know why this happened to him, God answered him inwardly:

# Where God May Be.

## Chapter 18.

The Maiden said: "My Father, I have learned in some measure what God is, but I would also like to know where he is." The Servant spoke: "The opinion of the learned is that God is not in one certain place, but everywhere, and everything in all. The learned also say that one sometimes arrives at the knowledge of the things themselves through their name; now, however, a Teacher <note>Likely referring to St. Thomas Aquinas or Dionysius the Areopagite</note> calls the first and most prominent name of God, *Being* <note>original: *Esse*; Latin for 'to be' or 'existence'</note>, the Essence. Upon this Essence, and upon his bare simplicity, cast your eyes, so that you let go of this or that being which can be divided and separated, and look only upon the Being to which nothing of non-being is mixed. For what is nothing denies that which is something; likewise, that which is something is a denial of that which is not. What is yet to become, or has been, is not present; that mixed being, or that,"

<meta>catchword: not</meta>

<column-break/>

"not-being, cannot be known, but only from the consideration of the total Being. This Being is not separate, belonging to this or that creature, for every separate or separable being is mixed with the external, whereby it can take on something else; from this it is to be concluded that the Divine and inexpressible Substance <term>Substance: *Substanz*; the essential nature or underlying reality of something, rather than its outward appearance</term> in itself is the total Being, which through its presence sustains all separate being. How great now is the blindness of human reason, that it cannot experience that without which it can know or see nothing! When the bodily eye looks earnestly upon many kinds of colors, it does not see the light through which it sees all other things—or when it does see it, it nevertheless pays no attention to it. So it is with our soul’s eye, when it [looks] upon these..."

# Addition of Several Lofty Questions

<margin>The nature of God's goodness.</margin>
...ness <note>Continuing from the previous page's "Gott-heit" or "Gütig-keit" (Godhead or Goodness).</note> constrains Him so that He does not keep His blessedness for Himself alone, but wishes to communicate it in a more generous way both within and outside of Himself; from this it necessarily follows that the highest good pours itself out in the highest and closest manner, and this indeed upon and into the most present, internal, self-existing, Personal, natural, inconceivable, self-sufficient, infinite, and perfect being; what is shared with creatures, however, takes its origin from the eternal, infinite goodness of God. The scholars say that creatures flow, as if in a circle, from the end back to their beginning. For just as the outpouring of creatures within the Godhead <note>original: "Gottheit"</note> is the origin of the creatures, so too are they led back again to God. Yet there is some difference between the sharing of creatures and the sharing of God; for because the creature is a separate and divided being, its sharing is also separate and divided. When a fleshly father begets a son, he shares something of his substance with him, but not himself entirely, because he has a separate being; but the sharing of God is all the more internal and heartfelt the more excellent the good—namely, He Himself—is. Because He then surpasses all goods in an infinite way, it is necessary that the communication of His substance correspond entirely, which cannot happen without the communication of the essence, or the outpouring according to the properties of the Persons <note>Referring to the three Persons of the Trinity.</note>; here you can behold, with the clarified eye of reason, the purest goodness of the highest good, which in its essence is the present and actual origin of loving itself in a natural and voluntary way; thus you see

<column-break/>

without doubt the most excellent and transcendent outpouring of the Word <note>The Logos or Son.</note> from the Father, from whose generation and speaking all things spring forth; you also see in the highest good and in the highest outpouring within the Godhead the most holy Trinity <note>original: "Dreyfaltigkeit"</note>: the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Since the highest outpouring then springs from the highest essential goodness, it follows from this that in the highest Trinity there is the highest and (so to speak) most compatible co-essentiality <term>co-essentiality: "mitwesenheit," the state of sharing the same divine essence or substance</term>, or communion of substance, as well as the highest equality and unity of being, which the Persons have in the most lovely communication, as one undivided substance and unseparated power of the three Divine Persons. 
At this, the Maiden cried out: "Ah, I swim in the Godhead no differently than an atom <note>The text says "At-", likely "Atömlein," a common mystical metaphor for a tiny speck of dust dancing in a sunbeam.</note> flies through the air."

the Trinity of the Divine Persons can exist with the unity of the essence cannot be said with words; yet, as much as can be understood, *St. Augustine* <note>A 4th-century Doctor of the Church whose writings on the Trinity were foundational.</note> says that in the Godhead the Father is the beginning of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. *St. Dionysius* <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century mystical theologian.</note> says that the outflow of the Godhead is in the Father, who in a natural way communicates to the unspeakable Word, which is the Father's Son; and that He communicates Himself lovely through the generosity of the will to the Son, and in turn the Son pours Himself out into the Father through the clarity of the will, so that the Father loves the Son and the Son loves the Father; this is a reciprocal love and is called the Holy Spirit. ->of the Blessed Henry Suso.<-

...where he says: In the outpouring of the Word from the heart of the Father, reason requires that God the Father contemplates Himself in His understanding and perceives the Divine essence entirely; for if the Divine essence were not presented to the Father’s understanding, then the received Word could not be God, but would be a creature, which however is false. Here there is unity of essence and Trinity of Person. For certain proof of this distinction, the high-flying eagle John <note>John the Evangelist is traditionally symbolized by the eagle because his Gospel "soars" to the heights of divine theology.</note> says: John 1 <note>original: "Ioan. 1"</note>, "The Word was in the beginning with God." Regarding the procession of the Holy Spirit, it is to be known that God the Father always clearly beholds and knows Himself through His understanding, and through this knowledge presents Himself, and this is the Word, or the Son of God; and in that the Father knows Himself most perfectly in all blessedness, He loves Himself and His Son with infinite love; with that same love the Son loves the Father, and the love of both these is the Holy Spirit, who is indeed distinct in Person, but is of one essence in the Godhead with the Father and the Son. Now, when the Word of God goes forth from the Father’s sight according to the form of nature with distinction of Person, this outflow from the Father is called the birth; but when this outflow occurs under the name of the will and of love, from whence the third Person in the Godhead proceeds from the outflow of love, from the Father...

<column-break/>

...and goes out from the deep abyss of His express Image, then it can be called neither the Son nor a born Person. But when love occurs in a rational or spiritual way within the will itself, as an affection or bond of love in the lover toward the beloved, the outpouring of the will belongs to the third Person, who is Love and is called the Holy Spirit. Here, the human being is changed by the Divine light in such a secret and hidden way that no one but an experienced person can notice it. The Maiden <note>The "Maiden" is a character representing the soul seeking wisdom.</note> said: This is truly a heartfelt and Catholic teaching; but there are some of such subtle understanding who deny all these things mentioned here about God, and imagine that to one who desires and loves the highest perfection, God Himself is a harmful and hindering means; for such a person must set aside God, the spirit, and appearances, and betake themselves only to the bright-shining truth, which they imagine they have grasped.

The Servant <note>The "Servant" is Henry Suso's persona.</note> answers: This is an open error; therefore avoid it and follow the Catholic faith. Commonly we understand God as a Lord and Creator of all things, who lets no evil go unpunished and no good work unrewarded; so then God is terrifying to sinners, as can be read in Job: *I always feared God like the surging waters.* <note>original: "Ich förchtet Gott allzeit / wie die auffwallende wäſſer." Referencing Job 31:23.</note> Others serve God out of hope for reward, and to them God is the most generous Lord, who can reward everything richly. But whoever is well-practiced in virtues, has rooted out all vices which God hates through frequent mortification, and serves God out of pure, fervent love, he loves God...
