For such a person does not honor God in that [servile] manner, but rather loves Him as his most beloved friend, and is freed from the servile fear of which Paul says in Romans 8 <note>original: "Rom. 8"</note>: "You have not received a spirit of slavery, that you should fear again." Thus, God remains the God and Lord of such a <term>God-conformed</term><note>German: "Gottgleichförmigen" - describing a person whose will and nature have been aligned with God's.</note> human being, yet he does not honor Him in such a tangible or external way, because he has stepped closer to Him through love. 

How this same spirit must be laid aside, I will likewise explain: when someone at the beginning of his conversion perceives himself to be a creature made of body and soul, he renounces the body and all sensuality, joins himself to the spirit, and subjects the flesh to it. All his inward activity is then a contemplation of how he may reach the <term>supersubstantial</term><note>German: "vberwesentlichen" - referring to a reality that exists beyond the level of created beings or "substance."</note> spirit, take hold of it, and unite his spirit with that one. Such people are called "hidden saints." 

But whoever has practiced this for a long time, and the supersubstantial spirit draws him, and yet he cannot reach it, then he feels his own powerlessness, which comes from himself. He then surrenders and gives himself over entirely to the Divine power. In turning away from himself, he turns toward the Divine power with contempt for himself and his sensuality, and places himself into the immeasurability of the Highest Being. In this retreating, the spirit as it were forgets itself and loses itself, as Paul says in Galatians 2 <note>original: "Gal. 2"</note>: "I live, but now not I," and Christ Himself speaks in Matthew 5 <note>original: "Matt. 5"</note>: "Blessed are the poor in spirit." Thus the spirit remains as far as its essence is concerned, but retreats in regard to the properties of sensuality. I also wish to explain the difference between the right truth

<column-break/>

and uncertain appearances. The unmediated contemplation of the simple Godhead is nothing other than certain and indubitable truth; and every appearance, the more it is free of rational forms and the more it is similar to pure contemplation, the more <unclear>glorious</unclear> <note>OCR clipped: "herzliche" reconstructed as "herrlicher"</note> it is. 

Some had visions in order to <unclear>prophesy</unclear> <note>OCR clipped: "vmb zu sagen" - likely "about future things"</note>, such as Jeremiah and others; similar appearances still often happen to the intimate friends of God, sometimes while they are awake, sometimes in <unclear>sleep</unclear> <note>OCR clipped: reconstructed as "schlaff"</note>, in silence, and in the withdrawal of the <unclear>outer</unclear> <note>OCR clipped: reconstructed as "eusserlicher"</note> senses. A Teacher says that angels appear to some more often in sleep than when they are awake, because in sleep they are less burdened with many external <unclear>affairs</unclear> <note>OCR clipped: reconstructed as "geschäfften"</note> than when they are awake. 

However, regarding whether the appearances occurring in sleep are to be held as true—like those of King Pharaoh concerning the seven fat and seven lean oxen, and similar dreams mentioned in Holy Scripture—it is to be noted that they sometimes deceive and sometimes are in accordance with the truth. It is said of Saint Augustine that he heard from his mother <note>Saint Monica</note> that such grace had been granted to her by God; whenever she saw something in her sleep, God had simultaneously given her the discernment to easily distinguish whether it was a common and worthless dream, or whether it was a legitimate vision. Whoever has obtained this grace from God can judge more certainly and easily in this matter, and he alone can express it who receives it.

# On the Highest Retreat of a Loving Soul or Spirit.

## The 20th Chapter.

The Maiden said: I desire to know nothing more, and to be instructed from Holy Scripture, than in what manner the reason of a well-practiced person should aim for the highest goal in the infinitely deep abyss, so that this rich experience may agree with the Scripture.

To this, the Servant gave her a rational answer from Holy Scripture to this effect, concerning the secret understanding; such an excellent person pays heed in simple stillness to the meaningful word of our Savior, where He says: John 12 <note>original: "Joan.12"</note>: "Where I am, there also shall my servant be." Now, whoever sets before himself for imitation that hard word, "where," which the Son of God endured while dying on the Cross, then it is possible—indeed, according to His promise, it is certain—that such a person may feel the lovely "Where" of the Son's Divinity in a rational and most blessed manner in time and in eternity, more or less, and enjoy it as much as possible. But where is the lovely "Where" of the Divine Word? In the <term>exemplary light</term><note>German: "Ebenbildlichen liecht" - In Rhenish mysticism, this refers to the eternal prototypes or "ideas" of all things as they exist within the Divine Mind.</note> of the Divine Unity, which according to its unspeakable name is "nothing" <note>This refers to "negative theology," the idea that God is so far beyond human concepts that He cannot be described as a "thing" or any specific being.</note>; according to the turning inward, it is an essential rest and silence; according to the inward-remaining outflow, it is the Trinity of Persons; according to its 

<column-break/>

property, it is a light unto itself; according to its uncreated power, it is a being that brings forth all things, where the spirit loses itself and, as far as its own activity is concerned, is annihilated; this is the highest goal and the infinite "Where," in which, so to speak, the spirituality of all spirits ceases, and in which having lost oneself constitutes eternal salvation and bliss. So that you may understand it better, know that in the exemplary light of Divine Unity there is an inwardly springing fountainhead of the personal outflow from the eternal Godhead; for the Trinity of Persons is Unity in nature, and the Unity of nature is in the Trinity of Persons. The Unity works through the Trinity, and the Trinity has its power in the Unity, as Saint Augustine <note>original: "H. Augustinus"</note> almost says: the Trinity of Persons encompasses within itself the Unity, or its natural being; therefore each Person is GOD, and the Godhead is Unity according to nature. The Unity, however, appears clearly in the Trinity; but the Trinity, as it is drawn inward, appears purely in the Unity, as the Unity has purely embraced the Trinity within itself. The Father is the origin of the Son; the Son comes from the Father according to the distinction of the Person,

This "death" of the spirit consists in this: that in its departure, it feels no distinction in its own essence; yet, after its departure or outflowing, it maintains a distinction according to the Trinity of Persons and allows all things to be with distinction as they are, as the Servant of Wisdom <note>Suso's frequent name for himself in his writings.</note> has explained in detail in the *Little Book of Truth*.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the Maiden and the Servant (the author, Henry Suso), moving from the theoretical description of the spirit's "annihilation" in God to the practical and scriptural basis for such a state. It specifically draws upon the "Apophatic" or "Negative" theology of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite.</meta>

-># Addition of several high questions<-

There is one more thing to note here: namely, that in the aforementioned withdrawal of the spirit, a simple light shines forth from the Divine Unity. The three Divine Persons send this light upon the pure substance of the human spirit; and from the radiance of this light, the spirit withdraws from itself and the operation of its own powers. This happens when the spirit, in its innermost part, has withdrawn outside of itself into the unrecognizable Godhead, and has lost itself in the most restful silence of the most radiant Godhead and the simple Unity. In this *Where* <note>original: "Ubi." In medieval philosophy, "Ubi" (where) refers to the category of place or location; here it refers to a spiritual state beyond physical space.</note> that knows no intermediary, consists the highest Blessedness.

**The Maiden says:** In what way shall we arrive there?

**The Servant answers:** Of this, **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century Christian philosopher whose writings on "mystical darkness" deeply influenced medieval mysticism.</note> writes to **Timothy** in the following way:

> But you, my dearest Timothy, exercise yourself diligently in beholding the secret things; leave the senses and the intellectual activities, and all recognizable things—that which is, and that which is not—

<column-break/>

> and so that you may be united with Him who is above all being and surpasses all knowledge, attend secretly with all your strength to yourself. For when you withdraw from yourself and from all things, free, bare, and pure, you will flee unhindered to the supersubstantial <note>original: "vberwesentlichen." This refers to God being "beyond" the category of "being" or "essence" as humans understand it.</note> radiance of the Divine darkness.

A little before this, he says:

> O supersubstantial Trinity, venerable in Godhead and goodness, overseer of Divine and Christian Wisdom, lead and guide us to the unknown, most brightly shining and highest peak of the secret conversations <note>original: "gesprächen," referring to mystical discourse or communion.</note>, where the simple, bare, and unchangeable mystery of the Godhead is opened and discovered according to the over-shining and overflowing darkness of the silence that teaches in secret. In the midst of the darkness, that which is invisible and cannot be touched shines most heartily; with the most excellent radiance, it fills the eyes of the spirits—which are indeed incorporeal.

***

# Concluding speech and explanation of all that has been mentioned
## and cited.

### The 21st Chapter.

**The Maiden says:** You speak indeed from your own experience, and are well-taught in Holy Scripture, according to the Catholic faith, concerning the simple Godhead and the outflow and return of the spirit. But because your words are very dark <note>meaning "obscure" or "difficult to understand."</note>, I would like to have them explained to me according to your understanding through some parables <note>original: "gleichnuß," meaning similes, metaphors, or parables used to explain spiritual truths.</note>, and to have what has been said at length briefly summarized, so that it might stick all the more firmly to my weak

<column-break/>

memory.

**The Servant answers:** How can one represent in a form that which is without form? And how can one explain what surpasses all sense and human reason? For every parable that one gives is infinitely more unlike than it is like. Nevertheless, so that forms may be excluded by forms <note>A mystical teaching: using a metaphor to replace a physical image, eventually leading the mind to discard all images.</note>, I will, through several parables—as much as can happen—[speak] of the aforementioned...

# Of the Blessed Henry Suso.

To say something briefly about the aforementioned high matters—namely, how they are to be understood. A wise teacher says that God, according to His Godhead, is like a great circle whose center is called **Everywhere**, but whose circumference is **Nowhere**. <note>This famous definition, often attributed to Hermes Trismegistus or Alan of Lille, describes God as being both infinitely present and beyond all boundaries.</note> Now consider, and imagine: when someone throws a large stone into standing water, it immediately creates a circle in the water. That same circle, through its force, creates another, and this one a third; and the circles extend according to the strength of the first throw. Indeed, the force of the throw could be so great that it creates more circles than the water could contain. 

Let the first circle be presented as an example, so that through it you may understand the almighty power of the Divine Nature, which is infinite in the **Father**. Out of Himself, He creates a circle equal to Himself—namely, the second Person, who is the **Son**. And from these two circles comes the third, which is the **Holy Spirit**. In this unfathomable abyss of Divine Nature, the Father speaks and brings forth the **Word** <note>The "Word" (Logos) refers to the second person of the Trinity, the Son, through whom all things were created.</note>, the second Person in the Godhead, who nonetheless remains inwardly within the Divine Essence. This Word has taken on human nature. If one wishes to describe this through a likeness, take the form of a human, from whose inward parts or heart an identical form breaks forth, and is constantly led back again to its origin. 

This spiritual and <term>supersubstantial</term> <note>original: "vberwesentliche." A key term in medieval mysticism meaning "beyond all being" or "above all essence."</note> birth of the Word is the complete cause and manner of the creation of all spirits and all things. The highest and supersubstantial Spirit has made man so noble that He shines upon him out of His eternal Godhead; and this is the

<column-break/>

**Image of God** in the reason, which is also eternal. From the great circle, which signifies the eternal Godhead (to speak by way of likeness), spring small circles which, in an unequal way, can indicate the high courage of their understanding. However, because many turn away from this dignity, they defile the Image of God within them and surrender themselves to bodily and worldly lusts. When they cling to these with great desire, they are overtaken by sudden death. 

But whoever is wise betakes himself with this gleaming <term>soul-spark</term> <note>original: "Seelen füncklein." In Rhineland mysticism, this refers to the innermost, divine core of the human soul that remains uncorrupted and capable of direct union with God.</note> to that which is steadfast and eternal, from whence he took his origin; he renounces all transitory creatures and clings to the Truth alone. So that you may also learn how the spirit shall return to God, mark my words:

**Firstly**, he must apply himself to turn away bravely and nimbly from the pleasures of the world and from all vices; and through constant prayer, through laudable and holy exercises by which he makes the flesh subject to the spirit, he must turn toward God.

**Secondly**, he shall give himself up freely and magnanimously to accept all adversity sent to him by God or by creatures.

**Thirdly**, he shall press the **Suffering of Christ**, His teaching, His conversation, and His most gentle life upon his heart, setting Him before himself as an example and for imitation. 

Afterward, he shall put aside outer business, betaking himself to peaceful silence and to the silent rest of the soul. He should do this with strong **resignation**, just as if he had died to himself, so that he no longer looks upon himself, but only

<meta>The catchword "die" (the) at the bottom indicates the start of the next page's first sentence.</meta>

### Addition of Several High Questions

...seek the honor and the praise of the Heavenly Father and His Son / and will behave humbly and lovingly toward all people / toward enemies as well as friends. A person devoted to such practices is deprived of the working of the outward senses / which were previously very busy with outward things / and the spirit attains a falling away from the higher powers / according to their natural working / and tastes something supernatural. Now when the spirit loses itself after the clinging of nature / it goes further inward / and through the circle / which signifies the eternal Godhead / it attains rich perfection; but the spirit's wealth is contained within its own form / in that it rises without the burden of sin through Divine power in its enlightened understanding; where it experiences the everlasting influence of Divine comfort / and can thus weigh things wisely / and carry them out reasonably / as the manner / and its distinction requires / and thus stands orderly freed through the Son in the Son / yet it still sees outward things in their own nature, and contemplates them wisely / and with distinction. This can be called a departure of the spirit / because it transcends all time and place / and has withdrawn into God through inward, loving contemplation. Whoever can free themselves further in this case / and penetrate deeper / and whom God wishes to help through powerful ecstasy in a special and excellent way / as happened to St. Paul / and others / as St. Bernard <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot and influential mystic often cited by Suso.</note> testifies / and could be proven / there the created spirit is seized by the supersubstantial <note>original: *vberwesentlichen* – a term in German mysticism describing God’s being as "beyond essence" or "above all being."</note> Spirit of God / and is raptured to where it cannot reach through its own power; during this ecstasy it loses all 

<column-break/>

forms / and all multiplicity / forgets itself and all things / so that outside of God it thinks neither of itself / nor anything else / and is sunk with the three most holy Persons <note>The Holy Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note> into the deep abyss of the Godhead / where it tastes its Blessedness according to the highest purity; Here there is no more intention to act / or to exert oneself / because the beginning and the end have become one / and the spirit / in that it has departed from itself / is united with God. But whether the departure of the spirit / which also happens to people in this temporal life / is permanent / or impermanent / or how one is raptured more or less into time above time / and departs from oneself / and is placed into the (One) that knows no forms / has been sufficiently explained.

Here consider, my daughter / that the explicit images and words / which have been brought forth through parables / are as unlike the unimagined truth / as a black Moor is to the brightly shining sun. <note>This was a common rhetorical trope in the 14th–16th centuries used to illustrate the absolute greatest possible contrast between two things.</note>

he wrote to her in his last letter in the following manner: "Well then, my daughter, renounce all creatures <note>In mystical theology, "creatures" refers to all created things as opposed to the Creator.</note> and cease from inquiring further in the future; listen yourself to what the LORD speaks within you; you have more reason to rejoice because that which is denied to many has been granted to you, and even though you have endured heavy labor and pain because of it, they have now vanished. ### The Little Book of the Nine Rocks.
# OF DR. HENRY SUSO,
->Who is renowned for the holiness of his life.<-
### Preface to the Little Book of the Nine Rocks.

I ask all people to diligently observe the heartfelt and memorable instructions of this book. For whoever reads this book diligently from beginning to end, or hears it read, will be moved, as it were, toward improvement—unless it be that he willfully chooses to perish in his vices. If he is pious and desires to be converted to God, he will be clearly instructed here—provided he is willing to take note—by what path he should journey to his origin and beginning, namely to God. For here one can easily learn where one is stuck, by what one is hindered, and what keeps him imprisoned and entangled. Thus, this book is written for everyone in common, whether they are entangled in sins or appear to shine with excellent holiness, which they will come to understand during the reading. It comprises four parts: the first, how a <term>Friend of God</term> <note>The "Friends of God" (Gottesfreunde) were a 14th-century mystical movement of clergy and laity who sought a deep, internal union with God.</note> was driven by Divine wisdom to write this book; the second, how strange visions and appearances were presented to him; the third, how he also clearly saw and recognized the vices of those who profess the faith of Christ; the fourth, how he saw a high mountain, divided by nine rocks, upon which rocks the Christians dwelt, each of which was higher than the other, until one reached the summit of the mountain.

# Of Emperors and Kings.

### The 15th Chapter.

**God.** Look now at those who live in the highest worldly dignity, namely Emperors and Kings, also their wives, their splendor, and pride. In former times, when one was elected, he resisted with great diligence, because out of humility he considered himself unworthy of it. But if one was elected Roman Emperor, he accepted the administration of the Empire indeed with the highest humility and fear; he held himself therefore as a servant of Christ, surrendered to Him his body, soul, wealth, means, and honor, and because he relied on the help of God, he endeavored to bring about peace and unity in the Church, and fought and struggled

in a humble, lowly <note>original: "niderträchtigen" — in this medieval context, the word signifies being low-positioned or humble of heart, rather than the modern German meaning of "despicable" or "vile."</note>, obedient, and resigned ground of the soul, of which they—just like others—possess little.

# Of Dukes, Counts, and Barons.

### The 16th Chapter.

**God.** See also what kind of life the
Dukes, Counts, Barons, <note>original: "Freyherren" — literally "Free Lords," a rank of nobility that held their land directly from the Emperor.</note> and
their wives lead. In former times they gave
their body and life for the honor of God in
danger, so that the Church and their sub-
jects might live in peace and rest;
there was also a Divine bravery in them,
united with honor; they did not
lack in human diligence;
their spouses were provided with such good manners
and humility, and of such an unblamable
life, that whoever was with either them
or their husbands was encouraged to the
improvement of life and was made to blush with shame
at the thought of committing anything against
decency and good manners. There was in the

<column-break/>

Princely women no insolence, pride, <note>original: "hoffart" — a specific term for sinful arrogance or vanity, often listed as the first of the seven deadly sins.</note>

oppress their subjects against

own souls—to the shame and injustice
of God.

**Man.** Lord, I pray thee, have
mercy on them.

# Of Craftspeople.

## The 19th Chapter.

**God.** Behold also the dangerous life
of the craftspeople <term>craftspeople: artisans and skilled manual laborers, such as weavers, smiths, or masons</term>, how greed

<column-break/>

# Of Peasants.

## The 20th Chapter.

**God.** In this wretched and sorrowful
time, the peasants in the villages also
live just like cattle, without any fear of
God; they cast all good and honorable
customs to the wind; they obey and
follow their lusts with all their might.
They are entirely cunning and proud,
possessing an evil spirit and heart,
so that the hellish enemies <note>original: "höllische Feind" — a common reference to demons or the devil.</note> rule over
and possess them with all their power.
Certainly, if God were not hindered by
the prayers of His friends, He would
treat them quite differently because
of their godlessness.

<column-break/>

**Man.** Most gracious God, if my
prayer might have any influence with
you, I would ask you to spare them.
**God.** I endure their life as much as I
can, but if I am forced, I will let all
their affairs go to ruin. In former times,
one saw such piety, simplicity, discipline,
and humility in them that God was
gracious to them in every way.
**Man.** Lord, I have nothing else to
say, except that you, for the sake of your
goodness, should have mercy on your
Church.

# Of Worldly Women.

## The 21st Chapter.

**God.** Look now at where the women have gone, and where their modesty has fled. See how they trample all fear of God and womanly modesty underfoot; for in these dangerous times they are much more shameless and willful than the men. Yet I would not have this understood of pious and honorable women (for many are still found who lead an honorable and virtuous life), but I speak only of those who are devoted to this world—whether they be spiritual <note>original: "geist." (geistlich) — referring here to nuns or women in religious orders who have become worldly.</note> or secular—who seek to please people in words, works, clothes, and manners more than God, and who also cast their time, heart, and mind upon creatures <note>In medieval theology, "creatures" refers to anything created (people, objects, status) as opposed to the Creator.</note>. Such women are undoubtedly nothing other than murderers' dens <note>original: "Mördergruben" — a biblical allusion suggesting they are places where souls are spiritually "slain" through temptation.</note>, and even though the goodness of God suffers them, bears with them, and looks through His fingers <note>An idiom meaning to overlook or tolerate something for a time.</note>, it still avails nothing. Meanwhile, they want to be regarded and held as honorable women, though they often stink more filthily before God than common harlots; for the latter live in sin with some fear, but not like the former with audacity and stubbornness; certainly they are much more pleasing to the devils than the common women, because they [the devils] obtain greater gain and profit from them. See how filthily and shamelessly they go into the assembly of men; if common women had gone about so exposed in former times, the honorable

<column-break/>

women would have been ashamed from their hearts. See them so unrestrained above and below, and walking about so exposed that they should rightly be ashamed before the eyes of all men. Look at their clothing, their wantonness <note>original: "geilheit" — in this context, it implies a mixture of excessive luxury, physical lust, and social провокация.</note> in walking, gestures, words, works, and their whole life among men, their willfulness in their eyes and all external senses? What is now of discipline and womanly modesty? Believe me, many women are found who daily commit probably a hundred mortal sins, and yet they wish to be held for honorable matrons, and they are not ashamed of those sins. Therefore, hold it for certain: when a male person sees such an unrestrained and wanton woman, who walks so shamefully, and as it were bare and naked before his and all other men’s faces, whatever he then thinks to himself—which often happens—that if he could only have her, he would fulfill his will with her: as often as such occurs with a deliberate mind, so many mortal sins he commits, even if the deed and the work itself do not follow; hold for certain, I say, that such a woman partakes in all these sins and is guilty of them, because with her frivolous clothing and the aforementioned sins, she gives the first cause and occasion for it, whether it happens in the churches, on the streets, or elsewhere. If a man is kindled to lust through such an occasion...

# The Book of the Blessed Henry Suso

[human] nature is so weakened, corrupted, and destroyed, and the majority of people—not only those living in the state of marriage, but also others, such as priests, monks, laity, and cloistered persons of both sexes—are full of lust and unchastity. This is so pervasive that few remain who are not stained in some way; if not in the actual deed, then in other ways, such as through conversation or through inner or outer efforts and trouble taken to please others. Certainly, if God wanted to destroy the world because of sin, as He did before in the time of Noah (Genesis 7), He would have to do so daily; perhaps some omen of this will soon come to pass. 

For a few years now, people have been lovingly warned and exhorted by God through poisonous diseases <note>Likely a reference to the Black Death or similar recurring plagues of the 14th century.</note>, hunger, war, and other plagues. However, little benefit or improvement has followed, for the Church shows itself so ungrateful and forgetful, as if these things had happened a thousand years ago. If they do not improve their lives, Almighty God will finally, in His righteous judgment, grow weary and allow people to murder one another. For everyone strives to surpass the other; all are inclined toward murder and killing. Also, pride and arrogance have gained such the upper hand that sins are no longer even considered sins. In former times, people were not as godless as they are now. It is only right that people should surrender themselves to Divine Love, for when death is near, the evil spirit applies all his diligence to bring a person to destruction. He places their whole past life before their eyes with such terror that many 

<column-break/>

of them despair in this state, even those who were otherwise of good hope. But God is so angered by others that they remain in the greatest pains until the Last Day <note>The Day of Judgment.</note>, and they do not know whether they dwell in Hell or in Purgatory. These are the people who, hardened in their wickedness, postpone the improvement of their lives until the moment of death, and only then, for the first time, feel a slight sorrow for their sins. 

These, as has been said, God disciplines with such great wrath that He does not wish to remember them, and He does not allow His friends <note>A reference to the "Friends of God" (*Gottesfreunde*), a medieval mystical movement to which Suso belonged.</note> to pray for them. Believe me, people will be dealt with far more terribly than many of them imagine. The evil spirits strive with all diligence and all their strength to bring a person to a fall at the very last. Whatever strength they possess, however, has been given to them by the sins of humanity. Do you want to know what brought the Jews to destruction?

**The Person.** I would very much like to know.

**God.** Greed and their secret sins destroyed them. Now, if God also wanted to root out the Christians because of their secret and open sins, He would have nothing else to do but allow them to be murdered and destroyed, which might perhaps happen soon. See now how people are struck with the arrows of lust, unchastity, pride, and greed—vices which God hates most because they are the cause of hatred and envy, as well as all other vices. With these, cities and monasteries, secular and spiritual people, priests and laity, are filled, so that it is unnecessary to lay the blame from one to another, because each and every one is deserving of punishment. And when each...

## Short Preface to the Nine Rocks.

No one can reach God unless they possess <note>Or "attain a place upon."</note> one of these rocks. However, if one wishes to order their life so that they may behold the origin from which the noble soul sprang, they must have a courageous and undaunted heart and climb over all these rocks until they reach the highest. There, they will be instructed on where they must hasten. Praiseworthy is the one who does not fear to climb the mountain along with its many rocks, for in this life they will carry away the victory from all their enemies, and in the future life, the greatest dignity and glory.

# The Book of the Blessed Henry Suso

**Man.** Lord, I pray you: does this soul shine in its origin as I behold it now?

**God.** Rest assured that if God were to let you look upon such a soul as it is in its origin—namely, created according to the **Image of God**—your nature could neither endure it, nor could your senses grasp what it was. But now God has let you see such a beautiful soul so that you might express these visions in words and record them in writing for the benefit and warning of the Church.

**Man.** Thy will be done.

**God.** Open your inner eyes and look on high. Immediately, the man saw the mountain rising in such a way as if it wished to touch the heavens; it was so spread out that he could not oversee it with his sight. Upon the mountain, however, there were **nine rocks**, each one higher than the next, until one reached the peak of the mountain. These rocks were also very wide and broad, terrifying and wonderful to behold.

**Man.** Tell me, my Heart, <note>In Suso’s writing, "Heart" is an intimate address for the Divine or the personified Wisdom.</note> what does it mean that I see this terrifying mountain for a second time?

**God.** Behold what is upon the mountain and who dwells there.

**Man.** May it happen to me according to your pleasure. In that same moment, the man found himself upon the lowest rock, which was nevertheless so high that from it he could see the entire earth; at the same time, he saw a great net drawn and stretched through the whole world, except for the high mountain. Because he was frightened, he spoke to the Lord: "What does this mean?"

# Of Nine Rocks.

**Man.** Lord, will they attain salvation?

**God.** If they die without mortal sin <note>original: "Todsünd" — in medieval theology, a grave sin that "kills" the life of grace in the soul.</note>, they will be saved; however, they live in greater danger than they realize, for they persuade themselves that they can simultaneously obey and serve God and nature <note>In this context, "nature" refers to worldly or fleshly desires as opposed to the spirit.</note>, which is difficult, indeed almost impossible. They will hardly be able to persevere. But if they do persevere, they will indeed be saved, but they must endure great anxieties, terrifying pain, and the torments of Purgatory <note>original: "Fegfeuers"</note>. According to God's decree, they must remain there for as long a time until they have atoned for even the slightest transgression most precisely and perfectly, and have made full satisfaction. For nothing committed here is so small that it must not be paid for there. But when they reach Heaven after suffering these torments, they will receive a small reward compared to other pious people, because their labor, practice, and love for God were very slight. Meanwhile, the man saw many of them being pushed down from the rock in great haste and falling under the net.

**Man.** Lord, what does it mean that these are thrown down so quickly?

**God.** They have consented to mortal sin, and the rock cannot bear them. He also saw, in many places, certain people tearing themselves out of the net who were black or lead-colored, as if they had lain dead under the earth for a long time.

**Man.** What does this mean?

**God.** These are the people who lay under the net and the snares in mortal sin under the power of the devils, but have now received repentance and sorrow; therefore

<column-break/>

the evil spirits no longer have power over them, but must release them from the snares.

**Man.** What does their blackish, leaden color mean?

**God.** Their repentance or pain has not yet been made perfect through confession, penance, and satisfaction <note>original: "Beicht, buß, vnd gnugthuung" — the three traditional steps of the Sacrament of Penance.</note>; once this occurs, they will be like the inhabitants of this rock. Furthermore, he saw upon the mentioned rock many people in the flower of their youth—namely, youths, maidens, men, priests, laypeople, monks, nuns, and of every rank and order, none excepted—who all at once threw themselves with joy into the nets and snares.

**Man.** What does it mean that these enter the net with such haste?

**God.** Here you must remember the parable seen above regarding the fish, which fell from their highest origin down the mountain, drifted through the whole world, and were caught and entangled in many nets along the way. For through that parable, God intended to signify those people whom you see here running under the net. For when they come to full understanding and ought to turn back to their beginning, they obey their own nature like the foolish fish; and with all diligence and deliberate will, they place themselves under the nets of this deceitful world, which is full of the devils' snares. The devils strive with all effort and labor to drive people into these, for there are countless numbers of them in the world.

**Man.** Lord, as I see it, no one will escape these snares except one who turns away from them with a brave spirit <note>original: "tapffern gemüht"</note>.

**Man.** Lord, does the evil spirit still have power over those who dwell on the lowest rock?

**God.** He has no power against them unless they themselves wish it, so long as they keep themselves from mortal sins <note>original: "Todtsünden" — sins that "kill" the life of grace in the soul</note>. Yet he has good confidence, because he keeps them busy with worldly affairs and scatters their thoughts. He also notices that they are inclined toward worldly honors and prosperity. And although they do not wish to commit any mortal sin, they are nevertheless not far from the snare <note>original: "garn" — literally a net or yarn, used here as a metaphor for a trap</note>. Their life and actions hang in great danger, because the hellish enemy strives with great diligence to bring them into his ropes. For he holds them back with a hook <note>original: "Angel" — a fishing hook or a baiting device</note> so that they do not find the right road to their origin <note>meaning their source in God</note>, but rather deviate from it.

**Man.** Lord, what kind of hook is this? What kind of life do these people lead, and what is their nature?

<column-break/>

they imagine they can serve God and nature <note>original: "natur" — referring here to the "lower nature" or fleshly desires rather than the physical world</note> at the same time, which is nevertheless very dangerous and uncertain. They indeed wish to be pious people and commit no mortal sin, but only so that they might be very dear to God because their own life pleases them. Therefore, they strive after no more perfect life, but wish to die as they are, because they commit no mortal sin. If someone tells them their life is in danger and wants to compel them to tame their nature, they do not obey him, but rather the evil spirit, who leads them by the rope of their own evil nature and for whom they are diligent to live. For they look only to themselves and act according to their own will, imagining their life and manner to be entirely safe, though they hang in the greatest danger because they are near the snare.

**Man.** When they die, do they also attain salvation?

**God.** Certainly, provided they die without mortal sin. However, they must endure unspeakable pain in Purgatory <note>original: "Fegfeyr" — the place of purification</note> because of all the delights and lusts of nature which they indulged in without necessity. Believe me, if someone were aware of the punishment one must endure for the slightest sin committed against God or the pleasure of nature—before committing even a venial sin <note>original: "lästliche sünd"</note>—he would much rather have his head struck off every day or suffer some other death. Yet the aforementioned people are not only visited with these pains, but must also be deprived of eternal bliss <note>original: "seligkeit" — the joy of heaven</note> for a time because of the voluntary pleasure of their nature.

In this way, he brings them into a spiritual pride <note>original: "geistliche hoffart" — a state where a person becomes proud of their own religious practice or perceived holiness</note> which they themselves do not recognize, and they imagine themselves to be so wise that they need no other counsel or help; thus, he finally causes them to be satisfied with this life and to wish to die in it.
**Man.** Yet they have surrendered and subjected themselves to the friends of God <note>A term for a loose network of 14th-century mystics (Gottesfreunde) who sought a deeper interior life</note>; why then do these friends not teach them the right and nearest way?
**God.** The friends of God well know and recognize the hook which has been cast to them by the Devil; but they fear that, if they were to deal with them somewhat more harshly, they might fall entirely into the net and become worse than before. If they

<column-break/>

remain upon this rock, they will be much dearer and more pleasing to God than the inhabitants of the lowest rock, because they attack their nature more harshly and strictly, and therefore are closer to their beginning.
**Man.** My Heart <note>A common mystical term of endearment for God</note>, must they also one day endure the pain of Purgatory?
**God.** Yes, certainly; and indeed they will receive great and heavy torments, but nonetheless lesser than the inhabitants of the first rock, for which they shall also be partakers of a greater reward. Hold this for certain: whoever desires to come to his origin must climb over all the rocks of this mountain until he reaches its summit.
**Man.** My Heart, I know that you are so kind, faithful, and merciful that if someone were to trust you with their whole heart, and with an undaunted heart renounce all creatures, choose you as a friend, turn to you with all their strength, and cling to you, they should always enjoy your help and with all speed climb over all these rocks.
**God.** It is so. Whoever is of a bold and manly spirit, and also of a steadfast will, God stands by him without any doubt and accompanies him further; but there are few of those at this time.
**Man.** Lord, have mercy.

## Of the Fourth Rock.

### The 26th Chapter.

**God.** Look toward the height. The man saw some climbing from the third to the fourth rock, but they soon fell back, and some even fell under the net. And as the man looked down, one fled quickly toward it, climbed the mountain with great speed, and in a single run reached the fourth rock.

**Man.** Lord, what does this mean?
**God.** Those from the fourth rock who fell under the net signify those who have ascended to the fourth rock with rigorous exercises and much diligence; but when they should have climbed ever higher, they allowed themselves to be overcome by the hellish enemy through their own flesh.

They are indeed often tested to see if they wish to resign themselves, but it does no good; for when the light of resignation is offered to them by God, immediately Satan casts the hook of their exercises—which they perform out of their own judgment and self-interest—to them. With the cord of their stubbornness <note>original: "eigensinnigkeit"</note>, he holds them back, with which they perform all their labor. For the cunning spirit is certain that if they were to give themselves over entirely and submit to those in God's stead who are better acquainted with the way of God, God would immediately grant them the fruit and taste of their great exercises and labor, and would lead them through secret, previously hidden, and unknown ways.

**Man.** These people please me very well, because they are pleasant and lovely to look upon.

**God.** It is indeed true; yet they are easily moved to anger, and many also to other vices. Although they guard themselves according to their ability, they nonetheless occasionally become entangled in these things, and this is because they have not yet rightly resigned, have not yet died away <note>The concept of "dying to the self" or "dying to the world" before physical death</note> entirely to worldly matters, and are not yet founded in true surrender. Yet, they are in greater friendship with God than all those before. But hold for certain that the others go by a far different path than the one they are traveling now.

**Human.** My heart and God, there must be very many of these people in our times.

**God.** How can there be many, when you yourself see how small the number is of those who, for the love and honor of God, are willing to renounce and deny these temporal, transitory, and natural things? When will they ever be persuaded to give up that which they have for that which is eternal, infinite, and inexpressible?

**Human.** The majority understand the instruction that all temporal things should be forsaken and denied in such a way as if they were to strip themselves entirely of temporal goods and possessions; for this reason, they are frightened.

**God.** Whoever desires to reach this **eighth rock** must unload all temporal goods that could create any hindrance between God and him—or must at the very least hold himself toward them in such a way that he accounts them as nothing, nor claims them as his own. Instead, he should use them to soar upward toward God rather than being hindered by them. He who, in the midst of his riches, looks not upon himself but upon the honor of God, will be given the necessary means of life by God; and whatever is left over, he gives it all back to God the Lord, to whom it actually belongs.

**Human.** I rejoice greatly, for I believe the inhabitants of this rock have reached their **origin**. <note>term: origin (original: "Ursprung") — In medieval German mysticism, this refers to the soul's return to its source in the Divine essence, moving beyond the "created" self.</note>

**God.** Not at all; rather, they are the closest of all those you have seen before. They are provided with more frequent and more radiant gifts of **grace** <note>original: "Gnaden gaaben"</note> than all the others, and great and rare things are shown to them by God, though still through images and forms.

<column-break/>

**Human.** What exists beyond these analogies, images, and forms?

**God.** Sometimes a small radiance from the **origin** is shown to these people, which they cannot depict with any form or express with words.

**Human.** I hope that these people will have nothing to atone for.

**God.** They still have something to suffer in **Purgatory**. <note>original: "Fegfeuer" — a place of purification after death.</note>

**Human.** What is that? And why do they still find it so difficult to reach their origin?

**God.** The evil spirit has fastened them with **two great hooks**, so that they do not escape out of his hands.

**Human.** What kind of hooks are they?

**God.** As has been said, a small radiance of the origin has appeared to them, which they have pursued with such desire to receive more and more; but this is not entirely helpful for reaching perfection, because they are still stained with a certain secret blemish of their **own will**, which they neither recognize nor wipe out.

**Human.** Which is the second hook?

**God.** God has led them on strange ways and shown them strange appearances under many different forms; upon these, they have placed their affection with a certain sense of **spiritual possessiveness**, <note>term: spiritual possessiveness (original: "eigenthümbligkeit") — The subtle sin of "owning" one's spiritual experiences or taking personal pride in God's gifts.</note> and they do not notice it themselves. But it is known to God the Lord. Nevertheless, He does not wish to withdraw this spiritual grace from them; rather, He spares them because He knows well the hidden "ground" in their soul which they themselves do not recognize. And this is the second hook with which they are held back by the Enemy, so that they do not reach their origin.

**God.** Look up now with joy.
The **Human** saw the ninth rock so high that he could hardly reach it with his sight, just as if he were looking at the highest heaven; he saw few go from the eighth to the ninth, and even if they reached its height, some fell back. They often exerted themselves to go up again, but fell back so often that barely three of those remaining seemed to stay; those who had fallen back were held almost for dead.

**Human.** Lord, <note>original: "Herz" — Literally "Heart," used here as an intimate, mystical form of address for God.</note> what does this fall mean, and why do so few remain here?

**God.** What is high and laborious is difficult to climb; because few in this life wish to stand in danger until death, few come here. When they see the **set-apart life**, <note>original: "abgeſonderte leben" — A life totally secluded from worldly concerns and dedicated to the Divine.</note> they fall back out of fear.

**Human.** My Lord, this grieves me from my heart.

**God.** Look up now with joy.
Amidst these words, he found himself led onto the ninth high, broad, awesome, and great rock, and it seemed

<column-break/>

to him that if all the aforementioned rocks were melted together, they would not be as high, large, broad, and beautiful as the ninth. Upon it indeed few dwelt, but they caused him greater joy than all the previous ones.

**Human.** Why does this so beautiful rock have so few inhabitants?

**God.** This rock was not created by God to be inhabited by few; know that here is the **gate** that leads to the **origin**, <note>term: origin (original: "vrsprung") — The primordial essence of God where the soul finds its ultimate home.</note> from whence all created things in Heaven and on Earth flow forth.

**Human.** Why do these people appear so weak on the outside and shine on the inside like **angelic spirits**? <note>original: "Engliſche geiſter" — In this archaic German context, "Englisch" refers to "Engel" (angels), not the English nation.</note>

**God.** It is no wonder that they have become weary and weak from climbing such high rocks; for all the blood and the marrow of their bones is dried up; therefore their powers are weak.

**Human.** How then can they remain in this life?

**Human.** I fear nothing, because you, my God, have suffered so much for my sake. My God, do with me, your most miserable creature, what pleases you in time and in eternity. After the human had thus **resigned** <term>Resigned: "Resignirt," a key term in Rhineland mysticism (Gelassenheit) meaning the total surrender of one's own will to God.</term> himself, the gate of the **Origin** <term>Origin: "vrsprung," the divine source from which the soul flows and to which it returns.</term> was immediately opened to him, and he saw his beginning; however, this vision lasted scarcely a moment. He pondered this earnestly within himself, and the more he thought, the less he could recognize what it had been. He thought to describe the vision he had held, but could neither express it in words nor compose it in writing. Later, he wanted to make it known through parables <note>original: "gleichnussen," meaning allegories or metaphorical comparisons.</note>, but likewise was not able to do so; he strove to reach it with his senses and reason, but had to surrender his understanding. He strove to recognize it properly, but the more he composed <note>original: "dichtet," meaning to mentally frame or poeticize.</note>, the lesser his knowledge became, for whatever he had otherwise heard or seen was not to be compared with this. There-

<column-break/>

-fore he said to the Lord: I am bewildered by your words, when you said I should behold and describe what cannot be written, since not even an angel can speak of it, nor does my understanding reach where I have been or what I saw; I am indeed full of joy, which I cannot withhold or hide.

**God.** The smallest joy that one feels in God is greater than if all worldly joy were struck together.

**Human.** Yet I wonder that my heart does not burst with joy; oh, may I ask you where I have been and what I saw? For I can neither express it with words nor describe it with a pen.

**God.** You have seen your **Origin**; but do not wonder that you are unable to express or describe it, for if a person were endowed with the reason and senses of all other people who have ever been on earth, they could not, by their own strength, grasp the slightest part of what you have seen. Therefore, do not strive to grasp such things, because it surpasses all understanding; for when you saw this, all creatures fell away from you, and the **Redeemer** <note>original: "Erlöser," referring to Jesus Christ.</note> himself gave himself to you as your food. You were in the school where the **Holy Spirit** is the schoolmaster; and when your soul entered this school, you saw everything filled with the writings of the true light and of **discretion** <term>Discretion: "bescheidenheit." In this mystical context, it refers to the spiritual gift of discernment or the humble awareness of the boundary between the Creator and the creature.</term>. Through this beholding, the soul was filled with inexpressible joy and, with great zeal and exultation, went out of itself into these writings, until, filled with the true light, [it attained] true discretion.

### Of the Nine Rocks

...done. In this school, such an abundance of love has been poured into your soul by the supreme Teacher that it filled even the body.

**Human.** As soon as I gazed upon the Origin, I felt such a wondrous, new, and inexpressible love in my soul that I would gladly have borne all the pain of all the souls in Purgatory <note>original: "Fegfewr"</note> so that they might be freed from their sufferings; such was my pity for them. In my nature, I felt such love—even though nature recoils in horror—that I became so enamored with your suffering and death that I sought and desired every trial, cross, and death for the honor and glory of your death. And if it were pleasing to you, I would suffer the trials, crosses, and pain of all people for the sake of all the sinners in the world.

**God.** Know that you have attained this love and this most glorious gift of grace in the most excellent school of the Holy Spirit.

**Human.** It would have been my highest joy, for your praise and honor, to bear the trials of all people.

**God.** Know that no one experiences such high grace from God except those who have reached this level <term>level: "staffel," literally a step or rung on a ladder, referring to the spiritual stages represented by the nine rocks.</term>.

**Human.** If it be your will, I would gladly suffer the pain of all the damned for all eternity for your honor, so that it might be known and revealed to all people what you have allowed me, an un-

<column-break/>

-worthy person, to see out of pure goodness.

**God.** Ah, if only the rest of humanity would bravely renounce their own will and manfully climb these nine rocks, obeying God in this matter; he would without doubt lead them with his help to where he has led you.

**Human.** I know of no person for whom I would not wish this from my heart, just as I do for myself, for I marvel at my own great joy.

**God.** Take care that you do not trust too much in this great grace; for when it pleases God, he will withdraw it all to himself again and leave you in such poverty and ignorance as if you had never received anything from God.

**Human.** Lord, do not take my words amiss; I am so in love with you that I believe you could do nothing, within all your power, that could be vexing to me. For everything will be acceptable to me; whether you give me something or take it away, it is equally dear and precious to me.

**God.** See that what happened to St. Peter <note>original: "H. **Human.** Lord, I surrender myself entirely to your goodness and mercy.

## He speaks further of the inhabitants of the ninth rock.

### Chapter 33.

**God.** Well then, behold once more all the rocks and the net <note>The "net" is a recurring mystical metaphor in this text representing the entrapments of the world or the reach of divine providence over humanity.</note> which is stretched across the entire world. The human looked beneath the net and there became aware of two people: one was as beautiful and radiant as an angel, but the other was as hideous and misshapen as the devil, though he still possessed the form of a human.

**Human.** My Lord <note>original: "Herz," literally "Heart," used here as an intimate address to God</note>, who are these people?

**God.** The black one, who is misshapen like the devil, was formerly an inhabitant of this rock, but he was cast out from it just like Lucifer. This happened because he took a vain pleasure in himself, spoke much of this to other people, and wished to be something and be esteemed of his own accord. But now he is the most foul creature in the world, because his teaching is stained with error and heresy <note>original: "Ketzerey"</note>, and for that reason, one must guard against him even more than against the devil. So many followed him under the net <note>original: "vnder dem Garn," referring to the mesh of the net</note> that it grieved this Human to the heart, because such a thing causes the greatest harm to Christians.

**Human.** How can one recognize these deceitful people?

**God.** Their teaching leads to a sweet, pleasant, soft, and delicate life, toward which nature is already inclined at this time.

**Human.** Who is the other one, so brightly shining under the net?

<column-break/>

**God.** He also saw his own origin and lived in this most lovely company of men, but out of great love and mercy toward his neighbor, he placed himself under the net and joined himself to poor sinners. He did this so that he might perhaps convert one through divine assistance and draw them away from sin; for he recognizes with what great danger Christians lie beneath the net. Therefore, he wishes to suffer death if only he might lead them away from sin, because he knows that the godless must endure a severe judgment after this life.

**Human.** Lord, does Christendom have many such shining and beautiful people?

**God.** There are so few of them that you would look upon the number with sorrow.

**Human.** Is there any fear in them?

**God.** They fear only one thing: that they might not satisfy God the Lord and might not follow his image <note>original: "ebenbilde," referring to the *Imitatio Christi* or the Imitation of Christ</note> as fully as they would wish. Otherwise, they fear neither fire, nor hell, nor the devil, nor men, nor death, nor life; rather, all fear has been taken from them, except for filial fear <term>filial fear: "kindliche forcht," a theological term for the fear of a child who does not want to offend a loving parent, as opposed to "servile fear" which is the fear of punishment.</term>, which remains in them as long as they live.

**Human.** Do they desire to live any longer?

**God.** Yes, certainly; but they desire nothing else than to follow the true image of Christ Jesus until their end. Their greatest cross is seeing the great [wickedness] <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "wi" (likely for "widrigkeit" or "wickedness")</note> of Christians...

# The Book of the Blessed Henry Suso

**Human.** Lord, it is terrifying for all who wish to amend their lives that they nevertheless place no trust in your friends, because they do not understand their speech.

**God.** How should they be able to understand them, since their lives are so vastly different? They say, "We do not know you"; yet they are not worthy to know them, because they will not obey their words. Indeed, for a person who strives for a better life, it is very necessary to seek a Friend of God <note>original: "Freund Gottes." This refers to the *Gottesfreunde*, a 14th-century lay and clerical mystical movement that emphasized an inner, personal union with God over outward ritual.</note>, to surrender to him, to speak with him, and to guard oneself with all diligence against the hypocrites and heretics who now run about everywhere. They use many guileful and subtle words that are listened to more than the truth of Holy Scripture. Thus, it is necessary to flee beneath the cross of Christ and to avoid the deceitful company and evil counsel of these godless people.

**Human.** I understand; if a simple person were to turn to you fully and steadfastly, if he were ready to live for you alone and renounce all creatures, you would immediately grant him your help and grace.

**God.** God would be ready, provided He found fitting vessels. People now seek only themselves and therefore rarely receive the grace of God, because they are not capable of it; for they do not commit themselves to the inner life with true humility. If one were to do so, God would show him greater things than before.

**Human.** If many were to behave in this way, I do not doubt that you would be merciful to your Church.

**God.** In times past, God was

<column-break/>

not as merciful as He is now, for now He endures much, suffers, spares, warns, and waits from day to day. Many years ago, the Father was indeed determined to destroy the world, but the Son begged Him to change His mind.

**Human.** Lord, I pray you, remember your bitter suffering and death, have mercy on your Church, and wait for a while until you bring about its improvement; can you not then bring it into a better state, so that it might fear you more?

**God.** What should God do? Do you not see that all is lost? Many live very godlessly and without any divine fear; therefore, God the Father can no longer endure it.

**Human.** Oh my Lord, have mercy on them.

**God.** How shall God have mercy? They are so deeply mired in vices that Divine Justice can no longer bear it. When the time comes, then your prayer, and the prayers of all the Friends of God, shall cease; and God the Father will allow His Son to avenge all the shame and injustice that has been done to Him, and which is being done in these perilous times.

**Human.** Lord, I know nothing more to say than that you should show mercy; now allow me to put one more question to you, and thereafter no more. Those who are deemed worthy to see their origin <note>The "origin" (vrsprung) refers to the mystical concept of the soul returning to its source in the Divine Essence.</note>, do they then enjoy full joy in this temporal life?

**God.** They are filled with unspeakable joys, but this joy of temporal blessedness is as unlike the joys of future happiness as time is to eternity.

### Laurentius Surius of the Carthusian Order wishes the favorable reader health and welfare.

**W**hat has been mentioned in the little book of the nine rocks and their inhabitants is, in some places, dark and difficult to understand. Therefore, for your sake, I have wished to include a brief explanation and interpretation of the aforementioned rocks, which was prepared by Dr. Henricus Harphius <note>Also known as Hendrik Herp (d. 1477), a prominent Franciscan mystic who systematized Suso’s teachings.</note> of the Order of Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans.</note>, who is likewise distinguished by his holiness of life and learning.

## A brief and clear explanation of the nine rocks, through nine steps of true salvation and self-denial.

->Described by the man renowned for holiness of life and learning,<-
->Father Henricus Harphius of the Order of Friars Minor.<-

**T**he first step of self-denial is possessed by those who are so surrounded by the fear of God that, for God’s sake, they wish to avoid all mortal sins. This is the first approach to the likeness of God; for just as we separate ourselves from God through the unlikeness of sin, so we dispose ourselves and return to Him through the likeness of His grace and our virtues. To this, the royal prophet David also exhorts us in Psalm 33 <note>original: "Psal. 33." In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 34:5. The author uses the Vulgate numbering common in the 14th–17th centuries.</note>: Draw near to Him and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be

<column-break/>

put to shame. But the number of these people is small when compared to those who live in sin, and their radiance is still dark, like a mist, so that they can hardly recognize, avoid, or know their mortal sins. Their life stands in danger, their conscience is anxious, and their senses are surrounded by many temptations by which they are incited to vices. Their health and salvation are very doubtful, and the hellish enemies <note>Demons or diabolical forces.</note> hope greatly that they will fall into sin and be damned, because they think it is enough if they simply avoid mortal sin.

### A Short Explanation of the Nine Rocks

...over your servant; and teach me your laws; specifically, how I should perform the external bodily exercises of virtue. Nevertheless, the evil enemy <note>The devil or a demonic influence seeking to distract the soul.</note> holds them in a state of blindness, so that they never see the height of spiritual exercises. Their primary exercises consist of suffering hunger, thirst, and cold; keeping watch, fasting, wearing hair-shirts <note>Garments made of coarse animal hair worn against the skin as a penance to mortify the flesh.</note>, and praying. These are undoubtedly pleasing to God and necessary for a spiritual life, but of the internal exercises, and how they should mortify <note>term: mortify (German: abtödten). To "kill off" or subdue the selfish desires and ego to make room for God.</note> themselves according to the **inner man**, they know nothing. Therefore, it happens that they are still held back by natural love and affection toward their flesh, or their spiritual friends and acquaintances. They believe this love is permissible for them, yet they do not notice how much harm it causes; for it brings overabundant worry and restlessness of heart, so that they do not reach the inner man. Instead, they are daily confused and wounded by countless, impure, and restless impulses, and are burdened with anxieties and cares that stem from natural love, even if these things appear to be good and virtuous.

The **fourth step** <note>The author uses "steps" or "levels" to describe the soul's ascent toward God.</note> is held by those who give themselves not only to external bodily exercises and works, but also to internal spiritual ones. These include the internal prayer of the soul, sighing, sweet compassion, loving desires, and the like, which belong to the inner man according to the inspiration and working of the Holy Spirit. These, too, are blinded by the hellish spirit,

<column-break/>

in that they perform all their exercises toward the end and goal of gaining perceptible devotion and love. For in all their exercises, they seek and desire much more their own delight and pleasure, which arises from perceptible devotion, rather than the pure, clear, naked, and acceptable Will of God. Therefore, they often boast of their enlightenment and spiritual sweetness, and they despise those who are weighed down by the burden of temptations and are deprived of such sweetness. Out of pure arrogance, they also say with heart and mouth the words of David:
> "The light of your countenance is sealed over us; you have given joy to my heart." <note>original: "Es ist gesiegelt vber vns das liecht deines Angesichts/ du hast freud in mein hertz geben." This is a translation of Psalm 4:6–7.</note>
Such people seem to be correct in their own judgment; they keep their own will and do not truly surrender themselves to the Divine Will. For although they may seem to offer and surrender themselves entirely—with all they are and can do—to God with great fervor as long as grace and perceptible sweetness last (as if for voluntary humility, for contempt of self, for trials, for misery, for mistrust, for death, and the like), as soon as the perceptible grace is withdrawn and they then encounter a disgrace, persecution, adversity, or evil, they allow their **unmortified nature** to be seen through impatience, restlessness, sadness, murmuring, and the like. This is because they still have that unmortified love toward themselves within them, through which the hellish enemy seeks to ruin them, whom they follow in all things.

<summary>This page distinguishes between purely external religious practices (the third step) and the internal spiritual exercises of the fourth step, warning that even internal devotion can be undermined by a selfish desire for "spiritual sweetness" rather than true surrender to God's will.</summary>

# Of the Blessed Henry Suso.

...to have surrendered to God; they thus remain devoted to their own will through the secret pull of nature, although they do not know this. They desire that God follow their will more than they follow the will of God, both in good fortune and in misfortune, and in lack of comfort as much as in the abundance of all sensible graces.
   On the **fifth step** stand those who, in all their works, in all they do or leave undone, renounce their own will in favor of Divine pleasure. However, because they have not been practiced or strengthened in this intention for long, they find themselves in this regard often weak and wavering, even though they regret it. This happens because the desire or inclination toward **mortification** <note>term: mortification (German: abtödtung). The spiritual practice of "killing off" one's selfish desires and ego to become more receptive to God's will.</note> has not yet taken root in them due to a lack of practice; therefore, they still feel within themselves the spirit of inconstancy—now they renounce all their own will, and soon again they waver in that same intention. In their person, **David** says in **Psalm 138**: <note>original: "Psal. 138." In the Vulgate numbering used here, this is Psalm 138; in most modern Bibles, it is Psalm 139:11.</note>
> I said, perhaps darkness (that is, adversities) will cover me / but the night shall also be my light for my desires / that is, in the joys of overabundant grace; the night / that is, the remembrance of adversity / to which I then voluntarily surrender myself / is my enlightenment / that is / a brief access to God / through which I am enlightened;
now, if these people surrendered all their own will without contradiction of the mind, even in all adversity, with heartfelt inclination, pleasure, and humility

<column-break/>

of spirit, and presented themselves entirely to the most pleasing will of God, they would receive great benefit from it. Through Divine enlightenment, they would recognize the most hidden paths of virtue, which are otherwise unknown to almost everyone.
   The **sixth step** is occupied by those who, through manifold desires and long practices, completely renounce all their own will without "barking back" <note>original: "widerbellen." A vivid term meaning to grumble, talk back, or resist like a dog snapping at a command.</note>, with a firm resolution to persevere in the most pleasing will of God. Because they are more abundantly enlightened in understanding, they see and recognize that all things serve the salvation of the souls of the pious and God-loving; they say with the **Psalmist** in **Psalm 26**: <note>original: "Psalm. 26." In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 27:1.</note>
> The Lord is my light / and my salvation / whom should I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life / of whom shall I be afraid?
Yet they still have this flaw: they chase after **spiritual comfort** <note>term: spiritual comfort (German: geistlicher trost). The pleasant emotional or sensory feeling of God's presence. Mystics warned that seeking this feeling for its own sake was a form of "spiritual gluttony."</note> far too much, upon which they rely. They easily endure all adversity but possess only this comfort and demand it from God as if it were their own property. Now, the intention to enjoy this comfort is not entirely pure and Divine; this is evident because they have no peaceful heart until they regain that sensible comfort according to their wish. It is to be known here that, although it is not evil in itself to desire a sensible comfort or devotion from God with a right intention, it is nevertheless to be attributed to a certain imperfection, which deviates from the right and true denial of oneself, even if few perceive this.

### A Brief Explanation of the Nine Rocks

...because such a person does not completely surrender himself to God without the heart reclaiming its own; <note>The original German "wiederbellung" implies a "reclaiming" or "retraction" of the heart's submission—essentially a spiritual backsliding where the ego tries to take back control.</note> so that God may work in the same in every way, even in abandonment and adversity, according to His most pleasing Will. And though he already recognizes that this ought rightly to happen, he nevertheless does not strive to give himself fully to God. Therefore, it happens that he does not progress in further exercises and virtues, because he cannot see or recognize the hidden inclination of nature, nor the subtle and disorderly attachments.

The **seventh step** is assigned to those who know how to use both hands skillfully and usefully—namely, the right hand of good fortune and prosperity, and the left hand of adversity—saying with the Prophet:
> **Psalm 107.** O God, my heart is ready to accept good fortune according to Your will; again, O God, my heart is ready to endure adversity according to Your pleasure. <note>original: "Psal. 107." In the Vulgate, this is Psalm 107; in modern Bibles, it is Psalm 108:1.</note>

Such people desire to satisfy the Will of God in all things, both internally and externally, in intention and in love, no differently than a shadow follows its body. To this belongs the saying of that loving soul:
> **Song of Solomon 2.** I sat down under the shadow of him whom I desired, and his fruit is sweet to my throat. <note>original: "Cant. 2." Short for Cantica Canticorum, the Song of Songs.</note>

Whereby it is to be known that God is the Light, but the humanity of Christ is the Body from which the shadow springs; and that His most perfect life is the shadow under which we should rest and follow Him completely; then the spiritual fruits are very sweet, because God

<column-break/>

illuminates such people with many secret gifts and insights. Such people are not disturbed in the night of adversity and discouragement, as they are grounded in pure love, through which they are not only taught to do great things, but also to suffer adverse things, as **David** says:
> **Psalm 138.** For even the darkness is not dark before You; that is, adversity will be illuminated in You like the day of prosperity, or the sensible spirit; as is Your light, so will also be Your darkness. <note>original: "Psalm 138." Corresponding to modern Psalm 139:12. The "sensible spirit" refers to the part of the soul that perceives spiritual feelings and consolations.</note>

For such people enjoy rest in adversity, thus receiving fittingly and clearly <note>The OCR "dentlich" is likely "deutlich" (clearly) or "ordentlich" (orderly).</note> the illumination and spiritual gifts. Through these, the memory is made right and showered with wondrous, hidden thoughts; the understanding is illuminated; and the loving soul or will is ignited with the heat of Divine love. But because abundance is dangerous to the unwary, it sometimes happens that they partly misuse such overabundant gifts out of a subtle and hidden ignorance, in that they ground themselves too much and rely upon the bestowed gra- graces <note>The OCR "Ga- Gnaden" reflects a printer's error where the first syllable of the word for "graces" was repeated.</note> given to them. Although they do not recognize or notice it, it happens to them because they do not desire those same graces if they were withdrawn in a disorderly way; <note>This suggests they are attached to the "feeling" of grace rather than God himself.</note> they are not careful to see if they are imprudently enjoying the grace bestowed on them by God. As long as they do not die to this piece of themselves, they cannot reach the highest perfection.

The **eighth step** is assigned to those who surrender themselves purely and clearly to the Divine Will, in whatever manner He wishes to deal with them in time or eternity. They allow nothing of self-interest <note>The German "eigenhümbliches" refers to "propriety" or "self-ownership"—the mystical concept of the ego claiming credit or possession of spiritual states.</note> to remain within them, nor any attachment or inclination toward creatures or even the gifts of God. If they possess temporal goods, their hearts cling to them as little as if they did not have them. They do not pride themselves on God’s gifts any more than if they had not received them. God visits these people more often than others with great and secret graces and reveals strange things to them through parables <note>original: "gleichnussen"; these are spiritual images or metaphors used to communicate divine truths.</note> because they have come very close to God. Although such revelations are sometimes granted to the imperfect, it is not without danger to their souls unless they show themselves grateful and proceed with great diligence in all virtues and the mortification of themselves. Yet, as far as common experience is concerned, high and super-essential <note>original: "vberwesentliche"; a term from Dionysian theology meaning "beyond all being" or "transcendent."</note> revelation remains hidden from these men, which is received without images—indeed, above all forms and parables—so that their highest dwelling in the spirit is the **highest darkness**, which surpasses all contemplation. They thus cry out with David in **Psalm 17**:
> For You enlighten, O Lord, my lamp; that is, You enlighten the rational powers with spiritual knowledge. My God, enlighten also my darkness, into which I am raised through the essential contemplation of Your face. <note>original: "Psalm. 17." This follows the Vulgate numbering; in modern Bibles, this is Psalm 18:28.</note>

However, this contemplation is not granted to them if they accept God's gifts

<column-break/>

or revelations in such a way that they imagine they still lack something in and through these gifts that they desire from God (even if it is not necessary), or because they cannot do without the granted divine gifts and revelations as readily as they desire them. Therefore, a secret self-interest lies hidden within them, which is punishable before God. For their mind should be as free from these things as if they had received nothing; they should only marvel at the Divine goodness and generosity, giving Him praise and thanks that He deigns to give His hidden graces to such low and unworthy sinners. They should surrender themselves to God with such resignation <note>In this context, "resignation" means total, active surrender of one's will to God, rather than passive giving up.</note> that they are ready not only to be deprived of the granted graces and revelations but also to endure all kinds of abandonment and adverse falls. This is primarily because the perfect life does not actually consist in gifts and revelations; rather, these are only loving gifts of God through which He declares His most generous goodness and with which He draws and entices many who are weak in spirit toward the perfect life. From this, one must only note how completely all self-interest must be extinguished and dead in whoever wishes to attain the contemplative life in a rightful manner.

On the **ninth step** stand those who, through powerful exercises and with ascending, most fervent desires for the love of God, have almost consumed their flesh, blood, and the marrow in their bones.

<meta>This page serves as the preface to the biography of the mystic Henry Suso.
