Life of the Blessed Henry Suso.

[A horizontal typographical headpiece consisting of two rows of repeating ornamental fleur-de-lis motifs.]

## Friar Laurentius Surius of the Carthusian Order wishes the
### kindhearted reader all blessing and prosperity.

<note>Laurentius Surius (1522–1578) was a famous Carthusian monk and hagiographer who translated many mystical works into Latin, making them accessible to a wider European audience.</note>

**Master HENRY Suso**, renowned for the holiness of his life and many <term>miracles</term> <note>original: *Mirackelen*</note>, led from his youth a life that few people are capable of following. He had a <term>spiritual daughter</term> <note>refers to Elsbeth Stagel (c. 1300–1360), a Dominican nun who recorded Suso's life and teachings</note> who was noble by birth, but even nobler in the fear of God. She secretly investigated much of his life and wrote it down; when he discovered this, he demanded to see the manuscript and burned part of it in a fire. However, what remained was published under a pseudonym. He never mentions himself by name, but everywhere calls himself the <term>Servant of Wisdom</term> <note>original: *Weißheit Diener*; Suso's preferred title, reflecting his devotion to "Eternal Wisdom"</note>, so that he might avoid vain glory. In this account of his life, one finds many things through which even ice-cold hearts may be most fervently kindled to love God. To be sure, those who are <term>beastly</term> <note>original: *Viehische*; referring to people driven by animal instincts and worldly desires rather than spiritual reason</note> and devoted to this world are prone to take offense at such things; however, those who wish to please God rather than men must pay this no heed. Our Lord wished to present holy people to us as examples, so that—since we are little moved by words alone—we might at least be encouraged and ignited by the lives and deeds of others; for deeds move us more than words.

I ask you, kindhearted reader, to examine this life with all diligence, for from it a great benefit will be granted to your soul.

## Life of the Blessed Henry Suso / his excellent words / and works / not all / but only several / very useful to read.

---

->The First Chapter.<-

In Germany, there was a man of the Religious Profession, a Dominican / a **Swabian** <note>Swabia is a cultural and linguistic region in southwestern Germany, a major center for German mysticism in the 14th century.</note> by fatherland / whose name is written in the **Book of Life** <note>A biblical reference (Philippians 4:3, Revelation 20:12) to the record of those destined for heaven.</note> / he wished / that he might be a **Servant of Wisdom** <note>original: *Weißheit diener*; This was Suso's preferred self-designation to maintain humility.</note> / and be so named / it happened however that he came into the acquaintance of a holy / and by God enlightened Person / who was burdened with misery / and temptations / this person desired to hear from the aforementioned Servant of Eternal Wisdom something of what he had suffered in his own Person / so that her tempted spirit might be strengthened / and she did this as often as he came to her / and through these secret questions she learned from him the manner of his beginning and progress / also several exercises / and temptations / which he secretly revealed to her out of spiritual friend- and fellowship. When she sensed some comfort / and instruction to be drawn from this / she wrote everything down / for her own / and others' use / yet secretly and by stealth / so that he would be aware of nothing.

When he noticed this **spiritual theft** <note>original: *geistlichen diebstal*; refers to her recording his words without permission.</note> / he rebuked her / and forced her to give him her Writings / thus threw everything / that he had received from her / into the Fire. When the other part was given to him / and he wished to clear it away in the same manner / it was

<column-break/>

forbidden to him through Divine revelation / thus what remained was not consumed by the Fire / which he mostly wrote with his own hands / to which also after his death many heartfelt instructions were added under his name by the Servant of Eternal Wisdom. The beginning of his **conversion** <note>original: *bekehrung*; in a monastic context, this refers to a deepening of faith or a "turning" from worldly habits to total devotion.</note> happened in his eighteenth Year / and although he had already worn the **religious Robe** <note>original: *geistliche Kleyd*; refers to the white tunic and black mantle of the Dominican habit.</note> for five Years / he was still of an unquiet spirit / and although he was already protected by God from heavy sins / which could harm his good name / he yet considered common / and petty sins to be small matters / nonetheless God so arranged it with him / that wherever he turned to desired / and things pleasant to his senses / he was not quiet nor satisfied in his heart / but it seemed to him as if something yet remained / which would bring rest / and peace to his lively spirit. In this unrest / and disturbance he found himself in a bad state / for he was always pricked with internal thorns of conscience / but could not help himself / until the most gracious **GOD** redeemed him through a certain conversion. # Of certain struggles of the new Pupil, or Disciple of Christ.
## Chapter 2.

When this grace was granted to him by God, several struggles immediately arose within him, through which the Devil sought to hinder his salvation; these were of this nature: the inner impulse of God required a complete turning away from all hindrances and means <note>original: *mitteln*; in this context, it refers to worldly attachments or intermediaries that stand between the soul and God.</note> from him; on the other hand, temptation fought back and threw such thoughts at him: perhaps with a mature mind, it is easy to start something, but difficult to finish it. The internal calling of God showed him the **Omnipotence** and working of the **Holy Spirit**; on the contrary, Temptation said that one should indeed not doubt the Omnipotence of God, but it was uncertain whether this path was pleasing to Him. Later, this was shown to him as a certainty, because God has promised that He will help and stand by all those who begin this in His name. 

When grace triumphed in this conflict, another thought crept into his heart under the appearance of friendship <note>A common theme in Suso's writing: the "voice of reason" or "false friendship" that encourages a comfortable, middle-of-the-road religious life instead of total devotion.</note> and advised him thus: "It is praiseworthy and right to improve your life, yet do not be hasty; rather, begin modestly so that you may reach the end. Give your body food and drink, be kind to yourself, and meanwhile avoid sin; be as pious in and for yourself as you wish, but with moderation <note>original: *mit dem mittel*; literally "with the middle," referring to avoiding extremes of asceticism.</note>, so that no one takes outward offense at you, as people are prone

<column-break/>

to say: 'as long as the heart is good, all is good.' You can be among people and nonetheless practice virtue; others also hope to be saved, even though they spend their lives in such [ordinary] practices." 

With these and similar thoughts he was attacked, but **Eternal Wisdom** overturned this deceitful advice thus: "He who wishes to hold an eel—a slippery thing—by the tail, and wishes to begin a holy life with lukewarmness, will be deceived on both sides; for when he thinks he holds this or that fast, it slips from his hands. So too, he who wishes to bring the untamed and undisciplined body, which is accustomed to a soft life, into servitude, [finds it difficult]; and whoever wishes to enjoy the world and nonetheless serve God fully, pursues an impossible thing, as Holy Scripture in **Matthew 6** <note>Reference to Matthew 6:24: "No man can serve two masters."</note> and the words of Christ attest. If you then wish to renounce all things, do so with brave courage." 

When he remained firm in these thoughts, he finally withdrew with boldness and trust from all things. In the midst of this, his lively spirit suffered many a 'death' (so to speak) as he separated himself from vain company, until—driven by natural weakness—he sought to refresh and amuse his mind with them; but as it usually happens...

# How he spiritually married Eternal Wisdom.
## The 4th Chapter.

The entire manner of his life was an everlasting diligence in how he might enjoy the presence and conversation of Eternal Wisdom. From his youth, his heart was entirely devoted to love. Eternal Wisdom, however, shows herself in Holy Scripture no differently than as one most loving, who dresses and adorns herself so that she may please everyone; who uses more charming speech and address, and presents herself in a lovely form so that all hearts fall in love with her. Meanwhile, she reveals the deception and inconstancy of other mistresses, but on the contrary, displays her own steadfastness and friendliness. Through this, his young heart was drawn, just as a panther with its lovely scent lures other animals to it. <note>In medieval bestiaries (books of animal lore), the panther was said to have a sweet-smelling breath that attracted all other creatures to follow it. Here, Suso uses it as a metaphor for the irresistible attraction of God's wisdom.</note> Eternal Wisdom very often uses this same manner of sweetness and friendly invitation to love, especially in the Song of Songs, in the Book of Wisdom, and in the "Wise Man." <note>original: *beym weisen Man*; Suso is likely referring to the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) or Proverbs, which were often attributed to "the wise man" Solomon.</note> When these books were read at the table, <note>In Dominican monasteries, it was customary for a brother to read scripture or holy texts aloud while the others ate in silence.</note> he was gladdened, ignited with desire, and thought thus within himself: "I will try my luck to see if I might enjoy the love of this friend, of whom such great things are said, and if I might partake in her friendship; for my young and lively heart must necessarily be embraced by love." He often took note of her; she often came

<column-break/>

into his mind and spirit, and she pleased him well. Once at the table, he heard these words read from her: *Sap. 7 & 8* <note>original: *Sapientia* (the Book of Wisdom). The following text is a paraphrase of Wisdom chapters 7 and 8, along with Proverbs 3.</note> "Wisdom is more beautiful than the sun; she shines above the stars, and the day is not to be compared to her. I have loved her and have sought her diligently from my youth; and I have undertaken to marry her as my bride, for I have had a great love for her beauty. Because of her, I shall be held in honor among the people and the Council; because of her, I shall have immortality and an eternal memory among those who come after me. When I come home, I would find rest with her; for her company has nothing unpleasant or bitter, but only joy and delight. Wisdom founded the earth and established the heavens; through the Lord's wisdom, the depths have broken forth and the clouds are filled with dew. Whoever attains her walks with confidence on his way, and his foot shall not stumble. When he sleeps, he has nothing to fear; he will rest, and his sleep shall be sweet." When he heard these and similar honey-sweet words, his heart received these thoughts: "O, if such a pure and lovely friend could be granted to me, I would be the most fortunate of men." On the contrary, he was deterred by opposing thoughts: "How can you love what you have never seen nor known?"

## The 4th Chapter.

Better is a handful with certain possession than a house full of uncertain hope. Whoever desires to build a high house and to possess the friendship of a powerful person—to whom he is very unequal—is often deceived in his hope and departs hungry. The companionship of this female friend <note>Suso personifies Wisdom as a "friend" or "bride," a common theme in the biblical Book of Proverbs.</note> would not be to his disadvantage, provided she allowed her lovers to care well for the body; but now she says: **Prov. 21. Yes, sleep a little more, sleep a little more, fold your hands together that you may sleep, so poverty will come like a wanderer, and want like an armed man. Prov. 6.** See whether anyone else prescribes such strict rules to their lovers. Soon he received this divine thought: It is an old law and property of love that lovers suffer adversity and heavy things; there is no lover without a Cross, and whoever is devoted to love is a martyr. How much more reasonable is it, then, that one who desires to win such an esteemed bride and friend should meanwhile suffer something adverse? See how much bitter chance, annoyance, and labor the lovers of this world must endure, whether it brings them joy or sorrow. Through these and similar inspirations, he was strengthened to persevere, and this happened to him often. At times he was of good will; at times he turned his love somewhat toward temporal things. # How he wrote the saving Name of Jesus upon his heart.
---
### The 5th Chapter.

At that same time, a great fire was poured into his soul, and his heart was violently inflamed. When he felt the heat one day and burned, as it were, with love for Jesus, he went into his small cell and gave himself over to meditation in secret, speaking thus to the Lord:

> "Ah, my God, if only I could think of a sign of love that would be a constant reminder of the love between me and you—something that would testify to me that I love you and you love me most fully, so that I might never forget it."

Under this most fervent zeal, he removed the <term>scapular</term> <note>A part of a monk's habit consisting of a long piece of cloth worn over the shoulders.</note> from his chest, seized an iron stylus, and looked at his heart, saying:

> "Almighty God, give me strength and power today to fulfill my desire, for you must be written upon my heart today."

As he said this, he began to pierce the flesh over the place of his heart with the stylus, moving the stylus up and down until he had written the name of Jesus upon the flesh covering his heart. Meanwhile, the blood flowed over his body into his lap; he looked at this with great joy in his heart, and because of his great love, he regarded the pain as very little. When he had done this, he went thus bloodied out of the cell and into the choir, and fell upon his knees before the <term>crucifix</term>.

> "Ah, my Heart," he said, "you sole love of my heart and <term>soul</term>, look upon my great desire; I cannot press you entirely into myself. Fulfill, O Heart, what is still remaining; press yourself into the depths of my heart and mark your holy Name in me so that you may never be torn out of my heart

<column-break/>

again." For a long time, this wound of love remained open; finally, it was healed, and the Name of Jesus remained upon his heart as he had desired. The letters were the width of a straw and the length of a finger joint, and he carried this name upon his chest until death. As often as his heart was moved, this Name also moved, and it was—especially in the beginning—very painful to him. He hid and concealed this with all diligence, and never let anyone see it in secret, except for one close and spiritual friend. Whenever he encountered something adverse later on, he would look at this sign and immediately felt relief. At times, in secret conversation with the Lord, he used to say:

> "The lovers of this world fasten the image or portrait of their mistresses to their clothes, but I have written you, my most beloved Heart, into my heart and blood."

Once, after coming from prayer following <term>Matins</term> <note>The service of morning prayer, traditionally held in the middle of the night or very early dawn.</note>, he sat in his cell upon a chair and placed the book called the <term>Vitas Patrum</term> <note>Latin for "Lives of the Fathers," a popular medieval collection of stories about the early desert monks.</note> under his head instead of a cushion. Because of this, he fell into an ecstasy, and it seemed to him as if a light went out from his heart; at the same time, he saw in his heart a golden cross set with many pearls, in which the Name of Jesus appeared very elegantly. He immediately covered his heart with his religious habit and struggled to suppress the bright-shining radiance so that no one might see it, but the rays spread out beyond all measure, so that he could not hide their power or their light.

## On several previews of Divine consolation, with which the new beginning students of Christ are lured.

### The 6th Chapter.

When he, according to his custom, had come out of <term>Matins</term> <note>The earliest of the monastic prayer services, traditionally held in the middle of the night or at very early dawn.</note> into his chapel, he sat down upon his chair to rest for a while. It was a short rest, until the watchers announced the day; at this he awoke, fell upon the earth, and greeted the rising Morning Star—namely, the most excellent Queen of Heaven. Just as the little birds in summer greet the breaking day with joy, so he too wished to honor the Mother of the Eternal Sun with lovely devotion, and thus spoke the most delightful greeting to her with a sweet and pleasing voice of the heart. As he was then settling himself to rest, he heard in his soul a strange sound, at which he was startled with all his heart; this sound was very sharp, and from that hour on he felt it every time the Morning Star rose, and he heard these words:

> *Mary, the Star of the Sea, has come forth at her rising.* <note>original: "Stella Maria Maris processit ad ortum."</note>

> The Star of the Sea who has arisen is Mary, the Mother of Jesus Christ.

This song resounded within him beyond the course of nature, so that he rejoiced from his heart and sang along. After the song, he heard this voice: "The more lovely you embrace me, and the more purely you kiss me, the more lovely and friendly you shall embrace me in eternity." After these words, his eyes were opened and flowed richly with tears. He then greeted the Morning Star according to his custom; soon he added another morning greeting, kissing the earth to

<column-break/>

honor the Eternal Wisdom, with the most devout prayer which he was accustomed to write in spiritual books, the beginning of which is:

> *My soul has desired,* etc.

The third greeting he performed by kissing the earth to honor the highest Seraphic, burning angelic spirit, who burns with the hottest love toward the Eternal Wisdom, so that this same spirit might also ignite his own heart with the most fervent love toward God, to burn entirely within and to set all other men aflame with fiery speeches and instructions. This threefold greeting he performed every morning when he awoke. Once, during the time of <term>Shrovetide</term> <note>The period of festivities and preparation immediately preceding the fast of Lent.</note>, he had delayed his prayer so long that the watchers announced the breaking day. Therefore, he thought to himself: "Rest a little before you greet the Morning Star." And while his senses enjoyed some rest in the meantime, the Angelic spirits sang with a high voice the most lovely <term>Responsory</term> <note>A type of chant in liturgical worship where a verse is sung by a soloist and answered by the choir.</note> from Isaiah 60:

> *Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem,* <note>original: "Surge, illuminare Ierusalem"</note>

Thus his eyes were opened, and from the abundance of his heart, hot tears ran down his cheeks. ## How he conducted himself when he was to go to table, and likewise at table.

It seemed to him in a vision that someone reached him an apple with these words: “Take it and enjoy it, for in this you seek your delight.” He replied that he sought no pleasure except in Eternal Wisdom; on the contrary, the voice accused him of lying, declaring that he had an immoderate desire for apples. The large apples he cut into four pieces; three of these he ate in honor of the Most Holy Trinity; the fourth he ate in the love with which the heavenly Mother and Virgin gave her little Son, the tender little Jesus, apples to eat. And this piece he ate along with the peel, because small children are accustomed to eating apples in such a manner. But from the birth of Christ onward, and for some time thereafter, he did not eat the fourth piece, but offered it up to the Immaculate Virgin so that she might present it to her little Son, out of whose love he wished to do without it during that time. If he were occasionally too greedy in eating and drinking, he covered his face with a blush of shame before his venerable Spouse <note>original: "Epons," referring to Eternal Wisdom as his spiritual bride</note>; if he had sinned somewhat in this at the table, he imposed a penance upon himself. Once, a stranger came to him, mentioning that it had been told to him in a vision that if he wished to keep an orderly meal, he should go to the Brother and learn his custom and manner.

In Swabia <note>original: "Schwabenland," a region in southwestern Germany where Suso lived and worked</note>, where he was born, it was the custom on New Year’s Day for foolish youths to go through the streets at night and request a wreath from their sweethearts; that is, they sing, letting lovely melodies be heard, and strive by all means and ways so that their lady friend might give them a crown or a wreath. ### Concerning the words: "Lift up your hearts." <note>original: "sursum corda"</note>

### Chapter 11.

His friends occasionally asked him what he thought about when he said the words "Lift up your hearts" <note>original: "Sursum corda"</note> during the Mass, the meaning of which is that the hearts of all people should sigh toward God. For he spoke these words with such devotion that all listeners could be moved by them. ## How he kept the Carnival.

### Chapter 13.

On the Saturday before Septuagesima Sunday <note>The third Sunday before Lent, traditionally the time when the "Alleluia" is removed from the liturgy and a period of pre-Lenten preparation begins.</note>, at which time the "Alleluia" ceases and worldly people devote themselves to all manner of folly because of the approaching Carnival <term>Fasznacht: the German Carnival season of revelry and feasting before the fast of Lent begins</term>, he arranged a spiritual Carnival in his heart in the following way: He thought of the momentary joy of the carnal Carnival and how the greater part of people, for the sake of a short pleasure, fall into eternal misery and lamentation. Thus, he prayed the 50th Psalm, **Have mercy on me, O God** <note>Psalm 51 in modern Bibles; a primary prayer of repentance.</note>, etc., to the honor of Almighty God for all the sins, shame, and

<column-break/>

wrongs that would be inflicted upon Him during this most wanton time. He called it the "Peasants' Carnival," as for those who know nothing better. Secondly, he considered the prelude of the heavenly life, how God still plays, as it were, through divine comfort with His friends even in this mortal body. He also immediately recalled with praise and thanksgiving that which had been shown to him by God, and he delighted himself in God his Lord. At the beginning of his conversion, he was granted a spiritual Carnival by God...

# Life of the Blessed Henry Suso

### How a Heavenly Carnival was granted to him in the following manner:

At Carnival time <note>German: *Faßnacht-zeit*. In the Middle Ages, this was a period of intense feasting and often rowdy behavior before the fasting of Lent began.</note>, he had gone one day before Compline <note>The final church service of the day.</note> into the warm room to warm himself, for he was both very cold and hungry; yet thirst plagued him even more when he saw others eating meat and drinking wine. Because he himself was hungry and thirsty, he felt an inner urging, went out, and sighed from his heart.

In that same night, it seemed to him in a vision as if he were in the infirmary, and from outside he heard a heavenly song of such sweetness that no sound of a lute could be compared to it. The voice was like that of a twelve-year-old schoolboy. The Servant of Wisdom forgot all food and drink, listened diligently to the melody, and said with fervor of heart: "Who might be singing outside like that? For such sweetness in singing I have never heard on Earth." 

The beautiful youth, who was present right there, replied: "Know that the youth sings for your sake." The Servant says: "Ah, that God would be mindful of me! I beg you, heavenly youth, tell him to sing more." He began to sing with a clear voice and finished three heavenly songs. After their completion, it seemed to him as if the youth flew through the air to the window of the Servant's cell and reached through it a little branch with red berries, just like strawberries. The aforementioned youth, however, took the branch from the boy's hands and gave it with joy to the Servant with these words: "Well then, my brother and companion, take these red fruits from your most beloved **Lord**, from this most beautiful youth, the eter-

<column-break/>

-nal King's Son, whom you have just now heard <insert>singing</insert>, sent to you as a gift. How very much he loves you!" When he heard this, the brother, with a joyful but <unclear>blushing</unclear> face, <insert>took</insert> the basket <note>The text likely refers to the "little branch" mentioned earlier as a container of fruit.</note> of fruits and says: "Ah, lucky <insert>me</insert>, to whom such a desired gift from an excellent and divine youth is presented, which gladdens me from <insert>the heart</insert>!" 

He then turned to the youth and to other blessed <unclear>spirits</unclear> <note>original: "stern" – likely *Geistern* (spirits) or *Gefährten* (companions).</note> present there: "You most beloved friends," he says, "is it not right that this gracious and heavenly youth be loved by me most diligently? Rightly should I fulfill his most pleasing <insert>will</insert> in every way." He turned <insert>back</insert> to the aforementioned youth and says: "O most beloved, do I have the right intention?" 

<insert>The youth</insert> smiled sweetly and says: "Your intention is good in every way, and rightly should you <insert>love</insert> the one who loves you before many others; therefore love him fervently, and be certain that you also, before many others, will have to endure great adversities, and <insert>prepare</insert> yourself at the same time." He says: "I will very gladly do <insert>so</insert>, and I beg you, permit <insert>me</insert> to show <insert>my gratitude</insert>, so that I may thank him for this so excellent gift and grace."

Thus the vision was ended; when he came to himself, he <insert>offered</insert> God praise and thanks for the shown heavenly <note>original: "nacht" – short for *Faßnacht* (Carnival).</note> Carnival.

# How he observed the first day of May.
## Chapter 14.

The night before the first day of May, he set up for himself, according to the custom of other men, a green tree <note>The "Maypole" or "May-tree" was a common folk custom; Suso adapts this secular celebration into a private religious devotion.</note>, which he thereafter honored every day for a long time. Among all other trees that have ever grown, though they be very beautiful, he could find none greener than the tree of the Holy Cross, which is much more radiant and greener in grace, virtues, and all kinds of adornment than all other trees. Under this tree, he made for himself six decorated branches, and each branch he wished to adorn especially with choice things which the lovely summer can bring. He sang to himself the hymn: <note>original: "Salve crux sancta"</note> **Hail, holy Cross**; Likewise: **Hail, you heavenly tree of eternal salvation**, upon which the fruit of eternal wisdom has grown. Firstly, for your adornment, I offer you, in place of all red roses, inward love; Secondly, in place of all creeping or ground-lying

<column-break/>

violets, prostrate humility. Thirdly, in place of all fragrant lilies, the purest embrace; Fourthly, in place of all kinds of well-formed and greening flowers, which any forest, meadow, tree, or field has brought forth or will bring forth in this pleasant spring, the spiritual foot of the heart <note>In medieval mystical language, the "feet of the soul" often represented the movements of the will and the affections (desire and love) toward God.</note>; Fifthly, in place of the singing of all birds flying in the air, which they have ever let be heard upon the branches of the trees, the praise of the unending soul; Sixthly, in place of the adornment of all things with which every green branch is clothed in the lovely springtime, my heart praises you today with a spiritual song of praise, beseeching you that you, as a blessed tree, would be helpful to me, so that I may praise you in this temporal life in such a way that I may become worthy to enjoy your life-giving fruit in eternity. In this manner, he observed the first day of May.

He was indeed frightened by these words, yet he endeavored to set his mind upon them, and began to learn what he had not known before, and surrendered himself entirely to the will of God. From that time on, he was accustomed to practice every night in the Chapter House <term>Capitelhauß: the room where the monks gathered for daily business and readings</term> in all the things which Christ had done in His Passion; he went from one corner to another. Finally, after He was condemned to death before the judgment seat, he set out with Him on the way which the Lord Jesus went from the judgment seat to the Mount of **Calvary** <note>original: "Calvariæ"</note> under the heavy Cross. When he came to the porch of the Chapter House, he kissed with bended knees the footprints of his Lord, who, condemned to death, turned around and hastened to the place of His martyrdom. Here he recited the 21st Psalm: <note>In the Vulgate, this is Psalm 21; in modern Bibles, it is Psalm 22.</note>
> **My God, my God, look upon me, etc.**

Thus he went through the door onto the churchyard, or the cloister walkway. He had imagined four streets for himself, through which he wished to walk with his Lord.

Through the first street, he went with Him to His death with this desire: that he might leave friends, possessions, and temporal goods, and be deprived of all comfort with Christ, and live to His praise in voluntary poverty.

In the second street, he resolved to despise all temporal honor and dignity, and to allow himself to be mocked by the world, because our Lord became a worm and no man, a reproach of men, and despised by the people.

At the beginning of the third street, he bent

<column-break/>

his knees again, kissing the earth, and renounced all unnecessary rest, comfort, and physical pleasure, for the honor of the most tender crucified body of the Lord Jesus; and he set before his eyes what is written: that His strength was dried up like a potsherd <note>A piece of broken pottery; a metaphor for extreme fragility and dehydration.</note>, and He was brought into the dust of death. And as the pains drove Him forth in a piteous manner, he thought how all eyes and hearts should weep bitterly over this.

In the middle of the fourth street, he fell upon his knees, just as if before the gate through which the Lord was to go out; he thus went before Him and prayed Him that he might not go to His death without his companionship, but rather let him die at the same time, because it was necessary for the Lord to pass by him. There he imagined it so firmly as if it were truly happening, and spoke this prayer:

Thus he let Him pass by. Afterward, he bent his knees toward the most blessed Queen of Heaven, Mary, who appeared before him with great heartache; he took heed of her mournful gestures, her hot tears, piteous sighs, and also her countenance and very sorrowful form, and said once:

With this scourge <note>A scourge or "Geissel" was a whip used for religious penance, often with multiple thongs.</note>, he went at night before Matins <note>The earliest monastic prayer service, held in the middle of the night.</note> into the choir before the Most Holy Sacrament, and struck himself very hard for a long time until the brothers became aware of it; then he stopped. On the Feast of Saint Clement [November 23rd], at the onset of winter, he once made a general confession, and in the quiet of the night, he locked himself in his chamber, bared his body down to his hair-shirt <term>hair-shirt</term><note>A garment made of coarse animal hair worn against the skin as a form of penance.</note> undergarment, and struck his arms and shins with the pointed scourge so severely that the blood ran from his body no differently than if he had been pierced through with a sword. In the scourge was a curved spike, like a hook, which pulled out the flesh it caught; at that time, he struck his body so hard and so long that the scourge shattered into three pieces, and the spikes flew against the wall, with only one part remaining in his hands. There he stood, all bloody, looked at himself, and saw the wretched state of his body, so that in some measure he appeared like the cruelly mangled Christ; out of pity for himself, he wept bitterly. In the winter cold, as he was entirely naked and bloody, he fell on his knees and prayed to the Lord that He would blot out his sins.

Afterward, on Quinquagesima Sunday <note>The Sunday before Ash Wednesday and the start of Lent.</note>, while the brothers were at the table, he went

<column-break/>

into his chamber, took off his clothes, and struck himself so that the blood again ran profusely from him; and because he dealt himself harder blows, a brother heard the sound of the scourge, ran to him, and stopped him. But so that his pain would be even greater, he rubbed the wounds with salt and vinegar. On the Feast of Saint Benedict [March 21st], the day on which he had been born into this wretched world, he went into his chapel during the midday meal, bolted it, took off his clothes, and began to scourge himself. He struck the "heart-vein" <note>original: "herß ader"</note> on his left arm, which is called the *mediana* <note>original: "mediam" — The median cubital vein, traditionally used in bloodletting.</note>, from which the blood ran so plentifully that it moistened not only his feet but the ground; because of this, the arm swelled and turned a blue color. He was terrified by this and dared not strike any more. At the same time that he was thus striking himself, a holy virgin named Anna was praying in another city. In a vision, she was led to the place where he was scourging himself. She took pity on the terrible wound and stepped closer to him; as he intended to strike with his arm outstretched, she placed herself in the way, and it seemed to her that she received the blow upon her own arm. When she returned to herself, she found the mark of the blow on her arm in black and blue colors, and she kept this certain sign of truth on her body for a long time afterward.

# On Moderation in Drinking.

## The 20th Chapter.

He once took upon himself a difficult practice / and prescribed for himself a meager portion of drink / and so that he would not violate this either at home / or abroad, he devised for himself a small drinking vessel / and carried it with him whenever he went out. In the greatest thirst, it was merely a refreshment for his parched mouth / just as when one pours a little juice for a sick person with a burning fever. For a very long time, he abstained from wine / and only used it on the feast of Easter to honor the Great Mystery <note>The Great Mystery refers to the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note>. When he was very thirsty / and would not allow himself relief with either wine / or water, he once looked up toward heaven / and felt internally such a divine prompting: Mark how I, in former times, surrounded by the agonies of death, stilled the greatest thirst with gall and vinegar / even though all springs of water belong to me / because they were created by me / like all other things for use / and for human sustenance; so you also / if you wish to follow in my footsteps / suffer all lack / and poverty willingly. Once, before Christmas, he renounced all bodily comforts / and besides his usual practices, he also employed these three trials.

The first / was that at night, after Matins <term>Matins: the earliest monastic prayer service, usually held in the middle of the night or at dawn</term>, he remained before the high altar with bare feet until the day broke / during the longest nights.

<margin>Of</margin> The second / was that neither by day / nor night would he go to warm places / nor would he warm his hands at the altar / even though his

<column-break/>

# How he was sent to a rational school of true resignation AND
## surrender of himself.
### The 21st Chapter.

Once, after Matins <note>The first prayer service of the monastic day, held in the early morning hours.</note>, while sitting on his stool, he was caught up in a vision during his meditation. It seemed to him in the vision that he saw a beautiful youth come from heaven and speak with him in the following way: "You have been exercised long enough in the lower schools <note>A reference to Suso's previous twenty years of extreme physical mortification, such as wearing a spiked cross and hair shirts.</note>; now it is time that you ascend. Come, go with me, for I will lead you to an eminent school of this temporal life, where you can apply yourself to the very best science <note>original: "wissenschafft"; here meaning a branch of spiritual knowledge or a discipline of the soul.</note>, which will grant you true peace and bring the good beginning to the desired end." 

At this, he stood up with joy; the youth took his hand and led him (as it seemed to him) into a spiritual landscape where an imposing house, in form and shape like a monastery, stood. Spiritual people lived there and applied themselves to the aforementioned science. Upon his entry, they received and greeted him kindly, and soon hurried to the Superior, or Rector, and announced to him the arrival of one who wished to apply himself to their art and science. He answered that he must examine him to see what was to be hoped for from him. When he had examined him, he smiled and said: "Certainly, this guest of ours will become an excellent Master in our science, if he will with 

<column-break/>

all diligence surrender himself to being enclosed in the House of Discipline <note>original: "Zuchthauß"; in this context, a place of spiritual training and correction rather than a modern prison.</note>." Because the Servant <note>Suso often refers to himself in the third person as "the Servant of Eternal Wisdom."</note> did not entirely understand these words, he turned to the youth who had led him there and asked: "Tell me, my dearest one, what kind of school is this, and what is the nature of its science of which you have made mention?" 

The angelic youth answered: "The excellent science in this school is nothing else than a complete denial and surrender of oneself, so that one dies to oneself in such a way that, however God shows Himself—either through Himself or through His creatures, in good fortune or misfortune—one is always of good cheer with self-denial (as much as human weakness allows) and seeks only the praise and honor of God, just as Jesus Christ always conducted Himself toward His Father." 

This pleased the Servant of Wisdom, and he said he certainly desired to apply himself to this science, and that nothing so vexing would happen to him that could turn him away from this intention. Immediately, he began to build a house for himself and to busy himself with many restless affairs. The youth forbade him this and said that this art requires a quiet and spiritual leisure <note>original: "müssiggang"; here referring to the mystical concept of "Gelassenheit" or being still and "idle" from worldly activity to focus on God.</note>, and the less one does,

# Of several burdensome denials of self.
## The 22nd Chapter.

After God had forbidden the Servant the aforementioned external practices which had nearly taken his life, his emaciated nature was so greatly rejoiced that when he remembered the hard bonds, the Cross <note>Suso previously wore a wooden cross with thirty iron nails against his bare back.</note>, and the like, he wept for joy. These thoughts floated in his heart: "My LORD and God, in the future I will lead a quiet life, do myself some good, quench my thirst with water and wine, and sleep without bonds upon my straw mattress; for I have often wished for such comfort before my death. I have exhausted my strength enough; now I will rest." Such audacious thoughts overcame him, for he did not know what God intended for him. When he had been burdened and pleased by these thoughts for several weeks, he sat once upon his stool,

<column-break/>

and contemplated the saying from Job, Chapter 7: *The life of man is a struggle upon Earth* <note>original: "Des menschen leben ist ein streit auff Erden"; referring to Job 7:1.</note>. This youth stepped toward him and put the clothes on him, with these words: "Know that you have been a foot soldier until now; now GOD will have you be a rider <note>original: "Reuter"; here meaning a knight or cavalryman. And he said to the youth: "Since it so pleases God that I should be of the Order of Knighthood, if only I had achieved this dignity with glory in a battle, it would be all the more pleasant to me." # Chapter 19.

The Servant <note>The "Servant" is the title Henry Suso used for himself throughout his autobiography to maintain humility.</note> trembled in his whole body and threw himself onto the earth in the shape of a cross. With a sorrowful voice and heart, he prayed that if it were possible according to God’s divine goodness, He might release him from this; if not, then His eternal and divine will should be done. When he had lain in this anxious prayer for some time, he heard an internal voice speaking to him: "Be of good cheer; I will be with you myself and ensure that you overcome everything happily." He stood up and surrendered himself into the hands of God. In the morning, as he sat sorrowfully in his chamber after the **Holy Sacrifice of the Mass** <note>original: "Meßopffer"; the Eucharistic service.</note>, weighing everything in his mind while also being afflicted by the winter cold, he heard an internal voice telling him to look out the window. And behold, a dog was running through the monastery cloister, carrying an old cloth in its mouth; it was playing a strange game with it, for it would toss it up and down and tear it with its claws. The Servant looked toward heaven and sighed, hearing these words inwardly: "In the very same way, you will be tossed about in the mouths of your brothers." He thought: "Since it cannot be otherwise, surrender yourself willingly to it; and just as that cloth endures all mistreatment in silence, so must you do also." So he went down, took the cloth, and kept it for many years as a precious thing; and whenever he felt he might lose his patience, he would pull out the cloth so that by looking at it, he might recognize his duty and remain in silence. Whenever he occasionally turned his face away from his persecutors with displeasure, he was inwardly rebuked with these words: "Remember how I, your Lord, did not turn my most beautiful face away from those who struck and mocked me." Immediately, he would turn back to them with a gracious countenance. When, in the beginning,

<column-break/>

he encountered a **Cross** <term>Cross: In mystical literature, a "cross" refers to any suffering, trial, or humiliation sent by God for the soul's purification.</term>, he thought: "O my God, if only I could be released from this trial." When you carry a cross, you must not look toward its end, as if you will then enjoy rest; rather, as long as the cross lasts, humble yourself and prepare yourself to accept another one with the same spirit. Follow the example of a young maiden gathering roses, who is not satisfied with picking only one rose from the thorns, but picks many of them; you must do the same. Be ready, as soon as one cross departs, to accept another immediately." Among other **Friends of God** <note>original: "freunden Gottes"; a 14th-century mystical movement in the Rhineland focused on a personal, interior relationship with God.</note> who prophesied his future crosses to him was a holy virgin. She said that during the **Solemnity of the Angels** <note>The Feast of St. Michael and All Angels.</note>, after Matins, she had prayed fervently to the Lord for him. In a vision, she saw the Servant in a place where a large, wide rose garden with lovely white and red roses grew over him. When she raised her eyes to heaven, she saw the sun rising, shining brightly without clouds. In the light, or rather in the rays, stood a beautiful young boy in the form of a **Crucifix**. A ray came out of the sun and into the Servant’s heart with such power and effect that all his limbs and veins were set on fire. But the thick rose garden, filled with roses, stood in between and tried to separate the sun’s brilliance from his heart; yet it could not, because the brightly shining rays, with their great power, penetrated every bush and hedge and poured themselves into the Servant's heart. Afterward, she saw the young boy leave the sun and said to him: "Where are you going, O beautiful child?" "To my most beloved..."

The Servant said. She <note>Likely "Eternal Wisdom," often personified as a female figure in Suso's writings.</note> spoke: "Most graceful child, what does the radiance of the sun on his chest signify?" The child replied: "I have flooded his heart with such clarity that the radiance of light shall reflect back from him, break forth, and guide and draw many hearts to me; and the thick rose garden <note>In medieval mysticism, the "rose garden" often symbolizes a place of both beauty and thorns—here representing Suso’s impending trials and spiritual labor.</note> shall not be able to prevent this, which signifies the manifold Cross still awaiting him, so that it might be heartfully accomplished in him." Because a secluded life is very useful for a beginner, it seemed advisable to him that he should be separated from all human companionship and the entire world in his monastery for longer than ten years. When he rose from the table, he would go into his chapel and would speak to neither man nor woman at the gate, nor look at them. He had set certain and short limits for his eyes, which they were not allowed to exceed—namely, five feet. He remained at home at all times and went neither into the city nor to nearby places, but applied himself to solitude. This, however, did not help him, but in that same year he had to endure such a Cross <note>A metaphorical term for suffering or a heavy spiritual burden.</note> that he and others felt compassion for him. So that he might more easily endure the solitude of the chapel, in which he had locked himself for ten whole years without iron <note>original: "ohne eisen"; likely meaning he was not physically chained or forcibly imprisoned, but remained there by his own spiritual vow.</note>, he asked a painter to depict on the wall the ancient Fathers <note>The "Desert Fathers," early Christian hermits whose ascetic lives served as models for medieval monks.</note>, their sayings, and other godly things that would encourage a troubled and tempted person toward patience. But by God’s providence, he did not attain his desire in this case either, for when the painter began to sketch the images of the Fathers with charcoal, he immediately felt pain in his eyes and could not complete the work he had begun. He therefore asked for permission to go away until he felt better.

<column-break/>

When he asked him how much time might be required until he felt better, the painter replied that three months might pass. The Servant told him to set up the ladder again; so he climbed up, laid his hands on the images, touched the painter's poorly-seeing eyes with them, and said: "In the power of God and the holiest of the Fathers, I command you, O painter, that you return here tomorrow with healthy eyes." In the morning, he came back fresh and healthy and gave thanks to God and him for the gift of healed eyes. The Servant, however, did not attribute this good deed to himself, but to the holy Fathers. It seemed at that time as if God had given power to all devils and men to torment him, for the devils plagued him in every way most cruelly by day and by night. It happened once that he felt a desire to eat meat—for he had abstained from it for many years. As soon as he had satisfied his desire by eating meat, a devil appeared before him in a vision and spoke this verse: *While the food was still in their mouths, the wrath of God came upon them* <note>original: "Da die Speiß noch in ihrem Mund war/ da kam der zorn Gottes vber sie"; a reference to Psalm 78:31, describing the punishment of the Israelites in the wilderness.</note>. And with a great cry, he spoke to those standing around: "This monk is guilty of death; I will attack him for this!" But when the others would not allow this, he brought out a large borer <note>A tool used for drilling holes; an auger.</note> and said to him: "Since I am permitted to do nothing else to you, I will now torment your body with this borer, pierce your mouth, and so distress you that the pleasure you received from eating meat shall be atoned for." Immediately he set the borer to his mouth, from which his cheeks, teeth, and mouth swelled to such an extent that for three days he could put neither meat nor anything else into his mouth, except what he took in by sucking.

## Concerning the Manifold Cross.

### The 25th Chapter.

He once came to a small town; not far from there was a crucifix <note>Original: "Crucifixbild."</note> in a small house, as is customary, and there was a common rumor that many miracles <note>Original: "Mirackel."</note> occurred there. Therefore, the people offered many wax images and wax for the praise of God. <note>Wax images were "ex-votos"—offerings shaped like limbs or people, given in thanks for a healing.</note> When he came to the crucifix, he bowed his knees, prayed, and went with his companion to the inn. Meanwhile, a seven-year-old girl had seen him praying there. The following night, thieves broke in and took all the wax away. In the morning, the cry went through the town to the citizen who was the guardian of this image; he immediately inquired who might have committed this spiritual theft. The aforementioned girl said she knew the perpetrator, and when she was forced to reveal him, she pointed out the Servant, saying he had prayed there late in the evening and had gone from there into the town. The citizen immediately believed these words of the girl and spread the lies everywhere, so that the rumor went through the entire city, and everyone held the Servant to be a church thief. Meanwhile, many judgments were passed against him, regarding with what punishment one should do away with such a godless

<column-break/>

man. When he understood this, he was greatly terrified, although he knew himself to be innocent; he sighed to God and said:
> Lord, if I indeed should and must suffer, if you would send me such a Cross that did not dishonor my name, I would gladly bear it; but because you allow such things to happen to me which diminish my name, it is entirely repugnant to me.

He remained in the city, however, until everything was settled. It happened in another city that a great rumor resounded about him, which spread not only through the city but through the entire land. In that same city was a monastery in which there was a stone crucifix, the size of Christ, as it was said. Once during Lent, however, fresh blood was seen on the side of the image. The Servant went there with others so that he might see this wonder; when he saw the blood, he stepped closer and received it upon his finger before many onlookers. There was, however, a great gathering of people, and they forced him to say publicly what he had seen and touched. He told everything that had happened and did not conclude whether it had occurred in a divine or human way,

# Of a severe trial that befell him through a Brother.

## The 27th Chapter.

Once, a lay brother <note>A lay brother was a member of a religious order who focused on manual labor rather than the liturgical duties of a choir monk or priest.</note> was given to him as a traveling companion, whom he took with him reluctantly because the man was somewhat deranged in his mind; for the brother remembered all the things that had been done to him by other companions in a mischievous way. Nevertheless, he submitted himself to the will of his superior and took him along. Around noon, they came to a village where a fair was being held and many people were gathered. The lay brother was wet from the rain; therefore, he went into a house to dry himself by the fire and said to Wisdom <note>Suso frequently refers to himself as the "Servant of Eternal Wisdom," and in this text, "Wisdom" is used as a title for Suso himself.</note> that he could go no further, and that he should perform what he had to do without him, for he wished to wait for him there. But as soon as the Servant had gone out, the lay brother rose from the fire and sat at the table among the rowdy company of merchants who were there seeking their profit. When they saw the Brother loaded with wine and overcome by it, as he cast his eyes to and fro, they attacked him as if he had stolen a cheese. Meanwhile, as the godless people vexed the poor wretch in this way, five other armed men came, terrible to behold, seized the Brother, and cried out that he was carrying poison about; for at that time there was a common rumor of poison <note>This refers to the historical "well-poisoning" panics of the 14th century, often associated with the Black Death, where travelers and marginalized groups were falsely accused of spreading the plague.</note>. They captured him and made such a great uproar that nearly all the people ran to the scene. Because he saw himself captured and wished to be

<column-break/>

released from his bonds, he turned to those standing around and said: "Hear me, and I will immediately reveal everything to you." Everyone listened in great silence, and he said: "You see that I am not altogether wise, therefore I am held in little regard; but my companion is a bold and cunning man. It was commanded him by the Order that he should poison all the wells from this place all the way to Alsace; for he is traveling there and will devastate everything along the way with poison. Therefore, seize him quickly, otherwise we will carry out this murder; for he has thrown a sack full of poison into the well of this village, so that all who drink from the well shall die from the poison. This is the reason why I remained here and did not go with him, because I cannot endure it; and so that you may be certain of the truth, you will find a large sack with him, in which one carries books, which he has filled with poison and many golden pennies which the Jews have given to him and to our Order so that he might perform this cruel deed." When these cruel and rowdy people understood this, they cried out with a great shout: "Let him be pursued at once!" One immediately seized a spear, another an axe, the third whatever first came to his hands. They ran like madmen, breaking into houses and doors where they thought to find him, stabbing with their swords through the boards and straw.

# About a Murderer.
## The 28th Chapter.

---

As he once came from Lower Germany <note>The "Lowlands" or northern territories along the Rhine.</note> and traveled along the Rhine river toward the Upper Land <note>The "Highlands," referring to the mountainous regions of Southern Germany or Switzerland.</note>, he had a young companion who was well-equipped for the journey. One day, the Servant could not keep pace with him because he was sick and weary; instead, he remained nearly half a mile behind him. He looked behind him from time to time, hoping he might meet a companion with whom he could pass through the upcoming forest, for evening was approaching, and the forest was large and dangerous because of murderers. Before entering the woods, he stood still for a moment and waited for a fellow traveler. In the meantime, he saw two persons walking hurriedly toward him, one of whom was a beautiful young woman, the other a terrifying man. In the man's hands was a spear, and at his side a long sword; he was dressed in an old black coat. Because of the terrifying appearance 

<column-break/>

of the large man, the Servant looked around trembling to see if anyone was following him; but there was no one. He thought to himself: "My Heart and my God, what kind of people are these? How will I be able to go through this large and monstrous forest? What will happen to me?" He then made the sign of the Holy Cross upon his chest and entered the forest. When he had gone a little way, the woman came to him and asked him who he was and what his name was. He told the woman his name. She replied: "Sir, I know you well by name; I pray you, hear my confession." She began to confess and said: "Honorable Sir, I lament my misfortune to you. See the man who follows us; he is a murderer, and he kills people in the forest and other places, taking their money and clothes, and sparing no one. This man deceived me, [leading me away] from Fr<unclear>ancisco</unclear> <note>Likely referring to a location or perhaps "Friedland," though the text cuts off.</note>..."

## On Dangers by Water.

### The 29th Chapter.

Once, according to his custom, he had traveled to Strasbourg; <note>Strasbourg was a major center for the "Friends of God" movement, of which Suso was a part.</note> on the return journey, he fell into a terrible whirlpool of the Rhine, and at the same time the book which he had recently written <note>original: "das buch/ welches er etwas zuvor gemacht" — This likely refers to his most famous work, *The Little Book of Eternal Wisdom*.</note> fell in, because the Evil Enemy <note>The "böse Feind" is a common historical term for the Devil.</note> was entirely hateful toward him. Since he was then in mortal agony through the force of the river and began to sink down, and no one came to his aid, it happened through God's most gracious providence that just then a young soldier from Prussia <note>original: "Preussen" — refers to the lands of the Teutonic Knights.</note> came across from Strasbourg, who threw himself into the turbulent river and rescued both the Servant and his companion from death. Another time he traveled somewhere out of obedience in the winter; and as he had traveled all day until evening without food in the wind and in harsh, raw, and cold air on a cart, they came to a murky, deep, and fast-flowing water. The servant who drove the wagon came too close to the edge of the bank out of carelessness and overturned the wagon; the Servant fell immediately from the wagon and fell backward into the water. The wagon struck right upon him, so that, being pinned down by the wagon, he could turn nowhere nor help himself; therefore he was carried far under the water with the wagon until he reached a mill, where there ran

When the wagon was moved, they pulled him entirely wet onto the land, and his clothes immediately froze to his body because of the great cold, so that his teeth chattered. He stood for a while in such distress <note>original: "anfechtung" — a term for spiritual or physical trial/temptation.</note> and cried out to God: "O my heart, what shall I do, what shall I begin? The night is coming on; there is no house or village here where I could warm and dry myself; if I should die thus, it would certainly be a wretched death." And as he turned his eyes here and there, he saw from afar a village on a mountain; he went there as best he could, completely wet and frozen. It was already night when he went to the houses and asked for lodging for God's sake, but he was turned away everywhere, because no one took pity on him. Therefore he cried out with a loud voice to the Lord: "O God, it would have been better for me if you had let me drown in the water, for there I would have perished more quickly and better than having to freeze to death here." These pitiful words were overheard by a peasant who had previously turned him away; he took pity on him and led him into the house, where he nevertheless had a miserable night.

# On a sweet reckoning that he once held with God.

->The 31st Chapter.<-

Sometimes the Servant would go into the infirmary <note>The "Krancken hauß" was the part of the monastery dedicated to the care of the sick and elderly.</note> so that he might refresh his sick body in some small way. When he sat silently at the table according to his custom, he was attacked with harsh, mocking words, which at first seemed very painful to him. It caused him such sorrow that hot tears often ran down his face and fell into his mouth along with his food and drink. Therefore, he lifted his eyes and sighed to God: "Ah, most kind God, is my misery and sorrow not enough for you, with which you strike me day and night, unless even the humble food I enjoy is turned into bitterness?" This happened to him often. Once, he stood up from the table and could not restrain himself, but went into his private little chamber and prayed thus to God: "O most kind Lord and ruler of the world, show yourself kind and merciful toward me, a wretched man. Today I must hold a reckoning with you, and I cannot refrain from it. And although you owe nothing to anyone, nor are you bound in any matter because of your Majesty, yet it befits your infinite goodness that you let a troubled soul <term>angefochtenes gemüht: a spirit undergoing spiritual trials or "assaults" of doubt and despair</term> find restoration within your grace—especially when it can complain of its need to no other, and can obtain comfort from no other. See, my Lord, I take you as my witness, you who know all things, that I have always had an upright and pious heart from my mother's womb.

<column-break/>

I have never withdrawn a compassionate heart from anyone in trouble, and I have never been able to hear anything of my neighbor—whether he were present or absent—which could be a burden to him. My companions will bear me witness that I have rarely interpreted the actions of my brother, or any other person, in the worst way, neither before the authorities <note>Original: "Obrigkeit" — referring to the monastic superiors or local officials.</note> nor before others. Indeed, I have much more often interpreted all human actions for the best, as much as I was able. If I could not, I remained silent, or at least fled from the place so that I might not hear such things. But when I perceived that someone's honor was diminished, I replaced it with great friendship out of compassion, so that his good name might be more easily restored. I was called a faithful father of the wretched, and I was a special friend to all the friends of God. Whoever came to me troubled and distressed received at least some counsel from me, so that they went from me well-comforted and joyful. For I wept with those who wept and was troubled with the troubled, until I comforted them as if with motherly kindness. Never has someone been so opposed to me that I did not immediately forgive him everything, just as if he had never offended me, if he only showed me a friendly face. And my heart—what do I say of humans?—for even the need and distress of irrational animals <note>Original: "vnvernünfftigen Thier" — literally "un-reasoning animals," the standard term for beasts that lack human speech and logic.</note> and birds, which I either saw...

<meta>This page continues the "reckoning" or spiritual dialogue between the Servant (Henry Suso) and God, focusing on the transition from merely enduring suffering to actively responding with kindness to one's persecutors.</meta>

seen or heard, it moved my heart so much that I prayed to Almighty God to come to their aid. Whatever lives on earth has experienced mercy and goodwill from me. Yet you, O most kind God, allow some—whom the Apostle calls "false brothers" <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 11:26, where St. Paul speaks of the dangers he faced from within his own community.</note>—to set themselves quite cruelly against me, as is well known to you, O Lord, and evident to everyone; therefore, console me through yourself." After he had refreshed his soul with God in this way for a long enough time, he enjoyed a quiet peace and felt this answer from God within him: "Your childish reckoning, which you have set up with me, comes from this: that you do not always pay attention to the words and gestures of the suffering Jesus Christ. Know that it is not enough for God, as far as you are concerned, that you are of a kind and compassionate heart; rather, he requires something even more perfect from you. For he wills that when someone attacks you in an inhuman way with words and gestures, you should not only endure it more joyfully, but also die to yourself in such a way that you do not go to sleep until you go to that person and—with friendly and lovely as well as gentle words and gestures, as much as is ever possible—soothe and still his anger and cruelty. For through such gentleness and humility, you take the sword out of his hands and weaken his malice. This is the ancient path to perfection which Christ showed to his disciples when he said: *Behold, I send you out as lambs among wolves.* <note>original: "Sihe ich schicke euch wie die Lämmer vnder die Wölff" — a reference to Matthew 10:16.</note>" Afterward, when the Servant came to himself, this way of perfection seemed very difficult and troublesome to him. He could not think of it without irritation, and with even greater irritation he struggled to enter upon it; yet he surrendered himself voluntarily and applied all diligence

<column-break/>

to learn how to walk on this path. Later it happened that a lay brother <term>Laybruder: a member of a religious order who was not ordained as a priest and often performed manual labor</term> spoke to him in a boastful way and insulted him greatly. He bore it with patience and silence and thought he had now done enough. But inwardly he was warned that he must do something more. In the evening, when the lay brother wanted to go into the infirmary, the Servant waited for him at the door. As soon as he came out, the Servant prostrated himself at his feet and asked him humbly, saying: "Dearest spiritual brother, I beg you for the honor of God, if I have been burdensome to you in any matter or have offended you, that you would forgive such a wretched man for God's sake." The brother stood silent at first; afterward, he said with a clear voice: "Oh, what strange things you do! You have never done me any harm—no more than anyone else—but I have greatly offended you and attacked you with my biting tongue. Therefore, I beg you earnestly to forgive me." Thus his mind was made still and peaceful. Once, when the Servant was sitting at the table in the infirmary, a brother attacked him with defiant words. To this man, he turned kindly and smiled as if the brother had shown him a great favor. At this, the brother felt such remorse that he not only remained silent but also showed a friendly face. After the meal was finished, the brother told this in the town, saying: "Today I was made so ashamed at the table, the likes of which has never happened to me; for when I wantonly set upon the Servant with words, he showed me such a friendly face that I was made red with shame; and this example of his will always be useful and helpful to me."

# How he once, through great affliction, came nearly to the point of death.
## Chapter 32.

IT happened at one time that for many nights in a row he was awakened from sleep with great terror, and immediately began to pray the 21st Psalm, *My God, my God, look upon me* <note>original: "Mein Gott / mein Gott sehe auff mich" — This is the opening of Psalm 21 in the Vulgate (Psalm 22 in modern English Bibles), which contains the words spoken by Jesus on the Cross: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?"</note>, which the Lord Jesus, hanging on the Cross and in his final distress, said and spoke when he was abandoned by the Father and all creatures. This repetition, as soon as he awoke, greatly terrified the Servant; therefore, he cried out to his Lord hanging on the Cross with bitter tears and said: "Alas, my Lord and God, must I then bear a new cross with you? If it is so, I pray you, fulfill in me, a miserable man, your innocent and most holy death; stay with me and help me to overcome all affliction <term>anfechtung: a term used by Suso to describe intense spiritual trials, temptations, or mental assaults that test a believer’s faith.</term>." When the afflictions that had been signaled to him arrived afterward, they began to increase daily, and finally reached the point that they brought him—who was otherwise weak—nearly to death. For once, when he had gone to sleep late outside of his monastery, he fell into such a state of weakness that he thought he would die immediately, for not a single vein in him moved. When a pious and devout person noticed this—someone whom he had converted to God with great effort and labor—they ran to him in distress, feeling his chest and heart to see if life was still in him. But his heart was as still as that of a dead man; the person was terrified, wept, and cried out with a lamentable voice: "Alas, my God, see

<column-break/>

how today that excellent heart is extinguished and died out, which for so long a time carried you within it with great fear of God, and which preached and proclaimed you with words and writings to countless wayward people. Alas for this sorrowful cry, that the noble heart should rot, and that it is not permitted to live longer for your praise and the comfort of many people!" During this weeping, the person occasionally touched his heart, mouth, and arms, desiring to know whether he was dead or alive, but felt no movement. The face was pale, the mouth black, and no life remained, just like a dead body that one would want to bury immediately. This lasted for nearly two hours. While he lay in such a trance <term>verzückung: a state of mystical ecstasy or being "carried away" from the physical senses to experience the divine.</term>, his spirit enjoyed no other object or sight than God and His Divinity; the True One, the Truth, and the eternal Unity. But before he had begun to become weak and entranced out of himself, he had started to speak quite friendlily with God in this manner: "O Eternal Truth, whose inexhaustible abyss is known to all creatures, I, your miserable servant, seem now to have reached my end, as the powerlessness of my strength testifies. Because I am drawing my last breath, I speak with you, Almighty God, whom no one can lie to and whom no one can deceive, for all things are manifest to you. You alone know how..."

# How one should attribute <term>anfechtungen: intense spiritual trials, temptations, or assaults of the soul</term> to God with praise and thanksgiving.

## The 33rd Chapter.

As the Servant <note>Henry Suso refers to himself throughout his biography as "the Servant" to maintain a posture of humility.</note> one day brought his trials to mind and weighed within them the hidden judgments of God, he turned to God with sighs and spoke: "Lord, the Cross and these outward trials seem outwardly to be nothing other than sharp stings and thorns which pierce the flesh and the soul. Therefore, let some fruit of salvific instruction grow out of these rough thorns, so that we miserable ones might bear the Cross all the more patiently, to the praise and honor of God." When he had desired this from God for a long time and with great zeal, he was caught up in an inner ecstasy above himself, deprived of his physical senses, and he heard the Lord speak these loving words to him: "I will, in this present time, reveal to you the excellence and dignity of my life, and make known to you how one who is tried should direct all his suffering to the honor of God." When he heard this, his soul as it were melted away, and out of a great overflow of the heart, he stretched out the arms of his soul toward Heaven and Earth, giving thanks to God with unspeakable desire of the heart in this manner: "Until now I have praised you, my Lord, in my writings, and incited everything in creation that can be pleasing to you to your praise; but now I am forced to offer a new and previously unheard-of praise, which until now was unknown even to myself, for I have only now learned it in trials; and it is this: I desire with my whole heart that all

<column-break/>

the crosses and adversity which I have ever suffered, also all the anguish and pain, the bitterness of all wounds, the agony of all the sick, the sighs of all the sorrowful, the laments <note>original: "laſter" — in this context, it refers to the "cries" or "complaints" of those weeping, though it can also mean "vices" or "burdens."</note> of all those who weep, the shame and contempt of the oppressed, the poverty of widows, orphans, and the needy, the hunger and thirst of all the poor, the shed blood of all martyrs, the renunciation of one's own will in persons of young and blooming age, the strict works of penance of all the friends of God, all secret and public trials which I, or any other miserable person, have suffered in body, goods, honor, and fortune or misfortune, or what I shall yet suffer until death—that all this, O Heavenly Father, may reach toward your praise and toward the honor and glory of your only-begotten Son into all eternity. Furthermore, I, your miserable servant, desire with a patient and thankful mind and with all loyalty to stand in the place of all those who are tried—who perhaps do not know how to use their Cross correctly—to represent them. I direct all their trials and burdens to your praise, and in their stead, I offer everything to you for the praise of your only-begotten Son and for the comfort of the afflicted, whether they are still in the flesh of this present world or without the body in the world to come. I ask you, all you who are tried and miserable, you who bear the Cross with me: turn your eyes toward me, incline your ears to me; it is right that we should be overcome with joy and comfort, even though we are tried, in consideration of our..."

# The 31st Chapter

g 2

...of our most worthy Head, Jesus Christ, who first endured the manifold Cross in such a way that while living on Earth, He never experienced a single joyful day. If in a humble, lowly, and unimpressive lineage <note>The original German "geschlecht" refers to one's family line or ancestry.</note> only a single rich man were found, the whole lineage could without doubt boast of him. O most kind Jesus, you excellent Head of all Cross-bearers, be merciful to us; and when we lack patience in any <term>anfechtung: intense spiritual trials or assaults of the soul</term>, may you make that good before your heavenly Father. 

Lord, remember how you showed your help to one of your servants when he almost despaired in his adversity, and said: "My son, be of good cheer, look upon me. See, I am born of noble parents, yet I am a poor and needy man in this world; I was at once the most tender and the most wretched; I came from the greatest joys, nevertheless I fell into the bitterest Cross and suffering." Well then, we who are the brave soldiers of the highest Emperor, let us not become faint-hearted; we who follow the noble Commander, let us courageously carry the Cross after him. If the trial brought no other benefit than that we would become all the more similar to that brightly shining mirror, Jesus Christ—the more truly we follow him—this alone would be great enough. I maintain that even if God, after this life, were to give an equal reward to those who endure adversity and those who endure none, we should still rightly carry the Cross to be conformed to Him; for a lover unites himself and makes himself conformed to his beloved however, wherever, and whenever he can.

<column-break/>

But, O Jesus, you most invincible King, how do we dare or desire to be conformed to you in suffering? How great a difference is there between your trials and ours? You alone suffered the heaviest pain, though you had not deserved it. Where can anyone else boast that he has deserved no trial? For even if he suffers on one hand without his own fault, on the other hand he is still deserving of punishment. Therefore, we who have ever suffered any trial sit in a circle and place you, our most pleasant friend, in the center, and we stretch out our parched veins <note>A mystical metaphor for a soul "thirsting" for divine relief or grace.</note> toward you, the life-giving fountain of all grace. 

For just as the soil, which is cracked from dryness, is accustomed to pull the rain into itself abundantly, so also we wretched and punishable ones—the more we are bound to you, with hearts and minds all the more expanded and spread out, we receive you into ourselves. And just as you have testified with your holy mouth, we also wish—against all others' wills—to be washed in your richly flowing wounds and to be cleansed of all guilt and punishment, from which praise and honor grow for you, and we obtain grace from you; for through the power of your precious Blood, all our sin is blotted out.
