# How God still delights and comforts the afflicted in this world within their tribulations.

## The 34th Chapter.

ON an Easter feast, the <term>Servant of Wisdom: Henry Suso’s preferred way of referring to himself in his writings</term> was of good cheer. As he sat in his usual place where he was accustomed to take a little rest, he desired to know from God what kind of delight He would give in this world to those who had suffered much for Him. Meanwhile, he was caught up in ecstasy, and through Divine enlightenment, he received this answer: All those who are tried shall rejoice from their hearts and bear their cross patiently, with the assurance that their patience shall be repaid with an infinite reward. Since they have died with me here, they shall likewise rise joyfully with me; for I will grant them three extraordinary joys of incomprehensible worth.

The first: whatever they shall desire of me in Heaven and on Earth, they shall obtain.

The second: I will impart to them my Divine peace, which neither Angels, nor Men, nor Devils, nor any creatures shall be able to take from them.

The third: I will so inwardly embrace them that, being united with me, they shall remain with me eternally; they in me, and I in them. And just as it is very difficult for an afflicted heart to pray for something for a long time and not receive it, so for one hour of present trial, my mutual love shall not cease for a single moment, but shall begin here and always re-

<column-break/>

main, as human weakness will be able to bear it more or less according to its capacity.

The Servant of Wisdom was highly gladdened by these pleasant words. When he came to himself, he leaped from his chair and began to laugh so that it echoed in the chapel, and said joyfully to himself: "If anyone has endured anything adverse, let him come forward and complain. It seems to me that I have suffered nothing on Earth; I truly do not know what the cross and trial are. But of joy and exultation I can speak; behold, I have the choice to desire what I will, which is denied to those who turn away from the right path; what more can or will I desire?"

Among these words, he turned with his understanding toward the Eternal Truth and said: "I beseech you, most kind Jesus, as the Eternal Truth, that you give me this to understand, insofar as it can happen—for it is hidden from many blinded people." Immediately he was inwardly instructed thus: Those who conduct themselves according to <term>mortification: the practice of 'dying' to worldly desires or the ego</term> and self-denial, so that they die to themselves and all creatures (of whom there are but a small number), their mind and soul are so rapt in God that they know almost nothing of themselves, but rather see themselves and all other things in their first origin <note>In mystical theology, the 'first origin' refers to the state of all things as they exist eternally in the mind of God before creation.</note>; therefore, they are so delighted by all the works and deeds of God as if God had done nothing

# Concerning the first beginning of a newly starting spiritual person.
## The 36th Chapter.

Although the beginning for all virtuous people is different / one being of this nature / and another of that / nonetheless I wish to instruct you somewhat regarding the beginning of a godly life. I know a certain man in Christ / who initially cleansed his conscience with me through a complete confession / and thereafter applied himself to reveal his sins to an understanding and modest Confessor / to go forth from him / as from the representative of God / clean and unstained with sins forgiven / just as Christ (Luke 7) forgave all the sins of **St. Mary Magdalene** / when she wept / and washed the feet of Jesus with her tears / so was the nature of that man's beginning. When the Maiden <note>original: "Jungfraw." Because, however, for certain reasons she could not confess to him orally / she reflected upon her whole life / which in truth was entirely inno-

<column-break/>

-cent / and unstained / and where, in her own opinion, she had ever sinned / she wrote it upon a large **wax tablet** <note>original: "wächsene tafel." A common writing surface made of wood covered with wax, inscribed with a stylus; it could be sealed for privacy.</note> / and sent it to him thus sealed / and asked for Absolution regarding it. ## Concerning the first instructions / examples / or figures of a newly beginning spiritual man / and how his exercises should be joined with discretion <note>original: "bescheidenheit." In this context, it refers to the spiritual gift of discernment or moderation rather than modern "modesty."</note>.

### The 37th Chapter.

After the Servant had purified himself in the very beginning of a better life through confession / he set before his mind the circle or goal / in which he enclosed himself for the spiritual watch / and held himself in check. The first circle was his bedchamber / the chapel and the choir / herein he thought himself to be safe. The second circle was the whole monastery up to the gates. The third was the gate itself / where he had need of great foresight and power; whenever he went outside these three barriers / he felt / as if there were no difference between him / and the wild beasts / which have gone out from their dens / and are surrounded by hunters / for whom without doubt great diligence and skill are necessary to defend themselves. In the beginning of his conversion he had chosen for himself a lonely place / namely a chapel / where he attended to his devotion also through images / but especially when he was still a youth / he had Eternal Wisdom <term>Eternal Wisdom: In Suso's theology, "Sapientia" (Wisdom) is a personification of the Divine—specifically the Second Person of the Trinity—whom he pursued as a mystical lover or "Spouse."</term> painted for him on parchment / which rules over heaven and earth / and with miraculous beauty and exquisite form surpasses the ornament

<column-break/>

of all creatures / therefore he had taken her in his youth as a bride and friend. This very beautiful image he carried with him / as long as he had to travel around for the sake of his studies / and placed it before his eyes at the window of his bedchamber / looking at it often with inward delight of the heart; finally he placed it with a special intention in the chapel. What other images he had / which would be suitable for him and all beginning spiritual persons / can be sufficiently perceived from the figures and sayings of the ancient Fathers <note>The Desert Fathers: early Christian hermits and monks who lived in the Egyptian desert in the 3rd and 4th centuries.</note> / which were painted in the chapel / and partly written there / yet the meaning is expressed more than the words themselves.

Abbot Arsenius asked the angel what he should do / that he might be saved / there it was said to him: Flee / keep silent / and rest <note>original: "Fliehe / schweige / vnd ruhe." This is the famous Latin ascetic maxim "Fuge, tace, quiesce."</note>. In a vision the angel read to the Servant from the *Life of the Fathers* this saying: The origin and fountain-head of all good is to remain constantly within oneself.

Abbot Theodorus: Purity of the heart gives greater knowledge / than studying.

### The 73rd Chapter.

Abbot **Moses**: Sit in your cell / and it will instruct you in all things. <note>Moses the Black (c. 330–405 AD), a former bandit who became a Desert Father, often emphasized that the cell itself is the monk's greatest teacher.</note>

Abbot **John**: Keep your outer man in silence / and the inner man in purity.

**Again**: A fish outside of the water / and a monk outside of his cell both sink to the bottom / and perish.

The holy **Anthony**: The chastisement <term>casteyung: physical discipline or fasting</term> of the body / the devotion of the heart / and the withdrawal from people bring about / and make plain the state of chastity.

**Again**: Wear no clothing / which savors of vanity; the first battle of a newly beginning cleric is / to fight bravely against the vices.

Abbot **Poemen**: Be angry with no one / even if he threatens to strike out your right eye. <note>The original text uses "Abbot Pastor," which is the Latin translation of the Greek name "Poemen," meaning "Shepherd."</note>

Abbot **Isidore**: An angry person displeases God / even if he performs great signs.

**Hyperichius**: He commits a lesser sin / who eats meat on forbidden days / than he who cuts down the honor of his neighbor. <note>This highlights the spiritual priority of charity over mere ritual fasting.</note>

Abbot **Pior**: It is very evil to criticize the faults of others / and not to inspect one's own.

**Zacharias**: He must be highly despised / who wishes to be perfect.

**Nestor**: You must first become a donkey / before you attain Divine Wisdom. <note>A metaphor for humble, silent service and the patient endurance of burdens.</note>

An **elder**: You must always be immovable in good fortune and misfortune / just like the deceased.

**Elias**: A pale face / a lean body / humble gait and

<column-break/>

conduct adorn a cleric very well.

**Hilarion**: One must withhold the fodder from a lusty horse / and from a willful body.

An **elder**: Take the wine away from me / for the death of the soul is hidden within it.

**Poemen**: He is not to be called a monk / who still complains / who cannot subdue anger / who cannot avoid much chatter / and who cannot endure the contempt of himself.

**Cassian**: As Christ behaved while dying on the Cross / so should we arrange our manners.

Abbot **Anthony** says to a brother: My brother / take heed of your salvation / otherwise neither God / nor I will be able to advise / or help you.

When a woman begged Abbot **Arsenius** // that he would be mindful of her before God: But I / he says / pray to God / that I may completely forget you. <note>A classic example of monastic "detachment," where the monk avoids even spiritual attachments to individuals to focus solely on God.</note>

**Macarius**: I lead my body astray / because it leads me astray / and attacks me with many temptations.

Abbot **John**: I have never been obedient to my own will // and have never taught others with words // what I had not first done myself in deed.

An **elder**: Many beautiful words without good works are to be esteemed like a tree / that has many leaves / and little fruit.

**Nilus**: He who deals much with the world // must of necessity receive many wounds.

An **elder**: If you can do nothing else in the cell / then at least preserve its walls for the love of God. <note>The advice implies that simply staying in one's place of prayer is a victory, even if the monk feels unproductive.</note>

**Hyperichius**: He who lives chastely / is honored here / and crowned by God.

**Apollonius**: Resist in the beginning / and crush the serpent’s head. <note>This refers to stopping sinful thoughts at their very first appearance before they take root.</note>

**Agathon**: For three years I carried a stone in my mouth / so that I might learn to keep silence.

When an elder was asked by a youth / how long he must remain silent / he gave this answer: until he is asked to speak.

The holy **Syncletica**: Rejoice when you are sick / for God is mindful of you. Do not attribute the cause of your sickness to fasting / because even those who do not fast become sick. If you are attacked by temptations of the body / rejoice likewise / because another Paul can be made out of you. <note>Syncletica of Alexandria (c. 270–350 AD) was one of the "Desert Mothers" (Ammas); she compares the struggle with the flesh to the trials of the Apostle Paul.</note>

**Joannes**: The sun has never seen me angry.

**Paphnutius**: It is of no use to have begun well / unless one perseveres until the end.

The Abbot **Moses**: Whatever is contrary to the purity of the heart / that is to be avoided / even if it appears to be good.

**Cassian**: The goal of all perfection consists in this / when the soul with all its powers is moved and drawn into the one thing / which is God.

<column-break/>

The Servant sent these figures / and sayings of the Fathers to his spiritual daughter / with the intention / that she should also discipline her body according to the example of the host of Fathers / which she also did; she began to discipline <term>Castleyen: physical mortification or penance</term> herself with hair shirts and furs / with terrifying bonds / with sharp iron nails / and the like. When the Servant understood this / he commanded her thus: My daughter / if you have resolved within yourself to lead a spiritual life according to my counsel / as you have requested of me / then cease from this great stringency / and hardness / for it is not suited to your female weakness / and your delicate nature. Christ does not say; "Take my cross upon your shoulders," but rather; "Each shall take up **his** cross upon himself." Matt. 16. Do not desire the stringency of the ancient Fathers / nor seek to follow the heavy exercises of your spiritual father / but take from this what is endurable for your weak body / so that you may indeed kill the vices in you / but live long according to the body / for this is a heartfelt / and very useful exercise for you. When she, however, desired to know why the Servant had undertaken such stringent exercises / which he advised neither her / nor others to undertake / he directed her to the writings of the Fathers / saying: It is written / that some of the Fathers led an almost inhuman and incomparably stringent life / so that in these times delicate people hear of it with terror / for they do not notice / how much fervent love united with virtue can do and suffer for God’s sake / for to a true lover even all impossible things become possible through God. Thus speaks David. Psal. 18. In my God I shall leap over a wall. <note>original: "In meo Deo transiliam murum." Suso uses this to explain that his own extreme penances were a result of a specific divine "drive" not intended for everyone.</note>

On the contrary, we read in the writings of the **Holy Fathers** that some omitted this severity, even though they all strove toward the same goal. The Holy Apostles **Peter** and **John** were not led in the same way. Who can say and explain everything, other than that "God is wonderful in his saints"? <note>original: "Gott wunderbarlich iſt in ſeinen heyligen." This is a reference to Psalm 68:35 (Psalm 67:36 in the Vulgate).</note> And according to the multitude of His greatness, He wishes to be praised in different ways.

Finally, we are not all endowed with the same qualities of nature and body; therefore, what is beneficial to one is harmful to another. If someone cannot endure such severity, let him not think that he is thereby prevented from attaining **perfection** <term>vollkommenheit: a state of spiritual maturity and union with God, often the goal of monastic life</term>, although such delicate and soft people should not, on the other hand, despise or interpret for the worst the rough exercises and severe works of penance performed by others. 

Let everyone take heed of themselves, what God requires of him, and satisfy Him, setting all other things aside. It is much better to maintain a moderate and modest way of life than one that is too severe; because it is difficult to hit the middle mark, it is better to deviate slightly from the middle than to exceed it too much. For it often happens that when nature is deprived of too much in an internal, disorderly way, one must later give in to it far too much; although in this regard many Holy Fathers also overstepped out of burning fervor. Such a severe way of life and the aforementioned examples apply to those who are far too merciful to themselves, living softly and misusing their untamed and willful bodies to their own harm—which cannot be said of you and your kind. God has many kinds of crosses,

<column-break/>

with which He chastises <term>casteyet: from the Latin 'castigare', meaning to discipline or purify through suffering</term> and tests His friends. I believe God wishes to lay a cross upon you that is no less burdensome than this bodily chastisement; bear this, then, with patience.

Not long after, God afflicted the **Virgin** <note>This refers to Elsbeth Stagel (c. 1300–1360), a Dominican nun and Suso's spiritual daughter who helped preserve his writings.</note> with long-lasting illnesses, so that she remained afflicted by them until her death. Therefore, she wrote to the **Servant** <note>Henry Suso often referred to himself in the third person as "the Servant of the Eternal Wisdom."</note> that it had happened to her according to his words. The Servant gave her this written answer: 

"My most beloved daughter, not only has God foretold your cross through me, but He has also attacked and hurt me in you, especially because I have no one else who will assist me in the future with equal diligence and loyalty in writing books." 

Therefore, the Servant prayed to God from his heart for you, that if it pleased Him, He would restore your health. But when he was not heard immediately according to his wish, he spoke out of a **friendly anger** <note>A term for "holy boldess," where a mystic speaks familiarly or even argumentatively with God.</note> that in the future he would write no more books about Him, and also omit the **Morning Greeting** <term>Morgengruß: a specific daily devotion or prayer ritual Suso practiced</term> to which he was accustomed, unless He restored your health.

While he sat down in the **chapel** in his usual manner during this disturbance of heart, he was caught up in ecstasy and saw a great number of **angels** entering the chapel, singing a heavenly song for his consolation; for they knew that he was then highly tempted and troubled. When they asked him why he was so distressed and did not sing with them, he confessed to them the concern of his heart, because God would not hear his prayer. They exhorted him to be at peace and to betake himself to rest, because God had sent the illness for your highest benefit, so that it might be your cross in this world, through which you—

# On Childlike Devotion in the Newly Commencing Spiritual Disciples of Christ.
## Chapter 38.

When the Servant <note>The "Servant" is the name Henry Suso used for himself in his writings to maintain humility.</note> visited the sick maiden <note>This refers to Elsbeth Stagel, a nun and Suso's spiritual daughter who recorded much of his life.</note>, she asked him to speak of spiritual matters that made no mention of severity <note>Referring to the harsh physical penances Suso was known for.</note>, but would yet be pleasant for a God-loving soul to hear. The Servant began to tell her something of his childlike devotion and said: When the Servant was still young, he kept this custom for a long time: whenever he was bled <note>Bloodletting was a common medieval medical practice; Suso turned this physical pain into a spiritual exercise.</note>, he would go to Christ hanging on the Cross, show him his wounded arm, and say:

> O Lord Jesus, my dearest friend, remember that among men the custom is that one friend goes to another when they have been bled, so that they may regain healthy blood; you, my heart, know that I love no one more than you, therefore I come to you, so that you may bless my wounds and grant me healthy blood.

When in his youth he was shorn <note>This likely refers to the monastic tonsure (shaving the head), which Suso reinterpreted as an offering of his physical beauty.</note> and appeared in a lovely form in his countenance, he betook himself to Jesus and said:

> O sweetest Jesus, if my face were more beautiful than all roses, the Servant would wish to offer this beauty to you alone; and though you already look upon the heart alone and do not care much for the outward appearance, yet my heart shows you its love, because

<column-break/>

take this trial from the providence <note>original: "vorsichtigkeit" - used here in the sense of divine foresight or providence.</note> of God as the most acceptable one.

> I turn to you alone, and to no other.

Whenever he put on a new garment, he went to his accustomed place and asked the Lord—since this garment was obtained through His bounty—that He would let it be salutary for him and let it be worn out according to His will. When in the springtime the beautiful little flowers grew forth, he refrained from touching or picking any until he had made a wreath of flowers for his spiritual friend, in which he placed the first flowers in honor of the Mother of God. Afterward, when it seemed to him to be time, he picked the flowers with many loving thoughts, carried them to his chamber, and wove a wreath; then he went into the choir or into the chapel of the Mother of God, knelt down before her image, and placed the wreath upon it with the intention <note>original: "intention" - Suso uses this Latin-derived term to describe the conscious spiritual purpose behind his action.</note> that, since she was the most beautiful flower of all and the springtime of his heart, she might not disdain the firstfruits of the flowers offered by her Servant. When he had once crowned this Child-bearing Woman with such a crown, he saw in a vision heaven open and the angelic spirits, adorned with shining garments, flying up and down—

This man’s diligence and desire were directed toward loving God from the heart and placing Him before all things, so that He might be loved by others above all else, and that he might draw them away from harmful and vain love. This indeed happened with many persons of both the male and female sex. But when the devil saw that his prey was being taken from him and given instead to God the Lord, he felt it deeply. He appeared to several pious people and threatened the Servant, saying that he intended to avenge himself upon him in every possible way. Meanwhile, the Servant came to a monastery <note>This likely refers to a "double monastery" where both monks and nuns lived in separate quarters but shared a church.</note> where both the men and the spiritual women lived according to their Rule. In this monastery, there were two spiritual persons, a man and a woman, who were very fond of each other with a special love and friendship. The devil had so painted this in their blinded hearts with the color of virtue that they believed it was no sin, but rather permitted to them by God. When the Servant was asked whether this friendship was in accordance with the will of God, he answered: "No; rather, your opinion is false and contrary to Christian teaching." He saw to it that this friendship was severed, and they afterwards lived chastely and purely. When this happened, a holy virgin named Anna saw a great multitude of devils gathered over the Servant. They cried out: "O rogue monk! Come, let us attack him and kill him!" They cursed him because he had driven them away with his warnings and advice. They also swore with cruel gestures and faces that they would always watch him and

<column-break/>

Even if he avoided every opportunity for scandal, this would nonetheless be brought about through their lies. The aforementioned Anna was terrified by this and prayed to the most holy Mother of God that she would assist him in all the approaching danger. To this, Mary kindly answered: "Without the permission <note>Original: *verhängniß*, meaning divine providence or what God allows to happen.</note> of my Son, nothing shall be harmful to him; but whatever He permits to happen to him shall be very useful and profitable for him." When she reported this to the Servant, he began to fear the plots of the devils. As was his custom in times of anxiety, he went to a chapel on a mountain which was consecrated to the honor of all the angels. He performed his prayer by walking nine times around the chapel in honor of the nine choirs of angels <note>In medieval theology, angels were organized into nine levels, such as Seraphim, Cherubim, and Archangels.</note>, and he begged them to stand by him in every hostile attack. Afterwards, he was led in a vision to a beautiful field where he saw a great number of holy angels who wished to assist him, and they comforted him with these words: "The Lord is with you, and He will not leave you in any anxiety or danger; therefore, do not cease to draw people to the love of God." Strengthened by this, he proved himself by continuing to lead all sorts of people to God. He even approached a terrifying and bold man, who had not gone to confession for eighteen whole years, with kind words and won over his soul, so that the man confessed his sins with such heartfelt repentance that they both wept bitterly; and this man died shortly there—

# Chapter 40.

...to the martyrs, with sadness; she gave as an answer: "Now the song of suffering goes before, but afterwards the joyful *Gaudeamus* <note>original: "Gaudeamus"; Latin for "Let us rejoice," the opening word of a traditional hymn of joy.</note> shall follow upon it." When he came to himself, he trembled and said:
> O kind Jesus, shall I carry the Cross <note>Suso frequently uses the "Cross" as a metaphor for personal trials and the imitation of Christ’s suffering.</note> again?
And as he was very troubled on the journey, his companion said, "Father, why are you so sad?" He answered: "Brother, here I must sing the Mass of the Martyrs," indicating it was revealed to him by God that he should be cruelly tempted; but because the brother did not understand it, he remained silent. Later, when he came into the city before Christmas, he was seized with such temptations that he humanly thought his heart must burst, for all comfort, all delight, all worldly honor, and whatever can delight a person was withdrawn from him. His Cross was of this nature: among others whom he desired to lead to God, a cunning and deceitful woman came to him under the guise of honest conversation, and she did this so secretly that the Servant did not notice it for a long time. This woman had previously fallen into sin with a man; with this vice she was still not satisfied, but wanted to attribute the child to an innocent person. Because of this committed sin, the Servant did not want to turn her away, but heard her Confession and provided her with all necessary and spiritual services, more than to other religious persons. After a long time, he and other trustworthy people found that she secretly remained in her previous sins; yet he kept this silent because he did not want to betray her publicly. Meanwhile, he gradually withdrew himself from her and no longer provided the previous spiritual services. When she noticed this, she commanded him not to do so, for if she were to be deprived of his services, she would give him the child, which was fathered by a world-

<column-break/>

ly man, and proclaim him as its father, and thus take away his honor and good name, so that people everywhere would have reports of him. At these words, he was terrified; in silence he sighed and said:
> Everywhere I am in anguish, not knowing where I should turn; if I do it, I am in pain; if I do it not, I find myself unwell; in all places, anguish and distress overtake me.
He considered what God would allow the Devil to do to him in this case; yet he finally took this counsel with God within himself: that it was more useful for his body and soul that he should choose, among two evils, rather to be separated from the godless woman, whatever might happen to his honor and good name. And he followed this counsel. Through this, she was so enraged that she ran here and there to clergy and laity, and out of godlessness, she highly shamed herself, only so that she might forge a Cross for the miserable man, and told everyone she had born the child from him. This disturbed those who believed her words, and so much the more as his holiness had been more widely renowned. This cut through his heart and soul, and he almost fainted from anguish and misery; he could neither sleep at night nor have rest by day. Therefore, he sighed to God and said:
> See, my Lord, the pitiable time is here; see, the hour is at hand; how can I endure the infinite tribulations of the heart? Oh, that I had died so that I might neither have seen nor heard this! When he saw the child crying, he pressed it to his breast and said:
> "My dearest child, stop crying. Should I kill you because I did not father you, and because I must endure heavy labor on your account? I cannot do you any harm, for you shall be my and God's child; as long as God grants me a morsel of bread, I will share it with you for the praise of God, and for your sake, I will suffer everything that comes my way."

When the cruel woman <note>Likely the midwife or accomplice who previously offered to kill the child.</note> heard this mournful voice from the one who was supposed to destroy the child, she was moved to her heart and began to cry aloud, so that the Servant <note>Suso refers to himself throughout his writing as "The Servant of the Eternal Wisdom."</note> had to quiet her, for he feared it might become known. When she had wept enough, he gave the child back to her, blessed her, and said:
> "May God bless <note>original: "benedeye," from the Latin benedicere</note> you, and may his holy angels protect you from all harm,"

and he ordered her to raise the child at his expense. After this, the godless woman—the child’s mother—slandered the Servant more and more, especially in places where she thought it would be most damaging to him. Because of this, many honest people took pity on him and often wished death upon the godless woman from God, the righteous Judge. Once, one of his relatives came to him and said:
> "Woe to that godless woman who attributes such a deed to you; I will certainly take revenge on her for your sake. I will hide myself on the long bridge of that river, and when she crosses it, I will push her into the water so that her cruelty may be avenged."

The Servant said:
> "Not so, my friend. God, to whom everything is known, knows that she falsely attributes this child to me; therefore I commend this matter to Him, that He may let her die or live according to His pleasure. And even if I could kill her without

<column-break/>

damaging my soul, I would still want to honor all chaste and honest women through her and let her live." The relative answered in anger:
> "It matters nothing to me whether I kill a woman or a man, if they had insulted me so."

The Servant spoke:
> "By no means, for such would be a great tyranny and a barbaric outrage; let me only suffer every cross <note>In this context, a "cross" refers to a spiritual trial or burden of suffering.</note> that God wishes to send me."

Once, in his greatest temptation <note>Suso often uses "temptation" to describe periods of intense spiritual or social trial.</note>, he sought some relief and comfort and therefore went to two friends who had faithfully stood by him in his time of prosperity. There, God let him see in truth how there is nothing permanent in created things, because he was insulted <note>original: "inuirt," a Germanized form of the Latin injuriari, meaning to be wronged or slandered.</note> more by them than by the common folk. One of them rebuked him harshly with words and turned his face from him, using insulting and blasphemous words. Among other things, he renounced all friendship and kinship with him because he felt ashamed of him. These words pierced his heart; therefore he said with a mournful voice:
> "O my brother, if God had plunged you into the mud pits <note>original: "kothlacken," referring to filthy gutters or puddles of manure.</note> where I lie, I would immediately jump in and pull you out; but for you, unfortunately, it is not enough to see me sunk so deep, but you also strive to trample me underfoot."

I complain of this then to the heart of the most kind Jesus, who was once most afflicted. But this friend told him to be silent, saying:
> "It is over for you; not only your sermons that you have given, but also your books will be rejected."

But he lifted his eyes up toward heaven and said:
> "I place my trust in Almighty God that my books and writings will one day be as acceptable as they ever were."

Such miserable comfort he received from his best friends. In that same city, several pious people had provided him with all necessary things up until that time; however, when this rumor reached them, they withdrew all help and friendship from him until they had heard the thorough truth, at which point they returned to him. One day, while he sought some rest, he was carried away in a trance into a beautiful landscape. There, someone spoke to his soul in this way: "Hear, hear a consoling word which I wish to read to you." Then let the Latin words from Isaiah chapter 62 be heard: <note>original: "No vocaberies ultra derelicta, &c."</note> *You shall no longer be called the Abandoned One, and your land shall no longer be called Desolate; but you shall be called: 'My delight is in her,' and your land: 'An inhabited land,' for the Lord takes pleasure in you.* These words were repeated to him a third and fourth time. He said out of wonder: "What does this frequent repetition mean?" "Because," the voice said, "you should trust strongly in God, for he will also give the necessities of life to his earthly friends—that is, to their mortal bodies—and what they lack in one place, he will restore in another; so God will also do for you according to his goodness." And all this later happened so clearly that many of them laughed out of joy and praised God, whose eyes had previously shed hot tears. It happened to this tormented man no differently than to a poor animal which has been torn apart and eaten by lions, whose bones still give off some scent, toward which the wasps and hungry flies swarm; they gnaw at the remaining bones in great heaps and carry the marrow away with them into the air. In such a manner was this miserable man slandered and belittled by the clergy <note>religious figures</note> under the outward appearance and cloak of "spiritual concern," so that they might amuse themselves out of a sense of friendship, though

<column-break/>

there was no loyalty in them. At times, the thought occurred to him: "If one must suffer something from Jews, heathens, or openly wicked people, it is still bearable; but those who torment me boast of being your friends, therefore my cross is all the more unbearable." But when he weighed everything rightly, he blamed them not, but attributed everything to God. However, when he was particularly struggling with impatience, he received this answer internally: "Remember that the Lord Jesus wished to endure in his company not only the holy John, his most beloved disciple, and the holy Peter, his faithful vicar, but also the unclean Judas. But you, who desire to follow Christ, why do you endure your 'Judas' with such ill-will?" Soon another thought gave this answer: "Ah, kind Jesus, if your tormented friend had only one Judas, it would be bearable; but now every corner is filled with them, so that when one leaves, five more take his place." To this, he received this answer internally: "He who is of good courage must look upon no one as his 'Judas,' but rather as a co-worker of God, through whom he must be exercised for his salvation. When Judas kissed Jesus, He called him his friend. 'My friend,' He said, 'why have you come?'" As he was being led astray in this manner, one small comfort remained to him which gave him strength: that the rumor had not yet reached the highest Prelates <note>high-ranking officials</note> of the Dominican Order. # The Life of the Blessed Henry Suso.

...as happens to those who endure their **Purgatory** <term>Purgatory: a state of suffering or purification after death; Suso suggests some experience this cleansing while still alive through earthly trials</term> here through illness, poverty, and the like; or those whom He allows to be attacked by devilish men so that they might be freed from the terrifying face of the devils at death. Some suffer out of fervent love. There are also in this world some vain and hopeless **tribulations** <term>tribulations: spiritual trials or "anfechtungen," often involving doubt or emotional distress</term> which those must suffer who wish to satisfy the world, who undoubtedly buy the pain of Hell dearly; this can comfort pious, tempted people in their suffering. Some God calls quite kindly, that they should turn to Him, who nonetheless resist Him. Others He must seize by the hair through tribulation, as it were, pulling them to Himself with force, so that they do not escape from His hands. Others make their own **Cross** <note>In mystical tradition, the "Cross" refers to any personal burden or suffering that brings one closer to the experience of Christ</note> for themselves, because they value highly that which is nothing; which a certain tempted man experienced as he passed by a house and heard a woman crying piteously. For when he came into the house to comfort her, he asked what her concern was. She said she could not find a lost needle again. He soon went out and thought thus: "O foolish woman, if you had one of my burdens on your shoulders, you would not weep for a lost needle." Thus some tender people make themselves a Cross where there is none. The most glorious Cross is the tribulation that is like unto Christ; that is, just as God the Father laid upon His Son, and today still treats His friends by laying it upon them—not that anyone is without guilt alongside Christ—but just as Christ in His suffering behaved meekly as a lamb surrounded by wolves,

<column-break/>

so He also lays a great Cross upon His dear friends, so that we impatient ones might learn from their example to endure with patience and to overcome evil with good. Consider this, my lord, and do not bear your Cross unwillingly, wherever it may come from—if it is possible for a man, when he knows it comes from God, to accept it. The same woman said: "Father, the glorious Cross of which you spoke last—when one suffers for one’s own guilt—is granted to few. Now I would like to know how a sinner should overcome his tribulations through God’s help, for such a person does not seem to be 'tempted' in the holy sense, because he has forsaken God and is punished externally." The **Servant** <note>Henry Suso refers to himself as "The Servant" throughout the text as a sign of humility</note> answered: "I know a man who held this custom: whenever he committed some fault out of natural weakness, he behaved like a diligent washerwoman. She first cleans the clothes with diligence, then she throws them into clean water and thus drives away all impurity. He used to never rest until he reached the flowing, precious blood running from the **Wounds of Christ**. In this holy blood, he washed away all impurity and immersed himself entirely in the bloody, streaming brook, just as one is accustomed to wash small children in a warm bath. And this he did with the highest confidence that through the power of this blood all his sins would be extinguished; and this custom he kept at all times, whether he suffered with or without guilt."

# How some worldly people were drawn away from the love of temporal things and led to the love of God.

## The 43rd Chapter.

As the **Servant** <note>Henry Suso refers to himself throughout the text as "The Servant" of Eternal Wisdom.</note> applied himself to drawing people away from temporal love and leading them toward God, he noticed that in certain convents, several people wearing the habit of a religious order still possessed worldly hearts. Among these was one who had her "friends"—or lovers—which is a **spiritual poison** <term>spiritual poison: Suso uses this term to describe worldly attachments or romantic entanglements that distract a nun from her vows to God</term>. The Servant told her that she should renounce these friends and in their place embrace **Eternal Wisdom** <note>original: "ewige Weißheit"; Suso's personification of Christ as the object of mystical love</note>. This was difficult for her, as she was young, beautiful, and entangled in such matters; yet he finally brought her to the point where she was willing to obey him. However, when her will was later changed through the influence of others, the Servant said: "My daughter, cease this; see, I tell you beforehand, if you do not do it voluntarily, you shall have to do it against your will." Because she made light of his words, he prayed to God that He would draw her away from it, whether through good fortune or misfortune. Once, he even scourged himself until he bled and prayed that God would tame her, which indeed happened: for when she returned home, an unsightly hump <note>original: "vnstätiger hoger"; a physical deformity interpreted here as a divine intervention to protect her chastity</note> suddenly grew upon her back, which made her quite deformed. Thus, she was forced by necessity to give up what she otherwise would not have. In the same **uncloistered convent** <term>uncloistered: a religious house where the residents were not strictly confined and had more contact with the outside world</term> was another young, noble Virgin, who for many years had wretchedly consumed her heart and time with all sorts of people. She had become so blind to her state that she fled from the Servant like a wild animal, fearing that he might perhaps hinder her. This Virgin's biological sister begged the Servant to try and see if he might convert her to God. Because he considered this nearly impossible, he said: "I

<column-break/>

believe it would be easier to bend the heavens than to lead her away from this, for it can only happen through death." But she said: "I trust that <note>original abbreviation: "dʒ" for "das"</note> whatever you ask of God, He cannot refuse you." The Servant promised her his diligence. Because she always fled from his speech, he noticed that around **St. Margaret’s Day** <note>July 20th; a common feast day in the medieval calendar</note> she had gone into the field with others. He followed her secretly, walking around the field so that he might conveniently come upon her. When she noticed him, she turned her back to him, showed an angry face, and said: "Sir, why do you come to me? Go your way; you will accomplish nothing with me. I would rather lose my head than **confess** <term>beichten: the sacrament of penance where one admits sins to a priest</term> to you, and I would rather be buried alive than renounce my love." Her companion rebuked her and said he had only done this for the sake of her salvation. "I," she said, "will not deceive him, but will open my heart to him in word and deed." At these stubborn words and strange gestures, the Servant was terrified and turned so red with shame that he could not speak a word. The other Virgins were disturbed by the insolence of their companion. The Servant went away from there, looked toward heaven, sighed, and wanted to leave the place entirely; but God alone put this in his mind: "When someone wishes to do something for God and the world, he must not rest or give up so easily." This happened in the afternoon, after the **Lord's Supper** <note>original: "Abendmahl"; here likely referring to the midday meal or the afternoon liturgy</note> was held. As the Virgins went into the garden to attend to their business, the aforementioned Virgin went with them; and as they passed by the hospital where the Servant lived, he asked one of her companions...

...as happens to those who endure their **Purgatory** <term>Purgatory: a state of suffering after death to atone for sins; Suso argues that earthly suffering like illness or poverty can serve as a "Purgatory" while still alive</term> here on earth through sickness, poverty, and the like, or those whom He allows to be attacked by devilish people, so that in death they might be delivered from the terrifying face of the devils. Some suffer out of fervent love. There are also in this world some vain and hopeless **trials** <term>trials: original "anfechtungen," referring to spiritual struggles, temptations, or bouts of despair</term> which those must suffer who wish to satisfy the world; these people undoubtedly purchase the pain of Hell at a high price, a fact which can serve to comfort devout, afflicted people in their own suffering. Some God calls quite kindly, that they may turn to Him, yet they still resist Him. Others He must seize by the hair, as it were, through trials, and draw them to Himself by force, so that they do not escape His hands. Others make their own **Cross** <note>Cross: Suso uses the "Cross" as a metaphor for the specific spiritual burdens or sufferings God assigns to each person to refine their character</note> because they value things that are worthless, which a certain afflicted man experienced when he passed by a house and heard a woman crying piteously. For when he went into the house to comfort her, he asked what her trouble was. She said she could not find a lost needle. He soon went out again and thought:
> O foolish woman, if you had one of my burdens upon your shoulders, you would not weep for a lost needle.
Thus some delicate people make a Cross for themselves where there is none. The most heartfelt Cross is that trial which is like Christ's—that is, just as God the Father laid it upon His Son, and still today is accustomed to lay upon His friends; not that anyone is without guilt alongside Christ, but just as Christ in His suffering, like a lamb surrounded by wolves, behaved meekly

<column-break/>

and gentle, so He also lays a great Cross upon His <unclear>dear</unclear> friends, so that we impatient ones may learn from them to bear all things with patience and to overcome **evil with good**. Consider this, my <unclear>dear</unclear> friend, and do not carry your Cross unwillingly, from wherever it may come; it is possible for a person, if they know it comes from God, to accept it.
The **Soul-Lady** <note>Soul-Lady: likely a personified "Daughter of the Soul" or a spiritual student engaging in dialogue with the Servant</note> said: 
> Father, the heartfelt Cross <unclear>of</unclear> which you last spoke—when a person [recognizes] their guilt—comes to few. Now I would like to know how a sinner should overcome their trials through God's help; for such a person seems <unclear>not</unclear> to be tried [in the same way], because he has <unclear>angered</unclear> God and is punished outwardly. 
The **Servant** answered: 
> I know a man who kept this custom: whenever he committed some fault out of human weakness, he behaved like a diligent washerwoman. She first cleans the clothes with soap, then throws them into clean water, and thus drives out all impurity. In the same way, he would never rest until he reached the precious river of **Blood** flowing from the **Wounds of God** <note>Wounds of God: a central focus of late medieval devotion, emphasizing Christ's physical sacrifice as a source of healing</note>. In this holy Blood, he washed away all impurity and submerged himself entirely in the bloody, flaming stream, just as one is accustomed to wash small children in a warm bath. And this he did with the highest confidence that through the power of this Blood, all his sins would be blotted out; and this custom he kept at all times, whether he suffered with or without guilt.

# How several worldly people were drawn away from the love of temporal things and led to the love of God.

### The 43rd Chapter.

As the Servant <term>the Servant: the name Henry Suso uses for himself throughout his autobiography to emphasize his humility</term> applied himself to drawing people away from temporal love and leading them to God, he noticed that in certain cloisters <term>cloisters: religious houses or convents</term> several people wore the religious habit of their Order but possessed worldly hearts. Among these was a woman who had her "friends"—or lovers—which is a spiritual poison for those in religious life. The Servant told her to renounce these friends and instead take up **Eternal Wisdom** <note>original: "ewige Weißheit"; a central theme in Suso's work, personifying Divine Wisdom as a beloved figure</note>. This was difficult for her because she was young, beautiful, and entangled in such matters; yet, he finally brought her to the point where she was willing to obey him. However, when her will was changed back through the influence of other people, the Servant said: "My daughter, cease this; behold, I tell you in advance, if you do not do it willingly, you will be forced to do it against your will." Because she made light of his words, he prayed to God that He would draw her away from it either through good fortune or misfortune. Once, he scourged himself until he bled and prayed to God that He would tame her, which indeed came to pass: for when she returned home, a foul hump immediately grew upon her back, which made her completely misshapen; thus, she was of necessity forced to give up what she otherwise would not. In the aforementioned unenclosed cloister was another young, noble maiden who for many years had miserably consumed her heart and time with all kinds of persons; she was now so alienated that she fled from the Servant like a wild animal, for she feared perhaps being hindered by him. This maiden’s biological sister begged the Servant to try and see if he could convert her to God. Because he considered this almost impossible, he said: "I

<column-break/>

believe it would be easier to bend the heavens than to lead her away from this, because it can only happen through death." But she said: "I trust that whatever you ask of God, He cannot refuse you." The Servant promised her his diligence: because she always fled from his speech, he noticed that around **St. Margaret’s Day** <note>July 20th; a common way to mark time in the medieval calendar</note> she had gone into the fields with others. He followed her secretly, going around the field so that he might conveniently come upon her. When she noticed him, she turned her back to him, showed an angry face, and said: "Sir, why do you come to me? Go your way; you will accomplish nothing with me: I would rather lose my head than confess to you, and I would rather let myself be buried alive than renounce my love." Her companion rebuked her and said he had done this only for the sake of her salvation. "I," she said, "will not deceive him, but will open my heart to him with words and deeds." At these stubborn words and strange gestures, the Servant was terrified and became so red with shame that he could not speak a word. The other maidens were disturbed by the insolence of their companion, but the Servant went away from there, looked to heaven, sighed, and wanted to leave the place entirely; but God put this in his mind: if one wishes to do something for God and the world, one must not rest or give up so easily. This happened after midday; after the **evening meal** <gloss>original: "Abendmahl"; here referring to the daily meal rather than the Sacrament</gloss>, as the maidens went into the garden to attend to their business, the aforementioned maiden went with them, and as they passed by the hospital where the Servant was staying, he asked one of her companions,

When they came to the Servant <term>the Servant: Suso’s humble self-designation</term> and she sat with him in a public place, he said with sighs: "Well then, you most beautiful, chosen virgin of God, how long will you leave your most beautiful body and your heart to the Devil? Behold, God has made you so lovely and graceful in every way that it is unbefitting for such a beautiful, noble virgin to cling to any other lover than the all-beautiful God. Who plucks the beautiful rose more rightfully than He to whom it belongs? I pray you, noble and beautiful virgin, open your eyes; think of the friendship which begins here and remains in eternity. Mark what misery, unfaithfulness, pain, the cross, and harm to body, soul, and good name the lovers of the world must suffer, whether it be to their joy or sorrow, even though the sweet poison of love so befuddles their souls that they think neither of the harm to their temporal nor to their future life. Well then, my most beautiful and lovely daughter, if any natural noble qualities still be in you, give them to the noblest among all men, and cease from your folly; I promise you by my faith that God will receive you into His friendship and will share His friendship with you in the present and future life." This was a blessed little hour. For the words pierced the virgin's heart so that she immediately lifted up her eyes, sighed, and spoke with a courageous voice: "Well then, my heart and Father, today I give myself to God and to you, and am ready this hour to leave my depraved life, to surrender myself entirely to God according to your counsel and help, and to serve Him unto death."

His companion <note>likely a fellow monk traveling with him</note> said to him out of pity: "It is fitting for Divine goodness that through your toil souls are preserved." # How God one day, through the merits of the Servant, multiplied the drink for his friends.

## Chapter 44.

The Servant once came upon a journey, quite exhausted late in the evening, to a monastery where he wished to remain overnight. But since there was wine neither in the village nor in the monastery, a young woman said she had a small flask full of wine, "but what is such a thing," she said, "among so many?" For there were about twenty pious people there who wanted to hear the Servant’s sermon. The Servant ordered the flask to be brought forth and set upon the table; when this was done, they asked him to bless it. He did so in the name of the salutary Name of Jesus, and drank from it first, because he was tired from the journey, and gave all the others some to drink, and the flask, before the eyes of all on-
<column-break/>
-lookers, was set back on the table full, from which they drank for the second and third time, without any pouring in of beer or wine. But because they had a great desire to hear the word of God, no one noticed the Divine miracle-sign; <note>original: "wunderzeichē"</note> however, when they later clearly saw the omnipotence of God in the multiplication of the wine, they praised God and attributed this miracle to the Servant. This he could not endure, saying: "Do not hold me to be the author of this miracle, but rather that the Almighty God has refreshed this pious company according to their faith with spiritual and physical drink."

---

# Of several afflicted people who were very faithful to the Servant.

## Chapter 45.

The Servant had in a city two holy and trusted persons who lived according to the spirit in different manners. One was famous among people and had an abundance of Divine sweetness; the other was despised and always attacked by God with afflictions. <term>afflictions: spiritual trials or internal struggles, known in the original German as "Anfechtungen."</term> When they both died, the Servant desired to know how different their reward was in the other life, because they had lived so differently here. One morning the famous person appeared to him and said she must still suffer in Purgatory. When he asked why this was?
<column-break/>
She said for no other reason than because a spiritual pride <term>spiritual pride: "geistliche hoffarth," the sin of taking personal credit or feeling superior because of one's spiritual gifts or the praise of others.</term> had arisen in her soul from the praise she received, which she did not immediately resist; yet her pain would soon be ended. The other person, who had been oppressed here, came to God without hindrance. The Servant’s mother was also visited with heavy afflictions the entire time of her life, and this happened because of the different way of life between her and her husband. She indeed desired to live for God, but her husband was a lover of the world, which she heartily

# The 45th Chapter.

...deeply pained her. This woman had made it her habit to sink all her suffering into the Passion <term>Passion: the physical and spiritual suffering of Jesus leading up to and during his crucifixion</term> of Christ; before her death, she told the Servant, her son, that for thirty years she had never been to the Holy Mass <note>original: "H. Meß"</note> without weeping bitterly out of intense compassion for God and His Mother. She also said that once, out of great love for God, she fell into a sickness and lay in bed for twelve weeks with such burning desire for God that even the doctors noticed it and were edified by it.

Once, at the beginning of Lent, she went into a church where an image of the Taking Down of Christ from the Cross <term>Deposition: an artistic representation of Jesus being removed from the cross</term> stood upon an altar; before this image, she received a portion of the pain that Mary endured beneath the Cross. Out of this compassion, she felt such pain that she fell to the ground and neither heard nor saw anything; she was carried home and lay thus in bed until Good Friday <note>original: "Carfreytag"</note>. On that same day, as the Passion was being sung in the church, she died. At that time, the Servant was living in Cologne <note>original: "Cölln"</note> for his studies, to whom his mother appeared in a vision, saying joyfully: 

> "My dearest son, love God, and be assured that He will never leave you in any temptation. I have departed from the world, but I have not died; rather, I shall live eternally with God."

She kissed and blessed her son, then vanished before his eyes. He wept and cried out: 

> "O my holy and faithful mother, be faithful to me before the Lord!" 

When he was in his youth and went to his studies, he gained a faithful companion. This man once asked the Servant, after much conversation, that

<column-break/>

he would show him the Name of Jesus on his chest; <note>Henry Suso famously used a sharp stylus to carve the name of Jesus (IHS) over his heart as a permanent, physical mark of his devotion.</note> but he refused him. Finally, when he perceived his devotion, he satisfied him, opened his garment at the breast, and let him see the treasure. With this, the other man was not yet satisfied, but when he saw the name in the middle of the heart, he also laid his hands and his face upon it and began to weep bitterly, so that the tears flowed over the Servant's breast. Afterward, however, the Servant showed this name to no one else except one special friend of God, to whom God permitted it and who viewed it with the same devotion as the previous one. 

As these two companions had lived in friendship for a long time and were now to part from one another, they made this pact: that whoever among them died first, the other who remained living should, for an entire year, celebrate two Masses every week—one on Monday for the departed, the other on Friday for the Passion of Christ. Many years later, the Servant's companion died; and because the Servant had forgotten his promise of the Mass-readings, he did not perform them, though he was faithfully mindful of him. As he sat one morning in his chapel as if in a trance, his companion came to him in a vision and spoke with a lamenting voice: 

> "O Brother, where is your faithfulness? Alas, how have you forgotten me?" 

When he said that he was always mindful of him in the Mass, the companion answered that this was not enough; rather, he should pay the full debt of the Masses for him, so that the innocent Blood of Christ might descend into Purgatory <note>original: "Fegfewr"</note> and extinguish its fire; for thus it would happen that he would soon be released. This the Servant did, and soon after, the soul was delivered from its pains.

# How Christ Appeared to the Servant in the Form of a Seraph and Loved Him.
## The 46th Chapter.

Once the Servant turned very zealously to God, praying to be instructed in suffering. Therefore, there appeared to him in a vision the likeness of the crucified Christ in the form of a Seraph <term>Seraph: a high-ranking angel, typically depicted in medieval art with six wings</term> with six wings, two of which covered the head, two covered the feet, and with the remaining two he flew. On the two lowest wings was written: "Accept temptation <note>original: "anfechtung" - in this context, it refers to spiritual trials, tribulations, or attacks from others</note> willingly." On the middle ones: "Carry the Cross with patience." On the uppermost: "Learn to suffer in conformity with Christ." When he told this vision to a holy virgin <note>likely Elsbeth Stagel, a nun who was Suso's spiritual friend and biographer</note>, she said: "You will be placed at the head of a monastery; there, new trials await you through God’s providence, for your enemies will attack you and heavily oppress you; take hold then of patience, as the Seraph instructed you." He sighed and waited for the coming storm, which met him according to the virgin’s word. At that time, the monastery where he lived had received neither fruit nor wine for three years, and thus had fallen into great debt. The brothers went to council and chose the Servant of Wisdom—though against his will (for he knew of the impending Cross)—as Prior <term>Prior: the superior or administrative head of a monastery</term>. On the first day, he had the brothers called together by the ringing of the bell and told them they should call upon St. Dominic <note>Saint Dominic: the 13th-century founder of the Dominican Order (the Order of Preachers)</note>, because he had promised his brothers to stand by them in times of need when they sought him. There were two brothers, one of whom mockingly said to the other: "Look how foolish this Prior is, in that he

<column-break/>

commands us to entrust our need to God. Perhaps he thinks God will open the heavens and send us food and drink." The other answered: "Not only he, but we are all foolish for accepting him as our superior, since we already knew that he understands nothing of worldly matters and only looks toward heaven." Thus he was held in contempt. But he remained firm in his opinion and had a Mass for St. Dominic sung the next day, so that he might provide for them. As he stood in the choir lost in thought, the gatekeeper called him to a wealthy Canon <term>Canon: a priest who lives in a community attached to a cathedral or large church</term>, his good friend, who said to him: "Henry, know that you have no means of life, and this night I was admonished by God to help you; therefore, I give you initially twenty pounds of Constance weight <note>original: "Costnitzer gewicht" - referring to the currency or weight standard of the city of Constance</note>; trust in God, He will not leave you." He took the money with joy and had fruit and wine bought; thus he governed the monastery laudably during his rule and incurred no debt. This Canon, at his end, bequeathed much alms to the places he was fond of; later he called the Servant, as the Prior of the place, to him and gave him much money to distribute among the poor friends of God <term>Friends of God: "Gottesfreunde," a 14th-century movement of lay and clerical mystics focused on an internal, personal relationship with God</term>. As he was reluctant to take the money because he feared the trials <note>original: "anfechtungen"</note> that would later meet him, he finally allowed himself to be persuaded, went out, and distributed the money according to his promise, yet with trustworthy witnesses and a good accounting to his superiors. Yet there followed for him

# How the Servant’s face once shone three times like the sun during his sermon.

## The 48th Chapter.

As the Servant <note>Henry Suso usually refers to himself as "the Servant" or "the Servant of Eternal Wisdom."</note> was preaching very zealously one day in Cologne / there was also among others a newly-beginning cleric present who was greatly troubled <note>original: "angefochten" – this refers to spiritual trials, doubts, or temptations.</note> / and as he looked diligently at the Servant / he saw with the inner eyes the Servant’s face transformed into the most delightful clarity / and

<column-break/>

becoming three times as shining / as the sun / in clear weather / so that he could behold his face without hindrance / from this vision he was cheered in his trial / strengthened / and fortified in the spiritual life.

---

# Of the wholesome Name of Jesus.

## The 49th Chapter.

As the Servant once traveled from Upper Germany to Aachen to visit the Mother of God / while he was on the return journey / the most blessed Mary appeared to a young woman / saying: Behold, my Son’s Servant has returned / and has proclaimed his most sweet name far and wide / as did his Apostles in former times / for just as they desired to make known the faith / and Christ’s name to all people / so he strives to pour this name into all cold hearts / to cheer them / and to set them on fire / therefore after death he shall receive an equal reward with the Apostles. Afterwards this holy young woman saw in Mary’s hands a beautiful candle shining so greatly / that it illuminated the whole world; in the candle the name of Jesus was written everywhere. Mary said to the young woman / the burning candle signifies the name of Jesus / which truly enlightens all hearts / who

<column-break/>

accept / honor / and carry such a name with them. For this my Son has chosen his Servant / so that through his diligence this name may be ignited in many hearts / and they may obtain the fruit of eternal salvation. When the holy young woman / as the Servant’s spiritual daughter / noticed / that he had such a devotion to the most sweet name of Jesus / which he also had written upon his breast <note>Suso is famous for having physically carved the name of Jesus (IHS) over his heart as an act of extreme devotion.</note> / she also received a great love for it / and with all devotion she made it with red silk threads on small cloths / and let the Servant hold them to his breast / and speak a blessing over them / so that he might distribute them among the spiritual daughters. To this young woman it was revealed by God / that / whoever carried this name in this manner with them / and prayed an "Our Father" <note>original: "Vatter vnser"</note> daily to its honor / to them God would grant forgiveness of sins in life and grace in death. Which may Jesus Christ grant us. Amen.

# BY DOCTOR HENRY SUSO

## One Hundred Meditations on the Passion of Jesus Christ / revealed to him by God / though very short / yet very powerful / and devout.

### The Author's Preface.

Whoever wishes to briefly and devoutly contemplate the bitter and loving Passion of Christ, and desires to show themselves thankful to Him for their manifold temptations, let them take these one hundred meditations, expressed in few words, into their memory, so that they may internalize their meaning. Let them run through these daily with heartfelt devotion, accompanied by one hundred kisses of the earth <note>This refers to the practice of prostrating and kissing the ground as an act of humility and penance.</note> or in another way more convenient to them. As often as the most blessed Virgin is mentioned, they should say an Our Father, a Hail Holy Queen <note>original: "Salve Regina"</note>, or an Angelic Salutation <note>The "Hail Mary" or Ave Maria.</note>. For in this way were these meditations revealed by God to a spiritual person after Matins <note>The midnight or early morning prayer service of the Divine Office.</note>, as he stood before the crucifix and complained to God that he could not contemplate His Passion without great difficulty and annoyance, as he had often been afflicted by this deficiency until that time. However, the sighs or desires which are attached to the meditations on the Passion of Christ were added by the Brother <note>Henry Suso often refers to himself as "the Brother" or "the Servant."</note> himself, and done so briefly, so that every person might have some manner and opportunity to request something of God, or to sigh to God, according to each person's own affection.

### On Sunday / or at Matins.

1. I remind you, O most kind Jesus, of the bloody sweat which the unspeakable anguish of your most gentle heart pressed out of you in abundance after the Last Supper, as you prayed in the garden. 2. Remember your most cruel imprisonment, the terrifying binding, and the piteous leading away. 3. Remember, O kind Je-

<column-break/>

sus, with what hard blows they greeted you thereafter, sullied you with spit, and treated you most shamefully and unworthily by covering your eyes. 4. How you were judged in the morning before Caiaphas and condemned to death as an evildoer. 5. How your most sorrowful Mother looked upon you with great heartache. 6. How you were shamefully presented to Pilate, falsely accused before him, and also most unjustly by him

...unjustly condemned to death. 7. How Herod and his followers mocked you in a white robe as a fool <note>In the Gospel of Luke, Herod Antipas clothes Jesus in a "gorgeous" or "shining" white robe to mock his claims of kingship or wisdom</note>, you who are the eternal Wisdom of the Father. 8. How the cruel scourge and lash tore your most beautiful body. 9. How the sharp thorns and stings pierced your tender head, so that the streams of your precious blood flowed abundantly over your face. 10. How you, finally completely exhausted, accepted the sentence of death, and carrying your own Cross, were led to the place of your crucifixion with the highest disgrace.

### ->Prayer.<-

I beseech you, O LORD, my only hope and confidence: through the memory of all that has been said above, stand by me, a miserable soul, through your Fatherly goodness in all my anxieties and needs. Release me from the hard and heavy bonds of my sins. Preserve me from secret sins, and from public disgrace and shame. Protect me from the deceitful inspirations of the Devil, as well as from all opportunities and incitements to every vice. Let me feel your pain and the pain of your Mother with inward, heartfelt compassion. Show yourself a merciful Judge toward me at my final end. Teach me to despise the honor of the world, but to serve you wisely and rationally. Heal and wash away all my sins with your wounds. May my reason be strengthened and adorned against all temptations through the most cruel pains of your most holy Head. Finally, grant that I may bear all your Cross and suffering according to my ability and strength.

<column-break/>

Remember, O sweetest Jesus, how your bright-shining eyes, as you hung on the high wood of the Cross, were darkened and broken <note>In this context, "broken eyes" refers to the glazing over and loss of sight that occurs during the agony of death.</note>. 2. How your divine ears were filled with derision, mockery, and disgrace. 3. How they tormented your most excellent sense of smell with stinking filth. 4. How they filled your most holy mouth with the bitterest drink <note>A reference to the vinegar or gall offered to Jesus on the cross.</note>. 5. How they martyred your tender and sensitive feeling with heavy wounds.

[Prayer:] Lord, I beseech you, keep my eyes from frivolous and vain looking. My ears from useless gossip. Grant that I may regard all visible and physical things as dung. Grant that I may have a distaste for all temporal things. Take from me the superfluous and delicate care of my own body.

## On Monday, or at Prime <note>Prime is the second prayer service of the Divine Office, traditionally observed at 6:00 AM.</note>.

Remember also, O sweetest Jesus, how your most holy head hung down in great pain and hardship. 7. How your supple neck was cruelly struck. 8. How spittle and blood completely covered your most lovely face. 9. How your vivid form turned completely pale. 10. How the beauty of your entire body departed and withered.

### ->Prayer.<-

Lord, grant me to love and embrace the discomfort of my body, and to rest in you alone; to bear the evils of others with patience, to strive for contempt of myself, to extinguish all my evil desires and inclinations—

## On Friday / or at Vespers.
<note>Vespers is the traditional evening prayer service. In the Passion narrative, this is the time when Christ was taken down from the Cross (the Descent).</note>

Lord Jesus, remember: 1. How the sharp spear pierced your side. 2. How the rose-colored blood <note>original: "Rosenfärbige Blut"</note> flowed out. 3. How at the same time the water ran down. 4. With how much labor and pain you redeemed me. 5. How heartily and joyfully you won back my freedom.

## To the Virgin Mother.

O my special and only comfort after God, refuge of all sinners, most excellent Queen, ever-Virgin Mary, remember how you once stood beneath the Cross and saw your deceased Son; how often you piteously cast your eyes upon his dead body hanging before you. 2. With what

devotion and motherly affection you embraced his arms when he was taken down from the Cross. 3. With what faithfulness and love you pressed the bloody arms against your face. 4. How you kissed his fresh welts and wounds, and his pale face. 5. How many deadly wounds you received there in your heart. 6. How many frequent, mournful, and bitter sighs you let be heard. 7. How sad, how pale <note>original: "enfärbt" — literally "un-colored" or drained of color</note> and transformed your face was, which is otherwise the most beautiful among women. 10. How the infinite pains of your heart could not be comforted by any human being.

->Prayer.<-

Most gracious Lady, I remind you of all these things and I ask you: be a faithful protectress and guide of my life. Turn your motherly eyes graciously toward me. Maintain me faithfully, and protect me from my enemies under the wings of your most beloved Son. May your frequent kissing of his wounds reconcile him with me. May the deadly wounds of your heart obtain for me true heartfelt repentance. Let your deep sighs awaken in me an unceasing desire for God. Let your very troubled speeches and mournful words destroy in me all idle talk. Your sad gestures shall endure in me no unrestrained behaviors. May your comfortless heart cause me to regard all transitory love as nothing.

### To the sorrowful and most compassionate Mother.

Most Holy Virgin Mary, I pray, remember the unspeakable pain when the dead body of your Son was taken from your heart and out of your lap. 2. Think of the saddest departure from the tomb of your Son. 3. Of your footsteps and piteous strides. 4. Of the sorrowful heart, which sighed after the buried Son. 5. ### Prayer.

Amen.

# Exercises of the Eternal Wisdom.

[those] who, having turned back toward themselves, also reject, avoid, and root out all inordinate affections for all earthly things; but instead accept and choose the most excellent Wisdom as their Spouse and Friend. But if someone is so entangled with self-love that they think it almost impossible to disentangle themselves, let them make a good resolution and holy desire to withdraw from this harmful love, so that the grace and help of God may be granted to them; and then let them begin this exercise. However, those who are not ensnared by this love, but have nevertheless remained sluggish and negligent in the love of God until now: let these marry this Spouse anew, and renew their love with the inclination of new zeal. And Him whom they previously served as their Master out of fear of punishment, they shall henceforth strive to cling to and please with fervent zeal as their most beloved Bride, always contemplating the excellence, goodness, and presence of this, their Divine Bride or Bridegroom—whichever they wish to call him. For in God, or in the soul, there is no gender; rather, He is a pure and simple Spirit. <note>Suso emphasizes the mystical concept that the soul and God transcend human gender, though he uses the romantic language of "spiritual marriage" common in medieval mysticism.</note> O blessed and thrice-blessed are those who deserve to be admitted to his friendship in this life. But this marriage must not only happen internally in the soul; it must also be awakened externally because of fervor—yet secretly—through certain signs of devotion, in the following way.

Initially, whoever desires to be accepted into the Brotherhood of Eternal Wisdom must speak three Our Fathers <note>original: "Vatter vnser"</note> with as many Hail Marys <note>original: "Ave Maria"</note>, and secretly cast themselves upon the ground three times, thereby completely offering themselves up to the Eternal Wisdom.

<column-break/>

They should also ask of Him a token of the marriage; namely, a new grace as a sign of their love and loyalty toward each other, which neither death, nor life, nor any creature may ever harm or sever.

The zealous servants of Eternal Wisdom shall daily read the Hours, which are called: <term>The Office of Eternal Wisdom</term> <note>original: "Cursus æternæ sapientiæ." This was a popular medieval prayer cycle similar to the Little Office of the Blessed Virgin Mary.</note>. Whoever cannot read, or cannot speak these prayers, shall instead say seven Our Fathers with seven Hail Marys—namely, one Our Father for each of the canonical hours, etc. And this is done so that Eternal Wisdom may preserve their hearts and bodies, so that they are not ensnared by this world which is filled with vanities and dangers, but instead walk wisely and cautiously, protected from all evil, and led by the Lord on the right path to eternal salvation.

At the table, after the blessing is given and before they eat, they shall say an Our Father with an Angelic Salutation <note>The "Angelic Salutation" (German: "Englischen Gruß") is the Hail Mary, referring to the greeting given to Mary by the Archangel Gabriel.</note> as a spiritual alms for the needy souls in Purgatory; contemplating how dangerous it is to enjoy alms without gratitude, and how godly it is to assist the wretched who cannot help themselves, and with what great gratitude they [the souls in Purgatory] accept even the smallest crumbs that fall from the table of their hearts.

They shall also say an Our Father with the Angelic Salutation in honor of the most sweet and most wholesome Name of Eternal Wisdom, which is Jesus himself, so that the Lord may protect all disciples of Eternal Wisdom and his holy Catholic Church, and defend them from all the snares of the enemies, with these words: Blessed be the sweet Name of our
